## 1. Chemical Reactions and Equations
## CHEMICAL EQUATION
An atom of an element is represented by symbol, the molecule of a compound by a formula, and a chemical change is represented by an equation. Thus, the symbolic representation of an actual chemical change is a chemical equation.
## To write an equation -
(a) Substances which take part in chemical reaction (i.e., reactants) are usually written on left hand side and substances formed as a result of chemical reaction (i.e., products) are written on right hand side. The reactants and products are separated by an arrow head mark ( → ) which starts from reactants and points towards the products. Sign of equal to (=) may also be used in place of arrow head mark.
(b) Each reactant or the product is separated from one another by using plus sign ( + ) in between them.
The chemical equation written, following the above two steps, is skeletal chemical equation, as it does not have same number of atoms of each element on both sides of the arrow i.e. unbalanced chemical equation.
## BALANCED CHEMICAL EQUATION
A chemical equation in which number of atoms of each element is equal, both in products and reactants, is a balanced chemical equation.
## Example :
(i) Magnesium burns with oxygen and forms magnesium oxide.

## Features of the Balanced Equation \section*{Equation}
(a) The reactants appear on the left, and products appear on the right. The arrow joining them indicates the direction of reaction.
(b) An integer preceedes the formula of each molecule. These integers are known as stoichiometric coefficients. The quantitative relation among reactants and products is known as stoichiometry. The stoichiometric coefficient for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in the equation (iii) is 3 and that of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is 2 . When no number appears, we understand that the stoichiometric coefficient is 1 . The stoichiometric coefficient for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in this equation is 1 .
(c) The stoichiometric coefficients in a chemical equation are the set of smallest integers that gives a balanced equation. It refers to the relative number of molecules involved in the reaction.
(d) Charge is conserved in balanced equation. In this equation, all participants are neutral species, so charge is conserved regardless of the stoichiometric coefficients. For reactions that include ions, however, charge conservation must be explicitly addressed.
- The amount of product actually obtained in a reaction is called actual yield.

## BALANCING OF A CHEMICAL EQUATION
According to law of conservation of mass, "Mass can neither be created nor destroyed"
In a chemical reaction total mass of the reactant should be equal to total mass of the product. If not, then we need to balance chemical equation. Let us understand the balancing of a chemical equation :
There is no definite rule for balancing an equation. Therefore, it requires a good deal of skill and practice. The equation is balanced by a method called hit and trial method.
## Hit and Trial Method
Lets consider word equation of a reaction between nitrogen and hydrogen producing ammonia.
Nitrogen + Hydrogen ⟶ Ammonia
Steps involved in balancing the above equation are as following :
## Step-1
First of all write the skeletal equation for the reaction and count the number of atoms of each substance on either side of the equation.
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | | |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Element | Number of atoms in reactants | Number of atoms in product |
| N | 2 | 1 |
| H | 2 | 3 |
(Skeletalequation)
## Step-2
Balance the atom which is minimum in number, on either side of chemical equation. In the given equation, number of nitrogen is the minimum on the RHS.
To balance the nitrogen atom, multiply the nitrogen in RHS by 2, so that the number of nitrogen atoms becomes equal on both sides.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> (partly balanced equation) </mtext></mrow></math>
It should be noted that to equalise the number of atoms on both sides, we cannot alter the formulae of the compounds or elements involved in the reaction.
## Step-3
Still number of H atoms is not balanced. To equalise the number of H atoms, multiply the hydrogen molecule <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> on LHS by 3 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
## Step-4
Now examine the number of atoms of N and H in the new chemical equation.
| Elements | Number of atoms in reactants | Number of atoms in product |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| N | 2 | 2 |
| H | 6 | 6 |
The number of atoms of each element are equal on both sides. Thus, this equation is now balanced.
## Step-5
The above balanced equation does not give any information about the physical state of reactants and products.
In order to make the equation more informative, the physical states of reactants and products are mentioned along with their chemical formulae. These physical states are mentioned with the help of certain notations. These notations are -
(g) for gases, (l) for liquids,(s) for solid, (aq) for aqueous; The word aqueous (aq) is written if the reactant or product is present as a solution in water.
The balanced equation becomes
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
## Example :
Hydrogen reacts with chlorine to give hydrochloric acid.
(i) The skeleton equation of the above reaction :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(ii) To balance chlorine atoms, multiply the molecule HCl by 2 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Now, number of chlorine atoms and oxygen atoms are equal on both sides. Hence, the equation is balanced.
(iii) To make the chemical equation more informative, now write physical states of the reactants and products.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
## Implications of a Chemical Equation
A chemical equation conveys a large number of informations as described below.
## Qualitative information
(a) It tells us about the names of the reactants and products.
(b) It tells us about the physical states of the reactants and products.
## Quantitative information
(a) It expresses the number of molecules of reactants and products.
(b) It expresses the relative number of moles of the reactants and the products.
(c) It expresses the relative weight of the reactants and the products.
(d) It expresses the volume of the gaseous reactants and products.
## Example :
Ammonia gas is formed by the combination of nitrogen and hydrogen.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi></mrow></mrow></munder><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi></mrow></mrow></munder></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>28</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>6</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math>
The above equation expresses that-
(i) Nitrogen combines with hydrogen to form ammonia.
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, all three are in gaseous physical state.
(iii) One molecule of nitrogen combines with three molecules of hydrogen to form two molecules of ammonia.
(iv) 28 parts by weight of nitrogen has combined with 6 parts by weight of hydrogen to form 34 parts by weight of ammonia.
(v) One volume of nitrogen and three volumes of hydrogen combine together to give 2 volumes of ammonia gas.
## Limitations of a Chemical Equation
A chemical equation does not give the following informations :
(a) Conditions necessary for a chemical reaction : A chemical equation does not necessarily indicate the reaction conditions.
(b) Rate of reaction : It does not give any idea about the rate of the reaction, whether it is slow or fast.
(c) Change of heat : It fails to give any indication whether the heat is absorbed or evolved.
(d) Concentration : It does not give any indication about the concentration of the reactants.
(e) Mechanism : It fails to give any idea about the mechanism of the reaction.
(f) Nature of reaction : It fails to give any information about the nature of reaction, whether it is reversible or irreversible reaction.
## Removal of Drawbacks of a Chemical Equation
Limitations of chemical reactions have been partially removed.
(a) To express the concentration of a substance the word 'conc.' for concentrated and 'dil' for dilute are written just below the reactant or after the formula of the reactant, viz. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (conc.)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> (conc.) </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></munder><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
(b) If a substance formed in the reaction is gas, it is indicated putting an arrow pointing upwards after the formula.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>↑</mo></mrow></math>
If a substance is precipitated in the reaction, it is indicated by putting arrow pointing downwards after the formula.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>↓</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) Reversible reaction is indicated by the sign of reversibility ( ⇌).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>⇌</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>↑</mo></mrow></math>
(d) If a reaction take place at a particular temperature or pressure, it is expressed by writing above or below the arrow head.

## CHEMICAL REACTION
The process in which two or more substances reacts to form new substances, is called chemical reactions.
It involves making and breaking of bond between atoms to form new a substance, which describes the nature and specific characteristic of the reaction.
## Types of Chemical Reactions
Based on the specific characteristics and the nature of the reactions, chemical reactions have been divided into following types :
## 1. Synthesis or Combination Reaction

## 2. Decomposition Reaction
The reactions in which a substance is decomposed into two or more simpler substances, are known as decomposition reactions. Decomposition reactions involve the breaking of chemical bonds to form new substances. Hence, they require energy in the form of heat, light, electricity, etc.
Those reactions which absorbs energy in the form of heat are known as endothermic reactions.
Examples :
(i) When potassium chlorate is heated, it is decomposed into potassium chloride and oxygen.

## SOLUTION :
The description in the problem tells us what happens to the starting material: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> breaks apart into molecules of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>. An unbalanced form of the equation can be written from this description. Then we must balance each element in turn by inspection.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
## Step 1
First, count all atoms of each element on each side of the equation to see whether the elements are balanced:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
## Step 2
As we can see that nitrogen is already balanced. To balance the hydrogen atoms, we change the stoichiometric coefficient of water from 1 to 2 :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
## Step 3
This step balances nitrogen and hydrogen, but oxygen is not yet balanced. Oxygen must be balanced without changing the 1 : 1 ratio of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ratio of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>. These ratios must be retained to keep hydrogen and nitrogen in balance. Thus the only coefficient that can be adjusted to balance the oxygen atoms is that of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Two oxygen atoms are already present as in water and thus the remaining oxygen atom can be adjusted. by changing the coefficient of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
This balances the equation, but it is unrealistic from a molecular perspective because there is no such thing as half a molecule. To get rid of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> without unbalancing the reaction, we multiply all the coefficients by 2 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Now the reaction is balanced and reasonable from a molecular perspective.
Copper nitrate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> gives positive ring test of nitrate ion ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>), but after heating small amount of copper nitrate in dry boiling tube over the burner flame, it does not give positive ring test any more because it undergoes thermal decomposition reaction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## 3. Simple Displacement Reactions (Simple Substitution)
A displacement reaction occurs because a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one from a solution of its compound.

## Displacement reactions in solutions
A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from its compounds in solution. These are the sorts of things you observe in this type of reaction:
- The more reactive metal gradually dissolves.
- The less reactive metal coats the more reactive metal.
- The solution may change colour.
- The tube gets warm because these reactions are exothermic.
Here are two examples of these displacement reactions.
(a) Magnesium and copper sulphate solution
Magnesium is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper sulphate solution.

Double displacement reactions can be further classified as precipitation, gas formation, and acid-base neutralization reactions.

## 5. Oxidation-Reduction Reactions
(a) Oxidation reactions :
Oxidation is defined as a process in which a substance gains oxygen or loses hydrogen during a chemical reaction.
Examples :

Based on classical concept, oxidation reaction can also be defined as following:

## 2. Oxidation Number Concept
(a) Oxidation : According to this concept, increase in oxidation number of an element in a reaction is called oxidation.
(b) Reduction : According to this concept, decrease in oxidation number of an element in a reaction is called reduction.
Example :
Thus, here <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is oxidised to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> while <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is reduced to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
## OXIDATION NUMBER
It is the number of electrons lost or gained by an element during a chemical change in a particular compound.
## Or
It is defined as the formal charge present on an atom in a particular compound determined by certain arbitrary rules.
## Rules for Determining Oxidation Number
(i) O.N. of elements in free state or uncombined state is zero. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> etc has zero oxidation state.
(ii) O.N. of hydrogen is always +1 except in ionic metal hydrides where it is -1 .
(iii) O.N. of oxygen is -2 except in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> where it is +2 and in peroxides where it is -1 .
(iv) O.N. of metals is always + ve. For IA group elements it is +1 and for IIA group elements it is +2.
(v) O.N. of halogens is -1 in metal halides.
(vi) O.N. of ion or radical is the number of electrons it must gain or lose to acquire neutrality i.e. it is equal to the electric charge, e.g. for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> O.N., is -2 .
(vii) O.N. of an atom within compound can be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math> integer, zero or fraction.
(viii) The algebric sum of all the O.N. of elements in a compound is equal to zero.
(ix) The algebric sum of all the O.N. of elements in an ion is equal to net charge on the ion.
(x) Maximum O.N. of an element is equal to number of valence electrons i.e. group number.
(xi) Minimum O.N. of an element (except metals) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> (Group number -8 ).
A compound can undergo both oxidation as well as reduction, if the O.N. of one of its element is in between the maximum and the minimum value.
## For example,
Maximum O.N. of N is +5 and minimum O.N. of N is -3 .
O.N. of N is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is +3 . <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> can undergo oxidation and reduction both, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>. of N is between maximum and minimum value.

- Redox reactions involve the transfer of electrons, while in general acid-base reactions involve transfer of protons.
## Oxidizing Agent
- The substance which gives oxygen for oxidation is called an oxidizing agent.
- The substance which removes hydrogen is also called an oxidizing agent.
- The substance which undergoes gain of electron and oxidizes the other substance is called an oxidizing agent.
## Reducing Agent
- The substance which gives hydrogen for reduction is called a reducing agent.
- The substance which removes oxygen is also called a reducing agent.
- The substance which undergoes loss of electron and reduces the other substance is called a reducing agent.

## (A) Oxidation Number Method
In a balanced redox reaction, total increase in oxidation number must be equal to the total decrease in oxidation number. This equivalence provides the basis for balancing redox reactions.
The general procedure involves the following steps :
(a) Select the atom in oxidising agent whose oxidation number decreases and indicate the gain of electrons.
(b) Select the atom in reducing agent whose oxidation number increases and indicate the loss of electrons.
(c) Now cross multiply i.e. multiply oxidising agent by the number of lost electrons and reducing agent by number gained electrons.
(d) Balance the number of atoms on both sides whose oxidation number changes in the reaction.
(e) In order to balance oxygen atoms, add <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> molecules to the side deficient in oxygen. Then, balance the number of H atoms by adding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions to the side deficient in hydrogen.
(f) If the reaction occurs in basic medium, then add <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions, equal to the number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions, on both sides of the equation.

## (B) Ion Electron Method (Half Reaction Method)
The following steps are followed while balancing redox reactions (equations) by this method.
(a) Write the equation in ionic form.
(b) Split the redox equation into two half reactions, one representing oxidation half reaction and the other reduction half reaction.
(c) Balance these half reactions separately and then add by multiplying with suitable coefficients so that the electrons are cancelled.
Balancing is done as follows:
(i) Write both half reactions and then balance the atoms other than ' O ' and ' H '.
(ii) Balance oxygen atoms by adding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> molecules to the side deficient in oxygen. The number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> molecules added is equal to the deficiency of oxygen atoms.
(iii) Balance hydrogen atoms by adding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions equal to the deficiency, on the side which is deficient in hydrogen atoms.
(iv) If the medium of reaction is basic, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions equal in number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>are added to both sides of balanced equation.
(v) Balance the charge by adding electrons to the side which is rich in + ve charges. i.e. deficient in electrons. Number of electrons added is equal to the deficiency.
(vi) Multiply the half equations with suitable coefficients to equalize the number of electrons.
(vii) Add these half equations to get an equation which is balanced with respect to charge and atoms.

## EXOTHERMIC AND ENDOTHERMIC REACTION
Chemical reactions usually proceed with either liberation of heat or the absorption of heat. The constituent elements of a compound are bound by a chemical bond, during the chemical reaction or chemical change these bonds between the constituents of the reactants are broken and the products are formed having new bonds. Breaking of a chemical bond releases energy while formation of a chemical bond requires energy.
Therefore, when a chemical reaction liberates heat to the surroundings, it is said to be 'exothermic reaction' and when it absorbs the heat, it is said to be 'endothermic reaction'.
## Examples :
(i) Nitrogen and hydrogen combine together to form ammonia. This chemical reaction liberates heat to the surroundings and, therefore, it is exothermic reaction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>22.4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>
Here bond between two atoms of a nitrogen molecule and between two atoms of the three hydrogen molecules are broken and new bonds between nitrogen and hydrogen atoms are formed. Here the sum of energies needed to break nitrogennitrogen bond and hydrogen-hydrogen bond is less than the energy released during the formation of the bonds between nitrogen and hydrogen. Thus the heat (energy) is liberated to the surroundings. Therefore, this reaction is exothermic. Similarly the formation of sulphur trioxide from sulphur dioxide and oxygen is also exothermic reaction :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>42.00</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>
(ii) Nitrogen and oxygen combine together to form nitric oxide. Here the heat from the surroundings is absorbed. Therefore, this reaction is endothermic.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>43.2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mtext>. </mtext></mrow></math>
The sum of energies needed to break nitrogen-nitrogen and oxygen-oxygen bonds is much more than the energy released during the formation of the bonds between nitrogen and oxygen atoms. Therefore, heat energy is provided externally to complete the reaction. Thus this is reaction is endothermic.

## CORROSION (EROSION BY CHEMICAL ACTION)
For most of us, corrosion is the degradation of metals and is often called rust.Technically we can define it as an irreversible interfacial reaction of a material (metal, ceramic, polymer) with its environment which results in consumption of the material. Corrosion causes damage to car bodies, bridges, iron railings, ships and to all objects made of metals, specially those of iron. Corrosion of iron (rusting) is a serious problem. Every year an enormous amount of money is spent to replace damaged iron. Most metals corrode on contact with water (and moisture in the air), acids, bases, salts, oils, aggressive metal polishes, and other solid and liquid chemicals. Metals will also corrode when exposed to gaseous materials like acid vapors, formaldehyde gas, ammonia gas, and sulfur containing gases. Corrosion specifically refers to any process involving the deterioration or degradation of metal components. The best known case is that of the rusting of iron. Corrosion processes are usually electrochemical in nature, having the essential features of a battery.
When corrosion is localised and create small holes or pits in the metal, it is called pitting
Did You Know? corrosion. Pitting corrosion occurs much faster in areas where microstructural changes have occurred due to welding operations.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
There are two O atoms on the left-hand side and three O atoms on the right-hand side of the equation. This inequality of O atoms can be eliminated by writing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> in front of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> on the left-hand side of the equation.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Now multiply the entire equation by 2 to convert <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> to 3 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> i.e. </mtext><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
The above equation is the balanced equation for the formation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.

## RANCIDITY
The most important cause of deterioration in fats and fatty foods is oxidation. Oxidation of fats results in the replacement of an oxygen ion from a hydrogen ion in the fatty acid molecule. This substitution destabilizes the molecule and makes it possible for other odd chemical fragments to find a place along the chain. An unpleasant change in the flavor and odour of a food is develop, called rancidity. Unsaturated fats are more susceptible to oxidation than the saturated fats.
Factors which accelerate fat oxidation include trace metals (iron, zinc, etc.), salt, light, water, bacteria, and molds. Fat oxidation can be retarded by use of antioxidants (Antioxidants are compounds that inhibit chemical reactions with oxygen such as BHT, BHA, vitamin E, and vitamin C), by use of spices such as sage and rosemary, and by use of light and/or air tight wrapping.
Some high fat foods such as potato chips are packed in materials that protect them from light and oxygen and the containers are flooded with nitrogen to further exclude oxygen. The nitrogen also serves as a cushion to minimize breakage of the chips during transport.

## More
Oxidation reactions may involve highly reactive molecules called free radicals. Free radicals are molecules that have lost an electron and try to gain it by reacting with other molecules. This causes the substance to break down. Metals often catalyze reactions with oxygen. Another example would be the half eaten apple. The skinless area quickly oxidized causing the apple to turn brown. Antioxidants inhibit these changes by reacting with the free radicals before they can react with oxygen (free radical scavenging) or by reacting with the metals. Naturally occurring antioxidants may also work by interacting directly with oxygen.
Naturally occurring antioxidants include retinol (vitamin A) and tocopherols (vitamin E), found in many animals and plants; ascorbic acid (vitamin C), found in citrus and other fruits and vegetables; and beta carotene, found in deep orange and dark green vegetables. These may play a significant role in the prevention of cancer, heart disease, immune-deficiency diseases, and aging.
Synthetic antioxidants include butylated hydroxy toluene (BHT), butylated hydroxy anisole (BHA), and propyl gallate. Natural and synthetic antioxidants are added to food to prevent undesirable deterioration. Foods preserved with antioxidants include vegetable oils, bread, and cheese.
Antioxidants are frequently applied to the packaging materials of cereals and nuts.

## Passage
Oxidation number is defined as the charge which an atom of the element has in its ion or appears to have when present in the combined state with other atoms.
There are certain rules for assigning oxidation number. Some of these rules are given below.
- The oxidation number of all the atoms of different elements in their respective elementary states and allotropic forms is taken to be zero.
- The O.N. of a monoatomic ion is the same as the charge on it.
- The O.N. of hydrogen is +1 when combined with nonmetals and is -1 when combined with active metals called metal hydrides
- The O.N. of alkali metals (Li, Na, K, etc.) is always + 1 and that of alkaline earth metals ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, etc.) is +2 .
- The algebraic sum of the O.N. of all the atoms in a compound must be zero. In polyatomic ion, the algebraic
sum of all the O.N.'s of atoms of the ion must equal the charge on the ion.

12. Oxidation or reduction cannot take place alone. This is because if one substance loses oxygen, i.e., undergoes reduction, there must be another substance to take up this oxygen, i.e., undergo oxidation. Similarly, if one substance loses hydrogen, i.e., undergoes oxidation, there must be another substance to take up this hydrogen, i.e., undergo reduction. Hence, oxidation and reduction always take place together. That is why, these reactions are called redox reactions.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
10. Respiration is the most important biochemical reaction which releases energy in the cell. When we breathe air (oxygen) enters into our lungs and oxygen binds itself to haemoglobin present in red blood cells (RBC). It is then carried to million of cells present in our body. Respiration occurs in these cells and is accompanied by the combustion of glucose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> producing carbon dioxide ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) and water ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> ). A large amount of energy is released in this chemical reaction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2820</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Since the process is accompanied by release of energy so it is considered as an exothermic reaction.
11. During decomposition reaction a single reactant decompose to form two or more products, whereas in combination reaction two or more reactants react to form a single product. e.g.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (Combination reaction)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (Decomposition reaction)
12. Displacement reaction : - In this reaction an element which is more reactive displaces the other element which is less reactive from its salt solution. e.g.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

16. To prevent iron articles from rusting, we apply paint on it, by which iron does not come in contact with air and moisture which causes rusting.
17. When the oil and fat containing food is surrounded by unreactive gas nitrogen, oxygen become unavailable to cause oxidation and therefore prevent rancidity.
18. Corrosion : - It is a process in which metals are eaten up gradually by the action of air, moisture or a chemical on their surface. For example rusting of iron.
Rancidity - When fat and oil containing food is oxidised with air or oxygen, their smell and taste changes. This process is called rancidity.

2. Grapes when attached to the plants are living and therefore their own immune system prevents fermentation. The microbes can grow in the plucked grapes and under anaerobic conditions these can be fermented. This is a chemical change.
3. (i) Silver metal does not react with dilute HCl .
(ii) The temperature of the reaction mixture rises when aluminium is added because it is an exothermic reaction.
(iii) Reaction of sodium metal is found to be highly explosive because it is an exothermic reaction.
(iv) When lead is treated with hydrochloric acid, bubbles of hydrogen gas are evolved.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
4. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> It is a thermal decomposition reaction.
5. (A) When solutions are kept in copper container.
(i) Dilute HCl
Copper does not react with dilute HCl . Therefore, it can be kept.
(ii) Dilute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Nitric acid acts as a strong oxidising agent and reacts with copper vessel, therefore cannot be kept.
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Zinc is more reactive than copper ( Cu ) therefore, no displacement reaction occurs and hence can be kept.
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
Copper does not react with water. Therefore, can be kept.
(B) When solutions are kept in aluminium containers.
(i) Dilute HCl
Aluminium reacts with dilute HCl to form its salt and hydrogen is evolved. Therefore, cannot be kept.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(ii) Dilute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Aluminium gets oxidised by dilute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to form a layer of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and cannot be kept.

## ACIDS
The word "acid" comes from the Latin word acidus, meaning "sour" or "tart," since aqueous solutions of acids have a sour or tart taste. Lemon and orange taste sour because they contain citric acid and ascorbic acid (vitamin C). Another common acid is vinegar, which is the sour liquid produced when apple cider, grape juice, or other plant juices ferment beyond the formation of alcohol. Vinegar is a 5 percent aqueous solution of acetic acid.
Liebig defined acid as a compound containing one or more replaceable hydrogen(s). Acid dissociate in water and produce hydrogen ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>e.g. HCl is an acid and on dissolving in water it gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Hydrogen ions cannot exist alone but they exist after combining with water molecules. Thus hydrogen ion must always be shown as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> or hydronium ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

On the basis of sources acids can be classified into two groups. These are
(a) Organic acid: Acid obtained from plants material and animals is called organic acid. e.g citric acid (oranges \& lemons), acetic acid (vinegar), oleic acid (olive oil) etc.
(b) Mineral acid: Acid obtained from minerals is called mineral or inorganic acid. They do not contain carbon. e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> etc.
## Physical Properties of Acids
(a) Taste : Acids are generally sour in taste.
(b) Effect on indicator : Acid changes the colour of indicators as given in the table.
| Indicator | Change of colour | |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Litmus | From | To |
| Methyl orange | Blue | Red |
| Phenolphthalein | Orange | Red |
(c) Electrical Conductivity : Acids conduct electricity in aqueous solution, since they contain dissolved ions. For example, soluble acids like hydrochloric acid and sulphuric acid are used as electrolytes.
(d) Corrosive action : Strong acids are corrosive in nature. They corrode metals and release hydrogen gas. They can also burn skin. Know!
Acids are generally not corrosive except mineral acids <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> etc) and most of them are solids like organic acids (oxalic acid, tartaric acid, ascorbic acid, citric acid etc.)

## (2) Classification Based on the Strength of the Acid
Almost all the acids dissociate in water and produce hydrogen ion to a lesser or greater extent. The strength of an acid depends on the concentration of the hydrogen ions present in a solution. Greater the tendency to loose hydrogen ion in the solution, greater is the strength of acid. However, some acids do not dissociate to an appreciable extent in water such as carbonic acid. Therefore, these acids will have a low concentration of hydrogen ions present in a solution. Based on this, acids are classified as :
(i) Strong acids
An acid, which dissociates completely or almost completely in water, is classified as a strong acid.
Examples : Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, nitric acid etc.

## (3) Classification Based on the Concentration of the Acid
Concentration of an acid solution depends upon the percentage of the acid that is dissolved in water. Based on this, acids are classified as
CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC
(i) Concentrated acid : An acid, that has a relatively high percentage of the acid dissolved in the aqueous solution is classified as a concentrated acid. Example concentrated hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, nitric acid, acetic acid etc.
(ii) Dilute acid : An acid, which has a relatively low percentage of the acid dissolved in the aqueous solution is classified as a dilute acid. Examples : dilute hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, nitric acid, acetic acid etc.
## (4) Classification Based on the Basicity of an Acid
As we have studied that acid on dissociation in water produce hydrogen ion, the number of these replaceable hydrogen ions in an acid is known as the basicity of an acid. It is also evident that, one hydrogen ion or hydronium ion can react with one hydroxyl ion ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>).
(i) Monobasic acid
A monobasic acid has one replaceable hydrogen ion. Hence, these acids combine with one hydroxyl group of a base to form salt and water.
Since, monobasic acids have only one replaceable hydrogen ion, they form only one kind of salt.

## BASES
Like acids, bases also dissociate in water, but in place of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>they produce hydroxyl ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. Thus, a base is a compound which on dissolving in water yields hydroxyl ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. The characteristic property of a base is due to the formation of these negative hydroxyl ions. A base may be an oxide or a hydroxide of a metal. If a base is soluble in water, it dissociates to form a metal ion and negative hydroxyl ion. Substances that combine with acids to form salt and water are also called bases.
## Example:
Sodium hydroxide is a base, it gives sodium ion and hydroxyl ion when dissolved in water.

Ammonium hydroxide is also a base. In water, it dissociates to form ammonium ion and a hydroxyl ion.

Sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, calcium hydroxide and ammonium hydroxide are the common alkalis.

All alkalis are bases but not all bases are alkali. Alkali is a basic, ionic salt of an alkali or alkaline earth metal element. Alkalis are best known for being bases that dissolve in water. Whereas a base is most commonly thought of as a substance that can accept <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> ions. A soluble base is also often referred to as an alkali if hydroxide ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>are involved.

## Physical Properties of Bases
(a) Taste: Bases are bitter to taste. If you have ever gotten soap in your mouth, you have noticed its bitter taste. This bitter taste confirms presence of base in the soap.
(b) Feel: They are soapy and slippery to touch.
(c) Electrical conductivity: Some bases are good conductors of electricity. For example, soluble bases like sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are used as electrolytes.
(d) Corrosive action : Strong alkalis like sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are highly corrosive or caustic in nature. Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are commonly called caustic soda and caustic potash respectively. Organic tissues like skin, etc. get completely corroded by these two alkalis. However, the other alkalis are only mildly corrosive.
(e) Effect on indicator: Bases changes the colour of indicator as given in the table.
| Indicator | Change of colour | |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| Litmus | From | To |
| Methyl orange | Red | Blue |
| Phenolphthalein | Orange | Yellow |
| Turmeric | Colourless | Pink |

## CLASSIFICATION OF BASES
Bases can be classified in various ways, depending on the following factors:
## (1) Classification Based on the Strength of the Base
We have already studied that bases on dissociation produce hydroxyl ion ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>). The strength of a base depends on the concentration of the hydroxyl ion when it is dissolved in water. Based on this, bases are classified as,
(i) Strong base
A base that dissociates completely or almost completely in water is classified as a strong base. In other words, greater the tendency to loose hydroxyl ion in the solution, the stronger is the base.
Example: Sodium hydroxide : NaOH
Potassium hydroxide : KOH
Calcium hydroxide : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(ii) Weak base
A base that partially dissociates in water is classified as a weak base.
Example: Magnesium hydroxide : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Ammonium hydroxide : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

## (2) Classification Based on the Concentration of a Base
Concentration of a basic solution depends upon the percentage of the base dissolved in water. Based on this fact, bases are classified as,
(i) Concentrated base : A base that has a relatively high percentage of the base in its aqueous solution is classified as a concentrated base. Example concentrated sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, ammonium hydroxide etc.
(ii) Dilute base: A base that has a relatively low percentage of the base dissolved in its aqueous solution, is classified as a dilute base. Example dilute sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, ammonium hydroxide etc.
## (3) Classification Based on the Acidity of a Base
The acidity of a base is equal to the number of hydroxyl ions it has. It is also the number of hydrogen ions with which a base can combine as one hydrogen ion combines with one hydroxyl ion.
Based on the acidity bases can be classified as,
(i) Monoacidic base
It is a base that has only one hydroxyl ion. It combines with only one hydrogen ion. Hence, its acidity will be one.
Example : Sodium hydroxide, Potassium hydroxide: KOH , Lithium hydroxide: LiOH , Ammonium hydroxide: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Sodium hydroxide </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Hydrochloric acid </mtext></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Sodium chloride </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Water </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
## (ii) Diacidic base
It is a base that has two hydroxyl groups and combines with two hydrogen ions. Hence, its acidity will be two.
