A base that has three hydroxyl ions and can combines with three hydrogen ions. Hence, its acidity will be three.
Example: Aluminium hydroxide
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Aluminium hydroxide </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Hydrochloric acid </mtext></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Aluminium chloride </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Water </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
## - - Time to Check Your Knowledge - On the basis of acidity of bases, barium hydroxide is which type of base?
## Acid or a Base in a Water Solution:
The process of dissolving an acid or a base in water is a highly exothermic one. Care must be taken while mixing concentrated nitric acid or sulphuric acid with water. The acid must always be added slowly to water with constant stirring. If water is added to a concentrated acid, the heat generated may cause the mixture to splash out and cause burns. The glass container may also break due to excessive local heating. Mixing an acid or base with water results in decrease in the concentration of ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>/</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>per unit volume. Such a process is called dilution and the acid or the base is said to be diluted.
Learn More
## Indicators are substances which undergoes change in colour, smell or taste with respect to the change in medium. It helps to differentiate between acidic and basic medium. Indicators are of following types depending upon its source:
- Natural indicators can be extracted from a wide variety offlowers, fruits, roots, leaves and other parts of plants, e.g. tea leaves, beet roots, rose petals of various colours, red cabbage leaves, turmeric, black berries, and delphinium flowers. Litmus (a natural dye) is one of the most common and naturally available indicator. It is extracted from lichens (combination of algae and fungus). When this litmus is added to an acidic solution, it turns red and when added to a basic solution, it turns blue. It possess a purple colour in distilled water.
- Synthetic indicators are prepared from man made chemical substances like phenolphtalein, methyl orange etc.
Phenolphthalein is a synthetic indicator. It turns acidic solutions colorless and basic solutions pink. If the concentration of indicator is particularly strong, it can appear purple.
Methyl orange is also a synthetic indicator used more oftenly because of clear colour change. In a solution becoming less acidic, methyl orange moves from red to orange and finally to yellow with the reverse occuring for a solution increasing in acidity.
Depending upon the change in properties indicators are classified as:
- Halochromic indicator show change in color with respect to the change in medium, e.g: litmus, phenolphtalein, methyl orange etc. These indicators are generally used as acid-base indicators.
- Olfactory indicator causes change in odour/smell with respect to the change in medium. e.g: clove oil, onion, vanilla extract etc.
- Gustatory indicator causes change in taste with respect to the change in medium. e.g: Sour taste of milk indicates that the milk has became acidic, hence it is spoiled.
Universal indicators : It is a mixture of indicators often sold ready made solution which can indicate pH values, usually over a range of 3-11, by successive changes of colour

First add few drops of phenolphthalein solution and stir solution with glass rod properly then record your observation if there is any change. Now add few drops of ammonium hydroxide and stir solution with glass rod properly then again record your observation if there is any change. Then add few drops of vinegar solution and stir resulting solution properly with glass rod. Record change if any. Now in case you are not able to understand the reason of your recorded observations, consult your friend and discuss with your teacher.

theory_sections.markdown: ## 1. Chemical Reactions and Equations

## CHEMICAL EQUATION
An atom of an element is represented by symbol, the molecule of a compound by a formula, and a chemical change is represented by an equation. Thus, the symbolic representation of an actual chemical change is a chemical equation.

## To write an equation -
(a) Substances which take part in chemical reaction (i.e., reactants) are usually written on left hand side and substances formed as a result of chemical reaction (i.e., products) are written on right hand side. The reactants and products are separated by an arrow head mark ( → ) which starts from reactants and points towards the products. Sign of equal to (=) may also be used in place of arrow head mark.
(b) Each reactant or the product is separated from one another by using plus sign ( + ) in between them.
The chemical equation written, following the above two steps, is skeletal chemical equation, as it does not have same number of atoms of each element on both sides of the arrow i.e. unbalanced chemical equation.

## BALANCED CHEMICAL EQUATION
A chemical equation in which number of atoms of each element is equal, both in products and reactants, is a balanced chemical equation.

## Example :
(i) Magnesium burns with oxygen and forms magnesium oxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
(Skeletonequation)
(Balanced equation)
Note: Magnesium burns in air with a brilliant white light, and for this reason it is often used in flares and fireworks.
(ii) Magnesium also burns in an environment of carbon dioxide such as in a beaker full of dry ice.

Note: When the Haber synthesis is carried out industrially, immense numbers of molecules are involved, but for every one molecule of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> that reacts with three molecules of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, two molecules of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are produced.

## Features of the Balanced Equation \section*{Equation}
(a) The reactants appear on the left, and products appear on the right. The arrow joining them indicates the direction of reaction.
(b) An integer preceedes the formula of each molecule. These integers are known as stoichiometric coefficients. The quantitative relation among reactants and products is known as stoichiometry. The stoichiometric coefficient for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in the equation (iii) is 3 and that of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is 2 . When no number appears, we understand that the stoichiometric coefficient is 1 . The stoichiometric coefficient for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in this equation is 1 .
(c) The stoichiometric coefficients in a chemical equation are the set of smallest integers that gives a balanced equation. It refers to the relative number of molecules involved in the reaction.
(d) Charge is conserved in balanced equation. In this equation, all participants are neutral species, so charge is conserved regardless of the stoichiometric coefficients. For reactions that include ions, however, charge conservation must be explicitly addressed.
- The amount of product actually obtained in a reaction is called actual yield.

## BALANCING OF A CHEMICAL EQUATION
According to law of conservation of mass, "Mass can neither be created nor destroyed"
In a chemical reaction total mass of the reactant should be equal to total mass of the product. If not, then we need to balance chemical equation. Let us understand the balancing of a chemical equation :
There is no definite rule for balancing an equation. Therefore, it requires a good deal of skill and practice. The equation is balanced by a method called hit and trial method.

## Hit and Trial Method
Lets consider word equation of a reaction between nitrogen and hydrogen producing ammonia.
Nitrogen + Hydrogen ⟶ Ammonia
Steps involved in balancing the above equation are as following :

## Step-1
First of all write the skeletal equation for the reaction and count the number of atoms of each substance on either side of the equation.
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | | |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Element | Number of atoms in reactants | Number of atoms in product |
| N | 2 | 1 |
| H | 2 | 3 |
(Skeletalequation)

## Step-2
Balance the atom which is minimum in number, on either side of chemical equation. In the given equation, number of nitrogen is the minimum on the RHS.
To balance the nitrogen atom, multiply the nitrogen in RHS by 2, so that the number of nitrogen atoms becomes equal on both sides.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> (partly balanced equation) </mtext></mrow></math>
It should be noted that to equalise the number of atoms on both sides, we cannot alter the formulae of the compounds or elements involved in the reaction.

## Step-3
Still number of H atoms is not balanced. To equalise the number of H atoms, multiply the hydrogen molecule <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> on LHS by 3 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

## Step-4
Now examine the number of atoms of N and H in the new chemical equation.
| Elements | Number of atoms in reactants | Number of atoms in product |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| N | 2 | 2 |
| H | 6 | 6 |
The number of atoms of each element are equal on both sides. Thus, this equation is now balanced.

## Step-5
The above balanced equation does not give any information about the physical state of reactants and products.
In order to make the equation more informative, the physical states of reactants and products are mentioned along with their chemical formulae. These physical states are mentioned with the help of certain notations. These notations are -
(g) for gases, (l) for liquids,(s) for solid, (aq) for aqueous; The word aqueous (aq) is written if the reactant or product is present as a solution in water.
The balanced equation becomes
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## Example :
Hydrogen reacts with chlorine to give hydrochloric acid.
(i) The skeleton equation of the above reaction :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(ii) To balance chlorine atoms, multiply the molecule HCl by 2 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Now, number of chlorine atoms and oxygen atoms are equal on both sides. Hence, the equation is balanced.
(iii) To make the chemical equation more informative, now write physical states of the reactants and products.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## Implications of a Chemical Equation
A chemical equation conveys a large number of informations as described below.

## Qualitative information
(a) It tells us about the names of the reactants and products.
(b) It tells us about the physical states of the reactants and products.

## Quantitative information
(a) It expresses the number of molecules of reactants and products.
(b) It expresses the relative number of moles of the reactants and the products.
(c) It expresses the relative weight of the reactants and the products.
(d) It expresses the volume of the gaseous reactants and products.

## Example :
Ammonia gas is formed by the combination of nitrogen and hydrogen.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi></mrow></mrow></munder><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">V</mi></mrow></mrow></munder></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>28</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>6</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math>
The above equation expresses that-
(i) Nitrogen combines with hydrogen to form ammonia.
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, all three are in gaseous physical state.
(iii) One molecule of nitrogen combines with three molecules of hydrogen to form two molecules of ammonia.
(iv) 28 parts by weight of nitrogen has combined with 6 parts by weight of hydrogen to form 34 parts by weight of ammonia.
(v) One volume of nitrogen and three volumes of hydrogen combine together to give 2 volumes of ammonia gas.

## Limitations of a Chemical Equation
A chemical equation does not give the following informations :
(a) Conditions necessary for a chemical reaction : A chemical equation does not necessarily indicate the reaction conditions.
(b) Rate of reaction : It does not give any idea about the rate of the reaction, whether it is slow or fast.
(c) Change of heat : It fails to give any indication whether the heat is absorbed or evolved.
(d) Concentration : It does not give any indication about the concentration of the reactants.
(e) Mechanism : It fails to give any idea about the mechanism of the reaction.
(f) Nature of reaction : It fails to give any information about the nature of reaction, whether it is reversible or irreversible reaction.

theory_sections.topics: Removal of Drawbacks of a Chemical Equation
theory_sections.markdown:
## Removal of Drawbacks of a Chemical Equation
Limitations of chemical reactions have been partially removed.
(a) To express the concentration of a substance the word 'conc.' for concentrated and 'dil' for dilute are written just below the reactant or after the formula of the reactant, viz. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (conc.)

(b) If a substance formed in the reaction is gas, it is indicated putting an arrow pointing upwards after the formula.

(e) If the reaction is exothermic the energy released is expressed by plus ( + ) sign and if the reaction is endothermic, it is expressed by putting minus (-) sign on RHS.

## CHEMICAL REACTION
The process in which two or more substances reacts to form new substances, is called chemical reactions.
It involves making and breaking of bond between atoms to form new a substance, which describes the nature and specific characteristic of the reaction.

## Types of Chemical Reactions
Based on the specific characteristics and the nature of the reactions, chemical reactions have been divided into following types :

## 1. Synthesis or Combination Reaction
When two or more elements or substances combine together to form a new substance, the chemical reaction is known as synthesis or combination reaction. This type of reaction takes place in presence of heat, light or may require electricity.
Examples :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

(1) At a commercial scale, ammonia is manufactured by Haber's process.

(2) Ostwald process for manufacturing of nitric acid.

theory_sections.topics: Combination reactions can occur between following types of reactants:
theory_sections.markdown:
## Combination reactions can occur between following types of reactants:
(a) Combination reaction between two elements.
(a) Combination between two non-metals: When a mixture of hydrogen and chlorine is placed in sunlight, hydrogen chloride gas is formed.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Sunlight </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) Combination between a metal and a non-metal : When magnesium wire is burnt in air, magnesium oxide is formed.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) Combination reaction between two compounds.
These are the reactions in which two compounds directly combine to form a new compound.
(a) Calcium oxide directly combines with water to form calcium hydroxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) Calcium oxide directly combines with carbon dioxide gas to form calcium carbonate.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) Formation of sulphuric acid from combination of sulphur trioxide and water which is a major contributor to nasty and toxic acid rain.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(c) Combination reaction between a compound and an element.
In these reaction in which an element reacts with a compound to form a new substance.
Combination of oxygen with carbon monoxide produces carbondioxide gas.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## Learn More
Reaction between calcium oxide, also known as quick lime, with water produces calcium hydroxide (slaked lime). calcium hydroxide produced in the above reaction remains as a white suspension.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Quick lime </mtext></mrow></munder><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Slaked lime </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
It is filtered and solution containing soluble calcium hydroxide is used for white washing walls. Calcium hydroxide reacts slowly with the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in air to form a thin layer of carbonate on the walls. Calcium carbonate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is formed after two to three days of white washing and gives a shiny finish to the wall.
Combination reactions involve the formation of new bonds, and this process releases a large amount of energy in the form of heat. Those reactions which occur with the evolution of heat, are known as exothermic reactions.
Example : Formation of calcium hydroxide.
Quick lime reacts with water to form slaked lime. This reaction is highly vigorous as well as exothermic in nature.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Quick lime </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Slaked lime </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>

## 2. Decomposition Reaction
The reactions in which a substance is decomposed into two or more simpler substances, are known as decomposition reactions. Decomposition reactions involve the breaking of chemical bonds to form new substances. Hence, they require energy in the form of heat, light, electricity, etc.
Those reactions which absorbs energy in the form of heat are known as endothermic reactions.
Examples :
(i) When potassium chlorate is heated, it is decomposed into potassium chloride and oxygen.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

## Step 1
First, count all atoms of each element on each side of the equation to see whether the elements are balanced:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

## Step 2
As we can see that nitrogen is already balanced. To balance the hydrogen atoms, we change the stoichiometric coefficient of water from 1 to 2 :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

## Step 3
This step balances nitrogen and hydrogen, but oxygen is not yet balanced. Oxygen must be balanced without changing the 1 : 1 ratio of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ratio of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>. These ratios must be retained to keep hydrogen and nitrogen in balance. Thus the only coefficient that can be adjusted to balance the oxygen atoms is that of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Two oxygen atoms are already present as in water and thus the remaining oxygen atom can be adjusted. by changing the coefficient of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
This balances the equation, but it is unrealistic from a molecular perspective because there is no such thing as half a molecule. To get rid of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> without unbalancing the reaction, we multiply all the coefficients by 2 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Now the reaction is balanced and reasonable from a molecular perspective.
Copper nitrate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> gives positive ring test of nitrate ion ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>), but after heating small amount of copper nitrate in dry boiling tube over the burner flame, it does not give positive ring test any more because it undergoes thermal decomposition reaction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## 3. Simple Displacement Reactions (Simple Substitution)
A displacement reaction occurs because a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one from a solution of its compound.
When we immerse a strip of zinc metal in a blue aqueous solution of copper (II) and remove the zinc strip it looks as if it has changed into copper. Actually, what happened is that a coating of copper is formed on the metal strip.

## Learn More
To decide if a displacement reaction will happen or not, we must have the knowledge of activity series. In activity series the element placed above will displace the element placed below from its compound.
Now reactivity of different metals is decided on the basis of reactivity series.

## Displacement reactions in solutions
A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from its compounds in solution. These are the sorts of things you observe in this type of reaction:
- The more reactive metal gradually dissolves.
- The less reactive metal coats the more reactive metal.
- The solution may change colour.
- The tube gets warm because these reactions are exothermic.
Here are two examples of these displacement reactions.
(a) Magnesium and copper sulphate solution
Magnesium is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper sulphate solution.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mtext> Magnesium </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> Copper sulphate </mtext><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> Magnesium sulphate </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> Copper </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Displacement reaction in this reaction can be witnessed, as blue coloured solution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> becomes colourless due to formation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (see figure (a) below).
Figure (a) : Displacement of copper from copper sulphate solution
Figure (b) : Iron becomes coated with copper in this displacement reaction

## (b) Iron and copper sulphate solution
Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper sulphate solution.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mtext> iron </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> copper sulphate </mtext><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> iron sulphate </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> copper </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
In this reaction displacement could be witnessed, as blue coloured solution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> changes in green colour due to formation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (see figure (b) above).

## 4. Double Decomposition Reaction (Double Displacement Reaction) :
The reactions in which mutual exchange of ions takes place are known as double decomposition reactions. As a result of double decomposition reactions, two new substances are formed.
(a) Aqueous barium chloride reacts with sulfuric acid to form solid barium sulfate and hydrochloric acid.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(b) Sodium sulfide reacts with hydrochloric acid to form sodium chloride and hydrogen sulfide gas.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(c) Potassium hydroxide reacts with nitric acid to form water and potassium nitrate.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## CONNECTING TOPIC
Double displacement reactions can be further classified as precipitation, gas formation, and acid-base neutralization reactions.
1. Precipitation reactions : A precipitation reaction occurs when two solutions are mixed together and a solid separates from the solution. The solid part that forms and separates from the solution is called the precipitate.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>↓</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
2. Gas formation reaction : A double-displacement reaction in which one of the product formed is gas, is called gas formation reactions. For example, sulfide salts react with acids to form gaseous hydrogen sulfide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>↑</mo></mrow></math>
All gases are soluble in water to some extent, but only a few gases [like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ] are highly soluble.
3. Neutralization reactions : Neutralization reaction is a special kind of double displacement reactions. In an acidbase reaction, an acid reacts with equal quantity of a base. The acid-base reaction results in the formation of salt and water.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## 5. Oxidation-Reduction Reactions
(a) Oxidation reactions :
Oxidation is defined as a process in which a substance gains oxygen or loses hydrogen during a chemical reaction.
Examples :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></math>
Based on classical concept, oxidation reaction can also be defined as following:
(i) Removal of hydrogen : Chlorine oxidises hydrogen sulphide to sulphur by the removal of hydrogen.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>
(ii) Addition of oxygen : When carbon is heated in oxygen gas, carbon dioxide is obtained.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(iii) Addition of more electronegative element: Chlorine is added to stannous chloride to from stannic chloride.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) Reduction : Reduction is defined as a process which involves the loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen during a chemical reaction.

## 2. Oxidation Number Concept
(a) Oxidation : According to this concept, increase in oxidation number of an element in a reaction is called oxidation.
(b) Reduction : According to this concept, decrease in oxidation number of an element in a reaction is called reduction.
Example :
Thus, here <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is oxidised to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> while <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is reduced to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

## OXIDATION NUMBER
It is the number of electrons lost or gained by an element during a chemical change in a particular compound.

## Rules for Determining Oxidation Number
(i) O.N. of elements in free state or uncombined state is zero. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> etc has zero oxidation state.
(ii) O.N. of hydrogen is always +1 except in ionic metal hydrides where it is -1 .
(iii) O.N. of oxygen is -2 except in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> where it is +2 and in peroxides where it is -1 .
(iv) O.N. of metals is always + ve. For IA group elements it is +1 and for IIA group elements it is +2.
(v) O.N. of halogens is -1 in metal halides.
(vi) O.N. of ion or radical is the number of electrons it must gain or lose to acquire neutrality i.e. it is equal to the electric charge, e.g. for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> O.N., is -2 .
(vii) O.N. of an atom within compound can be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math> integer, zero or fraction.
(viii) The algebric sum of all the O.N. of elements in a compound is equal to zero.
(ix) The algebric sum of all the O.N. of elements in an ion is equal to net charge on the ion.
(x) Maximum O.N. of an element is equal to number of valence electrons i.e. group number.
(xi) Minimum O.N. of an element (except metals) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> (Group number -8 ).
A compound can undergo both oxidation as well as reduction, if the O.N. of one of its element is in between the maximum and the minimum value.

## For example,
Maximum O.N. of N is +5 and minimum O.N. of N is -3 .
O.N. of N is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is +3 . <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> can undergo oxidation and reduction both, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>. of N is between maximum and minimum value.

## REDOX REACTIONS
Those reactions in which oxidation and reduction takes place simultaneously, are known as redox reactions.

## Example :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
During this reaction lead oxide is losing oxygen and thus, being reduced. The hydrogen is gaining oxygen and thus being oxidised. Hence we can say that in a redox (oxidation-reduction) reaction one substance gets oxidised while the other one gets reduced.

Did You Know?
- Redox processes are very important as they play important role in governing a number of natural processes like corrosion, combustion, biological processes like respiration etc.
- Redox reactions involve the transfer of electrons, while in general acid-base reactions involve transfer of protons.

## Oxidizing Agent
- The substance which gives oxygen for oxidation is called an oxidizing agent.
- The substance which removes hydrogen is also called an oxidizing agent.
- The substance which undergoes gain of electron and oxidizes the other substance is called an oxidizing agent.

## Reducing Agent
- The substance which gives hydrogen for reduction is called a reducing agent.
- The substance which removes oxygen is also called a reducing agent.
- The substance which undergoes loss of electron and reduces the other substance is called a reducing agent.

## CONNECTING TOPIC
## REDOX REACTIONS

## (A) Oxidation Number Method
In a balanced redox reaction, total increase in oxidation number must be equal to the total decrease in oxidation number. This equivalence provides the basis for balancing redox reactions.
The general procedure involves the following steps :
(a) Select the atom in oxidising agent whose oxidation number decreases and indicate the gain of electrons.
(b) Select the atom in reducing agent whose oxidation number increases and indicate the loss of electrons.
(c) Now cross multiply i.e. multiply oxidising agent by the number of lost electrons and reducing agent by number gained electrons.
(d) Balance the number of atoms on both sides whose oxidation number changes in the reaction.
(e) In order to balance oxygen atoms, add <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> molecules to the side deficient in oxygen. Then, balance the number of H atoms by adding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions to the side deficient in hydrogen.
(f) If the reaction occurs in basic medium, then add <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions, equal to the number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions, on both sides of the equation.
