<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
Sol. Writing the oxidation number of all the atoms.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mover><mi>⟶</mi><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mover><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
There is change in oxidation number of Cu and N .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></mover><mi>⟶</mi><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mover><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(Oxidation no. of Cu increases by 2 )
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></mover><mi>⟶</mi><mover><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></mover></mrow></math>
(Oxidation no. of N decreases by 1 )
To make the increase and decrease of electrons equal, eq. (2) is multiplied by 2 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Balancing nitrate ions, hydrogen and oxygen, the following equation is obtained.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
This is the balanced equation.

## (B) Ion Electron Method (Half Reaction Method)
The following steps are followed while balancing redox reactions (equations) by this method.
(a) Write the equation in ionic form.
(b) Split the redox equation into two half reactions, one representing oxidation half reaction and the other reduction half reaction.
(c) Balance these half reactions separately and then add by multiplying with suitable coefficients so that the electrons are cancelled.
Balancing is done as follows:
(i) Write both half reactions and then balance the atoms other than ' O ' and ' H '.
(ii) Balance oxygen atoms by adding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> molecules to the side deficient in oxygen. The number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> molecules added is equal to the deficiency of oxygen atoms.
(iii) Balance hydrogen atoms by adding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions equal to the deficiency, on the side which is deficient in hydrogen atoms.
(iv) If the medium of reaction is basic, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions equal in number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>are added to both sides of balanced equation.
(v) Balance the charge by adding electrons to the side which is rich in + ve charges. i.e. deficient in electrons. Number of electrons added is equal to the deficiency.
(vi) Multiply the half equations with suitable coefficients to equalize the number of electrons.
(vii) Add these half equations to get an equation which is balanced with respect to charge and atoms.
EXAMPLE: Balance the following reactions by ion electron method.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msup><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>

## Sol. (a) Acidic Medium :
(i) Given equation
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(ii) Write both the half reactions.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi>⟶</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> (Reduction half reaction)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (Oxidation half reaction)
(iii) Atoms other than H and O are balanced
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></math>
(iv) Balance O atoms by the addition of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> to another side
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></math>
(v) Balance H atoms by the addition of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions to another side.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mn>14</mn><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC
(vi) Now, balance the charge by the addition of electrons (e).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mn>14</mn><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></math>
(vii) Multiply equations by a constant to get number of electrons same on both side. In the above case second equation is multiplied by 3 and then added to first equation.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mn>14</mn><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>→</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mn>14</mn><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></math>

## (b) Alkaline medium :
(i) Given equation
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msup><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>
(ii) Separate the two half reactions.

## EXOTHERMIC AND ENDOTHERMIC REACTION
Chemical reactions usually proceed with either liberation of heat or the absorption of heat. The constituent elements of a compound are bound by a chemical bond, during the chemical reaction or chemical change these bonds between the constituents of the reactants are broken and the products are formed having new bonds. Breaking of a chemical bond releases energy while formation of a chemical bond requires energy.
Therefore, when a chemical reaction liberates heat to the surroundings, it is said to be 'exothermic reaction' and when it absorbs the heat, it is said to be 'endothermic reaction'.

## Examples :
(i) Nitrogen and hydrogen combine together to form ammonia. This chemical reaction liberates heat to the surroundings and, therefore, it is exothermic reaction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>22.4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>
Here bond between two atoms of a nitrogen molecule and between two atoms of the three hydrogen molecules are broken and new bonds between nitrogen and hydrogen atoms are formed. Here the sum of energies needed to break nitrogennitrogen bond and hydrogen-hydrogen bond is less than the energy released during the formation of the bonds between nitrogen and hydrogen. Thus the heat (energy) is liberated to the surroundings. Therefore, this reaction is exothermic. Similarly the formation of sulphur trioxide from sulphur dioxide and oxygen is also exothermic reaction :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>42.00</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>
(ii) Nitrogen and oxygen combine together to form nitric oxide. Here the heat from the surroundings is absorbed. Therefore, this reaction is endothermic.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>43.2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mtext>. </mtext></mrow></math>
The sum of energies needed to break nitrogen-nitrogen and oxygen-oxygen bonds is much more than the energy released during the formation of the bonds between nitrogen and oxygen atoms. Therefore, heat energy is provided externally to complete the reaction. Thus this is reaction is endothermic.

## CORROSION (EROSION BY CHEMICAL ACTION)
For most of us, corrosion is the degradation of metals and is often called rust.Technically we can define it as an irreversible interfacial reaction of a material (metal, ceramic, polymer) with its environment which results in consumption of the material. Corrosion causes damage to car bodies, bridges, iron railings, ships and to all objects made of metals, specially those of iron. Corrosion of iron (rusting) is a serious problem. Every year an enormous amount of money is spent to replace damaged iron. Most metals corrode on contact with water (and moisture in the air), acids, bases, salts, oils, aggressive metal polishes, and other solid and liquid chemicals. Metals will also corrode when exposed to gaseous materials like acid vapors, formaldehyde gas, ammonia gas, and sulfur containing gases. Corrosion specifically refers to any process involving the deterioration or degradation of metal components. The best known case is that of the rusting of iron. Corrosion processes are usually electrochemical in nature, having the essential features of a battery.
When corrosion is localised and create small holes or pits in the metal, it is called pitting
Did You Know? corrosion. Pitting corrosion occurs much faster in areas where microstructural changes have occurred due to welding operations.

## RANCIDITY
The most important cause of deterioration in fats and fatty foods is oxidation. Oxidation of fats results in the replacement of an oxygen ion from a hydrogen ion in the fatty acid molecule. This substitution destabilizes the molecule and makes it possible for other odd chemical fragments to find a place along the chain. An unpleasant change in the flavor and odour of a food is develop, called rancidity. Unsaturated fats are more susceptible to oxidation than the saturated fats.
Factors which accelerate fat oxidation include trace metals (iron, zinc, etc.), salt, light, water, bacteria, and molds. Fat oxidation can be retarded by use of antioxidants (Antioxidants are compounds that inhibit chemical reactions with oxygen such as BHT, BHA, vitamin E, and vitamin C), by use of spices such as sage and rosemary, and by use of light and/or air tight wrapping.
Some high fat foods such as potato chips are packed in materials that protect them from light and oxygen and the containers are flooded with nitrogen to further exclude oxygen. The nitrogen also serves as a cushion to minimize breakage of the chips during transport.

## More
Oxidation reactions may involve highly reactive molecules called free radicals. Free radicals are molecules that have lost an electron and try to gain it by reacting with other molecules. This causes the substance to break down. Metals often catalyze reactions with oxygen. Another example would be the half eaten apple. The skinless area quickly oxidized causing the apple to turn brown. Antioxidants inhibit these changes by reacting with the free radicals before they can react with oxygen (free radical scavenging) or by reacting with the metals. Naturally occurring antioxidants may also work by interacting directly with oxygen.
Naturally occurring antioxidants include retinol (vitamin A) and tocopherols (vitamin E), found in many animals and plants; ascorbic acid (vitamin C), found in citrus and other fruits and vegetables; and beta carotene, found in deep orange and dark green vegetables. These may play a significant role in the prevention of cancer, heart disease, immune-deficiency diseases, and aging.
Synthetic antioxidants include butylated hydroxy toluene (BHT), butylated hydroxy anisole (BHA), and propyl gallate. Natural and synthetic antioxidants are added to food to prevent undesirable deterioration. Foods preserved with antioxidants include vegetable oils, bread, and cheese.
Antioxidants are frequently applied to the packaging materials of cereals and nuts.

## Passage
Oxidation number is defined as the charge which an atom of the element has in its ion or appears to have when present in the combined state with other atoms.
There are certain rules for assigning oxidation number. Some of these rules are given below.
- The oxidation number of all the atoms of different elements in their respective elementary states and allotropic forms is taken to be zero.
- The O.N. of a monoatomic ion is the same as the charge on it.
- The O.N. of hydrogen is +1 when combined with nonmetals and is -1 when combined with active metals called metal hydrides
- The O.N. of alkali metals (Li, Na, K, etc.) is always + 1 and that of alkaline earth metals ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, etc.) is +2 .
- The algebraic sum of the O.N. of all the atoms in a compound must be zero. In polyatomic ion, the algebraic
sum of all the O.N.'s of atoms of the ion must equal the charge on the ion.

## ACIDS
The word "acid" comes from the Latin word acidus, meaning "sour" or "tart," since aqueous solutions of acids have a sour or tart taste. Lemon and orange taste sour because they contain citric acid and ascorbic acid (vitamin C). Another common acid is vinegar, which is the sour liquid produced when apple cider, grape juice, or other plant juices ferment beyond the formation of alcohol. Vinegar is a 5 percent aqueous solution of acetic acid.
Liebig defined acid as a compound containing one or more replaceable hydrogen(s). Acid dissociate in water and produce hydrogen ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>e.g. HCl is an acid and on dissolving in water it gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Hydrogen ions cannot exist alone but they exist after combining with water molecules. Thus hydrogen ion must always be shown as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> or hydronium ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
On the basis of sources acids can be classified into two groups. These are
(a) Organic acid: Acid obtained from plants material and animals is called organic acid. e.g citric acid (oranges \& lemons), acetic acid (vinegar), oleic acid (olive oil) etc.
(b) Mineral acid: Acid obtained from minerals is called mineral or inorganic acid. They do not contain carbon. e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> etc.

## Physical Properties of Acids
(a) Taste : Acids are generally sour in taste.
(b) Effect on indicator : Acid changes the colour of indicators as given in the table.
| Indicator | Change of colour | |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Litmus | From | To |
| Methyl orange | Blue | Red |
| Phenolphthalein | Orange | Red |
(c) Electrical Conductivity : Acids conduct electricity in aqueous solution, since they contain dissolved ions. For example, soluble acids like hydrochloric acid and sulphuric acid are used as electrolytes.
(d) Corrosive action : Strong acids are corrosive in nature. They corrode metals and release hydrogen gas. They can also burn skin. Know!
Acids are generally not corrosive except mineral acids <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> etc) and most of them are solids like organic acids (oxalic acid, tartaric acid, ascorbic acid, citric acid etc.)

The gaseous hydrochloric acid formed, starts coming out of the tube.
Now, if we will place 'dry' blue litmus paper near the mouth of the tube it does not show any change, but if we place 'moist' blue litmus paper it turns red. Acids are corrosive in nature. While handling an acid, if it falls accidently on skin, clothes or wood it causes severe burns on the skin, it cuts hole in clothes and burns the wood producing black spots.

## (1) Classification Based on the Presence of Oxygen
(i) Oxy-acids
Oxy-acids are those, which contain oxygen in their composition.
Examples : Sulphuric acid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, Oxalic acid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, Nitric acid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, Acetic acid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
(ii) Hydracids
Acids which contain hydrogen together with other element and not any oxygen in their composition, are called hydracids. Examples: Hydrochloric and (HCl), Hydroiodic acid (HI), Hydrobromic acid (HBr).

## (2) Classification Based on the Strength of the Acid
Almost all the acids dissociate in water and produce hydrogen ion to a lesser or greater extent. The strength of an acid depends on the concentration of the hydrogen ions present in a solution. Greater the tendency to loose hydrogen ion in the solution, greater is the strength of acid. However, some acids do not dissociate to an appreciable extent in water such as carbonic acid. Therefore, these acids will have a low concentration of hydrogen ions present in a solution. Based on this, acids are classified as :
(i) Strong acids
An acid, which dissociates completely or almost completely in water, is classified as a strong acid.
Examples : Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, nitric acid etc.

## (3) Classification Based on the Concentration of the Acid
Concentration of an acid solution depends upon the percentage of the acid that is dissolved in water. Based on this, acids are classified as
CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC
(i) Concentrated acid : An acid, that has a relatively high percentage of the acid dissolved in the aqueous solution is classified as a concentrated acid. Example concentrated hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, nitric acid, acetic acid etc.
(ii) Dilute acid : An acid, which has a relatively low percentage of the acid dissolved in the aqueous solution is classified as a dilute acid. Examples : dilute hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, nitric acid, acetic acid etc.

theory_sections.topics: (4) Classification Based on the Basicity of an Acid
theory_sections.markdown:
## (4) Classification Based on the Basicity of an Acid
As we have studied that acid on dissociation in water produce hydrogen ion, the number of these replaceable hydrogen ions in an acid is known as the basicity of an acid. It is also evident that, one hydrogen ion or hydronium ion can react with one hydroxyl ion ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>).
(i) Monobasic acid
A monobasic acid has one replaceable hydrogen ion. Hence, these acids combine with one hydroxyl group of a base to form salt and water.
Since, monobasic acids have only one replaceable hydrogen ion, they form only one kind of salt.

(ii) Dibasic acid
A dibasic acid has two replaceable hydrogen ion. These acid combine with two hydroxyl groups of a base to form salt and water. It known as a dibasic acid. Such acids dissociate in two steps in water.

## BASES
Like acids, bases also dissociate in water, but in place of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>they produce hydroxyl ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. Thus, a base is a compound which on dissolving in water yields hydroxyl ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. The characteristic property of a base is due to the formation of these negative hydroxyl ions. A base may be an oxide or a hydroxide of a metal. If a base is soluble in water, it dissociates to form a metal ion and negative hydroxyl ion. Substances that combine with acids to form salt and water are also called bases.

## Example:
Sodium hydroxide is a base, it gives sodium ion and hydroxyl ion when dissolved in water.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>⇌</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Ammonium hydroxide is also a base. In water, it dissociates to form ammonium ion and a hydroxyl ion.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>⇌</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## Alkali
Alkalis are bases that dissociate in water to yield hydroxyl ion ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>). All alkalis are bases but not all bases are alkali. Alkali is a basic, ionic salt of an alkali or alkaline earth metal element. Alkalis are best known for being bases that dissolve in water. Whereas a base is most commonly thought of as a substance that can accept <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> ions. ## Physical Properties of Bases
(a) Taste: Bases are bitter to taste. If you have ever gotten soap in your mouth, you have noticed its bitter taste. This bitter taste confirms presence of base in the soap.
(b) Feel: They are soapy and slippery to touch.
(c) Electrical conductivity: Some bases are good conductors of electricity. For example, soluble bases like sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are used as electrolytes.
(d) Corrosive action : Strong alkalis like sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are highly corrosive or caustic in nature. Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are commonly called caustic soda and caustic potash respectively. Organic tissues like skin, etc. get completely corroded by these two alkalis. However, the other alkalis are only mildly corrosive.
(e) Effect on indicator: Bases changes the colour of indicator as given in the table.
| Indicator | Change of colour | |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| Litmus | From | To |
| Methyl orange | Red | Blue |
| Phenolphthalein | Orange | Yellow |
| Turmeric | Colourless | Pink |

theory_sections.topics: (1) Classification Based on the Strength of the Base
theory_sections.markdown:
## (1) Classification Based on the Strength of the Base
We have already studied that bases on dissociation produce hydroxyl ion ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>). The strength of a base depends on the concentration of the hydroxyl ion when it is dissolved in water. Based on this, bases are classified as,
(i) Strong base
A base that dissociates completely or almost completely in water is classified as a strong base. In other words, greater the tendency to loose hydroxyl ion in the solution, the stronger is the base.
Example: Sodium hydroxide : NaOH
Potassium hydroxide : KOH
Calcium hydroxide : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(ii) Weak base
A base that partially dissociates in water is classified as a weak base.
Example: Magnesium hydroxide : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Ammonium hydroxide : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

theory_sections.topics: (2) Classification Based on the Concentration of a Base
theory_sections.markdown:
## (2) Classification Based on the Concentration of a Base
Concentration of a basic solution depends upon the percentage of the base dissolved in water. Based on this fact, bases are classified as,
(i) Concentrated base : A base that has a relatively high percentage of the base in its aqueous solution is classified as a concentrated base. Example concentrated sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, ammonium hydroxide etc.
(ii) Dilute base: A base that has a relatively low percentage of the base dissolved in its aqueous solution, is classified as a dilute base. Example dilute sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, ammonium hydroxide etc.

theory_sections.topics: (3) Classification Based on the Acidity of a Base
theory_sections.markdown:
## (3) Classification Based on the Acidity of a Base
The acidity of a base is equal to the number of hydroxyl ions it has. It is also the number of hydrogen ions with which a base can combine as one hydrogen ion combines with one hydroxyl ion.
Based on the acidity bases can be classified as,
(i) Monoacidic base
It is a base that has only one hydroxyl ion. It combines with only one hydrogen ion. Hence, its acidity will be one.
Example : Sodium hydroxide, Potassium hydroxide: KOH , Lithium hydroxide: LiOH , Ammonium hydroxide: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

## (ii) Diacidic base
It is a base that has two hydroxyl groups and combines with two hydrogen ions. Hence, its acidity will be two.
Example : Iron (II) hydroxide: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, Magnesium hydroxide: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, Copper hydroxide: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, Zinc hydroxide : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, Lead hydroxide: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.

## (iii) Triacidic base
A base that has three hydroxyl ions and can combines with three hydrogen ions. Hence, its acidity will be three.
Example: Aluminium hydroxide

theory_sections.topics: Acid or a Base in a Water Solution:
theory_sections.markdown:
## Acid or a Base in a Water Solution:
The process of dissolving an acid or a base in water is a highly exothermic one. Care must be taken while mixing concentrated nitric acid or sulphuric acid with water. The acid must always be added slowly to water with constant stirring. If water is added to a concentrated acid, the heat generated may cause the mixture to splash out and cause burns. The glass container may also break due to excessive local heating. Mixing an acid or base with water results in decrease in the concentration of ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>/</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>per unit volume. Such a process is called dilution and the acid or the base is said to be diluted.

theory_sections.topics: Indicators are substances which undergoes change in colour, smell or taste with respect to the change in medium. It helps to differentiate between acidic and basic medium. Indicators are of following types depending upon its source:
theory_sections.markdown:
## Indicators are substances which undergoes change in colour, smell or taste with respect to the change in medium. It helps to differentiate between acidic and basic medium. Indicators are of following types depending upon its source:
- Natural indicators can be extracted from a wide variety offlowers, fruits, roots, leaves and other parts of plants, e.g. tea leaves, beet roots, rose petals of various colours, red cabbage leaves, turmeric, black berries, and delphinium flowers. Litmus (a natural dye) is one of the most common and naturally available indicator. It is extracted from lichens (combination of algae and fungus). When this litmus is added to an acidic solution, it turns red and when added to a basic solution, it turns blue. It possess a purple colour in distilled water.
- Synthetic indicators are prepared from man made chemical substances like phenolphtalein, methyl orange etc.
Phenolphthalein is a synthetic indicator. It turns acidic solutions colorless and basic solutions pink. If the concentration of indicator is particularly strong, it can appear purple.
Methyl orange is also a synthetic indicator used more oftenly because of clear colour change. In a solution becoming less acidic, methyl orange moves from red to orange and finally to yellow with the reverse occuring for a solution increasing in acidity.
Depending upon the change in properties indicators are classified as:
- Halochromic indicator show change in color with respect to the change in medium, e.g: litmus, phenolphtalein, methyl orange etc. These indicators are generally used as acid-base indicators.
- Olfactory indicator causes change in odour/smell with respect to the change in medium. e.g: clove oil, onion, vanilla extract etc.
- Gustatory indicator causes change in taste with respect to the change in medium. e.g: Sour taste of milk indicates that the milk has became acidic, hence it is spoiled.
Universal indicators : It is a mixture of indicators often sold ready made solution which can indicate pH values, usually over a range of 3-11, by successive changes of colour
Take 100 mL beaker and fill it upto 80\% with distilled water in your school laboratory. First add few drops of phenolphthalein solution and stir solution with glass rod properly then record your observation if there is any change. Now add few drops of ammonium hydroxide and stir solution with glass rod properly then again record your observation if there is any change. Then add few drops of vinegar solution and stir resulting solution properly with glass rod. Record change if any. Now in case you are not able to understand the reason of your recorded observations, consult your friend and discuss with your teacher.

## CHEMICAL REACTION
The process in which two or more substances reacts to form new substances, is called chemical reactions.
It involves making and breaking of bond between atoms to form new a substance, which describes the nature and specific characteristic of the reaction.
## Types of Chemical Reactions
Based on the specific characteristics and the nature of the reactions, chemical reactions have been divided into following types :
## 1. Synthesis or Combination Reaction
When two or more elements or substances combine together to form a new substance, the chemical reaction is known as synthesis or combination reaction. This type of reaction takes place in presence of heat, light or may require electricity.

## Combination reactions can occur between following types of reactants:
(a) Combination reaction between two elements.
(a) Combination between two non-metals: When a mixture of hydrogen and chlorine is placed in sunlight, hydrogen chloride gas is formed.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Sunlight </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) Combination between a metal and a non-metal : When magnesium wire is burnt in air, magnesium oxide is formed.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) Combination reaction between two compounds.
These are the reactions in which two compounds directly combine to form a new compound.
(a) Calcium oxide directly combines with water to form calcium hydroxide.

(b) Calcium oxide directly combines with carbon dioxide gas to form calcium carbonate.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) Formation of sulphuric acid from combination of sulphur trioxide and water which is a major contributor to nasty and toxic acid rain.

illustrations.title: ILLUSTRATION : 3
illustrations.problem: Ammonium nitrate, a colorless ionic solid used as a fertilizer, explodes when it is heated above <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>300</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>. The products are three gases: molecular nitrogen, molecular oxygen, and steam (water vapour). Find the type of chemical reaction and write a balanced equation for the explosion of ammonium nitrate.
illustrations.solution:
The description in the problem tells us what happens to the starting material: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> breaks apart into molecules of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>. An unbalanced form of the equation can be written from this description. Then we must balance each element in turn by inspection.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
## Step 1
First, count all atoms of each element on each side of the equation to see whether the elements are balanced:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
## Step 2
As we can see that nitrogen is already balanced. To balance the hydrogen atoms, we change the stoichiometric coefficient of water from 1 to 2 :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
## Step 3
This step balances nitrogen and hydrogen, but oxygen is not yet balanced. Oxygen must be balanced without changing the 1 : 1 ratio of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ratio of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>. These ratios must be retained to keep hydrogen and nitrogen in balance. Thus the only coefficient that can be adjusted to balance the oxygen atoms is that of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Two oxygen atoms are already present as in water and thus the remaining oxygen atom can be adjusted. by changing the coefficient of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
This balances the equation, but it is unrealistic from a molecular perspective because there is no such thing as half a molecule. To get rid of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> without unbalancing the reaction, we multiply all the coefficients by 2 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Now the reaction is balanced and reasonable from a molecular perspective.
Copper nitrate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> gives positive ring test of nitrate ion ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>), but after heating small amount of copper nitrate in dry boiling tube over the burner flame, it does not give positive ring test any more because it undergoes thermal decomposition reaction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

illustrations.problem:
Identify the substance that is oxidised and the substance that is reduced in the following reactions.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
illustrations.solution:
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Sodium metal is oxidised as it is gaining oxygen.
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

illustrations.title: ILLUSTRATION : 5
illustrations.problem: When aluminium metal is exposed to air, a protective layer of aluminium oxide ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) forms on its surface. The layer prevents further reaction between aluminium and oxygen, and it is the reason that aluminium beverage cans do not corrode. [In the case of iron, the rust, or iron (III) oxide, is too porous to protect the iron metal underneath, so rusting continues]. Write a balanced equation for the formation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
illustrations.solution:
The unbalanced equation is :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
We see that both Al and O appear only once on each side of the equation but in unequal numbers. To balance the Al atoms, we place 2 in front of Al :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
There are two O atoms on the left-hand side and three O atoms on the right-hand side of the equation. This inequality of O atoms can be eliminated by writing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> in front of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> on the left-hand side of the equation.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Now multiply the entire equation by 2 to convert <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> to 3 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> i.e. </mtext><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
The above equation is the balanced equation for the formation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
Place a small silver article (made up of pure silver) in open air for few days. Then record your observation. In case if there is any sort of change, then try to find out the exact reason for this change by discussing with your friends and teacher.
## RANCIDITY
The most important cause of deterioration in fats and fatty foods is oxidation. Oxidation of fats results in the replacement of an oxygen ion from a hydrogen ion in the fatty acid molecule. This substitution destabilizes the molecule and makes it possible for other odd chemical fragments to find a place along the chain. An unpleasant change in the flavor and odour of a food is develop, called rancidity. Unsaturated fats are more susceptible to oxidation than the saturated fats.
Factors which accelerate fat oxidation include trace metals (iron, zinc, etc.), salt, light, water, bacteria, and molds. Fat oxidation can be retarded by use of antioxidants (Antioxidants are compounds that inhibit chemical reactions with oxygen such as BHT, BHA, vitamin E, and vitamin C), by use of spices such as sage and rosemary, and by use of light and/or air tight wrapping.
Some high fat foods such as potato chips are packed in materials that protect them from light and oxygen and the containers are flooded with nitrogen to further exclude oxygen. The nitrogen also serves as a cushion to minimize breakage of the chips during transport.
## Learn
## More
Oxidation reactions may involve highly reactive molecules called free radicals. Free radicals are molecules that have lost an electron and try to gain it by reacting with other molecules. This causes the substance to break down. Metals often catalyze reactions with oxygen. Another example would be the half eaten apple. The skinless area quickly oxidized causing the apple to turn brown. Antioxidants inhibit these changes by reacting with the free radicals before they can react with oxygen (free radical scavenging) or by reacting with the metals. Naturally occurring antioxidants may also work by interacting directly with oxygen.
Naturally occurring antioxidants include retinol (vitamin A) and tocopherols (vitamin E), found in many animals and plants; ascorbic acid (vitamin C), found in citrus and other fruits and vegetables; and beta carotene, found in deep orange and dark green vegetables. These may play a significant role in the prevention of cancer, heart disease, immune-deficiency diseases, and aging.
Synthetic antioxidants include butylated hydroxy toluene (BHT), butylated hydroxy anisole (BHA), and propyl gallate. Natural and synthetic antioxidants are added to food to prevent undesirable deterioration. Foods preserved with antioxidants include vegetable oils, bread, and cheese.
Antioxidants are frequently applied to the packaging materials of cereals and nuts.

illustrations.solution:
