exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q10
exercises.problem:
When the gases sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide mix in the presence of water, the reaction is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. Here hydrogen sulphide is acting as -
(a) an oxidising agent
(b) a reducing agent
(c) a dehydrating agent
(d) a catalyst
exercises.solution: (b) Here <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow></mrow></math> is behaves as a reducing agent and oxidises to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q11
exercises.problem:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>→</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, reaction is an example of -
(a) redox reaction
(b) synthesis reaction
(c) neutralisation
(d) analysis reaction
exercises.solution: (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>~</mi></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>~</mi></mrow></munder></mrow><mrow><mtext> Reduction </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q12
exercises.problem:
A substance which oxidises itself and reduces other is known as -
(a) oxidising agent
(b) reducing agent
(c) both of these
(d) none of these

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q13
exercises.problem:
A redox reaction is one in which -
(a) both the substances are reduced.
(b) both the substances are oxidised.
(c) an acid is neutralised by the base.
(d) one substance is oxidised while the other is reduced.
exercises.solution:
In which of the following reactions, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> acts as a reducing agent?
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q14
exercises.problem:
In the following equations:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>, the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is-
(a) 1
(b) 2
(c) 3
(d) 4
exercises.solution: (b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q15
exercises.problem:
In the equation, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>→</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> nitric acid is acting as -
(a) an oxidising agent
(b) an acid
(c) a nitrating agent
(d) a dehydrating agent
exercises.solution: (b) The reaction represents a neutralisation reaction in which base <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> reacts with an acid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> to form salt <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and water <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q16
exercises.problem:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
The above reaction is an example of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo></mrow></math>
(a) combination reaction
(b) double displacement reaction
(c) decomposition reaction
(d) displacement reaction

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q17
exercises.problem:
White silver chloride in sunlight turns to -
(a) grey
(b) yellow
(c) remain white
(d) red
exercises.solution: (a) White silver chloride in sunlight turns to grey.

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q18
exercises.problem:
Black and white photography uses -
(a) decomposition of silver chloride.
(b) decomposition of silver bromide.
(c) both
(d) none of these

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q19
exercises.problem:
When copper powder is heated it gets coated with -
(a) black copper oxide
(b) yellow copper oxide
(c) red copper oxide
(d) None of these
exercises.solution: (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Black </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q20
exercises.problem:
Combination of phosphorus and oxygen is an example of-
(a) oxidation
(b) reduction
(c) rancidity
(d) None of these
exercises.solution:
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> (Oxidation) </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> (Oxidation) </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q21
exercises.problem:
Rusting of iron is an example of -
(a) reduction
(b) redox
(c) oxidation
(d) dissociation
exercises.solution: (b) 2 Fe (s) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (g) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>(aq) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> (aq) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> (l)

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q22
exercises.problem:
Which of the following does not corrode when exposed to the atmosphere?
(a) Iron
(b) Copper
(c) Gold
(d) Silver
exercises.solution: (c) Gold is least reactive hence does not corrode at all.

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q23
exercises.problem:
Take about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1.0</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in a test tube. Heat it over a flame, a colourless gas comes out. The reaction is called a
(a) decomposition reaction
(b) displacement reaction
(c) double decomposition reaction
(d) double displacement reaction
exercises.solution: (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q24
exercises.problem:
Hydrogen sulphide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a strong reducing agent. Which of the following reactions shows its reducing action?
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
exercises.solution:
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Oxidation </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>~</mi></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
In the given reaction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow></mrow></math> undergoes oxidation, hence behave as a reducing agent.

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q25
exercises.problem:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, the reaction is -
(a) redox
(b) neutralisation
(c) oxidation
(d) reduction
exercises.solution:
(a)
Oxidation and reduction both occur so the reaction is redox.

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q26
exercises.problem:
When copper turnings are added to silver nitrate solution, a blue coloured solution is formed after some time. It is because, copper -
(a) displaces silver from the solution
(b) forms a blue coloured complex with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) is oxidised to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(d) is reduced to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
exercises.solution: (a) Cu is more reactive than Ag .

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q27
exercises.problem:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>→</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. This is -
(a) oxidation
(b) reduction
(c) redox reaction
(d) none of these
exercises.solution: (b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>; reduction

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q28
exercises.problem:
A substance A reacts with another substance B to produce the product C and a gas D . If a mixture of the gas D and ammonia is passed through an aqueous solution of C , baking soda is formed. The substances A and B are
[NTSE]
(a) HCl and NaOH
(b) HCl and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) Na and HCl
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
exercises.solution:
(b)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Baking soda </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>&</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are HCl and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q29

Chemically the 'water gas' is
[JSTSE]
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> (gaseous)
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

exercises.solution: (d) Water gas → <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q30
exercises.problem:
The oxidation number of sulphur is -4 in
[KVPY]
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
exercises.solution:
(*) Let the oxidation state of S be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>&</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
None of these, option is correct.

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q31

(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q32
exercises.problem:
The schematic diagram is given below
[NTSE]
Which of the following is a correct statement?
(a) A and E are chemically same.
(b) A and D are chemically same.
(c) D and E are chemically same.
(d) C and E are chemically same.
exercises.solution:
(b)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>;</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q33
exercises.problem:
The oxidation states of P atom in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, respectively are

(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
exercises.solution:
(a) Let the oxidation state of P -atom in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q34
exercises.problem:
The process of respiration is :
[JSTSE]
(a) Oxidation reaction which is endothermic
(b) Reduction reaction which is endothermic
(c) Combination reaction which is exothermic
(d) Oxidation reaction which is exothermic
exercises.solution: (d) Respiration is oxidation and exothermic process.

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q35
exercises.problem:
Silver articles become black when exposed to air. It is due to the formation of
[JSTSE]
(a) Silver oxide
(b) Silver nitrate
(c) Silver chloride
(d) Silve sulphide
exercises.solution: (d) Layer of silver sulphide deposited on the silver articles when exposed to air.

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q36
exercises.problem:

Loss of weight during this experiment was 4.40 g . What is the weight of the empty test tube in this experiment?

(d) 2.008 g

key_points.text: Substances which take part in chemical reaction (i.e., reactants) are usually written on left hand side and substances formed as a result of chemical reaction (i.e., products) are written on right hand side. The reactants and products are separated by an arrow head mark ( → ) which starts from reactants and points towards the products. Sign of equal to (=) may also be used in place of arrow head mark.
Each reactant or the product is separated from one another by using plus sign ( + ) in between them.
Magnesium burns with oxygen and forms magnesium oxide.
(Balanced equation)
Magnesium also burns in an environment of carbon dioxide such as in a beaker full of dry ice.
The reactants appear on the left, and products appear on the right. The arrow joining them indicates the direction of reaction.

An integer preceedes the formula of each molecule. These integers are known as stoichiometric coefficients. The quantitative relation among reactants and products is known as stoichiometry. The stoichiometric coefficient for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in the equation (iii) is 3 and that of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is 2 . When no number appears, we understand that the stoichiometric coefficient is 1 . The stoichiometric coefficient for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in this equation is 1 .
The stoichiometric coefficients in a chemical equation are the set of smallest integers that gives a balanced equation. It refers to the relative number of molecules involved in the reaction.

Charge is conserved in balanced equation. In this equation, all participants are neutral species, so charge is conserved regardless of the stoichiometric coefficients. For reactions that include ions, however, charge conservation must be explicitly addressed.
The amount of product actually obtained in a reaction is called actual yield.
Nitrogen and hydrogen combine together to give ammonia. (Haber synthesis)

1. Read the following and answer any four questions from (i) to (v).
Chemical reactions involve the breaking and making of bonds between atoms to produce new substances. during a chemical reaction atoms of one element do not change into those of another element. Nor do atoms disappear from the mixture or appear from elsewhere. There are certain types of reactions. Reactions in which a single product is formed from two or more reactants is known as a combination reaction. Decomposition reactions are the reactions in which a compound breaks down into simpler compounds. Displacement and double displacement reactions are the one in which an atom or group of atom is replaced by another.Another type of reaction is redox reactions in which simultaneous oxidation and reduction takes place.

## Passage
Oxidation number is defined as the charge which an atom of the element has in its ion or appears to have when present in the combined state with other atoms.
There are certain rules for assigning oxidation number. Some of these rules are given below.
- The oxidation number of all the atoms of different elements in their respective elementary states and allotropic forms is taken to be zero.
- The O.N. of a monoatomic ion is the same as the charge on it.
- The O.N. of hydrogen is +1 when combined with nonmetals and is -1 when combined with active metals called metal hydrides
- The O.N. of alkali metals (Li, Na, K, etc.) is always + 1 and that of alkaline earth metals ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, etc.) is +2 .
- The algebraic sum of the O.N. of all the atoms in a compound must be zero. In polyatomic ion, the algebraic
sum of all the O.N.'s of atoms of the ion must equal the charge on the ion.

12. Oxidation or reduction cannot take place alone. This is because if one substance loses oxygen, i.e., undergoes reduction, there must be another substance to take up this oxygen, i.e., undergo oxidation. Similarly, if one substance loses hydrogen, i.e., undergoes oxidation, there must be another substance to take up this hydrogen, i.e., undergo reduction. Hence, oxidation and reduction always take place together. That is why, these reactions are called redox reactions.

An exchange of ions produces the compounds <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Both of these compounds are soluble, so no reaction occurs.
3. (a) Ammonia <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) Water <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> act as reducing agents
(c) Carbon monoxide (CO)
(d) Hydrogen
Hint-Reducing agents are those substances which have the ability of adding hydrogen or removing oxygen from the other substances.
4. (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
5. First, represent the name of the species involved as reactants and products with formulae and indicate their physical states.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Next, balance carbon. Place a coefficient of 3 in front of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to balance the carbons in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>. Balance the eight hydrogens in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> by adding a coefficient of 4 in front of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>3</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Now note that there are 10 oxygens on the right. On the left, one oxygen is in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> so nine are needed from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. To get an odd number of oxygens from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> we need to use a fractional coefficient, in this case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> (i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math> )
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>3</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Finally, we need to clear the fraction so that all coefficients are whole numbers. Multiply the whole equation by 2 and do a quick check.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>6</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
6. (a) Because aluminum oxide is the oxide of a metal, we would expect it to be an ionic solid. Indeed it is, and it has a very high melting point, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2072</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
(b) In its compounds, aluminum has a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> charge, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, the oxide ion is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, consequently, the formula of aluminum oxide is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Metal oxides tend to be basic and therefore reacts with acids to form salts and water. In this case the salt formed is aluminum nitrate, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. The balanced chemical equation is
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
7. In the activity series that Sn is higher in the series than Ag . Therefore Sn replaces <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> ions from solution.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(b) In the activity series, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is in higher position than Ag . Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> replaces <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, but the reverse reaction, the replacement of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>by Ag , does not occur. No reaction occurs.
8. (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>8</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## Exercise 2 Master NCERT (Textbook \& Exemplar)
## Text - Book Questions
1. Magnesium ribbon has a coating of basic magnesium carbonate on its surface, which is formed by a slow action of moist air on it. Therefore before burning it in air, it is cleaned by a sand paper which removes the protective layer of basic magnesium carbonate from the surface of magnesium ribbon, so that it can easily burn.
2. (i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

10. Respiration is the most important biochemical reaction which releases energy in the cell. When we breathe air (oxygen) enters into our lungs and oxygen binds itself to haemoglobin present in red blood cells (RBC). It is then carried to million of cells present in our body. Respiration occurs in these cells and is accompanied by the combustion of glucose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> producing carbon dioxide ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) and water ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> ). A large amount of energy is released in this chemical reaction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2820</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Since the process is accompanied by release of energy so it is considered as an exothermic reaction.

16. To prevent iron articles from rusting, we apply paint on it, by which iron does not come in contact with air and moisture which causes rusting.
17. When the oil and fat containing food is surrounded by unreactive gas nitrogen, oxygen become unavailable to cause oxidation and therefore prevent rancidity.
18. Corrosion : - It is a process in which metals are eaten up gradually by the action of air, moisture or a chemical on their surface. For example rusting of iron.
Rancidity - When fat and oil containing food is oxidised with air or oxygen, their smell and taste changes. This process is called rancidity.

## ACIDS
The word "acid" comes from the Latin word acidus, meaning "sour" or "tart," since aqueous solutions of acids have a sour or tart taste. Lemon and orange taste sour because they contain citric acid and ascorbic acid (vitamin C). Another common acid is vinegar, which is the sour liquid produced when apple cider, grape juice, or other plant juices ferment beyond the formation of alcohol. Vinegar is a 5 percent aqueous solution of acetic acid.
Liebig defined acid as a compound containing one or more replaceable hydrogen(s). On the basis of sources acids can be classified into two groups. These are
(a) Organic acid: Acid obtained from plants material and animals is called organic acid. e.g citric acid (oranges \& lemons), acetic acid (vinegar), oleic acid (olive oil) etc.
(b) Mineral acid: Acid obtained from minerals is called mineral or inorganic acid. They do not contain carbon. e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> etc.
## Physical Properties of Acids
(a) Taste : Acids are generally sour in taste.
(b) Effect on indicator : Acid changes the colour of indicators as given in the table.
| Indicator | Change of colour | |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Litmus | From | To |
| Methyl orange | Blue | Red |
| Phenolphthalein | Orange | Red |
(c) Electrical Conductivity : Acids conduct electricity in aqueous solution, since they contain dissolved ions. For example, soluble acids like hydrochloric acid and sulphuric acid are used as electrolytes.
(d) Corrosive action : Strong acids are corrosive in nature. They corrode metals and release hydrogen gas. They can also burn skin. Know!
Acids are generally not corrosive except mineral acids <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> etc) and most of them are solids like organic acids (oxalic acid, tartaric acid, ascorbic acid, citric acid etc.)

case_studies.title: CASE STUDY-1 : Get Closer to Acids
case_studies.description:
An acid is a substance, whose aqueous solution releases hydrogen ion.
CASE I : Are all compounds containing hydrogen acids?
When an acid is dissolved in water, then in solution it produces hydrogen ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. But compounds like glucose and alcohol do not dissociate in water to produce hydrogen ion. Therefore, even though they have hydrogen in their formula they are not acids.
## Think Out of the Box
Q. 1 You are given <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution and glucose solution which one do you think will show electrical conductivity and why?
Q. 2 Among the given substances, find whose property can be determined by universal indicator.
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

(vii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Q. 3 If you have to store sulphuric acid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> which container will you prefer metallic or ceramic, and why?
CASE II : To determine whether acid will show their acidic behaviourcas in absence of water.
Take sodium chloride in a boiling tube and add some concentrated sulphuric acid to it. Following reaction will take place,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
The gaseous hydrochloric acid formed, starts coming out of the tube.
Now, if we will place 'dry' blue litmus paper near the mouth of the tube it does not show any change, but if we place 'moist' blue litmus paper it turns red. This is because acids produces <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion only in presence of water, hence in absence of water they do not show acidic behaviour.
CASE III : While using an acid in lab, we notice a burned hole in our lab coat.
Acids are corrosive in nature. While handling an acid, if it falls accidently on skin, clothes or wood it causes severe burns on the skin, it cuts hole in clothes and burns the wood producing black spots.

## (2) Classification Based on the Strength of the Acid
Almost all the acids dissociate in water and produce hydrogen ion to a lesser or greater extent. The strength of an acid depends on the concentration of the hydrogen ions present in a solution. Greater the tendency to loose hydrogen ion in the solution, greater is the strength of acid. However, some acids do not dissociate to an appreciable extent in water such as carbonic acid. Therefore, these acids will have a low concentration of hydrogen ions present in a solution. Based on this, acids are classified as :
(i) Strong acids
An acid, which dissociates completely or almost completely in water, is classified as a strong acid.
Examples : Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, nitric acid etc.

## (3) Classification Based on the Concentration of the Acid
Concentration of an acid solution depends upon the percentage of the acid that is dissolved in water. Based on this, acids are classified as
CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC
(i) Concentrated acid : An acid, that has a relatively high percentage of the acid dissolved in the aqueous solution is classified as a concentrated acid. Example concentrated hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, nitric acid, acetic acid etc.
(ii) Dilute acid : An acid, which has a relatively low percentage of the acid dissolved in the aqueous solution is classified as a dilute acid. Examples : dilute hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, nitric acid, acetic acid etc.
## (4) Classification Based on the Basicity of an Acid
As we have studied that acid on dissociation in water produce hydrogen ion, the number of these replaceable hydrogen ions in an acid is known as the basicity of an acid. It is also evident that, one hydrogen ion or hydronium ion can react with one hydroxyl ion ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>).
(i) Monobasic acid
A monobasic acid has one replaceable hydrogen ion. Hence, these acids combine with one hydroxyl group of a base to form salt and water.
Since, monobasic acids have only one replaceable hydrogen ion, they form only one kind of salt.

The tribasic acids can combine with three hydroxyl groups. These acids have three replaceable hydrogen ions. ## BASES
Like acids, bases also dissociate in water, but in place of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>they produce hydroxyl ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. Thus, a base is a compound which on dissolving in water yields hydroxyl ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. The characteristic property of a base is due to the formation of these negative hydroxyl ions. A base may be an oxide or a hydroxide of a metal. If a base is soluble in water, it dissociates to form a metal ion and negative hydroxyl ion. Substances that combine with acids to form salt and water are also called bases.
## Example:
Sodium hydroxide is a base, it gives sodium ion and hydroxyl ion when dissolved in water.

Ammonium hydroxide is also a base. In water, it dissociates to form ammonium ion and a hydroxyl ion.

Sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, calcium hydroxide and ammonium hydroxide are the common alkalis.

All alkalis are bases but not all bases are alkali. Alkali is a basic, ionic salt of an alkali or alkaline earth metal element. Alkalis are best known for being bases that dissolve in water. Whereas a base is most commonly thought of as a substance that can accept <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> ions. A soluble base is also often referred to as an alkali if hydroxide ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>are involved.

Whether calcium oxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is alkali, base or both?
## SOLUTION
It serves as both. As we know that alkalis are bases that dissociate in water to yield hydroxyl ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. The calcium oxide dissolves in water to form calcium hydroxide which further ionises to give hydroxyl ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

## Physical Properties of Bases
(a) Taste: Bases are bitter to taste. If you have ever gotten soap in your mouth, you have noticed its bitter taste. This bitter taste confirms presence of base in the soap.
(b) Feel: They are soapy and slippery to touch.
(c) Electrical conductivity: Some bases are good conductors of electricity. For example, soluble bases like sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are used as electrolytes.
(d) Corrosive action : Strong alkalis like sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are highly corrosive or caustic in nature. Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are commonly called caustic soda and caustic potash respectively. Organic tissues like skin, etc. get completely corroded by these two alkalis. However, the other alkalis are only mildly corrosive.
(e) Effect on indicator: Bases changes the colour of indicator as given in the table.
| Indicator | Change of colour | |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| Litmus | From | To |
| Methyl orange | Red | Blue |
| Phenolphthalein | Orange | Yellow |
| Turmeric | Colourless | Pink |

## CLASSIFICATION OF BASES
Bases can be classified in various ways, depending on the following factors:
## (1) Classification Based on the Strength of the Base
We have already studied that bases on dissociation produce hydroxyl ion ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>). The strength of a base depends on the concentration of the hydroxyl ion when it is dissolved in water. Based on this, bases are classified as,
(i) Strong base
A base that dissociates completely or almost completely in water is classified as a strong base. In other words, greater the tendency to loose hydroxyl ion in the solution, the stronger is the base.
Example: Sodium hydroxide : NaOH
Potassium hydroxide : KOH
Calcium hydroxide : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(ii) Weak base
A base that partially dissociates in water is classified as a weak base.
Example: Magnesium hydroxide : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Ammonium hydroxide : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
