## Strontium hydroxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a strong or weak base?
## SOLUTION
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is a strong base as it ionises almost completely in water
## (2) Classification Based on the Concentration of a Base
Concentration of a basic solution depends upon the percentage of the base dissolved in water. Based on this fact, bases are classified as,
(i) Concentrated base : A base that has a relatively high percentage of the base in its aqueous solution is classified as a concentrated base. Example concentrated sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, ammonium hydroxide etc.
(ii) Dilute base: A base that has a relatively low percentage of the base dissolved in its aqueous solution, is classified as a dilute base. Example dilute sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, ammonium hydroxide etc.
## (3) Classification Based on the Acidity of a Base
The acidity of a base is equal to the number of hydroxyl ions it has. It is also the number of hydrogen ions with which a base can combine as one hydrogen ion combines with one hydroxyl ion.
Based on the acidity bases can be classified as,
(i) Monoacidic base
It is a base that has only one hydroxyl ion. It combines with only one hydrogen ion. Hence, its acidity will be one.
Example : Sodium hydroxide, Potassium hydroxide: KOH , Lithium hydroxide: LiOH , Ammonium hydroxide: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

## Acid or a Base in a Water Solution:
The process of dissolving an acid or a base in water is a highly exothermic one. Care must be taken while mixing concentrated nitric acid or sulphuric acid with water. The acid must always be added slowly to water with constant stirring. If water is added to a concentrated acid, the heat generated may cause the mixture to splash out and cause burns. The glass container may also break due to excessive local heating. Mixing an acid or base with water results in decrease in the concentration of ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>/</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>per unit volume. Such a process is called dilution and the acid or the base is said to be diluted.

## Indicators are substances which undergoes change in colour, smell or taste with respect to the change in medium. It helps to differentiate between acidic and basic medium. Indicators are of following types depending upon its source:
- Natural indicators can be extracted from a wide variety offlowers, fruits, roots, leaves and other parts of plants, e.g. tea leaves, beet roots, rose petals of various colours, red cabbage leaves, turmeric, black berries, and delphinium flowers. Litmus (a natural dye) is one of the most common and naturally available indicator. It is extracted from lichens (combination of algae and fungus). When this litmus is added to an acidic solution, it turns red and when added to a basic solution, it turns blue. It possess a purple colour in distilled water.
- Synthetic indicators are prepared from man made chemical substances like phenolphtalein, methyl orange etc.
Phenolphthalein is a synthetic indicator. It turns acidic solutions colorless and basic solutions pink. If the concentration of indicator is particularly strong, it can appear purple.
Methyl orange is also a synthetic indicator used more oftenly because of clear colour change. In a solution becoming less acidic, methyl orange moves from red to orange and finally to yellow with the reverse occuring for a solution increasing in acidity.
Depending upon the change in properties indicators are classified as:
- Halochromic indicator show change in color with respect to the change in medium, e.g: litmus, phenolphtalein, methyl orange etc. These indicators are generally used as acid-base indicators.
- Olfactory indicator causes change in odour/smell with respect to the change in medium. e.g: clove oil, onion, vanilla extract etc.
- Gustatory indicator causes change in taste with respect to the change in medium. e.g: Sour taste of milk indicates that the milk has became acidic, hence it is spoiled.
Universal indicators : It is a mixture of indicators often sold ready made solution which can indicate pH values, usually over a range of 3-11, by successive changes of colour

Concentration of an acid solution depends upon the percentage of the acid that is dissolved in water. Based on this, acids are classified as
CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC
(i) Concentrated acid : An acid, that has a relatively high percentage of the acid dissolved in the aqueous solution is classified as a concentrated acid. Example concentrated hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, nitric acid, acetic acid etc.
(ii) Dilute acid : An acid, which has a relatively low percentage of the acid dissolved in the aqueous solution is classified as a dilute acid. Examples : dilute hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, nitric acid, acetic acid etc.
As we have studied that acid on dissociation in water produce hydrogen ion, the number of these replaceable hydrogen ions in an acid is known as the basicity of an acid. It is also evident that, one hydrogen ion or hydronium ion can react with one hydroxyl ion ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>).
(i) Monobasic acid
A monobasic acid has one replaceable hydrogen ion. Hence, these acids combine with one hydroxyl group of a base to form salt and water.
Since, monobasic acids have only one replaceable hydrogen ion, they form only one kind of salt.

Like acids, bases also dissociate in water, but in place of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>they produce hydroxyl ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. Thus, a base is a compound which on dissolving in water yields hydroxyl ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. The characteristic property of a base is due to the formation of these negative hydroxyl ions. A base may be an oxide or a hydroxide of a metal. If a base is soluble in water, it dissociates to form a metal ion and negative hydroxyl ion. Substances that combine with acids to form salt and water are also called bases.
Sodium hydroxide is a base, it gives sodium ion and hydroxyl ion when dissolved in water.

Ammonium hydroxide is also a base. In water, it dissociates to form ammonium ion and a hydroxyl ion.

Sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, calcium hydroxide and ammonium hydroxide are the common alkalis.

All alkalis are bases but not all bases are alkali. Alkali is a basic, ionic salt of an alkali or alkaline earth metal element. Alkalis are best known for being bases that dissolve in water. Whereas a base is most commonly thought of as a substance that can accept <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> ions. A soluble base is also often referred to as an alkali if hydroxide ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>are involved.
Time to Check Your Knowledge
Whether calcium oxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is alkali, base or both?
It serves as both. As we know that alkalis are bases that dissociate in water to yield hydroxyl ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. The calcium oxide dissolves in water to form calcium hydroxide which further ionises to give hydroxyl ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

(a) Taste: Bases are bitter to taste. If you have ever gotten soap in your mouth, you have noticed its bitter taste. This bitter taste confirms presence of base in the soap.
(b) Feel: They are soapy and slippery to touch.
(c) Electrical conductivity: Some bases are good conductors of electricity. For example, soluble bases like sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are used as electrolytes.
(d) Corrosive action : Strong alkalis like sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are highly corrosive or caustic in nature. Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are commonly called caustic soda and caustic potash respectively. Organic tissues like skin, etc. get completely corroded by these two alkalis. However, the other alkalis are only mildly corrosive.
(e) Effect on indicator: Bases changes the colour of indicator as given in the table.

| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| Litmus | From | To |
| Methyl orange | Red | Blue |
| Phenolphthalein | Orange | Yellow |
| Turmeric | Colourless | Pink |

These reactions are known as neutralisation reaction.

Bases can be classified in various ways, depending on the following factors:
We have already studied that bases on dissociation produce hydroxyl ion ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>). The strength of a base depends on the concentration of the hydroxyl ion when it is dissolved in water. Based on this, bases are classified as,
(i) Strong base
A base that dissociates completely or almost completely in water is classified as a strong base. In other words, greater the tendency to loose hydroxyl ion in the solution, the stronger is the base.
Example: Sodium hydroxide : NaOH
Potassium hydroxide : KOH
Calcium hydroxide : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(ii) Weak base
A base that partially dissociates in water is classified as a weak base.
Example: Magnesium hydroxide : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

Concentration of a basic solution depends upon the percentage of the base dissolved in water. Based on this fact, bases are classified as,
(i) Concentrated base : A base that has a relatively high percentage of the base in its aqueous solution is classified as a concentrated base. Example concentrated sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, ammonium hydroxide etc.
(ii) Dilute base: A base that has a relatively low percentage of the base dissolved in its aqueous solution, is classified as a dilute base. Example dilute sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, ammonium hydroxide etc.
The acidity of a base is equal to the number of hydroxyl ions it has. It is also the number of hydrogen ions with which a base can combine as one hydrogen ion combines with one hydroxyl ion.
Based on the acidity bases can be classified as,
(i) Monoacidic base
It is a base that has only one hydroxyl ion. It combines with only one hydrogen ion. Hence, its acidity will be one.

A base that has three hydroxyl ions and can combines with three hydrogen ions. Hence, its acidity will be three.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Aluminium hydroxide </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Hydrochloric acid </mtext></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Aluminium chloride </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Water </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
We know that acidity of a base is equal to number of hydroxyl ions. Thus, barium hydroxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> having two hydroxyl group is a diacidic base.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Did You Know!
The process of dissolving an acid or a base in water is a highly exothermic one. Care must be taken while mixing concentrated nitric acid or sulphuric acid with water. The acid must always be added slowly to water with constant stirring. If water is added to a concentrated acid, the heat generated may cause the mixture to splash out and cause burns. The glass container may also break due to excessive local heating. Mixing an acid or base with water results in decrease in the concentration of ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>/</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>per unit volume. Such a process is called dilution and the acid or the base is said to be diluted.
Learn More
- Natural indicators can be extracted from a wide variety offlowers, fruits, roots, leaves and other parts of plants, e.g. tea leaves, beet roots, rose petals of various colours, red cabbage leaves, turmeric, black berries, and delphinium flowers. Litmus (a natural dye) is one of the most common and naturally available indicator. It is extracted from lichens (combination of algae and fungus). When this litmus is added to an acidic solution, it turns red and when added to a basic solution, it turns blue. It possess a purple colour in distilled water.
- Synthetic indicators are prepared from man made chemical substances like phenolphtalein, methyl orange etc.
Phenolphthalein is a synthetic indicator. It turns acidic solutions colorless and basic solutions pink. If the concentration of indicator is particularly strong, it can appear purple.
Methyl orange is also a synthetic indicator used more oftenly because of clear colour change. In a solution becoming less acidic, methyl orange moves from red to orange and finally to yellow with the reverse occuring for a solution increasing in acidity.
Depending upon the change in properties indicators are classified as:
- Halochromic indicator show change in color with respect to the change in medium, e.g: litmus, phenolphtalein, methyl orange etc. These indicators are generally used as acid-base indicators.
- Olfactory indicator causes change in odour/smell with respect to the change in medium. e.g: clove oil, onion, vanilla extract etc.
- Gustatory indicator causes change in taste with respect to the change in medium. e.g: Sour taste of milk indicates that the milk has became acidic, hence it is spoiled.
Universal indicators : It is a mixture of indicators often sold ready made solution which can indicate pH values, usually over a range of 3-11, by successive changes of colour

## CHEMICAL REACTION
The process in which two or more substances reacts to form new substances, is called chemical reactions.
It involves making and breaking of bond between atoms to form new a substance, which describes the nature and specific characteristic of the reaction.
## Types of Chemical Reactions
Based on the specific characteristics and the nature of the reactions, chemical reactions have been divided into following types :
## 1. Synthesis or Combination Reaction
When two or more elements or substances combine together to form a new substance, the chemical reaction is known as synthesis or combination reaction. This type of reaction takes place in presence of heat, light or may require electricity.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
## Combination reactions can occur between following types of reactants:
(a) Combination reaction between two elements.
(a) Combination between two non-metals: When a mixture of hydrogen and chlorine is placed in sunlight, hydrogen chloride gas is formed.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Sunlight </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) Combination between a metal and a non-metal : When magnesium wire is burnt in air, magnesium oxide is formed.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) Combination reaction between two compounds.
These are the reactions in which two compounds directly combine to form a new compound.
(a) Calcium oxide directly combines with water to form calcium hydroxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) Calcium oxide directly combines with carbon dioxide gas to form calcium carbonate.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) Formation of sulphuric acid from combination of sulphur trioxide and water which is a major contributor to nasty and toxic acid rain.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(c) Combination reaction between a compound and an element.
In these reaction in which an element reacts with a compound to form a new substance.
Combination of oxygen with carbon monoxide produces carbondioxide gas.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

examples.title: ILLUSTRATION : 2
examples.problem: Write balanced equations that predict the reactions of cesium metal with (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐠</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>; and (b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐠</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
examples.solution:
The reaction of Cs with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are simple combination reactions between two elements, one metal and one nonmetal, forming the compound CsH and CsCl ,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>

examples.title: ILLUSTRATION : 3
examples.problem: Ammonium nitrate, a colorless ionic solid used as a fertilizer, explodes when it is heated above <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>300</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>. The products are three gases: molecular nitrogen, molecular oxygen, and steam (water vapour). Find the type of chemical reaction and write a balanced equation for the explosion of ammonium nitrate.
examples.solution:
The description in the problem tells us what happens to the starting material: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> breaks apart into molecules of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>. An unbalanced form of the equation can be written from this description. Then we must balance each element in turn by inspection.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
## Step 1
First, count all atoms of each element on each side of the equation to see whether the elements are balanced:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
## Step 2
As we can see that nitrogen is already balanced. To balance the hydrogen atoms, we change the stoichiometric coefficient of water from 1 to 2 :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
## Step 3
This step balances nitrogen and hydrogen, but oxygen is not yet balanced. Oxygen must be balanced without changing the 1 : 1 ratio of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ratio of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>. These ratios must be retained to keep hydrogen and nitrogen in balance. Thus the only coefficient that can be adjusted to balance the oxygen atoms is that of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Two oxygen atoms are already present as in water and thus the remaining oxygen atom can be adjusted. by changing the coefficient of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
This balances the equation, but it is unrealistic from a molecular perspective because there is no such thing as half a molecule. To get rid of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> without unbalancing the reaction, we multiply all the coefficients by 2 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>O</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Now the reaction is balanced and reasonable from a molecular perspective.
Copper nitrate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> gives positive ring test of nitrate ion ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>), but after heating small amount of copper nitrate in dry boiling tube over the burner flame, it does not give positive ring test any more because it undergoes thermal decomposition reaction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

examples.title: ILLUSTRATION : 4
examples.problem:
Identify the substance that is oxidised and the substance that is reduced in the following reactions.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
examples.solution:
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Sodium metal is oxidised as it is gaining oxygen.

examples.problem: When aluminium metal is exposed to air, a protective layer of aluminium oxide ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) forms on its surface. The layer prevents further reaction between aluminium and oxygen, and it is the reason that aluminium beverage cans do not corrode. [In the case of iron, the rust, or iron (III) oxide, is too porous to protect the iron metal underneath, so rusting continues]. Write a balanced equation for the formation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
examples.solution:
The unbalanced equation is :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
We see that both Al and O appear only once on each side of the equation but in unequal numbers. To balance the Al atoms, we place 2 in front of Al :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
There are two O atoms on the left-hand side and three O atoms on the right-hand side of the equation. This inequality of O atoms can be eliminated by writing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> in front of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> on the left-hand side of the equation.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Now multiply the entire equation by 2 to convert <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> to 3 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> i.e. </mtext><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
The above equation is the balanced equation for the formation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
Place a small silver article (made up of pure silver) in open air for few days. Then record your observation. In case if there is any sort of change, then try to find out the exact reason for this change by discussing with your friends and teacher.
## RANCIDITY
The most important cause of deterioration in fats and fatty foods is oxidation. Oxidation of fats results in the replacement of an oxygen ion from a hydrogen ion in the fatty acid molecule. This substitution destabilizes the molecule and makes it possible for other odd chemical fragments to find a place along the chain. An unpleasant change in the flavor and odour of a food is develop, called rancidity. Unsaturated fats are more susceptible to oxidation than the saturated fats.
Factors which accelerate fat oxidation include trace metals (iron, zinc, etc.), salt, light, water, bacteria, and molds. Fat oxidation can be retarded by use of antioxidants (Antioxidants are compounds that inhibit chemical reactions with oxygen such as BHT, BHA, vitamin E, and vitamin C), by use of spices such as sage and rosemary, and by use of light and/or air tight wrapping.
Some high fat foods such as potato chips are packed in materials that protect them from light and oxygen and the containers are flooded with nitrogen to further exclude oxygen. The nitrogen also serves as a cushion to minimize breakage of the chips during transport.
## Learn
## More
Oxidation reactions may involve highly reactive molecules called free radicals. Free radicals are molecules that have lost an electron and try to gain it by reacting with other molecules. This causes the substance to break down. Metals often catalyze reactions with oxygen. Another example would be the half eaten apple. The skinless area quickly oxidized causing the apple to turn brown. Antioxidants inhibit these changes by reacting with the free radicals before they can react with oxygen (free radical scavenging) or by reacting with the metals. Naturally occurring antioxidants may also work by interacting directly with oxygen.
Naturally occurring antioxidants include retinol (vitamin A) and tocopherols (vitamin E), found in many animals and plants; ascorbic acid (vitamin C), found in citrus and other fruits and vegetables; and beta carotene, found in deep orange and dark green vegetables. These may play a significant role in the prevention of cancer, heart disease, immune-deficiency diseases, and aging.
Synthetic antioxidants include butylated hydroxy toluene (BHT), butylated hydroxy anisole (BHA), and propyl gallate. Natural and synthetic antioxidants are added to food to prevent undesirable deterioration. Foods preserved with antioxidants include vegetable oils, bread, and cheese.
Antioxidants are frequently applied to the packaging materials of cereals and nuts.

examples.solution:
It serves as both. As we know that alkalis are bases that dissociate in water to yield hydroxyl ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. The calcium oxide dissolves in water to form calcium hydroxide which further ionises to give hydroxyl ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

examples.solution:
We know that acidity of a base is equal to number of hydroxyl ions. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Very Short Answer Questions — Q2
examples.problem: Can a combination reaction be redox reaction?
examples.solution: Yes, a combination reaction can be a redox reaction.

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Very Short Answer Questions — Q3
examples.problem: What are the different types of reactions ?
examples.solution:
Different types of reaction are-
(i) Combination reactions
(ii) Decomposition reactions
(iii) Displacement reactions
(iv) Double decomposition reactions
(v) Redox reaction

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Very Short Answer Questions — Q4
examples.problem: What is a decomposition reaction ? Give example.
examples.solution:
The conversion of a single compound into two or more simpler substances is called as decomposition reaction. For example,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> mercury(II) </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> oxide </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> mercury </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> oxygen </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Very Short Answer Questions — Q5
examples.problem: Define displacement reaction.
examples.solution:
A reaction in which an atom or group of atoms present in a molecule is displaced by another atom is known as displacement reaction. For example,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Very Short Answer Questions — Q6
examples.problem: What happens when sodium reacts with water ?
examples.solution:
Sodium being more reactive than hydrogen, displaces hydrogen from water.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

examples.problem: Write the chemical equation and name the reaction when a solution of sodium chloride is mixed with a solution of silver nitrate and a white precipitate of silver chloride is formed.
examples.solution:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>↓</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (aq)

examples.problem: To balance a chemical equation, can we change the formulae of either reactants or products ?

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Short Answer Questions — Q1
examples.problem: In the refining of silver, the recovery of silver from silver nitrate solution involved displacement by copper metal. Write down the reaction involved.
examples.solution:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
The displacement reaction occurs because copper is more reactive than silver. Shining white deposit of silver is formed on the copper metal and the solution becomes blue due to the formation of copper nitrate.

(d) Potassium metal reacts with water to give potassium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Short Answer Questions — Q3
examples.problem: What is rancidity ?
examples.solution: When food material left for longer time, the fat and oil present in them undergoes oxidation process that results in change of taste and smell of the food and make it unfit for consumption. The process of such oxidation of fat and oil is known as rancidity.

examples.problem: A large piece of zinc metal is placed in a copper (II) sulfate, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, solution. The blue solution become colourless as copper metal falls to the bottom of the container. The resulting solution contains zinc sulfate, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Write balanced chemical equation for the reaction.
examples.solution:

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Short Answer Questions — Q10
examples.problem: Show that oxidation and reduction reactions go side by side by taking a suitable example.
examples.solution:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
If a substance gains oxygen during a reaction it is said to be oxidised and if a substance loses oxygen it is said to be reduced. In the above reaction carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide, while zinc oxide is reduced to zinc. Thus, oxidation and reduction reactions are going side by side in the above reaction.

(b) Reduction

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Short Answer Questions — Q12
examples.problem: Can oxidation or reduction take place alone? Why or why not? What are such reactions called?
examples.solution: Oxidation or reduction cannot take place alone. This is because if one substance loses oxygen, i.e., undergoes reduction, there must be another substance to take up this oxygen, i.e., undergo oxidation. Similarly, if one substance loses hydrogen, i.e., undergoes oxidation, there must be another substance to take up this hydrogen, i.e., undergo reduction. Hence, oxidation and reduction always take place together. That is why, these reactions are called redox reactions.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(A)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(B)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi></mrow></math> No reaction
(C)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(D)
Color change occurs in test tube A, B and D, no color change will be observed in test tube ( C ) becuase there is no reaction.
Al is most reactive because it displace copper and iron from their sulphate salts.

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Short Answer Questions — Q17
examples.problem:
Identify the type of reactions taking place in each of the following cases and write the balanced chemical equation for the reactions.
(a) Zinc reacts with silver nitrate to produce zinc nitrate and silver.
(b) Potassium iodide reacts with lead nitrate to produce potassium nitrate and lead iodide.
examples.solution:
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>→</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
As zinc is more reactive than silver, therefore it displaces silver from its nitrate solution.
It is a displacement reaction.
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(yellow)
A yellow precipitate of lead iodide is formed. It is a precipitation reaction.

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Short Answer Questions — Q18
examples.problem: 2 g of silver chloride is taken in a china dish and the china dish is placed in sunlight for sometime. What will be your observation in this case? Write the chemical reaction involved in the form of a balanced chemical equation. Identify the type of chemical reaction.
examples.solution:
When 2 g of AgCl taken in a china dish and placed in sunlight then it turns to black/grey metallic colured silver along with the liberation of chlorine gas.
The balanced chemical reaction will be-
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
This is a decomposition reaction. As the decomposition reaction is carried out by sunlight so it is called photolytic decomposition reaction.

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Short Answer Questions — Q19
examples.problem:
Mention with reason the colour changes observed when :
(i) silver chloride is exposed to sunlight.
(ii) copper powder is strongly heated in the presence of oxygen.
(iii) a piece of zinc is dropped in copper sulphate solution.
examples.solution:
(i) Photo decomposition of silver chloride takes place which results in formation of silver and colour changing to grey.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(ii) Copper undergoes oxidation and black coloured copper oxide is formed.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(iii) Zinc displaces copper from its solution and colour of the solution changes from blue to colourless.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mtext> (aq.) </mtext><mo>→</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mtext> (aq.) </mtext></mrow></math>

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Long Answer Questions — Q1
examples.problem: What are different types of combination reactions ?
examples.solution:
There are three different types of combination reactions:
(a) Combination of an element with another element to form a compound.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(b) Combination of two or more compounds to form a new compound.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(c) The combination of an element and a compound to form a new compound.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Long Answer Questions — Q2
examples.problem: A solution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is mixed with a solution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Predict what happens.
examples.solution:
The four ions involved are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. The combinations of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> produce the compounds NaCl and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. If both of these compounds are soluble, no reaction occurs. In this case, however, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is insoluble. Thus a reaction occurs which we can illustrate with a balanced chemical equation.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
The equation written in total ionic form is
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
The net ionic equation will be
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

examples.title: Assertion \& Reason — Long Answer Questions — Q3
examples.problem:
Balance the following equations
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
