theory_sections.topics: Arrhenius Concept of Acids and Bases
theory_sections.markdown:
## Arrhenius Concept of Acids and Bases
Svante Arrhenius in 1887, stated that acid ionizes in aqueous solution to produce hydrogen ions (which are protons), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, and anions; and a base ionizes in aqueous solution to produce hydroxide ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>and cations. Later studies of aqueous solutions provided evidence of a small, positively charged hydrogen ion combining with a water molecule to form a hydrated proton, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, which is called the hydronium ion.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Often, the hydronium ion or hydrated proton is represented as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Hydrogen chloride <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, a gas, is an acid because it dissolves in water to yield hydrogen ions and chloride ions. This aqueous solution of HCl is referred to as hydrochloric acid.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## Problems with Arrhenius theory :
(i) The solvent has no role to play in Arrhenius theory. An acid is expected to be an acid in any solvent. This was found not to be the case. For example, HCl is an acid in water, behaving in the manner Arrhenius expected. However, if HCl is dissolved in benzene, there is no dissociation, the HCl remaining as undissociated molecules. The nature of the solvent plays a critical role in acid-base properties of substances.
(ii) All salts in Arrhenius theory should produce solutions that are neither acidic nor basic. This is not the case. If equal amounts of HCl and ammonia react, the solution is slightly acidic. If equal amounts of acetic acid and sodium hydroxide are reacted, the resulting solution is basic. Arrhenius had no explanation for this.
(iii) The need for hydroxide as the base led Arrhenius to propose the formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> as the formula for ammonia in water. This led to the misconception that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> is the actual base, not <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
The Arrhenius theory of acids and bases will be fully supplanted by the theory proposed independently by Johnnies Bronsted and Thomas Lowry in 1923.

theory_sections.topics: Bronsted Lowry Theory of Acids and Bases
theory_sections.markdown:
## Bronsted Lowry Theory of Acids and Bases
By the definition of Thomas Lowry and J.N. Bronsted working independently in 1923, "an acid is a material that donates a proton and a base is a material that can accept a proton".
Consider the example of ionization of hydrochloric acid in water. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> acts as an acid by donating a proton to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> molecule which acts as a base.
Here, HCl act as an acid, because it has a proton available to be transferred.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> act as a base, since it gets the proton that the acid lost.
Now, here comes an interesting data on considering the reverse reaction
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>- is an acid, because it can give a proton.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>- is a base, since it has the capacity to receive a proton.
Notice that each pair, HCl and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>as well as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, differ by one proton ( symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>). These pairs are called conjugate pairs.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>⇌</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>
The acids are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>and the bases are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>.
Each conjugate pair has a proton donor and a proton acceptor. Acids are paired with bases. Each acid has, a proton available (an ionizable hydrogen) and conjugate base part. The acid ionizes releasing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion, whereas rest part of the original acid forms the conjugate base.
Nitric acid, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, dissociates (splits) into a hydrogen ion and a nitrate ion. The hydrogen almost immediately joins to a water molecule to make a hydronium ion. The nitrate ion is the conjugate base of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ion. In the second part of the reaction, water is a base (because it can accept a proton) and the hydronium ion is its conjugate acid.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Acid </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Base </mtext></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mrow><mtext> Conjugate base Conjugate acid </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mtext> </mtext></mrow></math>

## Problems with the theory
This theory works very nicely in all protic solvents (water, ammonia, acetic acid, etc.), but fails to explain acid base behavior in aprotic solvents such as benzene and dioxane. It also cannot explain reaction between acidic oxides ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) and basic oxides ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math> etc).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

theory_sections.topics: Lewis Theory of Acids and Bases
theory_sections.markdown:
## Lewis Theory of Acids and Bases
In 1923, G.N. Lewis introduced another theory of acids and bases which could successfully explain the cases where there is no role for protons.
The G.N. Lewis idea of acids and bases is broader than the Bronsted Lowry model. According to Lewis, acids are electron pair acceptors and bases are electron pair donors.

## Postulates :
(i) An acid is a substance which can act as an electron pair acceptor. The molecule or ion should be associated with shortage of electrons to act as an acid.
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>etc.
(ii) A base is a substance which can act as an electron pair donor. The molecule or ion should be associated with one or more lone pairs of electrons to act as a base.
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>etc.
(iii) Acid base neutralization can be defined as the transfer of an electron pair from a base to an acid.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>:</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>←</mo><mi>:</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

## Merits :
(i) This theory could explain even the acidic nature of those substances which do not contain hydrogen.
(ii) It could explain the neutralization reactions which do not involve any transfer of proton.

## Limitations:
(i) This theory failed to explain the acidic and basic nature of general acids and bases.
(ii) This theory could not explain the general neutralization reactions involving the formation of salt and water.
(iii) Generally, the acid-base reactions are fast reactions. But the formation of a coordinate bond is a slow process.
(iv) This theory cannot explain the relative strength of acids and bases.
## Learn

## More
- Substance which are capable of donating as well accepting proton are amphoteric substance. For example <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mi>𝐎</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>etc.
- Remember that an acid-base reaction is a competition between two bases for a proton. If the stronger of the two acids and the stronger of the two bases are reactants (appear on the left side of the equation), the reaction is said to proceed to a large extent.
- Amphiprotic solvents : These solvents influence the acid-base characteristics of solute i.e., they possess the tendency to accept proton (protophilic solvents e.g., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mi>𝐎</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, liq. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">N</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow></math> etc.) or they posses the tendency to give protons (protogenic solvents e.g., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mi>𝐎</mi></mrow></math>, liq. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> etc.)
- Aprotic solvents : Solvents which do not influence the acid-base characteristic of solute are called aprotic solvents. In such systems acid-base equilibrium is established only by the introduction of second acid or base. In other words aprotic solvents are those which neither donate nor accept the proton e.g., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, liquid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, etc.
- The species: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> can act both as Bronsted acids and bases. For each case give the corresponding conjugate acid and conjugate base.

## THE PH SCALE
So far, we have explained the strength of an acid or base in terms of ion concentrations. We have used qualitative terms like "concentrated", "dilute", "strong", and "weak". To improve accuracy we prefer to use quantitative terms. Instead of descriptive terms which could be misinterpreted, we use a number scale called the pH scale.
The term p in pH stands for "potenz" in German; meaning power and is the amount of hydrogen ions in a particular solution. The more ions, the more acidic, the solution is the fewer ions, the more alkaline (basic) the solution is.
The pH scale is used to rank solutions in terms of acidity or basicity (alkalinity). Since the scale is based on pH values, as the value of pH increases, concentration of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions decreases. The pH scale is often said to range from 0 to 14 . Anything below 7.0 is acidic, and has higher concentration of hydrogen ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>in the solution; whereas anything above 7.0 is alkaline, or basic and has higher concentration of hydroxide ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. The pH of a neutral solution is 7 .

theory_sections.topics: Approximate pH Values of Some Common Substances
theory_sections.markdown:
## Approximate pH Values of Some Common Substances
| Substance | pH value | Substance | pH value |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Hydrochloric acid | 1.0 | Bread | 5.5 |
| Sulphuric acid | 1.2 | Potatoes | 5.8 |
| Gastric juice | 2.0 | Rain water | 6.2 |
| Lemon | 2.3 | Milk | 6.6 |
| Vinegar (Acetic acid) | 2.8 | Pure water | 7.0 |
| Soft drink | 3.0 | Egg | 7.8 |
| Apple | 3.1 | Sea water | 8.5 |
| Grape | 3.1 | Ammonium hydroxide | 11.1 |
| Tomato | 4.2 | Sodium hydroxide | 13.0 |
| Banana | 4.6 | | |
| Battery acid, 1M sulphuric acid | 0 | Stomach acid, 0.1 M hydrochloric acid | 1 |
| Milk of magnesia, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | 8 | Washing soda, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | 9 |
| Milk of magnesia, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | 10 | Aqueous household ammonia, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | 11 |
| Lime water, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | 12 | Drano, 0.1 M NaOH | 13 |
| Drano, 1.0 M NaOH | 14 | | |
## CONNECTING TOPIC

## CALCULATION OF pH VALUE
Sorenson defined pH as the negative logarithm (to the base 10) of the hydrogen ion concentration expressed in moles per litre,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>is the hydrogen ion concentration in moles/litre.
Remember that sometimes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>is written, so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>means the same thing. The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 . For acids, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>; for bases, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>; for neutral substances, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>.
The negative logarithm is used because most of the pH values are positive numbers.
A change of one pH unit represents a ten-fold change in the concentration of hydronium and hydroxide ions. Thus, pH equal to 2 is ten times as acidic as pH equal to 3 , one hundred times as acidic as pH equal to 4 , one thousand times as acidic as pH equal to 5 , and so on. Similarly, pH equal to 13 is ten times as basic as pH equal to 12 and so on.
Example: The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>in a solution is measured to be 0.010 M . What is the pH ?
The solution is pretty straightforward. Plug the [ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>] value into the pH definition:
An alternate way to write this is:

## THE pOH VALUE
Sorenson defined pH as the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
So, the pOH can be defined in a similar way: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
In words, the pOH is the negative logarithm of the hydroxide ion concentration.
So let's try a simple problem: The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>in a solution is measured to be 0.0010 M . What is the pOH ?
The solution is pretty straightforward. Plug the [ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>] into the pOH definition:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><mn>0.0010</mn></mrow></math>
An alternate way to write this is: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Since the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>log</mi></mrow></math> of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is -3 , we have: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
pOH equal to 3 represents that solution is basic.

CASE - IV : Acids and bases reacts to form an adduct. Why?
According to Lewis concept, acids are electron pair acceptor and bases are electron pair donor.

## IONIC PRODUCT OF WATER（ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>𝐊</mi><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ）
Ionic product of water <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ，is the product of concentration of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion．
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
The value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is temperature dependent since it is an equilibrium constant．
Water is able to act both as acid and base．Water molecules in pure water can exist in both acidic and basic form which are equal in number and thus making it neutral．One <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> molecule donates proton and act as an acid and another <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> molecule accepts a proton and act as a base at the same time．This process can be better understood by the following reaction，
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Acid </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Base </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>⇌</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Conjugate </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> Acid </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Conjugate </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> Base </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
Since pure water is neutral， pH of water <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mo>∵</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math>）
We know that，concentration of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion is equal，in pure water．
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Taking negative log equation（i），
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
Putting the values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>from equation（ii）
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow></math>
Equation（iii）can also be written as，
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" /><mtd columnalign="center"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>∴</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math>

theory_sections.topics: IMPORTANCE OF PH IN EVERYDAY LIFE
theory_sections.markdown: ## IMPORTANCE OF PH IN EVERYDAY LIFE

## Blood pH
In order to function properly, the human body needs to maintain a blood pH between 7.35 and 7.45. Large deviation from this range is extremely dangerous. Values greater than 7.8 or less than 6.8 often results in death. Any condition in which the blood pH drops below 7.35 is known as acidosis. If the pH rises above 7.45 , it is known as alkalosis.

## Acid Rain
When pH of rain water is less than 5.6, it is called acid rain. When acid rain flows into the rivers, it lowers the pH of the river water. The survival of aquatic life in such rivers becomes difficult.

## pH of the Soil
Plants require a specific pH range for their healthy growth. The effect of soil pH has a significant role in the solubility of minerals or nutrients. Before a nutrient can be used by plants it must be dissolved in the soil solution. Most minerals and nutrients are more soluble or available in acidic soils than in neutral or slightly alkaline soils. Phosphorus is not readily soluble in the soil but is most available in soil with a pH range around 6.5. Strongly acidic soils ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mn>4.0</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5.0</mn></mrow></math> ) can have high concentrations of soluble aluminum, iron and manganese which may be toxic to the growth of some plants.
The soil pH can also influence plant growth by its effect on activity of beneficial microorganisms. Bacteria that decompose soil organic matter are as not found in strong acid soils. This prevents organic matter from breaking down, resulting in an accumulation of organic matter and the tie up of nutrients, particularly nitrogen, that are held in the organic matter.

## pH in Our Digestive System
It is very interesting to note that our stomach produces hydrochloric acid which helps in the digestion of food without harming the stomach. During indigestion the stomach produces too much acid which causes pain and irritation. To get rid of this pain, people uses bases called antacids. These antacids neutralise the excess acid.
Magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia), a mild base, is often used for this purpose.

theory_sections.topics: pH Change as the Cause of Tooth Decay
theory_sections.markdown:
## pH Change as the Cause of Tooth Decay
Tooth decay starts when the pH of the mouth is lower than 5.5. Tooth enamel, made up of calcium phosphate is the hardest substance in the body. Bacteria present in the mouth produces acids by degradation of sugar and food particles remaining in the mouth after eating. The best way to prevent this is to clean the mouth after eating food. Using toothpastes, which are generally basic, for cleaning the teeth can neutralise the excess acid and prevent tooth decay.

theory_sections.topics: Self Defence by Animals and Plants Through Chemical Warfare
theory_sections.markdown:
## Self Defence by Animals and Plants Through Chemical Warfare
When a honey bee or ant stings, they injects acid which causes pain and irrigation. In the similar way, stinging hair of nettle leaves cause pain when touched due to secretion of methanoic acid. Some naturally occuring acids are:
| Natural Source | Acid | Natural source | Acid |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Vinegar | Acetic acid | Sour milk (Curd) | Lactic acid |
| Orange | Citric acid | Lemon | Citric acid |
| Tamarid | Tartaric acid | Ant sting | Methanoic acid |
| Tomato | Oxalic acid | Nettle sting | Methanoic acid |

## SALT
Compounds formed by the neutralization reaction between an acid and a base are known as a salts.

## Acid + Base → Salt + Water
Salts are ionic compounds which dissociate to yield a positively charged ion other than hydrogen [ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>] and negatively charged ion other than hydroxide ion [ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>]. During salt formation, positive ion comes from base and negative ion comes from acid.

## Example:
The most familiar salt is sodium chloride, the principal component of common table salt. Sodium chloride, NaCl , and water, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>, are formed by neutralization of sodium hydroxide, NaOH (a base), with hydrogen chloride, HCl (an acid):
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
In sodium chloride <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, formation of positively charged ion, (sodium <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>) occurs from sodium hydroxide and negatively charged ion, chloride ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>) occurs from hydrochloric acid.
Note: Although best known salt is sodium chloride which is commonly known as common salt. It is important to know that salt is a general name and it does not refer only to sodium chloride. In fact sodium chloride is just one member of a huge family of salts. Some other examples of salts are magnesium sulphate, potassium nitrate, calcium carbonate etc.

## Family of Salts
The salts having same positive ions or same negative ions are said to belong to a family of salts. For example calcium chloride and calcium sulphate belong to same family of salts 'calcium salts' because they both contain the same positive ion, calcium ion. Similarly calcium chloride and sodium chloride belong to same family of salts 'chloride salts' as both contain the same negative ion, chloride ion.
A salt is a compound consisting of positive metallic ion and negative ion derived from an acid, if negative ions are capable of further ionization to yield <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>the salt is an acid salt, but if not, the salt is a normal salt.
## CONNECTING TOPIC
## CLASSIFICATION OF SALTS

## (i) Acidic Salts
Salt which produces acidic solution when added to water is acidic salt. The pH of the acidic salt solution is less than 7 . If a polybasic acid (Example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> etc.) is neutralised partly by a base, the salt formed is acidic. In other words such salts are produced by the replacement of only a part of acidic hydrogen of the polybasic acids by a metal. Thus the anions of these salts retain one or more hydrogen atom of the parent acid. Acid salt exhibits all the properties of an acid in solution.

## Acidic Salts :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> Sodium bisulphite </mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>;</mi><mspace width="1em" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> Potassium bisulphite </mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> Sodium bisulphate </mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>;</mi><mspace width="1em" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> Potassium bisulphate </mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>

## (ii) Normal Salts
When acid and base neutralise each other completely, the salt formed is a normal salt. The pH of the salt solution of normal salt is 7 . Normal salts are produced by the replacement of all replaceable hydrogen(s) present in the molecule of an acid by metal or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mrow /><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>group. Thus such salts contain neither replaceable hydrogen nor hydroxyl group in the formula.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> (Carbonic acid) </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Sodium Carbonate </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> (normal salt) </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
Aqueous solution of normal salts may be neutral, acid or alkaline depending upon the nature of the constituent acid and base.
Normal Salts :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mtext> (Potassium nitrate), </mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mtext> (Sodium sulphite) </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mtext> (Potassium chloride), </mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mtext> (Sodium sulphate) </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math>

## (iii) Basic Salts
Salts which produces basic solution when added to water is basic salt. The pH of the basic salt solution is more than 7.
This type of salts are formed by incomplete neutralization of a base with an acid or by partial replacement of hydroxy radicals of a diacids or triacidic base with an acid radical.
This type of salts contain a metallic cation, a hydroxy ion of a base and anion of an acid.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Basic salts: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
## Other types of Salt

## (1) Double Salts
Such salts are formed by mixing saturated solutions of two simple salts, followed by crystallisation of the saturated solution.

## Example :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> : Mohr's salt, it a is mixture of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (simple salt) and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (simple salt)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>24</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> : Potash alum, it is a mixture of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (simple salt) and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (simple salt).
Alum is used for purification of water.

## (2) Mixed Salts
Such a salt contains two or more acidic radicals or basic radicals other than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
They consists of a fixed proportion of two salts, often sharing either a common cation or common anion.
Examples : Sodium potassium sulphate, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (two basic radicals, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>)
Bleaching powder - <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (two acid radicals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>)

## (3) Complex Salts
Like double salts, complex salts are formed by mixing saturated solutions of two simple salts, followed by crystallisation of the solution.
These salts give a simple and a complex ion on dissociation.
Examples : Potassium mercuric iodide - <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>

## Learn More
(1) Deliquescent Salts :- These are water soluble salts which on exposure to the atmosphere, absorbs moisture from it and dissolves in it, and change into liquid state for example :- <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> etc.
(2) Efflorescent Salts :- These are crystalline hydrated salts which on exposure to the atmosphere lose their water of crystallization either partly or completely and change into a powder.

## Solubility of Salts
Some general observations about solubility of salts are listed below.
(i) All sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble in water.
(ii) All nitrites, nitrates and bicarbonates are soluble in water.
(iii) Sulphates (except those of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ) are soluble in water.
(iv) All metallic oxides and sulphides are insoluble in water.
(v) Chlorides (except those of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>) are soluble in water.
(vi) All metallic carbonates and phosphates are insoluble in water.
- Oxides and sulphides of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>are soluble in water.
- <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is soluble in hot water.
- Carbonates, hydroxides and phosphates of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>are soluble in water.

## Water of Crystallization
Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules present in the formula unit of a salt.
On the basis of water of crystallisation salts are classified as hydrated salts. Hydrated salts are those salts which contain a definite number of water molecules as water of crystallisation. Example
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>5</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> - Copper sulphate penta-hydrate. It is also called blue vitriol.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> - Calcium chloride hexa-hydrate. It has 6 molecules of water of crystallisation.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>10</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> - Sodium carbonate deca-hydrate. It is also called washing soda. It has 10 molecules of water of crystallisation.

## Hygroscopic Substances
These are substances which on exposure to atmosphere absorb moisture but do not change their original state after absorption.
For example :
CaO (quick lime), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (sulphuric acid), Silica gel.
## pH OF SALT SOLUTIONS

## Hydrolysis of Salts
It is commonly observed that different salts, on dissolution in water do not always form neutral solutions. For example, aqueous solution of copper sulphate is acidic whereas aqueous solution sodium acetate is basic in character. However, salts of strong acids and strong bases such as sodium chloride, potassium chloride etc. form neutral aqueous solution. Salt hydrolysis is the interaction of anion or cation of the salt with water molecules to produce an acidic, basic or neutral solution.
The pH of the solution gets affected by this interaction. The cations of strong bases (such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, etc.) do not hydrolyze and therefore, the solutions of salts formed by strong acids and strong bases are neutral and their pH is 7 . On the other hand, the solutions of the salts formed by strong acids and weak bases are acidic i.e., their pH is less than 7 . While the solutions of strong bases and weak acids are basic and their pH is greater than 7 .
Since salt on dissolution in water undergoes dissociation to form ions, salt hydrolysis is reverse of neutralization.
(a) Hydrolysis of salts of weak acid and strong base e.g. sodium acetate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, sodium carbonate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, sodium phosphate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> etc. give aqueous solution in alkaline range because on hydrolysis they form weak acid (not completely) ionisable) and strong base which is approximately completely ionised. Thus in this case, base overpowers the effect of weak acid and resulting solution is basic in nature. For example
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>⇌</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Weak acid </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Strong base </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
(b) Hydrolysis of salts of weak bases and strong acids e.g. ammonium chloride <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, copper sulphate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, aluminium chloride <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> etc. give aqueous solution in acidic range because on hydrolysis they form weak base (not completely ionisable) and strong acid (get completely ionised). Thus in this case acid over powers the effect of weak base and resulting solution is acidic in nature.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>⇌</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Weak base </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Strong acid </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
(c) Salts of weak acid and a weak base e.g. ammonium acetate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math>, ammonium carbonate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, aluminium phosphate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> etc on hydrolysis give almost neutral, solution.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>⇌</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Weak acid </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Weak base </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
(d) Salts of strong acid and strong base e.g. sodium chloride ( NaCl ), potassium nitrate ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ), sodium sulphate ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ). potassium chlorate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> etc. Such salts on hydrolysis produce equally strong acids and bases. Thus their solutions are neutral.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>⇌</mo><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Strong base </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Strong acid </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
