<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
## Properties of sodium bicarbonate
(a) It is a white powder with crystalline grains.
(b) It is weakly alkaline in nature.
(c) It neutralizes acids and breaks down proteins
Do not add baking soda to vegetables because it will cause them to lose nutrients. Baking soda is also known as Saleratus.
Use of sodium hydrogen carbonate
(a) It is used as a component of baking powder.
(b) It is used as a tenderizer in baking (in combination with an acid it releases <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ).
(c) It is used as a deodorizer because of its neutralizing action.
(d) It is used in laundry work for enhancing the detergents effectiveness because it stabilizes the pH level (acts as a buffer)
(e) It is added to swimming pool water to balance the pH and keep the water clear.
(f) In combination with an acid, baking soda undergoes a chemical reaction that releases bubbles of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Trapped in butter these <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> bubbles enable the baked food to rise. Baked foods treated with baking soda, therefore, generally have a light crumb and are areated with many holes left by escaping bubbles of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(g) It is used in fire extinguishers as baking soda undergoes a chemical reaction that gives off <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> which helps in extinguishing fire.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>↑</mo></mrow></math>
(h) It is used as abrasive cleaner. Baking soda's finely gritty texture makes it an excellent gentle abrasive cleaner. It is inexpensive, environment friendly, fragrance-free and safe for nearly all surfaces making it ideal for house-hold use.
(i) As a mild abrasive agent, baking soda can also be used in place of tooth-paste.
(j) When sprinkled around the exterior entrances and to foundations of homes, it may prohibit ants and other insects from crawling in, as it is irritating to their chitinous exoskeletons and they avoid it.

Baking soda is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> while washing soda is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. ## Properties
Gypsum when heated to 390 K loses water to give <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>. This is known as plaster of paris. When heated above 437 K , it becomes anhydrous <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. ## Plaster of Paris <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
## Method of preparation :
It is prepared by heating gypsum ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> ) to 373 K .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mn>373</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
The temperature should not be allowed to rise beyond 373 K as above this temperature whole of water of crystallization is lost.
## Properties
It is a white powder. When water is added to plaster of paris it evolves heat and quickly sets to a hard porous mass in about half an hour. The setting of plaster of Paris is accompanied by a slight expansion (about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> ) in volume so that it fills the mould completely and takes a sharp impression. The process of setting occurs as follows:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Plaster of paris </mtext></mrow></munder><munderover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> setting </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></munderover><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Gyssum </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> orthorhombic </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> dihydrate </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder><munderover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> hardening </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></munderover></mrow></math>
The first step is called the setting stage, and the second, the hardening stage. The setting of plaster of Paris is catalyzed by sodium chloride, while it is reduced by borax, or alum.
Uses
(a) It is used for producing moulds for industries like pottery, ceramics, etc.
(b) It is used for setting broken and fractured bones in the body.
(c) It is used for making statues, models and other decorative material.
(d) It is mixed with cement and so used in the building industry.

## Bleaching Powder, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
## Method of preparation :
If chlorine is passed for a considerable time over solid slaked lime, the product formed is bleaching powder. It is also known as chloride of lime. Bleaching powder, a solid combination of chlorine and slaked lime, introduced in 1799 by the Scottish chemist,
Charles Tennant. Bleaching powder is represented as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, though the actual composition is quite complex.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
In the laboratory bleaching powder is prepared by taking a gas jar full of chlorine and shaking a spatula measure of freshly prepared slaked lime into it. The colour of the chlorine disappears immediately. The product may be used to absorb chlorine from several more gas-jars before absorption is complete.
[Note : bleaching powder is actually a mixture of calcium hypochlorite <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, calcium chloride <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> with some slaked lime]
There are two types of calcium hypochlorite. These are (i) Dry form and (ii) Hydrated form
The hydrated form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is safer to handle. It was used as an transport substitute for free chlorine.
## Properties of bleaching powder
(a) It is a yellow white solid having a strong smell of chlorine.
(b) It is soluble in water. The lime present is always left behind as an insoluble salt.
(c) It has greater available chlorine than sodium hypochlorite, NaClO (liquid bleach). It contains about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>36</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> of available chlorine.
[Note : Available chlorine is that which can be removed by dilute acids and even by carbonic acid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> of the atmosphere.]
(d) Bleaching powder deteriorates if left in contact with the air and smells like chlorine because of action of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> of atmosphere i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> reacts with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and release <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and with HCl to form calcium chloride.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></math>
Extreme care should be used in handling bleaching powder. It should always be kept in dry place, away from any organic material. Bleaching powder undergoes self-heating and rapid decomposition accompanied by release of toxic chlorine gas.
## Uses:
(a) It is widely used as a bleaching agent for bleaching clothes.
(b) It is used for disinfection of drinking water or swimming pool water. For use in outdoor swimming pools, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> can be used as a sanitizer in combination with cyanuric acid stabilizers. Two stabilizers will reduce the loss of chlorine because of u.v. radiation.
(c) It is also used for bleaching cotton and linen.
(d) It is used in manufacture of chloroform <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
(e) It is used as an oxidising agent.
(f) It is also used in bathroom cleaners, household disinfectant sprays, mass and algae removers, and weed killers.

textbook_exercises.solution:
In the manufacture of sodium hydroxide, hydrogen gas and chlorine gas ( X ) are formed as by-products. When chlorine gas ( X ) reacts with dry slaked lime, it forms calcium oxychloride (bleaching powder) Y. The reactions are
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (Chlorine gas)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

textbook_exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Exemplar Questions — Q4
textbook_exercises.problem: A metal carbonate X on reacting with an acid gives a gas which when passed through a solution Y gives the carbonate back. On the other hand, a gas G that is obtained at anode during electrolysis of brine is passed on dry Y , it gives a compound Z , used for disinfecting drinking water. Identity <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> and Z .
textbook_exercises.solution:
The gas evolved at anode during electrolysis of brine is chlorine ( G ). When chlorine gas is passed through dry <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> produces bleaching powder (Z), used for disinfecting drinking water.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Slaked lime (Y) </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Bleaching powder (Z) </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
Since Y and Z are calcium salts, therefore X is also a calcium salt and it is calcium carbonate.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

exercises.solution:

In this reaction salt and water are formed. It is an acidbase neutralisation reaction.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Very Short Answer Questions — Q10
exercises.problem: What do you mean by the family of salts?
exercises.solution: Salts, having the same positive or negative radicals, are said to belong to the same family.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Very Short Answer Questions — Q11
exercises.problem: Name the products formed from the chlor-alkali process.
exercises.solution: These products are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Very Short Answer Questions — Q12
exercises.problem: Name the gas evolved when dilute sulphuric acid acts on sodium carbonate.
exercises.solution: Carbon dioxide.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Very Short Answer Questions — Q13
exercises.problem: Write the name and the chemical formula of the organic acid present in vinegar.
exercises.solution: Acetic acid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> is present in vinegar.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Very Short Answer Questions — Q14
exercises.problem: What is efflorescence ? Give an example.
exercises.solution:
It is a property due to which a crystalline substance loses water of crystallization when exposed to air and becomes amorphous e.g.,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>10</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> air </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Very Short Answer Questions — Q15
exercises.problem: What are alkalies ? Give example of an alkali.
exercises.solution: Soluble bases in water are called alkalies e.g. NaOH , KOH are alkalies.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Very Short Answer Questions — Q16
exercises.problem: Is water a strong acid or a weak acid ?
exercises.solution: Water is a weak acid as it is ionised to a small extent and produces only a small number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q1
exercises.problem:
What is meant by strong acids and weak acids ? Classify the following into strong acids and weak acids :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
exercises.solution:
An acid which is completely ionised in water and produces a large amount of hydrogen ions are called strong acids.
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. An acid which is feebly ionised or remains almost unionised in aqueous solution is called weak acid. Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q2
exercises.problem: What is water of crystallisation ? Give some examples of salts having water of crystallisation?
exercises.solution:
Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules present in one formula unit of a salt.
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>5</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>. Five water molecules are present in one formula unit of copper sulphate.
Some other salts with water of crystallisation are :
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>10</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> | Sodium carbonate decahydrate |
| :--- | :--- |
| | (Washing soda) |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> | Calcium sulphate dihydrate (Gypsum) |

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q3
exercises.problem:
Classify each of the following substances as a weak acid, strong acid, weak base, strong base.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(c) NaOH
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
exercises.solution:
(a) strong acid
(b) weak acid
(c) strong base
(d) weak base

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q4
exercises.problem:
Write the formulas of the acid and the base that formed the following salts.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
exercises.solution:
(a) KOH and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q5
exercises.problem: Write two observations you would make when quick lime is added to water.
exercises.solution:
(i) The solution becomes hot.
(ii) Quick lime forms milky solution with water.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q6
exercises.problem: How is plaster of paris chemically different from gypsum? How may they be interconverted? Write one use of plaster of paris.
exercises.solution:
Plaster of Paris is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
Gypsum is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mtext> Gypsum </mtext></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Caster of Paris </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Plaster of Paris </mtext></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Gypsum </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
It is used for plastering fractured bones.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q7
exercises.problem:
State the chemical property in each case on which the following uses of baking soda are based :
(i) as an antacid
(ii) as a constituent of baking powder.
exercises.solution:
(i) It is weakly alkaline in nature, therefore, it can neutralize excess of acid in the stomach.
(ii) It decomposes to form carbon dioxide which makes the bread or cake fluffy.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q8
exercises.problem: What happens to most of the molecules of a strong acid when the acid is mixed with water?
exercises.solution: When a strong acid is mixed with water, most of the molecules of strong acid dissociate to produce hydrogen ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. These <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions combine with water to produce hydronium ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. Hence most of the molecules of a strong acid get converted to hydronium ions when mixed with water.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q9
exercises.problem: A weak acid is added to a concentrated solution of hydrochloric acid. Does the solution become more acidic or less acidic?
exercises.solution: When a weak acid is added to a concentrated solution of hydrochloric acid, the solution becomes more acidic because it increases the hydronium ion concentration of the solution.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q10
exercises.problem: Write the chemical name and formula of washing soda. What happens when crystals of washing soda are exposed to air?
exercises.solution: Washing soda is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>10</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>. Its chemical name is sodium carbonate decahydrate. When washing soda is exposed to air, it loses water of crystallization and become amorphous.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q11
exercises.problem: Write the balanced equation in molecular form illustrating the complete neutralization of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
exercises.solution:
Complete neutralization requires one <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>for each <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> has three available <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> can only provide two <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions, the reaction requires two moles of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> for three moles of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q13
exercises.problem: Explain why, an aqueous solution of sodium sulphate is neutral while an aqueous solution of sodium carbonate is basic in nature.
exercises.solution:
Sodium sulphate get dissolved in water to form strong acid and strong base, so it is neutral.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
On the other hand, sodium carbonate gives strong base and weak acid in water, so it is basic in nature.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> strong base </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q17
exercises.problem: Identify the acid and the base from which sodium chloride is obtained. Which type of salt is it? When is it called rock salt? How is rock salt formed?
exercises.solution:
NaCl is obtained from the hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide base.
It is a neutral salt as it is obtained from strong acid and strong base.
Large crystals of solid salt are often brown due to impurities. This is called rock salt.
Beds of rock salt were formed when seas of bygone ages dried up.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q18
exercises.problem: Blue litmus solution is added to two test tubes A and B containing dilute HCl and NaOH solution respectively. In which test tube a colour change will be observed? State the colour change and give its reason.
exercises.solution:
Since blue litmus solution is added in both test tube, so the colour change is observed in test tube in which acid is present and color changes from blue to red.
Test tube A: Acid present (color change from blue to red)
Test tube B: Base present (color doesn't change, blue remains blue since NaOH is basic)

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q19
exercises.problem:
During electrolysis of brine, a gas ' G ' is liberated at anode. When this gas ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ' is passed through slaked lime, a compound ' C ' is formed, which is used for disinfecting drinking water.
(i) Write formula of ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> ' and ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> '.
(ii) State the chemical equation involved
(iii) What is common name of compound ' C '? Give its chemical name.
exercises.solution:
(i) ' G ' is Chlorine <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and ' C ' is bleaching powder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
(ii) Chemical equation :-
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>→</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(iii) Common name is bleaching powder and chemical name is calcium oxychloride.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q1
exercises.problem: What is observed when - (i) dilute sulphuric acid is added to solid sodium carbonate, (ii) hot concentrated sulphuric acid is added to sulphur, (iii) sulphur dioxide is passed through lime water ? Also write chemical equations to represent the chemical reaction taking place in each case.
exercises.solution:
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas is formed.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mtext> (dil.) </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas is formed.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mtext> (conc.) </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><mn>3</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
(iii) Lime water turns milky due to formation of calcium sulphite.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q2
exercises.problem: (i) Name the raw materials used in the manufacture of sodium carbonate by Solvay process. (ii) How is the sodiumhydrogencarbonate formed during Solvay process separated from a mixture of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ? (iii) How is sodium carbonate obtained from sodium hydrogen carbonate ? Mention the name of scientist who develop Solvay process and list four important uses of sodium carbonate.
exercises.solution:
(i) Sodium chloride <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, Ammonia <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, Limestone <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
(ii) It is done by filtration.
(iii) Sodium hydrogen carbonate is heated to get sodium carbonate.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
The process was developed by Ernest Solvay. Following are few important uses of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
(i) It is used for softening of hard water.
(ii) A mixture of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is used as a fusion mixture.
(iii) It is used as an important laboratory reagent both in qualitative and quantitative analysis.
(iv) It is used for the manufacture of glass, borax, soap and caustic soda ( NaOH )

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q3
exercises.problem: A compound X of sodium forms a white powder. It is a constituent of baking powder and is used in some antacid prescriptions. When heated, X gives out a gas and steam. The gas forms a white precipitate with limewater. Write the chemical formula and name of X and the chemical equation for its decomposition on heating. What is its role as baking powder and as an antacid?
exercises.solution:
' X ' is sodium bicarbonate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. It is a constituent of baking powder and is used as an antacid. When ' X ' is heated, it gives out <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and steam. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>↑</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> When <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is passed through lime water, it turns milky due to formation of calcium carbonate.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> Lime water Carbon dioxide White ppt.
Sodium bicarbonate as baking powder makes the cake and biscuits fluffy, and as antacid it neutralizes hyperacidity in the stomach.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q4
exercises.problem: Identify the compound of calcium which is yellowish white powder and is used for disinfecting drinking water. How is it manufactured ? Write the chemical equation for the reaction involved. What happens when it is left exposed to air? Mention its four important uses also.
exercises.solution:
The compound is bleaching powder. It is used for disinfecting drinking water.
It is manufactured by reaction of dry slaked lime with chlorine gas.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
If it is exposed to air, it reacts with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas and liberates chlorine gas.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (Chlorine gas)

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q5
exercises.problem: Is it possible for a salt to behave as a base ? Explain.
exercises.solution: (b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> acetic acid is known as vinegar.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q1
exercises.problem: Why does a solution of a strong acid conduct electricity better than a solution of a weak acid having the same concentration?
exercises.solution: This is due to difference in number of ion produced by them in solution.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q2
exercises.problem: Why does tooth decay start when the pH of mouth is lower than 5.5 ?
exercises.solution: Tooth decay start when the pH of mouth is lower than 5.5 because the acid in our mouth which is formed by the bacterial break down of sugar molecules becomes strong enough to attack the enamel of our teeth and causes tooth decay.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q3
exercises.problem: Which of the two soil, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> should be treated with powdered chalk to adjust its pH and why?
exercises.solution: Soil <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is too basic and soil <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is too acidic. Therefore plant growth in these soil affected badly. Most of the plant grow at the neutral <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> 7) of the soil. Soil B should be treated with powdered chalk to reduce its acidity. Powdered chalk act as base and react with excess acid present in the soil B.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q4
exercises.problem: Bee sting should treated with baking soda while wasp sting should treated with vinegar, why?
exercises.solution: When a bee stings a person, it inject an acidic liquid into the skin. To neutralise bee sting a mild base such as baking soda should be used. While wasp sting has alkaline nature therefore it should be treated with weak acid such as vinegar.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q5
exercises.problem: Explain why the pH in a person's mouth becomes lower after each meal.
exercises.solution: When we eat food, then the bacteria present in our mouth break down the sugar molecules in food to form acid. Because of the formation of acid from sugar molecule in the mouth, pH becomes less than 7 .

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q6
exercises.problem: When <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>5</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> dehydrated, its characteristic blue colour disappeared. Why?
exercises.solution: The presence of water of crystalisation in copper sulphate impart it blue colour. When <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>5</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> dehydrated water of crystalisation is lost therefore blue colour disappeared.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q7
exercises.problem: Explain why an aqueous solution of ammonium chloride is acidic in nature?
exercises.solution:
When ammonium chloride dissolved in water, it get hydrolysed to form ammonium hydroxide (weak base) and hydrochloric acid (strong acid). Hydrochloric acid completely ionised and produces large amount of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ions in the solution. Ammonium hydroxide is slightly ionised and produces small amount of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions. Aqueous solution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math> contains more of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions therefore it is acidic.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>⇌</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> weak base </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> strong acid </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q1
exercises.problem: "Sulphuric acid is a dibasic acid". Write the reaction equations to justify this statement and name the reaction products in the two cases.
exercises.solution:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
