examples.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q6
examples.problem: What happens to the corrosive properties of an acid and a base after they neutralize each other ? Defend your answer.
examples.solution: The corrosive properties of an acid and a base get very much diminished after they (i.e. acid and base) neutralize each other. Generally, salts are much less corrosive as compared to the acid and the base from which they are formed.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q7
examples.problem:
For making cake, baking powder is taken. If at home your mother uses baking soda instead of baking powder in cake,
(a) How will it affect the taste of the cake and why?
(b) How can baking soda be converted into baking powder?
(c) What is the role of tartaric acid added to baking soda?
examples.solution:
(a) Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate. On heating, it is converted into sodium carbonate which is bitter to taste.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) Baking soda can be converted into baking powder by the addition of appropriate amount of tartaric acid to it.
(c) The role of tartaric acid is to neutralise sodium carbonate and cake will not taste bitter.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q8
examples.problem: Name the acid present in ant sting and give its chemical formula. Also give the common method to get relief from the discomfort caused by the ant sting.
examples.solution: The acid present in ant sting is methanoic acid (formic acid). The chemical formula is HCOOH . To get relief one should apply any available basic salt e.g., baking soda <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> on it.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q1
examples.problem: You are provided with three test-tubes, one of them contains distilled water and the other two contain an acidic solution and a basic solution respectively. If you are given only red litmus paper how will you identify the contents of each test-tube?
examples.solution:
Dip a piece of red litmus paper separately in each of the given test-tubes. Note the changes in colour of litmus paper.
(i) The test-tube in which the colour of red litmus paper turns purple indicates neutral nature i.e. it contains water.
(ii) The test-tube in which the colour of red litmus paper turns blue indicates basic nature i.e. it contains the basic solution.
(iii) The test-tube in which the colour of red litmus paper remains unchanged indicates acidic nature i.e. it contains acidic solution.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q2
examples.problem: Why should curd and sour substances not be kept in brass and copper vessels?
examples.solution:
Sour substances generally contain an acid. Curd also contains an acid. The acid present in curd and sour
substances is likely to react with copper or brass vessels and forms certain salts which are poisonous in nature (i.e. toxic compounds). To avoid any such possibility, it is advisable not to store curd and sour substances in brass and copper vessels.
Note : Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q3
examples.problem: Which gas is usually liberated when an acid reacts with a metal? Illustrate with an example. How will you test for the presence of this gas?
examples.solution:
The gas usually liberated by the action of an acid with a metal is hydrogen <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
Metal + Acid ⟶ Salt + Hydrogen
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Test for presence of gas :
When the gas is passed through soap solution, the gas filled bubbles are formed. When a burning match stick is brought near the hydrogen gas filled soap bubbles, the bubbles burn with a pop sound. It shows the presence of hydrogen gas.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q4
examples.problem: Metal compound A reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce effervescence. The gas evolved extinguishes a burning candle. Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction if one of the compounds formed is calcium chloride.
examples.solution:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> dil <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> gas
Since the gas is formed with effervescence and extinguishes a burning candle, so the gas is carbon dioxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> dil. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Since the metal compound reacts with dil. HCl to produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, the metal compound is a carbonate. Because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is one of the products so the metal salt is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (calcium carbonate). The reaction that occurs is :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
Balancing the equation, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>↑</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q5
examples.problem: Why do <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> etc. show acidic character in aqueous solutions while solutions of compounds like alcohol and glucose do not show acidic character?
examples.solution:
The acids <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> etc.) have replaceable hydrogen atoms in their molecule and they release hydrogens ion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>in aqueous solution. Since they release <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion so they show acidic character.
Compounds, alcohol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and glucose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> fail to release <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions in their aqueous solution because of absence of replaceable hydrogen atom in their molecule.
Since they do not release <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion in aqueous solution so they do not show acidic properties in solution.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q6
examples.problem: Why does aqueous solution of an acid conduct electricity?
examples.solution:
In an aqueous solution, an acid dissociates to produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions and some other anion. Due to the presence of ions the aqueous solution of an acid conducts electricity.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>⇌</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q7
examples.problem: Why does dry HCl gas not change the colour of dry litmus paper?
examples.solution:
The change in colour of litmus is observed only in presence of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions (acidic nature) or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions (basic nature).
Since dry HCl gas fails to produce any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions so the colour of dry litmus paper does not change when it comes in contact of dry HCl gas.
Note : Acids produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions in aqueous solution.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q8
examples.problem: While diluting an acid, why is it recommended that acid should be added to water and not water to the acid?
examples.solution: It is because if water is added to acid, heat evolved will be very high and bottle may break. On the other hand, if acid is added to water heat evolved will be absorbed by water as it has high specific heat. Thus, it prevents any accidental chances.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q9
examples.problem: How is concentration of hydronium ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>affected when solution of an acid is diluted with water?
examples.solution:
The concentration of hydronium ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>decreases when solution of an acid is diluted with water.
Note : Mixing of an acid or base with water results in decrease in the concentration of ions ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>/</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>) per unit volume. Such a process is called dilution and the acid or base is said to be diluted.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q10
examples.problem: How is concentration of hydroxyl ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>affected when excess of base is dissolved in solution of sodium hydroxide?
examples.solution: Sodium hydroxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a strong base (i.e. it is completely ionised in solution). When more of NaOH is dissolved, more <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>will be produced and thus there will be an increase in concentration of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q11
examples.problem: You have two solutions A and B. The pH of solution A is 6 and that of solution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is 8 . Which solutions has more hydrogen ion concentration? Which of this is acidic and which one is basic?
examples.solution:
We know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>H</mi></mrow></math> of a solution is inversely proportional to its <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion concentration (i.e. lesser the pH more will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion concentration).
Thus the solution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi></mrow></math> with pH 6 has more <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion concentration than the solution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow></math> with pH 8 .
We also know that for an acidic solution the pH lies between 0 to 7 and for a basic solution the pH range is 7-14.
Thus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi></mrow></math> with pH 6 is acidic and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow></math> with pH 8 is basic.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q12
examples.problem: What effect does concentration of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ions have on the nature of a solution?
examples.solution:
The acidic nature of a solution is directly related to the concentration of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ions in solution. More the concentration of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ions in solution, more acidic will be the solution.
Thus if the concentration of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ions increases in a solution, the solution becomes more acidic in nature and if the concentration of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ions in a solution decreases it becomes less acidic in nature.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q13
examples.problem: Do basic solutions also have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ions? If yes then why are these basic?
examples.solution:
Yes, basic solution also have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ions present in them. Actually these solutions are prepared in water. Water is a weak electrolyte (slightly ionised) and produces <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>⇌</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
However, the number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions released by water is small in comparison to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions released by a base and also by water. Because of this (number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo></mrow></math>number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>), the solution is basic in nature.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q14
examples.problem: Under what soil condition do you think a farmer would treat the soil of his fields with quick lime (calcium oxide) or slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) or chalk (calcium carbonate)?
examples.solution: The farmer will treat the soil of his fields with quick lime (a basic oxide) or slaked lime (basic hydroxide) or chalk (a metal carbonate) if the soil is acidic. An acidic soil will react with these basic substances and a neutralization reaction will occur. In this way the acidic nature of the soil will get neutralized.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q15
examples.problem: What is the common name of the compound <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ?
examples.solution: Common name of this compound is bleaching powder.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q16
examples.problem: Name the substance which upon treating with chlorine gas gives bleaching powder. Write the chemical equation for the reaction.
examples.solution:
Slaked lime or calcium hydroxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Bleaching powder </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow><mrow><mtext> Slaked lime </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q17
examples.problem: Name the sodium compound which is used for softening hard water.
examples.solution: Washing soda or sodium carbonate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>10</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q18
examples.problem: What will happen if the solution of sodium hydrogen carbonate is heated? Write the chemical equation involved.
examples.solution:
Whence solution of sodium hydrogen carbonate is heated, it decomposes to give sodium carbonate with the evolution of carbondioxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q19
examples.problem: Write the chemical equation for reaction between plaster of paris and water.
examples.solution:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
Plaster of Paris Gypsum

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q1
examples.problem:
A solution turns red litmus blue. Its pH is likely to be -
(a) 2
(b) 4
(c) 5
(d) 10
examples.solution: (d) The red litmus solution turns blue in basic solution. The pH of basic solution is more than 7 .

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q2
examples.problem:
A solution reacts with crushed egg-shells to give a gas that turns lime water milky. The solution contains -
(a) NaCl
(b) HCl
(c) LiCl
(d) KCl
examples.solution:
(b) Since the gas produced turns lime water milky so the gas is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. The egg-shell is made of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> which reacts with an acid (dil. HCl ) to produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>↑</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>20</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></mrow><mtext> of </mtext><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mtext> will require </mtext><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>20</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>

examples.problem:

examples.solution:
(a) Zinc + Sulphuric acid ⟶
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Zinc sulphate </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> Hydrogen </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover></mrow></math>
(b) Magnesium + Hydrochloric acid ⟶
Magnesium chloride + Hydrogen
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(c) Aluminium + Sulphuric acid ⟶
Aluminium sulphate + Hydrogen
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(d) Iron + Hydrochloric acid ⟶
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Iron (II) chloride </mtext><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q6
examples.problem: Compounds such as alcohol and glucose also contain hydrogen but are not categorised as acids. Describe an activity to prove it.
examples.solution: From their chemical formula it is evident that both alcohol ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ) and glucose ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) contain hydrogen. But in their aqueous solution they do not produce any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion so they are not categorised as acids.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Exemplar Questions — Q1
examples.problem: A student prepared solutions of (i) an acid and (ii) a base in two separate beakers. She forgot to label the solutions and litmus paper is not available in the laboratory. Since both the solutions are colourless, how will she distinguish between the two?
examples.solution: Using chemical indicator like phenolphthalein or natural indicators like turmeric, china rose etc. Alternatively, with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution which gives effervescences of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> with acid, but not with base.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Exemplar Questions — Q2

examples.solution:
When zinc reacts with dilute solution of strong acid, it forms salt and hydrogen gas is evolved.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
When a burning splinter is brought near the mouth of the test tube, the gas burns with a pop sound.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Exemplar Questions — Q3
examples.problem: In one of the industrial processes used for manufacture of sodium hydroxide, a gas X is formed as by product. The gas X reacts with dry slaked lime to give a compound Y which is used as a bleaching agent in chemical industry. Identify X and Y giving the chemical equation of the reactions involved.
examples.solution:
In the manufacture of sodium hydroxide, hydrogen gas and chlorine gas ( X ) are formed as by-products. When chlorine gas ( X ) reacts with dry slaked lime, it forms calcium oxychloride (bleaching powder) Y. The reactions are
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (Chlorine gas)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
Y -Calcium oxychloride (bleaching powder)

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Exemplar Questions — Q4
examples.problem: A metal carbonate X on reacting with an acid gives a gas which when passed through a solution Y gives the carbonate back. On the other hand, a gas G that is obtained at anode during electrolysis of brine is passed on dry Y , it gives a compound Z , used for disinfecting drinking water. Identity <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> and Z .
examples.solution:
The gas evolved at anode during electrolysis of brine is chlorine ( G ). When chlorine gas is passed through dry <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> produces bleaching powder (Z), used for disinfecting drinking water.

## THEORIES OF ACIDS AND BASES
## Arrhenius Concept of Acids and Bases
Svante Arrhenius in 1887, stated that acid ionizes in aqueous solution to produce hydrogen ions (which are protons), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, and anions; and a base ionizes in aqueous solution to produce hydroxide ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>and cations. Later studies of aqueous solutions provided evidence of a small, positively charged hydrogen ion combining with a water molecule to form a hydrated proton, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, which is called the hydronium ion.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Often, the hydronium ion or hydrated proton is represented as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Hydrogen chloride <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, a gas, is an acid because it dissolves in water to yield hydrogen ions and chloride ions. This aqueous solution of HCl is referred to as hydrochloric acid.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

(i) The solvent has no role to play in Arrhenius theory. An acid is expected to be an acid in any solvent. This was found not to be the case. For example, HCl is an acid in water, behaving in the manner Arrhenius expected. However, if HCl is dissolved in benzene, there is no dissociation, the HCl remaining as undissociated molecules. ## Physical properties of metals
- Metallic lusture
- Usually solid (except Hg which is a liquid)
- Show ductility and malleability.
- Good conductor of heat and electricity.
## Chemical properties of metals
Chemical properties of metals
- Form basic oxides with oxygen (Al and Zn forms amphoteric oxides)
- Form metal oxide and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
- Na and K reacts violently with cold water.
- Mg reacts only with hot water.
- <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and Fe react with steam.
- Form salts and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas with acids.
- Reactive metals displaces less reactive metals from their solution.
## Reaction of metals with non metals
- Metal loses the valence electrons while non-metal accepts these electron to form ionic bond.
- Properties of ionic compounds :
- Generally solids and exist in the form of crystals.
- High melting and boiling points.
- Soluble in water, insoluble in kerosene, petrol etc.
- Conduct electricity in molten state and not in solid state.
## Chemical properties of non-metals
- with chlorine form covalent compounds.
- do not react with acids on room temperature. On heating oxidised to respective oxides.
- chlorine dissolves in water and form acidic solution.
- Hydrogen burns with a pop sound.
- C and S form oxide with oxygen.
## Physical properties of Non-metal
- poor conductors, weak and brittle.
- low density and non-sonorous.
Now-a-days we use large number of materials in our routine life. Only few of them occur naturally rest are obtained by converting naturally occuring raw material into more useful substances via chemical modification. At present the number of elements known to us is around 118. Out of which 92 elements are naturally occuring and the rest are man-made. Most of the elements are solid, but eleven out of them are in gaseous state at room temperature and two are liquid at room temperature (i.e., mercury and bromine).
## METALS
## Physical Properties of Metals
Some of the physical properties of metals are listed below.
(a) They have a shining surface called lustre when freshly prepared.
(b) They are ductile (they can be drawn into wires) and malleable (they can be beaten into thin sheets, due to this property metals can be rolled into sheets)
(c) They usually have a high melting points.
(d) They are usually hard and solid at room temperature.
(e) Metals are generally good conductors of heat, electricity and sound.
(f) Metals have high tensile strength and density.
Alkali and alkaline earth metals are extremely reactive, and are rarely encountered in their elemental or metallic form. Some metals like sodium are so soft that they can be cut even with knife. Some metals are magnetic in nature such as iron, cobalt and nickel. Steel is also magnetic in nature since it is an alloy with major composition of iron. Whereas, other metals are not magnetic.
## Why cutting tools are generally made up of metals ?
## SOLUTION :
This is because of hard and strengthful character of metal.
Take pieces of iron, copper and aluminium, the three common metals you came across very often in routine life. Now place first piece of iron on hard steel blog and hammer it with full power. Notice change in shape if any. Now place pieces of copper and aluminium on steel blog and hammer it in a similar manner and record your observations. What conclusion will you obtain about physical nature of metals?
Noble metals : Noble metals are those metals which are resistant to corrosion or oxidation, unlike most base metals. They are referred to noble metals, often due to their inertness. Examples include tantalum, gold, platinum, and rhodium. Precious metals: A precious metal is a rare metallic chemical element of high economic value. Chemically, the precious metals are less reactive than most elements, they have high lustre and high electrical conductivity. Historically, precious metals were important as currency, but are now regarded mainly as investment and industrial commodities. The best-known precious metals are gold and silver. While both have industrial uses, they are better known for their uses in art, jewellery, and coinage. Other precious metals include the platinum group metals: ruthenium, rhodium, palladium, osmium, iridium, and platinum, of which platinum is the most widely traded.
Base metals : In chemistry, the term 'base metal' is used informally to refer to a metal that oxidizes or corrodes relatively easily, and reacts variably with dilute hydrochloric acid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> to form hydrogen. Examples include iron, nickel, lead and zinc. Copper is considered as a base metal because it oxidizes relatively easily, although it does not react with HCl .
Ferrous metals : The term "ferrous" is derived from the latin word meaning "containing iron". This can include pure iron, such as wrought iron, or an alloy such as steel. Ferrous metals are often magnetic in nature.
## CONNECTING TOPIC
Alloy : An alloy is a mixture of two or more elements in solid state in which the major component is a metal. Most pure metals are either too soft, brittle or chemically reactive for practical use. Combining different ratios of metals in alloys modify the properties of pure metals to produce desirable characteristics. The aim of making alloys is generally to make them less brittle, harder, resistant to corrosion, or have a more desirable color and lustre. Examples of alloys are steel (iron and carbon), brass (copper and zinc), bronze (copper and tin), and duralumin (aluminium and copper). Alloys specially designed for highly demanding applications, such as jet engines, may contain more than ten elements. Stainless steel ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ) is used where resistance to corrosion is important. Al and Mg alloys are used for strength and light applications. Nickel based super alloys are used in high temperature appliances such as turbochargers, pressure vessels and heat exchangers. Generally, electrical conductivity of an alloy is less than that of pure metal.
Alloys have wide domestic and industrial applications, as alloy formation enhances the applicability of metals in various fields.

## Chemical Properties of Metals
## 1. Metal burns in air :
Many metals burn in the oxygen of air to produce a metal oxide
Metal + Oxygen → Metal oxide
The more reactive a metal is, the more violent the reaction when it is burnt in oxygen or air.
Example : Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Many metals tarnish in air. The metal slowly reacts with the oxygen of the air forming a dull layer of the metal oxide on the surface of the metal.
Very unreactive metals like gold and silver do not tarnish, they stay shiny.
The reactivity series :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>K</mi><mo>−</mo><mtext> Potassium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mtext> Sodium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mtext> Calcium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mtext> Magnesium </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> Burn very easily with a bright flame <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Al-Aluminium </mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Zn-Zinc </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Fe-Iron </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Pb-Lead </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Cu-Copper </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mtext> React slowly with air when heated </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable><mspace width="1em" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Ag-Silver </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Au-Gold </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> No reaction
Metal oxides are usually basic in nature but there are some metal oxides which show both acidic and basic behaviour. i.e. they react with both acids and bases. These are called amphoteric oxides. One of the most common example of an amphoteric oxide is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. It reacts in the following manner with acids and bases -
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Zinc, tin, lead and beryllium can also form amphoteric oxides.
Most metal oxides are insoluble in water but some of these dissolve in water to form alkali. For example, sodium oxide and potassium oxide dissolve in water to produce alkali as follows,

All metals do not react with oxygen at same rate, some metals are more reactive than others. This is because very reactive metals lose electrons easily. Metals such as sodium are very reactive and explosive in air. Hence, to protect them and to prevent accidental fires, they are kept immersed in kerosene oil. Whereas, metals such as gold are very unreactive, and therefore do not corrode or tarnish in air.
## Learn More
At ordinary temperature, the surfaces of metals such as magnesium, aluminium, zinc, lead, etc., are covered with a thin layer of oxide. The protective oxide layer prevents the metal from further oxidation. Iron does not burn on heating but iron fillings burn vigorously when sprinkled in the flame of the burner. Copper does not burn, but the hot metal is coated with a black coloured layer of copper(II) oxide. Silver and gold do not react with oxygen even at high temperatures.
## 3. Reaction of metal with acids :
When an acid reacts with metal, a salt and hydrogen are produced:
For example :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Acid + Metal </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> Salt + Hydrogen </mtext></mrow></math>
Sulfuric acid + Calcium ⟶ Calcium sulfate + Hydrogen
The salt that is produced depends upon the reactivity of metals with acids. Potassium, sodium, lithium and calcium all react violently with dilute sulphuric acid and dilute hydrochloric acid. It is dangerous to put these metals into an acid. The reaction is similar to the reaction with water, forming the metal salt (either sulphate or chloride) and hydrogen gas.
For example :

Magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, tin and lead react safely with dilute acid. Magnesium is the fastest and lead is the slowest among the six.
The reaction of zinc with sulphuric acid is often used to make a small amount of hydrogen in the laboratory.

The reaction is slow at room temperature but its rate can be increased by the addition of a small amount of copper(II) sulphate. Zinc displaces copper metal, which acts as a catalyst.
Hydrogen gas is not evolved when a metal reacts with nitric acid. But magnesium ( Mg ) and manganese (Mn) react with very dilute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to evolve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas.
Metals react with dil HCl to form corresponding chloride salt and hydrogen which is evolved as bubbles. The rate of formation of bubbles was the fastest in case of magnesium and the reaction is exothermic. In the case of copper, no bubbles were seen and the temperature also remains unchanged. This shows that copper does not react with dilute HCl .

Dilute nitric acid is added to zinc, aluminium and copper. Immediately thereafter, zinc and aluminum show no reaction. Copper, on the other hand, reacts immediately and produces brown <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> according to the following reaction.

Aluminum and zinc do not react even with concentrated nitric acid since, a thick and hard to dissolve, oxidative layer builds (passive oxidation) on the metal, that protects the metal against further assaults.
Acids are often used to dissolve metals or organic material. However, certain material are more difficult to dissolve. They require more potent and specialized acid solutions like aqua regia.
Aqua regia consists of 3 parts HCl to 1 part <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, it is an excellent oxidant, can dissolve gold and platinum, it produces yellow fumes to produce nitrosyl chloride, NOCl, chlorine gas, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, and water, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>.
Acid Piranha consists <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in the ratios, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, it is also an excellent oxidant and removes trace amount of organic residues.
For preparing piranha always add peroxide to sulfuric acid, never vice versa. This is a selfheating solution that may even boil when mixed.
## 5. Reaction of metal with solution of other metal salts:
A metal will displace (take the place of) a less reactive metal in a metal salt solution.
For example,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mtext> Iron + Copper(II) sulphate </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> Iron sulphate + Copper. </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>↓</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Copper(II) sulphate is blue, iron sulphate is pale green in colour.
During the reaction the blue solution loses its colour and the iron metal is seen to turn pink-brown as the displaced copper becomes deposited on it.
If a less reactive metal is added to a metal salt solution, there will be no reaction - nothing will happen.
For example, iron is less reactive than magnesium.
Iron + Magnesium sulphate ⟶ No reaction

## OCCURRENCE OF METALS
The earth's crust is a very big source of the metals. Metals occur in nature sometimes free but mostly in combined state. Metals like silver, gold, platinum etc. occur in free or native state. Most of the metals are found in the form of the compounds in the nature. These naturally occuring compounds of metals are known as minerals. In certain minerals, the percentage of a particular metal is high and these metals can be extracted profitably and such minerals are called ores. The process of extraction of metals from their respective ores is called metallurgy.
The unwanted rocky, earthy or sandy materials almost always associated with ores as impurities are called gangue or matrix.

## CONNECTING TOPIC
Extraction of ore is a complex process which comprises various steps. So before studying the topic of extraction we should understand the general principles of metallurgy. Although we will study all these principles in detail in class XIIth, for your better understanding a summary is given here.
## GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF METALLURGY
Metallurgy is an art of extracting metals from the ores. The ores are generally associated with a number of impurities and earthy matter. The extraction of metals from ores involves various steps as discussed below :
## 1. Grinding or Pulverisation
The large pieces of ores are broken into small pieces with the help of hammer. These pieces are crushed with crusher and finally powdered in stamp mills. This powdered form of ore is used for further processes.
## 2. Concentration
The ores, obtained from ore mine contain various types of impurities. The removal of various types of impurities from ores is known as concentration. The process by which ore is concentrated depends on the type of ore and gangue. This concentration is carried out by using one or more of the following methods :
(a) Gravity separation or hydraulic washing : This method is based on the difference in the density of ore and the density of impurities. The ore is crushed and finely powdered, sieved and then levigated in a stream of water. The lighter impurities are carried away by the stream of water and heavier ore particles settle down. Ores of tin, lead and iron are concentrated by this process.
## Gravity separation method
(b) Froth floatation process : This process is used in the concentration of sulphide ores like galena ( PbS ), zinc blende (ZnS) etc. The well powdered ore (taken in a tank) is mixed with water to which an oil (pine oil or eucalyptus oil) has been added. The whole mass is agitated by a blast of air sent through pipe as shown in figure. The froth (containing impurities) floats on the surface of the water, while heavy ore particles settle down. The froth along with the ore is removed from the surface of the water.
Froth floatation process for the concentration of sulphide ores.
Froth stabilizers are those chemicals which stabilise the froth e.g. cresols and aniline.
## Collectors :
These compounds attach themselves by polar groups to grains of minerals which then become water repellent and thus pass on into the froth. Examples are ethyl xanthate and potassium ethyl xanthate.
## Activators and depressants :
These compounds activate or depress the floating property of one of the components of the ore and thus help in the separation of different minerals present in the same ore. Copper sulphate is an example of activator, while sodium and potassium cyanides are the examples of depressants.

PbS is then easily separated from ZnS .
(c) Electromagnetic separation : This method is used when either the ore or the gangue is magnetic in nature. For example, tin stone contains <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> as impurity. The powdered ore is dropped on a moving belt passing over two magnetic rollers. The magnetic impurities (like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) get collected in a heap nearer the magnetic rollers, while the ore (free from impurity) is collected in a heap, away from the magnetic rollers.
Some metals are attracted to magnet and can behave as a magnet. Thus Iron, cobalt and nickel are described as magnetic materials.
There are two types of permanent magnets those from "hard" magnetic materials and those from "soft" magnetic materials. Hard magnetic materials tend to stay magnetized over a long period while soft magnetic metals can be magnetized but lose their magnetism quickly.
(d) Leaching : It is a chemical method used for concentration of ore in which crude powdered ore is allowed to react with suitable reagent. Ore reacts with added reagent to form soluble complex while impurities remain undissolved. Insoluble impurities are separated by filtration and ore is reprecipitated from soluble complex.
Note : This process is used for concentration of Al, Ag, Au ores etc.
## 3. Extraction of Metals
Metals are extracted from their concentrated ore by the reduction of metal oxides. The ore is converted to its oxide by one of following methods.
(a) Calcination : Calcination is the process of heating the ore in the presence of limited supply of air to a temperature insufficient to melt it. During calcination, moisture and volatile impurities are removed and the whole mass becomes porous. Here carbonates are converted into oxides by giving out carbon dioxide. Apart from carbonate ores, hydrated ores are also subjected to calcination for the removal of water of crystallization. Some examples are given below:
(i) The metal zinc and calcium are obtained from calamine <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and lime stone <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> respectively. ## 4. Reduction of Metal Oxides
(a) Smelting : Calcined or roasted ore is mixed with carbon or any other suitable reducing agent and flux, and heated strongly. Metal oxides are reduced to metal. Smelting is opposite of roasting which involves an oxidizing reaction.
Examples : When tin stone <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is heated strongly with carbon, tin metal is obtained.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>C</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
The zinc oxide obtained by calcination of zinc blende, when heated strongly with carbon gives zinc metal.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Similarly, lead metal is obtained by the reduction of lead oxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
