- Carbon is good reducing agent for oxides but not for sulphides.
- Due to cheapness and high availability, carbon is widely used as a reducing agent. The process is known as carbon reduction. The metals which are less electropositive, do not form carbides with carbon, they are reduced by this method e.g. oxides of Ph, Fe, Zn, Sn etc.
- Below <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>710</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math> is better reducing agent than carbon and reverse is true at temperature higher than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>710</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
Flux :
Ores contain some fusible impurities. These impurities are removed by adding certain substances. These substances are called flux. The flux to be used depends on the nature of impurities. If acidic impurities (such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) are present, basic flux (e.g., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math> etc.) are mixed and if the impurities present are of basic nature the acidic flux are used.
Slag :
Fusible compounds, formed by the combination of flux and impurities are known as slag. For example, if ferrous oxide is present as impurity in a metal it may be removed by adding silica as a flux. Ferrous oxide is removed as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (slag).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Generally, slags possess melting points lower than the metals. The slags are generally lighter and hence floats on the surface of molten metals from where it can be skimmed off from time to time.
(b) Aluminothermic process :
There are certain metals whose oxides can not be reduced by carbon. These metals are extracted by aluminothermic process. The metal oxides are thoroughly mixed with aluminium powder and a little <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in a crucible. The reaction is brought about by introducing a lighted magnesium ribbon. Since the reaction is exothermic, temperature reaches to about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>3000</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>. Metals like chromium and manganese can be extracted by this method.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>3</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
The reaction between iron (II) oxide and aluminium is called thermite reaction. Commercially, it is used in welding of iron tracks. It was discovered by German chemist Dr. Hans Goldschmidt. In this reaction, iron oxide (rust) and aluminium metal powder undergo a redox (oxidation-reduction) reaction to form molten iron metal.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
In fact, thermite reaction has been used for underwater welding, joining railway tracks or cracked machine parts.
(c) Precipitation method :
Those metals which are more reactive tend to displace less reactive metals. If an iron rod is placed in a copper sulphate solution the copper metal is precipitated and iron goes in solution. Zinc is more reactive than silver and gold in reactivity series and hence it precipitates these metals from their salt solutions. This method is used in the extraction of silver and gold.
## 5. Refining of Metals
The metals obtained by anyone of the above methods are not pure. The metals are refined by the following methods :
(a) By liquation : This method is used for the easily fusible metals like tin etc. Impure metal is placed on the inclined bed of a furnace and heated. The metal melts and flows out leaving behind the impurities.
For example, purification of Sn containing impurities of high m.p. like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow></math>. It is also used for purification of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math> etc.
Purification of tin metal by liquation process
(b) By distillation : Volatile metals like Zn and Hg etc. can be purified by this method. When these metals are heated, their vapours are formed leaving behind the impurities. The vapours are condensed to get pure metals.
(c) By oxidation : If the impurities present in the metals can be easily oxidised, these are removed by this method. Molten metal is stirred thoroughly in the presence of air. The impurities float on the surface of the molten mass in the form of a scum which can be easily separated.
(d) Electrolytic refining : The impure metal is taken as anode and the cathode consists of a pure metal. Cathodes and anodes are placed in a soluble salt of the metal taken as an electrolyte. Pure metal is gradually deposited on the cathode and impurities either settle down or dissolved in the solution and collected as anode mud. Large number of metals like copper, silver, gold and zinc are purified by this method. The metal of highest purity are obtained by this method.
(e) Thermal decomposition method : In these methods, the metal is converted into suitable volatile compound which is decomposed at high temperature to give pure metal.
(i) Mond's process or carbonyl process (Purification of Ni) :
This method is used for the purification of nickel. Impure nickel is allowed to react with carbon monooxide at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>80</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>. It gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, which is a volatile compound. Vapours of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> decomposes at about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> giving pure Ni ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>99.9</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> purity).
(ii) van-Arkel process :
It is also known as iodide refining method. This method is used for obtaining metals of very high purity. Common metals which are refined by this method are Ti, Zr, Hf, Si etc. In this method, metal is converted into a volatile compound (e.g., iodides) which is decomposed to obtain pure metal. Impurities are left behind as they do not react with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Impure metal </mtext><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> Metal iodide </mtext><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Very high temp. </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mtext> Pure metal </mtext><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
## EXTRACTION OF METALS ON THE BASIS OF REACTIVITY SERIES
The reaction of metals or their position in activity series can also give a great idea about extraction of metals.
## Extraction of Metals Placed Low in the Activity Series
Metals that are low in the activity series are very unreactive. The oxides of these metals can be reduced to metals by heating alone. For example, mercury is obtained from its ore, cinnabar (HgS), by the process of heating.
## Reduction using heat :

Copper can also be obtained in a similar manner from its sulphide ore <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
When concentrated cinnabar ore (HgS) is roasted the ore is converted to oxide. The reduction of cinnabar ore to oxide is a combination of roasting and reduction.
## Extraction of Metals Placed in the Middle of the Activity Series
Metals such as iron, zinc, lead, copper, etc., are present in the middle of the reactivity series. These are moderately reactive metals and are usually present as sulphides or carbonates. It is easier to reduce an oxide ore as compared to its sulphides and carbonates. If the ore is not an oxide ore, it is first converted to the oxide by the process of calcination or roasting.
Roasting : Sulphide ores are converted into oxides by heating strongly in presence of excess air, to form the corresponding oxides. Sulphur impurities escape as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas. ## Extraction of Metals Placed at the Top of the Activity Series
Metals such as sodium, magnesium, calcium, aluminium present on the top of the reactivity series are very reactive and cannot be obtained from their compounds by heating with carbon. This is because these metals have more affinity for oxygen than for carbon. Such highly reactive metals are obtained by electrolytic reduction of fused chlorides, e.g. sodium from sodium chloride in a "Downs cell". Similarly, calcium is obtained by the reduction of fused calcium chloride.

## Prevention of Corrosion
Iron and steel (alloy of iron) are most easily protected by paint which provides a barrier between the metal and air/water. Moving parts of machines can be protected by a water repellent oil or grease layer. Covering the surface with enamel and lacquers is another method.
Did You
Know?
- Material selection is the first step to eliminate or minimize corrosion. The following rule can help as initial guidelines for materials selection for corrosion prevention concerns.
1. Avoid dissimilar metals to prevent galvanic corrosion.
2. Select materials with compact insulating oxide or passive layer such as stainless steel or aluminum.
3. Avoid the usage of materials with localized non uniform stresses by stress relief heat treatment process.
(a) Alloying :
Iron or steel along with other metals can also be protected by 'alloying' or mixing with other metals (e.g., chromium) to make non-rusting alloys. Stainless steel is an example of a non-rusting alloy of iron and carbon. Brass, an alloy of copper with zinc is less expensive and non reactive.
(b) Galvanizing :
Coating iron or steel with a thin zinc layer is called 'galvanizing'. A thin layer of Zn is deposited by electrolysis in which iron/steel object is dipped in molten zinc using Zn as cathode. Zinc preferentially corrodes or oxidizes to form a zinc oxide layer that does not flake off like iron oxide rust. However, if the coated surface is scratched, the zinc again corrodes.
(c) Electroplating :
Electroplating is very common method to coat surface of iron by another metal to prevent corrosion. The process is usually done from aqueous electrolytes at room temperature. It is one of the most popular method to prevent corrosion on steel. Chromium, nickel or aluminium are some common plating metals for corrosion protection.

## NON-METALS
Seventeen elements are generally classified as non-metals; most are gases (hydrogen, helium, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, neon, chlorine, argon, krypton, xenon and radon) : and a few are solids (carbon, phosphorus, sulfur, selenium and iodine). Bromine is the only non-metal which is a liquid at room temperature.
All non-metals have following properties in common:
- They are dull.
- They are poor conductors of heat and electricity (they are insulators).
- They are weak and brittle (they easily break or shatter).
- They have a low density (they feel light for their size).
- They do not make a ringing sound when they are hit.
The most abundant non-metal in the earth's crust is oxygen, which constitutes about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>50</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> of the earth's crust. The next abundant non metal is silicon which constitutes about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>26</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> of the earth's crust.

## HOW DO METALS AND NON-METALS REACT
In earlier classes we learnt that, noble gases have a completely filled valence shell and hence show little chemical activity. We can, therefore, explain the reactivity of elements as a tendency to attain a completely filled valence shell. Let us have a look at the electronic configuration of noble gases and some metals and non-metals.
A sodium atom has one electron in its outermost shell. If it loses the electron from its M shell then its L shell now becomes the outermost shell and has a stable octet. The nucleus of this atom still has 11 protons but the number of electrons has become 10 , so there is a net positive charge giving us a sodium cation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. On the other hand, chlorine atom has seven electrons in its outermost shell and requires one more electron to complete its octet. When sodium and chlorine react with each other, the electron is lost by sodium atom which could be taken up by chlorine atom. After gaining an electron, the chlorine atom gets a unit negative charge, because its nucleus has 17 protons and 18 electrons in its <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> and M shells. This gives us a chloride anion
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. So both of these elements can have a give-and-take relation between them as follows (Fig.).
Sodium and chloride ions, being oppositely charged, attract to each other and are held by strong electrostatic forces of attraction to exist as sodium chloride ( NaCl ).
It should be noted that sodium chloride does not exist as molecules but aggregates of oppositely charged ions.
Let us see the formation of one more ionic compound, magnesium chloride.
## Formation of magnesium chloride
The compounds formed in this manner by the transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal are known as ionic compounds or electrovalent compounds and these ionic compounds exhibit electrostatic intermolecular forces.
## Properties of Ionic Compounds
(a) Physical nature : Ionic compounds are solids and are somewhat hard because of the strong forces of attraction between the positive and negative ions. These compounds are generally brittle and break into pieces when pressure is applied.
(b) Melting and Boiling points : Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points . This is because a considerable amount of energy is required to break the strong inter-ionic attraction.

Because it stays solid at such high temperatures, magnesium oxide remains unconductive, and is used for hightemperature electrical insulation.
(c) Solubility : Electrovalent compounds are generally soluble in water (polar solvent) and insoluble in solvents such as kerosene, petrol, (nonpolar solvents) etc.
(d) Conduction of electricity : The conduction of electricity through an aqueous solution involves the movement of charged particles. A solution of an ionic compound in water contains ions, which move to the opposite electrodes when electricity is passed through the solution. Ionic compounds in the solid state do not conduct electricity because movement of ions in the solid state is not possible due to their rigid structure. But ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state. This is possible in the molten state since the elecrostatic forces of attraction between the oppositely charged ions overcomes due to the heat. Thus, the ions move freely and conduct electricity.

## METALLOIDS
Metalloids are those chemical elements that exhibit properties of both metals and non-metals. They behave as non-metals physically and chemically and show electrical conductivity like metals. However, they are not good conductors of electricity like metals and are known as semiconductors.
The concepts of metalloid and semiconductor should not be confused. Metalloid refers to the properties of certain elements in relation to the periodic table. Semiconductor refers to the physical properties of materials (including alloys, compounds) and there is only partial overlap between the two.
The following elements are generally considered as metalloids :
- Boron (B)
- Germanium (Ge)
- Antimony (Sb)
- Silicon (Si)
- Arsenic (As)
- Tellurium (Te)
- Polonium (Po)
Metalloids characteristics include ability to form amphoteric oxides and ability to behave as semiconductors and semimetals. The metalloids are placed between metals and non-metals in the periodic table. There are seven metalloids in the periodic table that are placed in Group 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17. They form a zig zag step line in the periodic table. They are separated from the metals and non-metals by a line called the 'amphoteric line'. Metalloids like boron, germanium, arsenic are used as dopants in semiconductor chips. Metalloids are usually brittle in nature and behave as electrical insulators at room temperature.
## Uses of Metalloids
- Boron is found in boric acid - a mild antiseptic and insect killer.
- Silicon is used in computers and other electronics and it is used to make rubbery cookware that does not stick to the food. Silicon is also used in making solar energy devices.
- Germanium is used in fiber optics.
- Arsenic can be used with gallium in semiconductors, but it is generally used as an insecticide.
- Antimony is used in batteries, antifriction alloys, cable sheathing, matches, medicines, antiprotozoan drugs, plumbing, soldering (some "lead-free" solders contain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>%</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ), and a couple of other things.
- Tellurium is used in ceramics, semiconductors, and blasting caps.
- Polonium is a very rare natural element. It is found in uranimum ores but it is uneconomical to extract it. These are used in antistatic devices and for research purposes.
Note : Boron, germanium and arsenic, all are used as a dopant in semiconductor chips.

Some metals are chemically very reactive, whereas others are less reactive or unreactive. On the basis of vigourness of reactions of various metals with oxygen, water and acids, as well as displacement reactions, the metals have been arranged in a group or series according to their chemical reactivity. The arrangement of metals in a vertical column in the order of decreasing reactivities is called reactivity series of metals (or activity series of metals). In reactivity series, the most reactive metal is placed at the top whereas the least reactive metal is placed at the bottom. As we come down in the series, the chemical reactivity of metals decreases. Since the metals placed at the bottom of the reactivity series (like silver and gold) are less reactive, so they are usually found in free state (native state) in nature.

But when Zn is dipped in copper sulphate solution, it displaces copper from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> which is colourless. Reddish brown copper metal gets precipitated because Zn is more reactive than Cu.

3. (i) The metal that catches fire in open air and gives off white fumes is sodium.
(ii) The metal that forms two types of oxides and rusts in moisture is iron. The formulas of its oxides are: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mi>;</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
(iii) The metal used in stainless steel is chromium besides iron and carbon as it increases corrosion resistance character of steel.
(iv) The metal used in long distance cable wires is aluminium, because it is a light metal and a very good conductor of electricity.
(v) The metal added to gold to harden, is copper.
4. (i) Electrolytic refining : The impure metal is taken as anode and the cathode consists of a pure metal. Cathodes and anodes are placed in a soluble salt of the metal taken as an electrolyte. Pure metal gradually passes on to the cathode and impurities either settles down or dissolved in the solution called anode mud. Large number of metals like copper, silver, gold and zinc are purified by this method. The metal of highest purity are obtained by this method.

7. (i) Metals are electropositive elements. They can easily lose electrons to form ions.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
These electrons are relatively free to move. Due to mobility of electrons most metals conduct electricity.
(ii) The reaction of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> with heated alumina is known as thermite
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> Heat The reaction is highly exothermic. In the reaction aluminium acts as reducing agent and reduces <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to Fe and itself oxidises to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Due to large amount of heat produced, the iron is produced in molten state. Molted iron is used to join cracked machine parts.

## Physical properties of metals
- Metallic lusture
- Usually solid (except Hg which is a liquid)
- Show ductility and malleability.
- Good conductor of heat and electricity.

## Chemical properties of metals
Chemical properties of metals
- Form basic oxides with oxygen (Al and Zn forms amphoteric oxides)

theory_sections.markdown:
## Reaction of metals with non metals
- Metal loses the valence electrons while non-metal accepts these electron to form ionic bond.
- Properties of ionic compounds :
- Generally solids and exist in the form of crystals.
- High melting and boiling points.
- Soluble in water, insoluble in kerosene, petrol etc.
- Conduct electricity in molten state and not in solid state.

## Chemical properties of non-metals
- with chlorine form covalent compounds.
- do not react with acids on room temperature. On heating oxidised to respective oxides.
- chlorine dissolves in water and form acidic solution.
- Hydrogen burns with a pop sound.
- C and S form oxide with oxygen.

## Physical properties of Non-metal
- poor conductors, weak and brittle.
- low density and non-sonorous.
Now-a-days we use large number of materials in our routine life. Only few of them occur naturally rest are obtained by converting naturally occuring raw material into more useful substances via chemical modification. At present the number of elements known to us is around 118. Out of which 92 elements are naturally occuring and the rest are man-made. Most of the elements are solid, but eleven out of them are in gaseous state at room temperature and two are liquid at room temperature (i.e., mercury and bromine).
## METALS

## Physical Properties of Metals
Some of the physical properties of metals are listed below.
(a) They have a shining surface called lustre when freshly prepared.
(b) They are ductile (they can be drawn into wires) and malleable (they can be beaten into thin sheets, due to this property metals can be rolled into sheets)
(c) They usually have a high melting points.
(d) They are usually hard and solid at room temperature.
(e) Metals are generally good conductors of heat, electricity and sound.
(f) Metals have high tensile strength and density.
Alkali and alkaline earth metals are extremely reactive, and are rarely encountered in their elemental or metallic form. Some metals like sodium are so soft that they can be cut even with knife. Some metals are magnetic in nature such as iron, cobalt and nickel. Steel is also magnetic in nature since it is an alloy with major composition of iron. Whereas, other metals are not magnetic.

## CONNECTING TOPIC
Alloy : An alloy is a mixture of two or more elements in solid state in which the major component is a metal. Most pure metals are either too soft, brittle or chemically reactive for practical use. Combining different ratios of metals in alloys modify the properties of pure metals to produce desirable characteristics. The aim of making alloys is generally to make them less brittle, harder, resistant to corrosion, or have a more desirable color and lustre. Examples of alloys are steel (iron and carbon), brass (copper and zinc), bronze (copper and tin), and duralumin (aluminium and copper). Alloys specially designed for highly demanding applications, such as jet engines, may contain more than ten elements. Stainless steel ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ) is used where resistance to corrosion is important. Al and Mg alloys are used for strength and light applications. Nickel based super alloys are used in high temperature appliances such as turbochargers, pressure vessels and heat exchangers. Generally, electrical conductivity of an alloy is less than that of pure metal.
Alloys have wide domestic and industrial applications, as alloy formation enhances the applicability of metals in various fields.

## Chemical Properties of Metals

## 1. Metal burns in air :
Many metals burn in the oxygen of air to produce a metal oxide
Metal + Oxygen → Metal oxide
The more reactive a metal is, the more violent the reaction when it is burnt in oxygen or air.
Example : Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Many metals tarnish in air. The metal slowly reacts with the oxygen of the air forming a dull layer of the metal oxide on the surface of the metal.
Very unreactive metals like gold and silver do not tarnish, they stay shiny.
The reactivity series :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>K</mi><mo>−</mo><mtext> Potassium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mtext> Sodium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mtext> Calcium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mtext> Magnesium </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> Burn very easily with a bright flame <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Al-Aluminium </mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Zn-Zinc </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Fe-Iron </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Pb-Lead </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Cu-Copper </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mtext> React slowly with air when heated </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable><mspace width="1em" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Ag-Silver </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Au-Gold </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> No reaction
Metal oxides are usually basic in nature but there are some metal oxides which show both acidic and basic behaviour. i.e. they react with both acids and bases. These are called amphoteric oxides. One of the most common example of an amphoteric oxide is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. It reacts in the following manner with acids and bases -
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Zinc, tin, lead and beryllium can also form amphoteric oxides.
Most metal oxides are insoluble in water but some of these dissolve in water to form alkali. For example, sodium oxide and potassium oxide dissolve in water to produce alkali as follows,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
All metals do not react with oxygen at same rate, some metals are more reactive than others. This is because very reactive metals lose electrons easily. Metals such as sodium are very reactive and explosive in air. Hence, to protect them and to prevent accidental fires, they are kept immersed in kerosene oil. Whereas, metals such as gold are very unreactive, and therefore do not corrode or tarnish in air.

## Learn More
At ordinary temperature, the surfaces of metals such as magnesium, aluminium, zinc, lead, etc., are covered with a thin layer of oxide. The protective oxide layer prevents the metal from further oxidation. Iron does not burn on heating but iron fillings burn vigorously when sprinkled in the flame of the burner. Copper does not burn, but the hot metal is coated with a black coloured layer of copper(II) oxide. Silver and gold do not react with oxygen even at high temperatures.

## 3. Reaction of metal with acids :
When an acid reacts with metal, a salt and hydrogen are produced:
For example :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Acid + Metal </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> Salt + Hydrogen </mtext></mrow></math>
Sulfuric acid + Calcium ⟶ Calcium sulfate + Hydrogen
The salt that is produced depends upon the reactivity of metals with acids. Potassium, sodium, lithium and calcium all react violently with dilute sulphuric acid and dilute hydrochloric acid. It is dangerous to put these metals into an acid. The reaction is similar to the reaction with water, forming the metal salt (either sulphate or chloride) and hydrogen gas.
For example :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mtext> Sodium </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> Hydrochloric acid </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> Sodium chloride </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> Hydrogen </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>+</mo><mspace width="1em" /><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, tin and lead react safely with dilute acid. Magnesium is the fastest and lead is the slowest among the six.
The reaction of zinc with sulphuric acid is often used to make a small amount of hydrogen in the laboratory.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>↑</mo></mrow></math>
The reaction is slow at room temperature but its rate can be increased by the addition of a small amount of copper(II) sulphate. Zinc displaces copper metal, which acts as a catalyst.
Hydrogen gas is not evolved when a metal reacts with nitric acid. It is because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is a strong oxidising agent. It oxidises the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> produced to water and itself gets reduced to any of the nitrogen oxides ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ). But magnesium ( Mg ) and manganese (Mn) react with very dilute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to evolve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas.
Metals react with dil HCl to form corresponding chloride salt and hydrogen which is evolved as bubbles. The rate of formation of bubbles was the fastest in case of magnesium and the reaction is exothermic. The reactivity decreases in the order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. In the case of copper, no bubbles were seen and the temperature also remains unchanged. This shows that copper does not react with dilute HCl .
Time to Check Your Knowledge
Four experiments are set-up as shown below. A rapid evolution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas will be observed in the test-tube.

theory_sections.topics: 4. Reaction of metals with nitric acid :
theory_sections.markdown:
## 4. Reaction of metals with nitric acid :
Dilute nitric acid is added to zinc, aluminium and copper. Immediately thereafter, zinc and aluminum show no reaction. Copper, on the other hand, reacts immediately and produces brown <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> according to the following reaction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mi>⟶</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
Aluminum and zinc do not react even with concentrated nitric acid since, a thick and hard to dissolve, oxidative layer builds (passive oxidation) on the metal, that protects the metal against further assaults.
Acids are often used to dissolve metals or organic material. However, certain material are more difficult to dissolve. They require more potent and specialized acid solutions like aqua regia.
Aqua regia consists of 3 parts HCl to 1 part <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, it is an excellent oxidant, can dissolve gold and platinum, it produces yellow fumes to produce nitrosyl chloride, NOCl, chlorine gas, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, and water, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>.
Acid Piranha consists <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in the ratios, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, it is also an excellent oxidant and removes trace amount of organic residues.
For preparing piranha always add peroxide to sulfuric acid, never vice versa. This is a selfheating solution that may even boil when mixed.

theory_sections.topics: 5. Reaction of metal with solution of other metal salts:
theory_sections.markdown:
## 5. Reaction of metal with solution of other metal salts:
A metal will displace (take the place of) a less reactive metal in a metal salt solution.
For example,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mtext> Iron + Copper(II) sulphate </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> Iron sulphate + Copper. </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>↓</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Copper(II) sulphate is blue, iron sulphate is pale green in colour.
During the reaction the blue solution loses its colour and the iron metal is seen to turn pink-brown as the displaced copper becomes deposited on it.
If a less reactive metal is added to a metal salt solution, there will be no reaction - nothing will happen.
For example, iron is less reactive than magnesium.
Iron + Magnesium sulphate ⟶ No reaction
In these displacement reactions the metals are competing for the non-metal anion. Reactions using chlorides or nitrates can also be used.
The order of the metals in the reactivity series can be worked out by using these type of reactions.
For example, tin would be seen to displace lead from lead chloride but would not react with iron(II) chloride.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mtext> Tin </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> Lead chloride </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> Tin chloride </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> Lead </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mtext> Tin </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> Iron </mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext> chloride </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> No reaction </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> No reaction </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
Therefore, tin must be above lead but below iron in the reactivity series.
Copper would be seen to displace silver from silver nitrate but would not react with lead nitrate.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mtext> Copper </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> Silver nitrate </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> Copper nitrate </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> Silver </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mtext> Copper </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> Lead nitrate </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> No reaction </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> No reaction </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
Therefore, copper must be above silver but below lead in the reactivity series.
The arrangement of metals in the decreasing order of their activities is known as activity series. It is also known as reactivity series. A portion of this series is given as follows.
## THE REACTIVITY SERIES

theory_sections.topics: Reactivity Series (or Activity Series) of Metals

## OCCURRENCE OF METALS
The earth's crust is a very big source of the metals. Metals occur in nature sometimes free but mostly in combined state. Metals like silver, gold, platinum etc. occur in free or native state. Most of the metals are found in the form of the compounds in the nature. These naturally occuring compounds of metals are known as minerals. In certain minerals, the percentage of a particular metal is high and these metals can be extracted profitably and such minerals are called ores. The process of extraction of metals from their respective ores is called metallurgy.
The unwanted rocky, earthy or sandy materials almost always associated with ores as impurities are called gangue or matrix.

## CONNECTING TOPIC
Extraction of ore is a complex process which comprises various steps. So before studying the topic of extraction we should understand the general principles of metallurgy. Although we will study all these principles in detail in class XIIth, for your better understanding a summary is given here.

## GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF METALLURGY
Metallurgy is an art of extracting metals from the ores. The ores are generally associated with a number of impurities and earthy matter. The extraction of metals from ores involves various steps as discussed below :

## 1. Grinding or Pulverisation
The large pieces of ores are broken into small pieces with the help of hammer. These pieces are crushed with crusher and finally powdered in stamp mills. This powdered form of ore is used for further processes.

## 2. Concentration
The ores, obtained from ore mine contain various types of impurities. The removal of various types of impurities from ores is known as concentration. The process by which ore is concentrated depends on the type of ore and gangue. This concentration is carried out by using one or more of the following methods :
(a) Gravity separation or hydraulic washing : This method is based on the difference in the density of ore and the density of impurities. The ore is crushed and finely powdered, sieved and then levigated in a stream of water. The lighter impurities are carried away by the stream of water and heavier ore particles settle down. Ores of tin, lead and iron are concentrated by this process.

## Gravity separation method
(b) Froth floatation process : This process is used in the concentration of sulphide ores like galena ( PbS ), zinc blende (ZnS) etc. The well powdered ore (taken in a tank) is mixed with water to which an oil (pine oil or eucalyptus oil) has been added. The whole mass is agitated by a blast of air sent through pipe as shown in figure. The froth (containing impurities) floats on the surface of the water, while heavy ore particles settle down. The froth along with the ore is removed from the surface of the water.
Froth floatation process for the concentration of sulphide ores.
Froth stabilizers are those chemicals which stabilise the froth e.g. cresols and aniline.

## Collectors :
These compounds attach themselves by polar groups to grains of minerals which then become water repellent and thus pass on into the froth. Examples are ethyl xanthate and potassium ethyl xanthate.

## Activators and depressants :
These compounds activate or depress the floating property of one of the components of the ore and thus help in the separation of different minerals present in the same ore. Copper sulphate is an example of activator, while sodium and potassium cyanides are the examples of depressants.

## 3. Extraction of Metals
Metals are extracted from their concentrated ore by the reduction of metal oxides. The ore is converted to its oxide by one of following methods.
(a) Calcination : Calcination is the process of heating the ore in the presence of limited supply of air to a temperature insufficient to melt it. During calcination, moisture and volatile impurities are removed and the whole mass becomes porous. Here carbonates are converted into oxides by giving out carbon dioxide. Apart from carbonate ores, hydrated ores are also subjected to calcination for the removal of water of crystallization. Some examples are given below:
(i) The metal zinc and calcium are obtained from calamine <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and lime stone <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> respectively. When these ores are calcined, they are converted into oxides.

(ii) Haemetite <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is an ore of iron. Concentrated ore when calcined in a shallow kiln -
(1) Moisture and carbon dioxide are removed.
(2) Ferrous oxide present is oxidised to ferric oxide.
(3) Sulphur is removed as sulphur dioxide gas.
(4) The whole mass becomes porous.
(b) Roasting: It is a process which involves heating of ore in presence of excess of air. In this process, moisture and volatile impurities are removed. The ore itself is converted into oxides.
