exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q7
exercises.problem: Name two metals which can displace hydrogen from dilute acids and two metals which can not do so.
exercises.solution: Sodium and calcium can displace hydrogen from dilute acids as they lie above hydrogen in the reactivity series. Copper and silver can not displace hydrogen from dilute acids as they lie below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q8
exercises.problem: In the electrolytic refining of metal (M), name anode, cathode and electrolyte.
exercises.solution:
Anode : It is a rod or wire of impure metal M
Cathode : It is a rod or wire of pure metal M
Electrolyte : It is an aqueous solution of a soluble salt of the metal M.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q9
exercises.problem:
Pratyush took sulphur powder on a spatula and heated it. He collected the gas by inverting a test-tube over it as shown in the figure.
What will be the action of gas on
(a) dry litmus paper ?
(b) moist litmus paper ?
Write balanced chemical equation for the reaction taking place.
exercises.solution:
On heating sulphur will produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> (air) </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(a) It will not change the colour of dry litmus paper.
(b) It will change the colour of moist litmus paper from blue to red.
Note: The colour change of litmus paper is due to the formation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (sulphurous acid) by dissolution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q10
exercises.problem: State two ways to prevent rusting of iron.
exercises.solution:
The rusting of iron can be prevented by
(i) applying grease
(ii) applying paint
(iii) galvanisation (applying a thin coat of zinc)

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q11
exercises.problem: What type of oxides are formed when non-metals combine with oxygen ?
exercises.solution:
When non-metals combine with oxygen the oxides formed are either acidic or neutral e.g.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mo>→</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> neutral oxide </mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mo>→</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> acidic oxide </mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q12
exercises.problem:
Give reasons for the following:
(a) Platinum, silver and gold are used to make jewellery.
(b) Sodium, potassium and lithium are stored under oil.
(c) Aluminium is highly reactive metal but still used for making cooking utensils.
(d) Carbonate and sulphide ores are usually converted into oxides during the process of extraction.
exercises.solution:
(a) Platinum, silver and gold are very less reactive (found near the bottom in reactivity series) and are not affected by air, water or dil. acids. Because of
their low reactivity and their bright lustre, these metals are used for making jewellary.
(b) Sodium, potassium and lithium react with water (or moisture in air) producing a lot of heat along with evolution of hydrogen. As a result, the hydrogen gas thus produced catches fire. To avoid accidents these metals are not kept in air. They are kept under kerosene to avoid contact with air and water.
(c) When aluminium is exposed to air it reacts with oxygen (present in air) to form aluminium oxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. This <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> formed gets deposited on the surface of aluminium metal in the form of a thin coating which acts as a protective coating and due to its presence metal becomes unreactive. The formation of protective layer of aluminium oxide on the surface make highly reactive aluminium metal suitable for making cooking utensils.
(d) Since we can easily reduce the metal oxides to the metal using coke (C) or any other suitable reducing agent, so carbonates and sulphides are converted to the oxides form by process of roasting or calcination.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q13
exercises.problem: You must have seen tarnished copper vessels being cleaned with lemon or tamarind juice. Explain why these sour substances are effective in cleaning vessels.
exercises.solution: Copper metal reacts slowly with water, carbon dioxide and oxygen (all these present in air) and forms basic copper carbonate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> which gets deposited as a green layer on its surface. Lemon juice contains citric acid and tamarind juice contains tartaric acid. Both these juices which contain an acid react with basic copper carbonate to form soluble copper salts which are removed from the surface of copper metal and the surface of copper metal begins to shine.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q14
exercises.problem: Differentiate between metals and non-metals on the basis of their chemical properties.
exercises.solution:
Differences in chemical properties of metals and non-metals:
| Properties | Metals | Non-metals |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Nature of oxides | They generally form basic oxides which form alkalies with water. For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> Sodium hydroxide (alkali) | They form acidic oxides. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>8</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><mn>8</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> (acid) </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math> |
| Electrochemical nature | They are electropositive elements and form cation. They are liberated at cathode during electrolysis. Some metals like chromium \& manganese form some anions also with other elements like oxygen. | They are electronegative elements and form anions. They are liberated at the anode during electrolysis (exception: hydrogen). |
| Action of acids | They generally dissolve in mineral acids forming a salt with the evolution of a gas. For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | They either do not dissolve in mineral acids or form the corresponding oxyacids. For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><munderover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow /><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></munderover><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> |
| Solubility | They generally dissolve by a chemical reaction. | Many non-metals dissolve without any chemical change taking place. For example: chlorine, bromine or iodine dissolves in water. |

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q15
exercises.problem: A man went door to door posing as goldsmith. He promised to bring back the glitter on dull gold ornaments. An unsuspecting lady gave a set of gold bangles to him which he dipped in a particular solution. The bangles sparkled like new but their weight was reduced drastically. The lady got upset and after a futile argument, the man beat a hasty retreat. Can you predict the nature of solution used by the imposter?
exercises.solution: The man has used an aqua-regia solution (mixture of conc. HCl and conc. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in the ratio of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> by volume). Gold dissolves in aqua-regia and forms gold (III) chloride, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (auric chloride). Since, gold dissolves in aqua-regia, so a loss in mass of gold bangles occurred. Since the dull layer of gold was removed from its surface so there was original shine on the bangles. It is an excellent oxidant and highly corrosive.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q16
exercises.problem: Give reason as to why copper is used to make hot water tanks and not steel (an alloy of iron).
exercises.solution: Copper does not react easily with water unlike iron (constituent of steel) and it is better conductor of heat than steel so it can be used to heat the water uniformly. It is less efficient in conserving heat but this disadvantage is corrected with heat insulation.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q1
exercises.problem:
A student by mistake used a wet gas jar to collect sulphur dioxide. Which one of the following tests of the gas is likely to fail ?
(a) Odour
(b) Effect on acidified <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution
(c) Solubility test
(d) None of these

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q2
exercises.problem:
Silicon is used in :
(a) solar energy devices
(b) semiconductors
(c) transistors
(d) all of these
exercises.solution: (d) All are characteristics of metal.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q3
exercises.problem:
Which of the following is not a characteristics of metal ?
(a) Malleable
(b) Electropositive nature
(c) Ductile
(d) None of these

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q4
exercises.problem:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> (Steam) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, In the equation A and B are -
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></math> only

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Cuprous sulphide, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Cuprous oxide

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q41
exercises.problem:
The following observations are given for four metals:
[NTSE]
I. Metal H does not react with dilute HCl .
II. Metal K reacts with warm water.
III. Metal L does not react with water but displaces metal H from its aqueous salt solution.
IV. Metal M reacts with cold water.
Choose the correct decreasing order of reactivity of these metals amongst the following:
(a) M <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> L <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> H <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> K
(b) K <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> M <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> H <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> L
(c) M <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> K <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> L <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> H
(d) L <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> H <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> K <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> M
exercises.solution:
(c) Metals below hydrogen in a reactivity series does not react with dilute HCl . Medium reactive metals reacts with warm water and highly reactive metals react with cold water.
As per the given information <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> and M can be identified as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> respectively. So their reactivity order will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>></mo><mi>K</mi><mo>></mo><mi>L</mi><mo>></mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></math> i.e.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Directions — Q15
exercises.problem:
Among the following statements, the incorrect one is -
(a) Calamine and siderite are carbonates
(b) Argentite and cuprite are oxides
(c) Zinc blende and pyrites are sulphides
(d) Malachite and azurite are ores of copper
exercises.solution: The man has used an aqua-regia solution (mixture of conc. HCl and conc. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in the ratio of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> by volume). Gold dissolves in aqua-regia and forms gold (III) chloride, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (auric chloride). Since, gold dissolves in aqua-regia, so a loss in mass of gold bangles occurred. Since the dull layer of gold was removed from its surface so there was original shine on the bangles. It is an excellent oxidant and highly corrosive.

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Directions — Q16

(a) Cuprite
(b) Chalcocite
(c) Chalcopyrite
(d) Malachite
exercises.solution: Copper does not react easily with water unlike iron (constituent of steel) and it is better conductor of heat than steel so it can be used to heat the water uniformly. It is less efficient in conserving heat but this disadvantage is corrected with heat insulation.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(ii) Reduction: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

case_studies.title: CASE STUDY-1 : Properties of Metals
case_studies.description:
| Element | Symbol | Reactivity | Reaction with acids | Reaction with oxgen |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Potassium | K | Metals become more reactive | Metals displace hydrogen from acids with increasing vigour V | Metals above in the series forms more basic oxide |
| Sodium | Na | | | |
| Calcium | Ca | | | |
| Magnesium | Mg | | | |
| Carbon | C | | | |
| Zinc | Zn | | | |
| Iron | Fe | | | |
| Hydrogen | H | | | |
| Copper | Cu | | do not react with acids | |
| Silver | Ag | | | |
| Gold | Au | | | |
CASE III : Few metals like Na, Mg, Al and Zn reacts easily with dilute HCl whereas copper and silver do not react with dilute HCl or even with dilute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Why?
All those metals which are more reactive viz. lose electron more easily than hydrogen, displaces hydrogen from dilute acids to produce hydrogen gas. This happens because the more reactive metal gives electron easily and these electrons reduce the hydrogen ion of the acids to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas. So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math> or Zn gives electrons easily required for the reduction while Cu and Ag do not give electrons for the reduction. Therefore, Cu and Ag do not react with acids.
1. Generally, metals react with dil HCl or dil <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to give their chloride sulphates and when a metal reacts with dilute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas is not evolved. Why?
2. A zinc plate was dipped in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution. After certain time, iron from the solution was deposited on the zinc plate. State the reason why it happened. Write the chemical equation too.
CASE II : Potassium reacts violently with cold water to form KOH and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas. Ca and Mg has different reactivity with water, Ca forms <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> whereas <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> g does not react, it reacts only in hot condition. Metals like Al, Zn and Fe do not react with cold water or hot water. They react with steam to form a metal oxide and hydrogen. Why?

## OCCURRENCE OF METALS
The earth's crust is a very big source of the metals. Metals occur in nature sometimes free but mostly in combined state. Metals like silver, gold, platinum etc. occur in free or native state. Most of the metals are found in the form of the compounds in the nature. These naturally occuring compounds of metals are known as minerals. In certain minerals, the percentage of a particular metal is high and these metals can be extracted profitably and such minerals are called ores. The process of extraction of metals from their respective ores is called metallurgy.
The unwanted rocky, earthy or sandy materials almost always associated with ores as impurities are called gangue or matrix.

## CONNECTING TOPIC
Extraction of ore is a complex process which comprises various steps. So before studying the topic of extraction we should understand the general principles of metallurgy. Although we will study all these principles in detail in class XIIth, for your better understanding a summary is given here.
## GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF METALLURGY
Metallurgy is an art of extracting metals from the ores. The ores are generally associated with a number of impurities and earthy matter. The extraction of metals from ores involves various steps as discussed below :
## 1. Grinding or Pulverisation
The large pieces of ores are broken into small pieces with the help of hammer. These pieces are crushed with crusher and finally powdered in stamp mills. This powdered form of ore is used for further processes.
## 2. Concentration
The ores, obtained from ore mine contain various types of impurities. The removal of various types of impurities from ores is known as concentration. The process by which ore is concentrated depends on the type of ore and gangue. This concentration is carried out by using one or more of the following methods :
(a) Gravity separation or hydraulic washing : This method is based on the difference in the density of ore and the density of impurities. The ore is crushed and finely powdered, sieved and then levigated in a stream of water. The lighter impurities are carried away by the stream of water and heavier ore particles settle down. Ores of tin, lead and iron are concentrated by this process.
## Gravity separation method
(b) Froth floatation process : This process is used in the concentration of sulphide ores like galena ( PbS ), zinc blende (ZnS) etc. The well powdered ore (taken in a tank) is mixed with water to which an oil (pine oil or eucalyptus oil) has been added. The whole mass is agitated by a blast of air sent through pipe as shown in figure. The froth (containing impurities) floats on the surface of the water, while heavy ore particles settle down. The froth along with the ore is removed from the surface of the water.
Froth floatation process for the concentration of sulphide ores.
Froth stabilizers are those chemicals which stabilise the froth e.g. cresols and aniline.
## Collectors :
These compounds attach themselves by polar groups to grains of minerals which then become water repellent and thus pass on into the froth. Examples are ethyl xanthate and potassium ethyl xanthate.
## Activators and depressants :
These compounds activate or depress the floating property of one of the components of the ore and thus help in the separation of different minerals present in the same ore. Copper sulphate is an example of activator, while sodium and potassium cyanides are the examples of depressants.

## How NaCN acts as a depressant?
## SOLUTION :
NaCN when added to ore containing ZnS and PbS , it forms a complex with ZnS as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and prevent it from forming froth. PbS is then easily separated from ZnS .
(c) Electromagnetic separation : This method is used when either the ore or the gangue is magnetic in nature. For example, tin stone contains <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> as impurity. The powdered ore is dropped on a moving belt passing over two magnetic rollers. The magnetic impurities (like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) get collected in a heap nearer the magnetic rollers, while the ore (free from impurity) is collected in a heap, away from the magnetic rollers.
Some metals are attracted to magnet and can behave as a magnet. Thus Iron, cobalt and nickel are described as magnetic materials.
There are two types of permanent magnets those from "hard" magnetic materials and those from "soft" magnetic materials. Hard magnetic materials tend to stay magnetized over a long period while soft magnetic metals can be magnetized but lose their magnetism quickly.
(d) Leaching : It is a chemical method used for concentration of ore in which crude powdered ore is allowed to react with suitable reagent. Ore reacts with added reagent to form soluble complex while impurities remain undissolved. Insoluble impurities are separated by filtration and ore is reprecipitated from soluble complex.
Note : This process is used for concentration of Al, Ag, Au ores etc.
## 3. Extraction of Metals
Metals are extracted from their concentrated ore by the reduction of metal oxides. The ore is converted to its oxide by one of following methods.
(a) Calcination : Calcination is the process of heating the ore in the presence of limited supply of air to a temperature insufficient to melt it. During calcination, moisture and volatile impurities are removed and the whole mass becomes porous. Here carbonates are converted into oxides by giving out carbon dioxide. Apart from carbonate ores, hydrated ores are also subjected to calcination for the removal of water of crystallization. Some examples are given below:
(i) The metal zinc and calcium are obtained from calamine <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and lime stone <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> respectively. When these ores are calcined, they are converted into oxides.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></math>
(ii) Haemetite <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is an ore of iron. Concentrated ore when calcined in a shallow kiln -
(1) Moisture and carbon dioxide are removed.
(2) Ferrous oxide present is oxidised to ferric oxide.
(3) Sulphur is removed as sulphur dioxide gas.
(4) The whole mass becomes porous.
(b) Roasting: It is a process which involves heating of ore in presence of excess of air. In this process, moisture and volatile impurities are removed. The ore itself is converted into oxides.
## Examples :
(i) Zinc blende ( ZnS ), when roasted, is converted into zinc oxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(ii) Copper metal is extracted from copper pyrite ore. When this ore is roasted :
(1) Most of the sulphur is removed as sulphur dioxide.
(2) Arsenic and antimony are volatilised.
(3) Copper pyrite ore is converted into sulphides of iron and copper
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Partial oxidation of FeS and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow></mrow></math> also takes place
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></math>
Both calcination and roasting may be carried out in same reverberatory furnace. In calcination, air holes are partially or completely closed, while in roasting they are open.
## - Why sulphide ores are roasted first before reduction ?
## SOLUTION
It is because oxides of metals can be reduced more easily to free metals rather than sulphides of metals.
The differences between roasting and calcination are given below:
| Roasting | Calcination |
| :--- | :--- |
| 1. Heating in the presence of excess air. | 1. Heating in the presence of limited air. |
| 2. Roasting is applied on sulphide ores. | 2. Calcination is applied on carbonate ores. |
| 3. Sulphur dioxide is released. | 3. Carbon dioxide is released. |
| 4. Not used for dehydrating an ore. | 4. Can be used to drive out moisture from an ore. |
## 4. Reduction of Metal Oxides
(a) Smelting : Calcined or roasted ore is mixed with carbon or any other suitable reducing agent and flux, and heated strongly. Metal oxides are reduced to metal. Smelting is opposite of roasting which involves an oxidizing reaction.
Examples : When tin stone <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is heated strongly with carbon, tin metal is obtained.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>C</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
The zinc oxide obtained by calcination of zinc blende, when heated strongly with carbon gives zinc metal.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Similarly, lead metal is obtained by the reduction of lead oxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC CONNECTING TOPIC
- Carbon is good reducing agent for oxides but not for sulphides.
- Due to cheapness and high availability, carbon is widely used as a reducing agent. The process is known as carbon reduction. The metals which are less electropositive, do not form carbides with carbon, they are reduced by this method e.g. oxides of Ph, Fe, Zn, Sn etc.
- Below <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>710</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math> is better reducing agent than carbon and reverse is true at temperature higher than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>710</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
Flux :
Ores contain some fusible impurities. These impurities are removed by adding certain substances. These substances are called flux. The flux to be used depends on the nature of impurities. If acidic impurities (such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) are present, basic flux (e.g., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math> etc.) are mixed and if the impurities present are of basic nature the acidic flux are used.
Slag :
Fusible compounds, formed by the combination of flux and impurities are known as slag. For example, if ferrous oxide is present as impurity in a metal it may be removed by adding silica as a flux. Ferrous oxide is removed as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (slag).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Generally, slags possess melting points lower than the metals. The slags are generally lighter and hence floats on the surface of molten metals from where it can be skimmed off from time to time.
(b) Aluminothermic process :
There are certain metals whose oxides can not be reduced by carbon. These metals are extracted by aluminothermic process. The metal oxides are thoroughly mixed with aluminium powder and a little <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in a crucible. The reaction is brought about by introducing a lighted magnesium ribbon. Since the reaction is exothermic, temperature reaches to about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>3000</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>. Metals like chromium and manganese can be extracted by this method.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>3</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
The reaction between iron (II) oxide and aluminium is called thermite reaction. Commercially, it is used in welding of iron tracks. It was discovered by German chemist Dr. Hans Goldschmidt. In this reaction, iron oxide (rust) and aluminium metal powder undergo a redox (oxidation-reduction) reaction to form molten iron metal.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
In fact, thermite reaction has been used for underwater welding, joining railway tracks or cracked machine parts.
(c) Precipitation method :
Those metals which are more reactive tend to displace less reactive metals. If an iron rod is placed in a copper sulphate solution the copper metal is precipitated and iron goes in solution. Zinc is more reactive than silver and gold in reactivity series and hence it precipitates these metals from their salt solutions. This method is used in the extraction of silver and gold.
## 5. Refining of Metals
The metals obtained by anyone of the above methods are not pure. The metals are refined by the following methods :
(a) By liquation : This method is used for the easily fusible metals like tin etc. Impure metal is placed on the inclined bed of a furnace and heated. The metal melts and flows out leaving behind the impurities.
For example, purification of Sn containing impurities of high m.p. like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow></math>. It is also used for purification of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math> etc.
Purification of tin metal by liquation process
(b) By distillation : Volatile metals like Zn and Hg etc. can be purified by this method. When these metals are heated, their vapours are formed leaving behind the impurities. The vapours are condensed to get pure metals.
(c) By oxidation : If the impurities present in the metals can be easily oxidised, these are removed by this method. Molten metal is stirred thoroughly in the presence of air. The impurities float on the surface of the molten mass in the form of a scum which can be easily separated.
(d) Electrolytic refining : The impure metal is taken as anode and the cathode consists of a pure metal. Cathodes and anodes are placed in a soluble salt of the metal taken as an electrolyte. Pure metal is gradually deposited on the cathode and impurities either settle down or dissolved in the solution and collected as anode mud. Large number of metals like copper, silver, gold and zinc are purified by this method. The metal of highest purity are obtained by this method.
(e) Thermal decomposition method : In these methods, the metal is converted into suitable volatile compound which is decomposed at high temperature to give pure metal.
(i) Mond's process or carbonyl process (Purification of Ni) :
This method is used for the purification of nickel. Impure nickel is allowed to react with carbon monooxide at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>80</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>. It gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, which is a volatile compound. Vapours of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> decomposes at about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> giving pure Ni ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>99.9</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> purity).
(ii) van-Arkel process :
It is also known as iodide refining method. This method is used for obtaining metals of very high purity. Common metals which are refined by this method are Ti, Zr, Hf, Si etc. In this method, metal is converted into a volatile compound (e.g., iodides) which is decomposed to obtain pure metal. Impurities are left behind as they do not react with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Impure metal </mtext><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> Metal iodide </mtext><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Very high temp. </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mtext> Pure metal </mtext><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
## EXTRACTION OF METALS ON THE BASIS OF REACTIVITY SERIES
The reaction of metals or their position in activity series can also give a great idea about extraction of metals.
## Extraction of Metals Placed Low in the Activity Series
Metals that are low in the activity series are very unreactive. The oxides of these metals can be reduced to metals by heating alone. For example, mercury is obtained from its ore, cinnabar (HgS), by the process of heating.
## Reduction using heat :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Mercuric oxide </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover></mrow></mrow></math>
Copper can also be obtained in a similar manner from its sulphide ore <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
When concentrated cinnabar ore (HgS) is roasted the ore is converted to oxide. The reduction of cinnabar ore to oxide is a combination of roasting and reduction.
## Extraction of Metals Placed in the Middle of the Activity Series
Metals such as iron, zinc, lead, copper, etc., are present in the middle of the reactivity series. These are moderately reactive metals and are usually present as sulphides or carbonates. It is easier to reduce an oxide ore as compared to its sulphides and carbonates. If the ore is not an oxide ore, it is first converted to the oxide by the process of calcination or roasting.
Roasting : Sulphide ores are converted into oxides by heating strongly in presence of excess air, to form the corresponding oxides. Sulphur impurities escape as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas. For example,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi The zinc oxide is then reduced to zinc by a suitable reducing agent such as carbon.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Besides using carbon to reduce metal oxides to metals, highly reactive metals like sodium, calcium, aluminium etc. are also used as reducing agents because they can displace the metal of lower reactivity from their compounds, e.g. when manganese dioxide is heated with aluminium powder, the following reaction takes place.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mtext> Heat </mtext></mrow></math>
A great amount of heat is evolved in such reactions, hence metals are produced in the molten state.
Another example of this type of the reaction is the thermite reaction in which iron oxide reacts with aluminium to give iron and aluminium oxide evolving large amount of heat
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mtext> Heat </mtext></mrow></math>
## Extraction of Metals Placed at the Top of the Activity Series
Metals such as sodium, magnesium, calcium, aluminium present on the top of the reactivity series are very reactive and cannot be obtained from their compounds by heating with carbon. This is because these metals have more affinity for oxygen than for carbon. Such highly reactive metals are obtained by electrolytic reduction of fused chlorides, e.g. sodium from sodium chloride in a "Downs cell". Similarly, calcium is obtained by the reduction of fused calcium chloride.
At cathode :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
At anode :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
## STEPS INVOLVED IN THE EXTRACTION OF METALS FROM ORES
## CORROSION OF METALS
We have learnt that metals which are chemically active get corroded in presence of moist air. Corrosion is an oxidation reaction with atmospheric oxygen in the presence of water on the surface of a metal.
Rusting is the corrosion of iron on exposure to atmosphere.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Hydrated iron (III) oxide
Rusting is called as oxidation reaction because here iron gains oxygen <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>or iron atoms are losing electrons ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>→</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ). The equation is not need to be balanced and the amount of water ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ' is variable, from dry to soggy.
The major problem of corrosion occurs with iron (or steel) which is used as a structural material in industries like construction, infrastructure, bridges, rail transport, power transmission, ship building, automobiles, heavy industries etc.
Aluminium, another useful structural metal, also undergoes an oxidation reaction, but does not oxidize and corrode as quickly as its reactivity suggests.
- Iron corrodes more quickly than most other metals. Corrosion or rusting of iron is accelerated
Did You Know! in the presence of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and salt solution.
- Once a thin oxide layer of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> has formed on the surface of aluminium, it forms a barrier to oxygen and water to prevent further corrosion of aluminium.
Aluminium can be made harder, stronger and stiffer by mixing it with small amounts of other metals (e.g., magnesium) to make alloys. The alkali metals like sodium, used in chemistry laboratories and in some chemical industries, rapidly corrodes in air and needs to be stored under oil.
Copper and lead are both used in roofing solutions because neither is very reactive. The compounds formed on the surface do not flake away as easily as rust does from iron. Lead corrodes to a white lead oxide or carbonate and copper corrodes to form a basic green carbonate (combination of the hydroxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and carbonate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ).
In the past, both metals, copper and lead, have been used for piping but as lead is considered too toxic, copper is usually used. Non reactive metals like gold, platinum, mercury do not corrode.
Why people who live in coastal areas encounter more corrosion problems.
## SOLUTION
It is because the air in those areas is more humid and thus corrosion occurs faster in the presence of moisture.
## Prevention of Corrosion
Iron and steel (alloy of iron) are most easily protected by paint which provides a barrier between the metal and air/water. Moving parts of machines can be protected by a water repellent oil or grease layer. Covering the surface with enamel and lacquers is another method.
Did You
Know?
- Material selection is the first step to eliminate or minimize corrosion. The following rule can help as initial guidelines for materials selection for corrosion prevention concerns.
1. Avoid dissimilar metals to prevent galvanic corrosion.
2. Select materials with compact insulating oxide or passive layer such as stainless steel or aluminum.
3. Avoid the usage of materials with localized non uniform stresses by stress relief heat treatment process.
(a) Alloying :
Iron or steel along with other metals can also be protected by 'alloying' or mixing with other metals (e.g., chromium) to make non-rusting alloys. Stainless steel is an example of a non-rusting alloy of iron and carbon. Brass, an alloy of copper with zinc is less expensive and non reactive.
(b) Galvanizing :
Coating iron or steel with a thin zinc layer is called 'galvanizing'. A thin layer of Zn is deposited by electrolysis in which iron/steel object is dipped in molten zinc using Zn as cathode. Zinc preferentially corrodes or oxidizes to form a zinc oxide layer that does not flake off like iron oxide rust. However, if the coated surface is scratched, the zinc again corrodes.
(c) Electroplating :
Electroplating is very common method to coat surface of iron by another metal to prevent corrosion. The process is usually done from aqueous electrolytes at room temperature. It is one of the most popular method to prevent corrosion on steel. Chromium, nickel or aluminium are some common plating metals for corrosion protection.

CASE I : The highly reactive metals such as sodium is extracted by the electrolysis of their molten chloride. Aqueous solution of sodium chloride cannot be used in place of molten sodium chloride. Why?
Molten NaCl contains free <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions. Following two reactions take place at the two electrodes:
At cathode : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> (Reduction reaction)
At anode : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math>| (Negative electrode) |
| :--- |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>(Oxidation reaction) |
(Positive electrode)
During the electrolysis of a aqueous solution of NaCl , as soon as the sodium metal is formed at cathode, it will react with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> present in aqueous solution to form NaOH instead of sodium metal.
CASE II : In thermite process aluminium is used as a reducing agent instead of carbon while in case of reduction of ZnO, carbon is used instead of Al. Why?
When the reactivity of Zn and Fe is considered, Fe is less reactive than Zn. So strong reducing agent is required for iron oxide. During the thermite process large amount of heat is evolved, therefore this reaction is exothermic and is used in welding for joining the broken pieces of heavy iron objects.
Due to high reactivity, ZnO is easily reduced by carbon, hence, no need of Al. Aluminium is used as a reducing agent in those cases where the metal oxide is comparatively less reactive metal than zinc.

CASE III : General metallurgical process like (i) conversion of ore to oxide (ii) Refining (iii) Dressing of ore (iv) Extraction of metal (v) Concentration of ore, are used to find economically valuable metals. Arrange them in correct sequence and give the reason why these are selected for implementation? Metals are extracted from their ores through certain processes. The first is dressing of ore in this process, the racks of ore are broken down into small pieces and ground to powder. In order to remove gangue (in purities) second process that is called concentration of ore is used. This process increase the concentration of metal in the ore. After that ore is converted to oxide by using next step that is called conversion of ore to oxide. Generally two methods (roasting and calination) are used for this conversion. The oxide ores obtained from this process needs to be reduced to metal so extraction of metal is required. The metal so obtained in this process is not <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>100</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> pure and needs to be further purified. Thus, the proess that is called refining of ore is used. Therefore, correct sequence is (iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>→</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> iii <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

## NON-METALS
Seventeen elements are generally classified as non-metals; most are gases (hydrogen, helium, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, neon, chlorine, argon, krypton, xenon and radon) : and a few are solids (carbon, phosphorus, sulfur, selenium and iodine). Bromine is the only non-metal which is a liquid at room temperature.
All non-metals have following properties in common:
- They are dull.
- They are poor conductors of heat and electricity (they are insulators).
- They are weak and brittle (they easily break or shatter).
- They have a low density (they feel light for their size).
- They do not make a ringing sound when they are hit.
The most abundant non-metal in the earth's crust is oxygen, which constitutes about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>50</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> of the earth's crust. The next abundant non metal is silicon which constitutes about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>26</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> of the earth's crust.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Oxygen </mtext><mo>></mo><mtext> Silicon </mtext><mo>></mo><mtext> Phosphorus </mtext><mo>></mo><mtext> Sulphur </mtext></mrow></math>
Non-metals are major constituents of earth, air and oceans. Oxygen and nitrogen are the main constituents of air. Oxygen and silicon are the two major constituents of earth. Hydrogen and oxygen are the two major constituents of oceans.

Carbon in the form of graphite is the only non-metal which is a good conductor of electricity. Graphite is an allotrope of carbon and is used for making electrodes.

## Difference in physical properties of metals and non-metals
| Property | Metal | Non-metal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| State | They are solids at ordinary temperature and usually non-volatile (Exception: mercury which is a liquid) | They exist in all the three states, i.e. solid, liquid and gas. They are either gases or volatile liquids at low temperatures. (Exception: diamond and boron which are hard solids) |
| Density | Their density is generally high. | Their density is generally low. |
| Metallic lustre | They possess metallic lustre | Generally they do not possess metallic lustre. Exception: graphite and iodine |
| Malleability and ductility | They are malleable and ductile. They can be beaten into thin sheets and drawn into wires. Exception: Bi | They are neither malleable nor ductile. |
| Alloy formation | They form alloys with other metals and some non-metals | They do not form alloys (except carbon, silicon and phosphorus). |
| Thermal and electrical conductivity | They are good conductors of heat and electricity. Exception: lead which is a poor conductor of electricity. | They are poor conductors of heat and electricity. Exception: graphite and gas carbon |

| Property | Metal | Non-metal |

## HOW DO METALS AND NON-METALS REACT
In earlier classes we learnt that, noble gases have a completely filled valence shell and hence show little chemical activity. We can, therefore, explain the reactivity of elements as a tendency to attain a completely filled valence shell. Let us have a look at the electronic configuration of noble gases and some metals and non-metals.
A sodium atom has one electron in its outermost shell. If it loses the electron from its M shell then its L shell now becomes the outermost shell and has a stable octet. The nucleus of this atom still has 11 protons but the number of electrons has become 10 , so there is a net positive charge giving us a sodium cation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. On the other hand, chlorine atom has seven electrons in its outermost shell and requires one more electron to complete its octet. When sodium and chlorine react with each other, the electron is lost by sodium atom which could be taken up by chlorine atom. After gaining an electron, the chlorine atom gets a unit negative charge, because its nucleus has 17 protons and 18 electrons in its <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> and M shells. This gives us a chloride anion
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. So both of these elements can have a give-and-take relation between them as follows (Fig.).
Sodium and chloride ions, being oppositely charged, attract to each other and are held by strong electrostatic forces of attraction to exist as sodium chloride ( NaCl ).
It should be noted that sodium chloride does not exist as molecules but aggregates of oppositely charged ions.

## Formation of magnesium chloride
The compounds formed in this manner by the transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal are known as ionic compounds or electrovalent compounds and these ionic compounds exhibit electrostatic intermolecular forces.
## Properties of Ionic Compounds
(a) Physical nature : Ionic compounds are solids and are somewhat hard because of the strong forces of attraction between the positive and negative ions. These compounds are generally brittle and break into pieces when pressure is applied.
(b) Melting and Boiling points : Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points . This is because a considerable amount of energy is required to break the strong inter-ionic attraction.
