Because it stays solid at such high temperatures, magnesium oxide remains unconductive, and is used for hightemperature electrical insulation.
(c) Solubility : Electrovalent compounds are generally soluble in water (polar solvent) and insoluble in solvents such as kerosene, petrol, (nonpolar solvents) etc.
(d) Conduction of electricity : The conduction of electricity through an aqueous solution involves the movement of charged particles. A solution of an ionic compound in water contains ions, which move to the opposite electrodes when electricity is passed through the solution. Ionic compounds in the solid state do not conduct electricity because movement of ions in the solid state is not possible due to their rigid structure. But ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state. This is possible in the molten state since the elecrostatic forces of attraction between the oppositely charged ions overcomes due to the heat. Thus, the ions move freely and conduct electricity.

## METALLOIDS
Metalloids are those chemical elements that exhibit properties of both metals and non-metals. They behave as non-metals physically and chemically and show electrical conductivity like metals. However, they are not good conductors of electricity like metals and are known as semiconductors.
The concepts of metalloid and semiconductor should not be confused. Metalloid refers to the properties of certain elements in relation to the periodic table. Semiconductor refers to the physical properties of materials (including alloys, compounds) and there is only partial overlap between the two.
The following elements are generally considered as metalloids :
- Boron (B)
- Germanium (Ge)
- Antimony (Sb)
- Silicon (Si)
- Arsenic (As)
- Tellurium (Te)
- Polonium (Po)
Metalloids characteristics include ability to form amphoteric oxides and ability to behave as semiconductors and semimetals. The metalloids are placed between metals and non-metals in the periodic table. There are seven metalloids in the periodic table that are placed in Group 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17. They form a zig zag step line in the periodic table. They are separated from the metals and non-metals by a line called the 'amphoteric line'. Metalloids like boron, germanium, arsenic are used as dopants in semiconductor chips. Metalloids are usually brittle in nature and behave as electrical insulators at room temperature.
## Uses of Metalloids
- Boron is found in boric acid - a mild antiseptic and insect killer.
- Silicon is used in computers and other electronics and it is used to make rubbery cookware that does not stick to the food. Silicon is also used in making solar energy devices.
- Germanium is used in fiber optics.
- Arsenic can be used with gallium in semiconductors, but it is generally used as an insecticide.
- Antimony is used in batteries, antifriction alloys, cable sheathing, matches, medicines, antiprotozoan drugs, plumbing, soldering (some "lead-free" solders contain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>%</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ), and a couple of other things.
- Tellurium is used in ceramics, semiconductors, and blasting caps.
- Polonium is a very rare natural element. It is found in uranimum ores but it is uneconomical to extract it. These are used in antistatic devices and for research purposes.
Note : Boron, germanium and arsenic, all are used as a dopant in semiconductor chips.

A metal ' X ' displaces metal ' Y ' from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> aqueous solution. Which metal is more reactive ' X ' or ' Y '?
4. Name a non-metallic element which conducts electricity.
5. What are metalloids?
6. What is meant by galvanisation ?
7. Define gangue.
8. What is an amalgam ?
9. Which one of the following metals does not react with oxygen even at high temperatures ?
Calcium, Gold, Sodium
10. Name two metals which are both ductile as well as malleable.
11. Write the chemical equation for the reaction of hot aluminium with steam.
12. A green layer is gradually formed on a copper plate left exposed to air for a week in a bathroom. What could this green substance be ?
13. Name one non-metal and one metal which are in liquid state at room temperature.
14. Which one of the metal in the following metals is (a) most reactive (b) least reactive
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
15. Which chemical element is alloyed with copper to make bronze?
16. Name the main constituents of common brass.
17. Which two major constituents form the alloy duralumin?
18. Name the constituents of an alloy called German silver.
19. Choose a metal out of the following which reacts with hot water but not with cold water : Sodium, Magnesium, Iron
Mention the products formed during the reaction.
20. Choose the metal (from the list given below) which can displace zinc from zinc sulphate solution.
Lead, Copper, Magnesium, Silver.
Write the equation of the chemical reaction involved.
21. Which one is more reactive, Ag or Pt ?
22. Name two metals which can displace hydrogen from dilute HCl .
23. Write the chemical equation to represent the reaction taking place between sodium metal and cold water.
24. How is corrosion of iron prevented by coating it with a layer of oil?
25. Why do silver ornaments turn blackish after some time ?
## Short Answer Questions
## DIRECTIONS : Give answer in two or three sentences.
1. An atom X has seven valence electrons and another atom Y has two valence electrons. Write the formula of the compound formed between X and Y . Also predict the type of bond formed between them.
2. What happens when
(i) Iron nail is placed in silver nitrate solution.
(ii) Iron strip is dipped in zinc sulphate solution.
3. What is 24 carat gold ? How will you convert it into 18 carat gold ?
4. Name an ore of zinc other than zinc oxide. By what process can this ore be converted to zinc oxide.
5. What is the activity series of metals ? Rearrange the following metals in an increasing order of reactivity : Aluminium, Zinc, Mercury.
6. Write chemical equations for the reactions taking place when :
(i) Zinc sulphide is heated in air.
(ii) Reduction of lead oxide by carbon
7. Define the term 'alloy'. Write two advantages of making alloys.
8. Give reasons for each of the following :
(i) Germanium is called a metalloid.
(ii) Gold is known as a precious metal.
9. Give reasons why metals conduct electricity.
10. Write chemical equations to show the reactions taking place when :
(i) Zinc carbonate is calcined.
(ii) Carbon dioxide gas is bubbled into lime water for a long time.
11. State three reasons for counting sulphur amongst the non-metals.
12. Explain how the following metals are obtained from their compounds by the reduction process :
(a) Metal X, which is low in reactivity series.
(b) Metal Y, which is middle of the series.
(c) Metal Z, which is high up in the reactivity series.
13. How does the term ore differ from mineral? Give an example.
14. What are the three major steps involved in extraction of a metal after its ore is mined?
15. A metal X combines with a non-metal Y by the transfer of electrons to form a compound Z .
(i) State the type of bond in compound Z .
(ii) What can you say about the melting point and boiling point of compound Z ?
(iii) Will this compound dissolve in kerosene or petrol?
(iv) Will this compound be a good conductor of electricity?
16. Write one example of each of the following :
(i) Most malleable metal and most ductile metal.
(ii) The best conductor of heat and the poorest conductor of heat.
(iii) A metal with highest melting point and a metal with lowest melting point.
17. (i) A non-metal X exists in two different forms Y and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> is the hardest natural substance whereas Z is a good conductor of electricity. Identify <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> \& Z .
(ii) Anelement X , onreactionwithoxygen forms anoxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. The oxide when dissolved in water turns blue litmus red. State whether element X is a metal or a non-metal.
(iii) Name the metal which is alloyed with copper to make bronze.
18. A metal ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> ' is found in nature as its carbonate. It is used in the galvanization of iron. Identify ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> ' and name its ore. How will you convert this ore into free metal?
19. What is cinnabar? How is a metal extracted from cinnabar? Explain briefly.
## Long Answer Questions
1. Give reason for the following :
When a piece of copper metal is added to a solution of zinc sulphate, no change takes place, but the blue colour of copper sulphate fades away when a piece of zinc is placed in its solution.
2. Which of the following metals can displace hydrogen from hydrochloric acid solution? Write appropriate equations for reaction that occurs.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Also write a short note on active metals which can displace hydrogen from water.
3. Name the following:
(i) A metal that catches fire in open air and gives off white fumes.
(ii) A metal that forms two types of oxides and rusts in moisture; write their formulae also.
(iii) A metal used in stainless steel.
(iv) A metal used in long distance cable wires.
(v) A metal added to gold to harden it.
4. (i) Explain the process electrolytic refining.
(ii) Differentiate between the roasting and calcination processes used in metallurgy. Give an example of each.
5. Why does metal not evolve hydrogen gas with nitric acid?
6. (i) Write the steps involved in the extraction of pure metals in the middle of the activity series from their carbonate ores.
(ii) How is copper extracted from its sulphide ore? Explain the various steps supported by chemical equations. Draw labelled diagram for the electrolytic refining of copper.
7. Give reasons for the following:
(i) Most metals conduct electricity well.
(ii) The reaction of iron oxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> with heated aluminium is used to join cracked machine parts.
8. List in tabular form three chemical properties on the basis of which we can differentiate between a metal and a non-metal.
9. Write balanced chemical equations to explain what happens, when
(i) Mercuric oxide is heated.
(ii) Mixture of cuprous oxide and cuprous sulphide is heated.
(iii) Aluminium is reacted with manganese dioxide.
(iv) Ferric oxide is reduced with aluminium.
(v) Zinc carbonate undergoes calcination.
## Reasoning Based Questions
1. Explain why the surface of some metals acquire dull appearance when exposed to air for a long time ?
2. Why are metals highly electropositive in nature ?
3. Why does zinc liberate hydrogen gas when it reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid but copper does not?
4. Why is an ionic bond also called an electrovalent bond ?
5. Why is sulphide ore converted to its oxide before reduction?
6. Why a salt which does not conduct electricity in the solid state becomes a good conductor in molten state ? Explain.
7. Explain why, the galvanised iron article is protected against rusting even if the zinc layer is broken.
8. An iron knife kept dipped in a blue copper sulphate solution, colour of solution changes to light green. Why?
9. Articles made of aluminium do not corrode even though aluminium is an active metal.
10. Why do gold ornameants look new even after several years of use ?
11. Why does aluminium not react with water under ordinary conditions.
12. Hydrogen is not metal but still it has been assigned a place in the reactivity series of metal why?
13. When calcium metal is added to water, the gas evolved close not catch fire but same gas evolved on adding sodium metal to water catches fire. why?
14. Why, a solution of cane sugar does not conduct electricity but a solution of common salt is a good conductor of electricity.
15. Why are ionic compounds usually hard?
## HOTS Questions
1. A copper plate was dipped into a solution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. After sometime, a black layer was deposited on the copper plate. State the reason for it. Write the chemical equation of the reaction involved.
2. The oxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is unaffected by water. Outline a method by which a sample of metal X can be obtained from its ore. Give one reason as to why have you chosen this method.
3. Give reasons for the following :
(i) Silicon is considered as metalloids.
(ii) Carbon is not used for extraction of aluminium from aluminium oxide.
(iii) For producing hydrogen gas by reaction with hydrochloric acid, granulated zinc is preferred over block of zinc.
4. Give reasons for the following :
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> and Ca metals form hydrides by combination with hydrogen gas, but most other metals do not.
(ii) Zinc oxide is called an amphoteric oxide.
5. (a) What is corrosion of metals ? Name one metal which does not corrode and one which corrodes on being kept open.
(b) How will you show that the rusting of iron needs oxygen and moisture at the same time ?
6. Which of the following combinations would result in a displacement reaction? Write appropriate equations for any reactions that occurs.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi></mrow></math>
7. Metals replace hydrogen from acid, whereas non-metals do not. Why?

case_studies.title: Case Study Based MCQs
case_studies.description:
1. Read the following and answer any four questions from (i) to (v).
Elements can be classified as metals or non-metals on the basis of their properties. The easiest way to start grouping substances is by comparing their physical properties. Metals, in their pure state, have a shining surface. This property is called metallic luster. metals are generally hard. The hardness varies from metal to metal. some metals are used for making cooking vessels.
(i) Metals generally are
(a) reducing agents
(b) oxidising agent
(c) both oxidising and reducing agents
(d) None of these
(ii) The most abundant metal in the earth's crust is -
(a) iron
(b) copper
(c) aluminium
(d) mercury
(iii) The metal that reacts with cold water is -
(a) mercury
(b) sodium
(c) zinc
(d) tungsten
(iv) Metal present in chloroplast is
(a) Iron
(b) Copper
(c) Magnesium
(d) Cobalt
(v) Which of the following metal(s) catch fire on reaction with water?
(a) Sodium
(b) Potassium
(c) Magnesium
(d) both (a) and (b)
## Exercise 2 Master NCERT (Textbook \& Exemplar)
## Text - Book Questions
1. Give example of a metal which
(a) is liquid at room temperature.
(b) can be easily cut with knife.
(c) is the best conductor of heat.
(d) is the poorest conductor of heat.
2. Explain the meaning of malleable and ductile.
3. Why is sodium kept immersed in kerosene oil ?
4. Write the equations for the reactions of
(a) iron with steam
(b) calcium with water
(c) potassium with water
5. You are provided with following information :
| Metal | Solution to which metal is added | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | Iron (II) sulphate | Copper (II) sulphate | Zinc sulphate | Silver nitrate |
| A | No reaction | Displacement | - | - |
| B | Displacement | - | No reaction | - |
| C | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction | Displacement |
| D | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction |
Answer the following questions.
(a) Which is the most reactive metal ?
(b) What would you observe when B is added to solution of copper (II) sulphate ?
(c) Arrange the metals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and D in order of increasing reactivity.
6. Which gas is produced when a reactive metal reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid ? Write the chemical reaction when iron reacts with dilute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
7. What would you observe when zinc is added to a solution of iron (II) sulphate ? Write chemical equation that takes place.
8. Metallic oxides of zinc, magnesium and copper were heated with zinc, Mg and Cu . In which case the displacement reaction will take place ?
| Metals oxide | Zinc | Magnesium | Copper |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Zinc oxide | | | |
| Magnesium oxide | | | |
| Copper oxide | | | |
9. (i) Write electron-dot structures for sodium, magnesium and oxygen.
(ii) Show the formation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> and MgO by transfer of electrons.
(iii) What are the ions present in these compounds?
10. Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
11. Define the following terms :
(i) minerals
(ii) ores
(iii) gangue
12. Name two metals which are found in free state in nature?
13. What chemical process is used for obtaining a metal from its oxide ?
14. Which metals do not corrode easily ?
15. What are alloys?
## Text - Book Exercise
1. Which of the following will give displacement reactions?
(a) NaCl solution and copper metal
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution and aluminium metal
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution and silver metal
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution and copper metal
2. Which of the following methods is suitable for preventing an iron frying pan from rusting?
(a) Applying grease
(b) Applying paint
(c) Applying a coat of zinc
(d) All the above
3. An element can react with oxygen to give a compound with high melting point. This compound is also water soluble. The element is likely to be
(a) Calcium
(b) Carbon
(c) Silicon
(d) Iron
4. Food cans are coated with tin and not with zinc because
(a) zinc is costlier than tin.
(b) zinc has higher melting point than tin.
(c) zinc is more reactive than tin.
(d) zinc is less reactive than tin.
5. You are given a hammer, a battery, a bulb, wire and a switch:
(a) How would you use them to distinguish between samples of metals and non-metals ?
(b) Assess the usefulness of these tests to distinguish between metals and non-metals.
6. What are amphoteric oxides ? Give examples of two amphoteric oxides.
7. Name two metals which can displace hydrogen from dilute acids and two metals which can not do so.
8. In the electrolytic refining of metal (M), name anode, cathode and electrolyte.
9. Pratyush took sulphur powder on a spatula and heated it. He collected the gas by inverting a test-tube over it as shown in the figure.
What will be the action of gas on
(a) dry litmus paper ?
(b) moist litmus paper ?
Write balanced chemical equation for the reaction taking place.
10. State two ways to prevent rusting of iron.
11. What type of oxides are formed when non-metals combine with oxygen ?
12. Give reasons for the following:
(a) Platinum, silver and gold are used to make jewellery.
(b) Sodium, potassium and lithium are stored under oil.
(c) Aluminium is highly reactive metal but still used for making cooking utensils.
(d) Carbonate and sulphide ores are usually converted into oxides during the process of extraction.
13. You must have seen tarnished copper vessels being cleaned with lemon or tamarind juice. Explain why these sour substances are effective in cleaning vessels.
14. Differentiate between metals and non-metals on the basis of their chemical properties.
15. A man went door to door posing as goldsmith. He promised to bring back the glitter on dull gold ornaments. An unsuspecting lady gave a set of gold bangles to him which he dipped in a particular solution. The bangles sparkled like new but their weight was reduced drastically. The lady got upset and after a futile argument, the man beat a hasty retreat. Can you predict the nature of solution used by the imposter?
16. Give reason as to why copper is used to make hot water tanks and not steel (an alloy of iron).
## Exemplar Questions
1. Iqbal treated a lustrous, divalent element M with sodium hydroxide. He observed the formation of bubbles in reaction mixture. He made the same observations when this element was treated with hydrochloric acid. Suggest how can he identify the produced gas. Write chemical equations for both the reactions.
2. A non-metal A is an important constituent of our food and forms two oxides B and C. Oxide B is toxic, whereas C causes global warming.
(i) Identify <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and C .
(ii) To which group of periodic table does A belong?
3. An alkali metal A gives a compound B (molecular mass <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> on reacting with water. The compound B gives a soluble compound C on treatment with aluminium oxide. Identify <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and C and give the reaction involved.
4. Of the three metals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> reacts with cold water, Y with hot water and Z with steam only. Identify X , Y and Z and also arrange them in order of increasing reactivity.
5. A non-metal A which is the largest constituent of air, when heated with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in 1:3 ratio in the presence of catalyst ( Fe ) gives a gas B . On heating with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> it gives an oxide C . If this oxide is passed into water in the presence of air it gives an acid D which acts as a strong oxidising agent.
(i) Identify <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and D
(ii) To which group of periodic table does this nonmetal belong?
## Exercise 3
## Multiple Choice Questions
DIRECTIONS : This section contains multiple choice questions. Each question has four choices (a), (b), (c) and (d) out of which ONLY ONE is correct.
1. A student by mistake used a wet gas jar to collect sulphur dioxide. Which one of the following tests of the gas is likely to fail ?
(a) Odour
(b) Effect on acidified <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution
(c) Solubility test
(d) None of these
2. Silicon is used in :
(a) solar energy devices
(b) semiconductors
(c) transistors
(d) all of these
3. Which of the following is not a characteristics of metal ?
(a) Malleable
(b) Electropositive nature
(c) Ductile
(d) None of these
4. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> (Steam) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, In the equation A and B are -
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></math> only
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
5. Removal of impurities from ore is known as -
(a) crushing and grinding
(b) concentration of ore
(c) calcination
(d) roasting
6. Froth floatation method is used for the concentration of-
(a) oxide ores
(b) sulphide ores
(c) sulphate ores
(d) halide ores
7. Heating of concentrated ore in absence of air for conversion into oxide ore is known as -

Some metals are chemically very reactive, whereas others are less reactive or unreactive. On the basis of vigourness of reactions of various metals with oxygen, water and acids, as well as displacement reactions, the metals have been arranged in a group or series according to their chemical reactivity. The arrangement of metals in a vertical column in the order of decreasing reactivities is called reactivity series of metals (or activity series of metals). In reactivity series, the most reactive metal is placed at the top whereas the least reactive metal is placed at the bottom. As we come down in the series, the chemical reactivity of metals decreases. Since the metals placed at the bottom of the reactivity series (like silver and gold) are less reactive, so they are usually found in free state (native state) in nature.

## Reasoning Based Questions
1. Due to the formation of a thin layer of oxide, carbonate or sulphide on the surface some metal acquires dullness. For example, silver on exposure to air acquire a blackish tinge due to the formation of silver sulphide.
2. Metals are electropositive elements because they lose electrons very easily to form positively charged ions.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>→</mo><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></math>
3. Zn is above hydrogen while copper is below hydrogen in the activity series of metals. Therefore, zinc displaces hydrogen from dilute HCl while copper does not.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>→</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>→</mo><mtext> No reaction </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
4. An ionic bond is also called as electrovalent bond because of the involvement of electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions in the formation of ionic bond.
5. It is because oxygen can be easily removed from metal oxides by reacting it with carbon or aluminium or by electrolytic reduction, sulphur cannot be removed from metal sulphides easily.
6. In solid state, ionic compounds do not conduct electric current because the ions are held together in fixed positions by strong electrostatic forces and cannot move freely. When ionic solid is dissolved in water or melted, the crystal structure is broken down and ions become free to move and conduct electricity.
7. The galvanised iron article remains protected against rusting even if the zinc layer is broken because zinc is more easily oxidised than iron. So when zinc layer on the surface of galvanised iron article is broken, then zinc continues to corrode but iron article does not corrode or rust.
8. Iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution as it lie above copper in reactivity series and forms ferrous sulphate solution which is light green.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> (Blue) </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> (Light green) </mtext></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
9. It is because oxide layer is formed on the surface of aluminium due to which it does not react further because it is non-penetrating layer.
10. Gold is highly unreactive metal which remains unaffected by air, water vapour and other gases in this atmosphere. So gold does not corrode. That is why gold ornaments look new even after several years of use.
11. Aluminium does not react with water at ordinary temperature due to the presence of a thin but strong layer of aluminium oxide on its surface.
12. Hydrogen is not a metal but like metal it loses electrons and forms positive ions, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Therefore, it has been assigned a place in the reactivity series.
13. Calcium reacts with water to produce calcium hydroxide and hydrogen gas. The heat produced during the reaction is not sufficient to burn the hydrogen gas.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Sodium reacts vigorously with water to produce sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Large amount of heat is produced during the reaction which causes ignition of hydrogen gas.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> Heat
14. Common salt is an ionic solid. When ionic solid is dissolved in water, its crystal structure is break down and ions become free to move and conduct electricity. Cane sugar is a covalent compound therefore in its aqueous solution ions are not present hence do not conduct electricity.
15. Ionic compounds consists of oppositely charged ions and they attract each other very strongly. It forms a regular crystal structure. Therefore, ionic compounds are usually hard.
## HOTS Questions
1. The black layer was deposited on copper due to deposition of silver metal on it.
2. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is unaffected by water. It must be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. ' X ' is obtained from its ore by electrolytic reduction because aluminium itself is good reducing agent and cannot be obtained from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> by chemical reduction.
3. (i) Silicon is a metalloid because its properties resembles both with metals as well as non-metals.
(ii) Aluminium is stronger reducing agent than carbon, therefore, carbon cannot be used for extraction of Al from its oxide.
(iii) Granulated zinc has more surface area than block of zinc metal, therefore, it is used for preparation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas.
4. (i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> and Ca are strongly electropositive, therefore, they form hydrides with hydrogen.
(ii) Zinc oxide reacts with both acids as well as bases, therefore, it is called an amphoteric oxide.
5. (a) Corrosion is a process in which metal reacts with air and moisture from the atmosphere along with some dilute acid to produce coating on its surface. Iron corrodes readily when placed in open atmosphere whereas aluminium does not corrode easily.
(b) Take three test tubes and put iron nails in each of them. In the first test tube add <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> up to brim and leave no space for air. In the second test tube add fused <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> so as to absorb moisture. In the third test tube add water and leave space for air. Leave them for few days. Rusting will not take place in first and second test tubes. But rusting will take place in third test tube showing that rusting of iron requires both air and moisture.
6. The activity of the halogens decreases from top to bottom in the periodic table. Br is above I and Cl is above Br in the periodic table. Therefore, neither combination (a) nor combination (c) could result in reaction. Cl is above I in the periodic table, and so combination (b) results in a displacement reaction.
The more active halogen, chlorine, displaces the less active halogen, iodine from its compounds.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
7. Non-metals cannot supply electrons to convert <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> whereas metals can give electrons for conversion.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>→</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## Master NCERT (Textbook \& Exemplar)
## Text - Book Questions
1.
(a) Mercury (Hg)
(b) Sodium (Na)
(c) Silver (Ag)
(d) Lead (Pb)
2. Malleable : The property by virtue of which a substance can be beaten into sheets is known as malleability. The
substance that shows the property of malleability is known as malleable substance. Metals are malleable in nature.
Ductile : The property by virtue of which a substance can be drawn into wires is known as ductility. A substance that shows the property of ductility is known as ductile. Metals are ductile in nature.
3. Sodium is a very reactive metal. It reacts with air and water. If kept open in air it reacts readily with oxygen (present in air) to form sodium oxide. It also reacts with water (moisture present in air) to form sodium hydroxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
To preserve sodium metal, it is generally kept under kerosene oil so that neither air nor moisture may come in contact with metal.
4. (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> steam <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
5. In the reactivity series we find that order of reactivity of metals present in the salt solutions is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> Ag. Thus we can say that by looking at the information provided in the table, we can conclude that
(i) Metal A is more reactive than copper as it displaces copper from copper (II) sulphate and is less reactive than iron as it fails to displace iron from iron (II) sulphate.
(ii) Metal B is more reactive than iron and less reactive than zinc.
(iii) Metal C is more reactive than silver and less reactive than other metals (i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and Zn ).
(iv) Metal D is least reactive.
Thus
(a) The most reactive metal is B .
(b) Since B is more reactive than iron so it is also more reactive than copper hence it will displace copper from copper (II) sulphate solution. The blue colour of copper (II) sulphate solution will slowly fade.
(c) The arrangement of metals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and D in decreasing order of reactivity is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>></mo><mi>A</mi><mo>></mo><mi>C</mi><mo>></mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>.
6. When a reactive metal reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, the gas produced is hydrogen <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
Iron and dilute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> react to produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
7. The green colour of iron (II) sulphate solution will disappear. Zinc will gradually dissolve and iron will get precipitated at the bottom of the container.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

case_studies.description:
1. Solder is an alloy of tin and lead. Lead is used in making car batteries that means lead is metal C whereas tin is metal B.
Metals A and D are Zn and Fe because Zn is used to prevent Fe from corrosion.
2. In this process, cathode is attached to the negative terminal of the battery so it is negatively charged whereas anode is attached to the positive terminal of the battery so it has positive charge. During electrolysis, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> used as an electrolyte reaches the cathode and get reduced by receiving electrons from the cathode terminal.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Cathode : </mtext><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mtext> Copper metal </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
Resulted copper metal is deposited on the cathode. The impure anode is oxidised to the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ions by leasing electrons hence anode is dissolved into the electrolyte.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Anode </mtext><mi>:</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Therefore, the pure metal from the impure anode dissolves into the electrolyte that means it becomes thinner and thinner whereas an equivalent amount of pure metal from the electrolyte is deposited on the cathode that means it becomes thicker and thicker.

examples.problem: ## Why cutting tools are generally made up of metals ?
examples.solution:
This is because of hard and strengthful character of metal.
Take pieces of iron, copper and aluminium, the three common metals you came across very often in routine life. Now place first piece of iron on hard steel blog and hammer it with full power. Notice change in shape if any. Now place pieces of copper and aluminium on steel blog and hammer it in a similar manner and record your observations. What conclusion will you obtain about physical nature of metals?
Noble metals : Noble metals are those metals which are resistant to corrosion or oxidation, unlike most base metals. They are referred to noble metals, often due to their inertness. Examples include tantalum, gold, platinum, and rhodium. Precious metals: A precious metal is a rare metallic chemical element of high economic value. Chemically, the precious metals are less reactive than most elements, they have high lustre and high electrical conductivity. Historically, precious metals were important as currency, but are now regarded mainly as investment and industrial commodities. The best-known precious metals are gold and silver. While both have industrial uses, they are better known for their uses in art, jewellery, and coinage. Other precious metals include the platinum group metals: ruthenium, rhodium, palladium, osmium, iridium, and platinum, of which platinum is the most widely traded.
Base metals : In chemistry, the term 'base metal' is used informally to refer to a metal that oxidizes or corrodes relatively easily, and reacts variably with dilute hydrochloric acid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> to form hydrogen. Examples include iron, nickel, lead and zinc. Copper is considered as a base metal because it oxidizes relatively easily, although it does not react with HCl .
Ferrous metals : The term "ferrous" is derived from the latin word meaning "containing iron". This can include pure iron, such as wrought iron, or an alloy such as steel. Ferrous metals are often magnetic in nature.

Why potassium bromide (KBr) is non conducting in solid state but it conducts electricity in molten state or in aqueous solution.
examples.solution:
KBr is an ionic compound with high melting point. In solid state, movement of ions is not possible due to rigid structure. But in molten state or in aqueous solution electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions is less, thus, conduct electricity due to movement of ions.
Some common items you came across at home or in your chemistry lab are table salt, vinegar, sugar, marble, blue vitrol, potassium ferrocyanide, dilute hydrochloric acid, gelatine, alcohol and baking soda. Now classify ionic compound (s) out of these items. Also provide reasons to support your answer that why have you classified those compounds in category of ionic compounds.

examples.problem:
Give reason for the following :
When a piece of copper metal is added to a solution of zinc sulphate, no change takes place, but the blue colour of copper sulphate fades away when a piece of zinc is placed in its solution.
examples.solution:
(i) It is because copper is less reactive than Zn , therefore, it cannot displace Zn from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi></mrow></math> No reaction
But when Zn is dipped in copper sulphate solution, it displaces copper from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> which is colourless. Reddish brown copper metal gets precipitated because Zn is more reactive than Cu.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
