examples.solution:
The activity series of the metals, tells us that copper and silver do not displace hydrogen from solutions of acids. Aluminum is an active metal that can displace <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> from HCl and form aluminium chloride.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Very active metals can even displace hydrogen from water. However, such reactions of very active metals of Group IA are dangerous because they generate enough heat to cause explosive ignition of the hydrogen. The reaction of potassium, or another metal of Group IA, with water is also a displacement reaction:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q3
examples.problem:
Name the following:
(i) A metal that catches fire in open air and gives off white fumes.
(ii) A metal that forms two types of oxides and rusts in moisture; write their formulae also.
(iii) A metal used in stainless steel.
(iv) A metal used in long distance cable wires.
(v) A metal added to gold to harden it.
examples.solution:
(i) The metal that catches fire in open air and gives off white fumes is sodium.
(ii) The metal that forms two types of oxides and rusts in moisture is iron. The formulas of its oxides are: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mi>;</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
(iii) The metal used in stainless steel is chromium besides iron and carbon as it increases corrosion resistance character of steel.
(iv) The metal used in long distance cable wires is aluminium, because it is a light metal and a very good conductor of electricity.
(v) The metal added to gold to harden, is copper.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q4
examples.problem:
(i) Explain the process electrolytic refining.
(ii) Differentiate between the roasting and calcination processes used in metallurgy. Give an example of each.
examples.solution:
(i) Electrolytic refining : The impure metal is taken as anode and the cathode consists of a pure metal. Cathodes and anodes are placed in a soluble salt of the metal taken as an electrolyte. Pure metal gradually passes on to the cathode and impurities either settles down or dissolved in the solution called anode mud. Large number of metals like copper, silver, gold and zinc are purified by this method. The metal of highest purity are obtained by this method.
(ii) Roasting is a process in which ore is heated in presence of oxygen so as to convert it into oxide, e.g.,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Calcination is a process in which ore is heated in absence of air, e.g.,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> heat </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q5
examples.problem: Why does metal not evolve hydrogen gas with nitric acid?
examples.solution:
When metal reacts with nitric acid, hydrogen gas is not evolved. It is because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is a strong oxidising agent. It oxidises <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to produce water and itself reduced to any of the oxides of nitrogen ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ).
For example,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>&</mi><mn>8</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q6
examples.problem:
(i) Write the steps involved in the extraction of pure metals in the middle of the activity series from their carbonate ores.
(ii) How is copper extracted from its sulphide ore? Explain the various steps supported by chemical equations. Draw labelled diagram for the electrolytic refining of copper.
examples.solution:
(i) Extraction of Zn
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
(ii) Copper is found as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow></mrow></math> in nature and can be obtained from its ore just by heating in air.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><munderover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></munderover></mrow></math>
(2) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>6</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Step - 1 is the heating of sulphide ore of copper in the presence of excess of air. This process is known as roasting.
Step - 2 is the self reduction of copper.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q7
examples.problem:
Give reasons for the following:
(i) Most metals conduct electricity well.
(ii) The reaction of iron oxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> with heated aluminium is used to join cracked machine parts.
examples.solution:
(i) Metals are electropositive elements. They can easily lose electrons to form ions.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
These electrons are relatively free to move. Due to mobility of electrons most metals conduct electricity.
(ii) The reaction of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> with heated alumina is known as thermite
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> Heat The reaction is highly exothermic. In the reaction aluminium acts as reducing agent and reduces <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to Fe and itself oxidises to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Due to large amount of heat produced, the iron is produced in molten state. Molted iron is used to join cracked machine parts.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q8
examples.problem: List in tabular form three chemical properties on the basis of which we can differentiate between a metal and a non-metal.
examples.solution:
Difference between metal and a non-metal -
| | Metal | Non-metal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. | They react with oxygen to form basic oxides, which forms alkalies with water, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></math> | They react with oxygen to form acidic or neutral oxides. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> |
| 2. | They are electropositive elements and form cation. They are liberated at cathode during electrolysis. | They are electronegative elements and form anions. They are liberated at the anode during electrolysis. |
| 3. | They generally dissolve in mineral acids forming a salt with the evolution of hydrogen gas. e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | They either do not dissolve in mineral acids or form the corresponding oxy acids. e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> |

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q9
examples.problem:
Write balanced chemical equations to explain what happens, when
(i) Mercuric oxide is heated.
(ii) Mixture of cuprous oxide and cuprous sulphide is heated.
(iii) Aluminium is reacted with manganese dioxide.
(iv) Ferric oxide is reduced with aluminium.
(v) Zinc carbonate undergoes calcination.
examples.solution:
(i) Mercuric oxide decomposes to mercury and oxygen gas on heating.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(ii) When cuprous oxide is heated with cuprous sulphide, copper metal is obtained.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(iii) When manganese dioxide reacts with aluminium then it results into the formation of aluminium trioxide and manganese.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(iv) When Ferric oxide is heated with aluminium, iron metal is obtained.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(v) When zinc carbonate is heated in calcination process it converted to zinc oxide then it can be easily converted to metal.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>→</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q1
examples.problem: Explain why the surface of some metals acquire dull appearance when exposed to air for a long time ?
examples.solution: Due to the formation of a thin layer of oxide, carbonate or sulphide on the surface some metal acquires dullness. For example, silver on exposure to air acquire a blackish tinge due to the formation of silver sulphide.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q2
examples.problem: Why are metals highly electropositive in nature ?
examples.solution:
Metals are electropositive elements because they lose electrons very easily to form positively charged ions.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>→</mo><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q3
examples.problem: Why does zinc liberate hydrogen gas when it reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid but copper does not?
examples.solution:
Zn is above hydrogen while copper is below hydrogen in the activity series of metals. Therefore, zinc displaces hydrogen from dilute HCl while copper does not.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>→</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>→</mo><mtext> No reaction </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q4
examples.problem: Why is an ionic bond also called an electrovalent bond ?
examples.solution: An ionic bond is also called as electrovalent bond because of the involvement of electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions in the formation of ionic bond.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q5
examples.problem: Why is sulphide ore converted to its oxide before reduction?
examples.solution: It is because oxygen can be easily removed from metal oxides by reacting it with carbon or aluminium or by electrolytic reduction, sulphur cannot be removed from metal sulphides easily.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q6
examples.problem: Why a salt which does not conduct electricity in the solid state becomes a good conductor in molten state ? Explain.
examples.solution: In solid state, ionic compounds do not conduct electric current because the ions are held together in fixed positions by strong electrostatic forces and cannot move freely. When ionic solid is dissolved in water or melted, the crystal structure is broken down and ions become free to move and conduct electricity.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q7
examples.problem: Explain why, the galvanised iron article is protected against rusting even if the zinc layer is broken.
examples.solution: The galvanised iron article remains protected against rusting even if the zinc layer is broken because zinc is more easily oxidised than iron. So when zinc layer on the surface of galvanised iron article is broken, then zinc continues to corrode but iron article does not corrode or rust.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q8
examples.problem: An iron knife kept dipped in a blue copper sulphate solution, colour of solution changes to light green. Why?
examples.solution:
Iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution as it lie above copper in reactivity series and forms ferrous sulphate solution which is light green.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> (Blue) </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> (Light green) </mtext></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q9
examples.problem: Articles made of aluminium do not corrode even though aluminium is an active metal.
examples.solution: It is because oxide layer is formed on the surface of aluminium due to which it does not react further because it is non-penetrating layer.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q10
examples.problem: Why do gold ornameants look new even after several years of use ?
examples.solution: Gold is highly unreactive metal which remains unaffected by air, water vapour and other gases in this atmosphere. So gold does not corrode. That is why gold ornaments look new even after several years of use.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q11
examples.problem: Why does aluminium not react with water under ordinary conditions.
examples.solution: Aluminium does not react with water at ordinary temperature due to the presence of a thin but strong layer of aluminium oxide on its surface.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q12
examples.problem: Hydrogen is not metal but still it has been assigned a place in the reactivity series of metal why?
examples.solution: Hydrogen is not a metal but like metal it loses electrons and forms positive ions, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Therefore, it has been assigned a place in the reactivity series.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q13
examples.problem: When calcium metal is added to water, the gas evolved close not catch fire but same gas evolved on adding sodium metal to water catches fire. why?
examples.solution:
Calcium reacts with water to produce calcium hydroxide and hydrogen gas. The heat produced during the reaction is not sufficient to burn the hydrogen gas.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Sodium reacts vigorously with water to produce sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Large amount of heat is produced during the reaction which causes ignition of hydrogen gas.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q14
examples.problem: Why, a solution of cane sugar does not conduct electricity but a solution of common salt is a good conductor of electricity.
examples.solution: Common salt is an ionic solid. When ionic solid is dissolved in water, its crystal structure is break down and ions become free to move and conduct electricity. Cane sugar is a covalent compound therefore in its aqueous solution ions are not present hence do not conduct electricity.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q15
examples.problem: Why are ionic compounds usually hard?
examples.solution: Ionic compounds consists of oppositely charged ions and they attract each other very strongly. It forms a regular crystal structure. Therefore, ionic compounds are usually hard.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q1
examples.problem: A copper plate was dipped into a solution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. After sometime, a black layer was deposited on the copper plate. State the reason for it. Write the chemical equation of the reaction involved.
examples.solution: The black layer was deposited on copper due to deposition of silver metal on it.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q2
examples.problem: The oxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is unaffected by water. Outline a method by which a sample of metal X can be obtained from its ore. Give one reason as to why have you chosen this method.
examples.solution: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is unaffected by water. It must be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. ' X ' is obtained from its ore by electrolytic reduction because aluminium itself is good reducing agent and cannot be obtained from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> by chemical reduction.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q3
examples.problem:
Give reasons for the following :
(i) Silicon is considered as metalloids.
(ii) Carbon is not used for extraction of aluminium from aluminium oxide.
(iii) For producing hydrogen gas by reaction with hydrochloric acid, granulated zinc is preferred over block of zinc.
examples.solution:
(i) Silicon is a metalloid because its properties resembles both with metals as well as non-metals.
(ii) Aluminium is stronger reducing agent than carbon, therefore, carbon cannot be used for extraction of Al from its oxide.
(iii) Granulated zinc has more surface area than block of zinc metal, therefore, it is used for preparation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q4
examples.problem:
Give reasons for the following :
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> and Ca metals form hydrides by combination with hydrogen gas, but most other metals do not.
(ii) Zinc oxide is called an amphoteric oxide.
examples.solution:
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> and Ca are strongly electropositive, therefore, they form hydrides with hydrogen.
(ii) Zinc oxide reacts with both acids as well as bases, therefore, it is called an amphoteric oxide.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q5
examples.problem:
(a) What is corrosion of metals ? Name one metal which does not corrode and one which corrodes on being kept open.
(b) How will you show that the rusting of iron needs oxygen and moisture at the same time ?
examples.solution:
(a) Corrosion is a process in which metal reacts with air and moisture from the atmosphere along with some dilute acid to produce coating on its surface. Iron corrodes readily when placed in open atmosphere whereas aluminium does not corrode easily.
(b) Take three test tubes and put iron nails in each of them. In the first test tube add <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> up to brim and leave no space for air. In the second test tube add fused <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> so as to absorb moisture. In the third test tube add water and leave space for air. Leave them for few days. Rusting will not take place in first and second test tubes. But rusting will take place in third test tube showing that rusting of iron requires both air and moisture.

examples.problem:
Which of the following combinations would result in a displacement reaction? Write appropriate equations for any reactions that occurs.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi></mrow></math>

The activity of the halogens decreases from top to bottom in the periodic table. Br is above I and Cl is above Br in the periodic table. Therefore, neither combination (a) nor combination (c) could result in reaction. Cl is above I in the periodic table, and so combination (b) results in a displacement reaction.
The more active halogen, chlorine, displaces the less active halogen, iodine from its compounds.

examples.problem: Metals replace hydrogen from acid, whereas non-metals do not. Why?

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q1
examples.problem:
Give example of a metal which
(a) is liquid at room temperature.
(b) can be easily cut with knife.
(c) is the best conductor of heat.
(d) is the poorest conductor of heat.
examples.solution:
(a) Mercury (Hg)
(b) Sodium (Na)
(c) Silver (Ag)
(d) Lead (Pb)

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q2
examples.problem: Explain the meaning of malleable and ductile.
examples.solution:
Malleable : The property by virtue of which a substance can be beaten into sheets is known as malleability. The
substance that shows the property of malleability is known as malleable substance. Metals are malleable in nature.
Ductile : The property by virtue of which a substance can be drawn into wires is known as ductility. A substance that shows the property of ductility is known as ductile. Metals are ductile in nature.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q3
examples.problem: Why is sodium kept immersed in kerosene oil ?
examples.solution:
Sodium is a very reactive metal. It reacts with air and water. If kept open in air it reacts readily with oxygen (present in air) to form sodium oxide. It also reacts with water (moisture present in air) to form sodium hydroxide.

(a) Which is the most reactive metal ?
(b) What would you observe when B is added to solution of copper (II) sulphate ?
(c) Arrange the metals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and D in order of increasing reactivity.
examples.solution:
In the reactivity series we find that order of reactivity of metals present in the salt solutions is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> Ag. Thus we can say that by looking at the information provided in the table, we can conclude that
(i) Metal A is more reactive than copper as it displaces copper from copper (II) sulphate and is less reactive than iron as it fails to displace iron from iron (II) sulphate.
(ii) Metal B is more reactive than iron and less reactive than zinc.
(iii) Metal C is more reactive than silver and less reactive than other metals (i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and Zn ).
(iv) Metal D is least reactive.
Thus
(a) The most reactive metal is B .
(b) Since B is more reactive than iron so it is also more reactive than copper hence it will displace copper from copper (II) sulphate solution. The blue colour of copper (II) sulphate solution will slowly fade.
(c) The arrangement of metals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and D in decreasing order of reactivity is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>></mo><mi>A</mi><mo>></mo><mi>C</mi><mo>></mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q6
examples.problem: Which gas is produced when a reactive metal reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid ? Write the chemical reaction when iron reacts with dilute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
examples.solution:
When a reactive metal reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, the gas produced is hydrogen <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
Iron and dilute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> react to produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q7
examples.problem: What would you observe when zinc is added to a solution of iron (II) sulphate ? Write chemical equation that takes place.
examples.solution:
The green colour of iron (II) sulphate solution will disappear. Zinc will gradually dissolve and iron will get precipitated at the bottom of the container.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q8
examples.problem:
Metallic oxides of zinc, magnesium and copper were heated with zinc, Mg and Cu . In which case the displacement reaction will take place ?
| Metals oxide | Zinc | Magnesium | Copper |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Zinc oxide | | | |
| Magnesium oxide | | | |
| Copper oxide | | | |
examples.solution:
From the reactivity series we find the order of reactivity of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and Cu as
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
i.e., magnesium is most reactive and so it will displace zinc from zinc oxide and copper from copper oxide
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow></mrow></math> (displacement)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow></math> (displacement)
Zinc is less reactive than magnesium so it will not displace magnesium from magnesium oxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi></mrow></math> No reaction
Zinc is more reactive than copper so it will displace copper from copper oxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow></math> (displacement)
Since copper is least reactive it will neither displace Mg nor Zn from their oxides.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi></mrow></math> No reaction
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi></mrow></math> No reaction

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q10
examples.problem: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
examples.solution: Ionic compounds consists of oppositely charged ions i.e. positively charged cations and negatively charged anions. They are held together by strong electrostatic force of atraction. Therefore, ionic compounds have high melting points and boiling points.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q11
examples.problem:
Define the following terms :
(i) minerals
(ii) ores
(iii) gangue
examples.solution:
(i) The elements or compounds, which occur naturally in the earth's crust are known as minerals.
(ii) Those minerals from which an element can be extracted economically is called an ore.
(iii) The unwanted rocky, earthy or sandy materials almost always associated with ores as impurities are called gangue or matrix.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q12
examples.problem: Name two metals which are found in free state in nature?
examples.solution: Gold ( Au ) and Platinum ( Pt ).

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q13
examples.problem: What chemical process is used for obtaining a metal from its oxide ?
examples.solution: Reduction process.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q14
examples.problem: Which metals do not corrode easily ?
examples.solution: Au (gold) and Pt (Platinum), which are placed near the bottom of the activity series do not corrode easily.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q15
examples.problem: What are alloys?
examples.solution: Alloys are homogeneous mixtures of more than one metal or metals and nonmetals.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q2
examples.problem:
Which of the following methods is suitable for preventing an iron frying pan from rusting?
(a) Applying grease
(b) Applying paint
(c) Applying a coat of zinc
(d) All the above
examples.solution: (d) All the above methods are helpful in preventing iron pan from rusting.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q3

An element can react with oxygen to give a compound with high melting point. This compound is also water soluble. The element is likely to be
(a) Calcium
(b) Carbon
(c) Silicon
(d) Iron
examples.solution: (a) Calcium (Ca) combines with oxygen to form calcium oxide ( CaO ) which has a high melting point and dissolves in water to form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q4
examples.problem:
Food cans are coated with tin and not with zinc because
(a) zinc is costlier than tin.
(b) zinc has higher melting point than tin.
(c) zinc is more reactive than tin.
(d) zinc is less reactive than tin.
examples.solution: (c) Zinc is more reactive than tin (zinc is above tin in reactivity series) so it will react with organic acids (present in food) to form poisonous compounds. To avoid this food cans are coated with tin and not with zinc.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q5
examples.problem:
You are given a hammer, a battery, a bulb, wire and a switch:
(a) How would you use them to distinguish between samples of metals and non-metals ?
(b) Assess the usefulness of these tests to distinguish between metals and non-metals.
examples.solution:
(a) Using the hammer, strike both metal and non-metal (solid) and observe if any sound is produced. Metals produce sound when struck with hammer whereas non-metals do not produce sound when struck with hammer.
Note: Metals are sonorous; Non-metals are nonsonorous.
Also if we use hammer to convert the metal and non-metal (solid) in the form of sheet we will find that metals get converted to a sheet but non-metals will break. Note : Metals are malleable and ductile while non-metals are brittle.
The given material can be used to distinguish between metal and non-metal if we set up the electric circuit as shown below :
Insert the sample of metal and non-metal between the terminals A and B as shown in figure. We will observe that the bulb glows, when the sample introduced is that of a metals and the bulb does not glow when the sample introduced is that of a non-metal.
Note: Metals are good conductors of electricity whereas non-metals are bad conductors.
(b) From these tests it can be easily concluded that
- metals are malleable where as non-metals are not.
- metals are good conductors of electrictity whereas non-metals are not.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q7
examples.problem: Name two metals which can displace hydrogen from dilute acids and two metals which can not do so.
examples.solution: Sodium and calcium can displace hydrogen from dilute acids as they lie above hydrogen in the reactivity series. Copper and silver can not displace hydrogen from dilute acids as they lie below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q8
examples.problem: In the electrolytic refining of metal (M), name anode, cathode and electrolyte.
examples.solution:
Anode : It is a rod or wire of impure metal M
Cathode : It is a rod or wire of pure metal M
Electrolyte : It is an aqueous solution of a soluble salt of the metal M.

examples.problem:
