What will be the action of gas on
(a) dry litmus paper ?
(b) moist litmus paper ?
Write balanced chemical equation for the reaction taking place.
examples.solution:
On heating sulphur will produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> (air) </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(a) It will not change the colour of dry litmus paper.
(b) It will change the colour of moist litmus paper from blue to red.
Note: The colour change of litmus paper is due to the formation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (sulphurous acid) by dissolution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q10
examples.problem: State two ways to prevent rusting of iron.
examples.solution:
The rusting of iron can be prevented by
(i) applying grease
(ii) applying paint
(iii) galvanisation (applying a thin coat of zinc)

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q11
examples.problem: What type of oxides are formed when non-metals combine with oxygen ?
examples.solution:
When non-metals combine with oxygen the oxides formed are either acidic or neutral e.g.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mo>→</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> neutral oxide </mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mo>→</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> acidic oxide </mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q12
examples.problem:
Give reasons for the following:
(a) Platinum, silver and gold are used to make jewellery.
(b) Sodium, potassium and lithium are stored under oil.
(c) Aluminium is highly reactive metal but still used for making cooking utensils.
(d) Carbonate and sulphide ores are usually converted into oxides during the process of extraction.
examples.solution:
(a) Platinum, silver and gold are very less reactive (found near the bottom in reactivity series) and are not affected by air, water or dil. acids. Because of
their low reactivity and their bright lustre, these metals are used for making jewellary.
(b) Sodium, potassium and lithium react with water (or moisture in air) producing a lot of heat along with evolution of hydrogen. As a result, the hydrogen gas thus produced catches fire. To avoid accidents these metals are not kept in air. They are kept under kerosene to avoid contact with air and water.
(c) When aluminium is exposed to air it reacts with oxygen (present in air) to form aluminium oxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. This <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> formed gets deposited on the surface of aluminium metal in the form of a thin coating which acts as a protective coating and due to its presence metal becomes unreactive. The formation of protective layer of aluminium oxide on the surface make highly reactive aluminium metal suitable for making cooking utensils.
(d) Since we can easily reduce the metal oxides to the metal using coke (C) or any other suitable reducing agent, so carbonates and sulphides are converted to the oxides form by process of roasting or calcination.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q13
examples.problem: You must have seen tarnished copper vessels being cleaned with lemon or tamarind juice. Explain why these sour substances are effective in cleaning vessels.
examples.solution: Copper metal reacts slowly with water, carbon dioxide and oxygen (all these present in air) and forms basic copper carbonate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> which gets deposited as a green layer on its surface. Lemon juice contains citric acid and tamarind juice contains tartaric acid. Both these juices which contain an acid react with basic copper carbonate to form soluble copper salts which are removed from the surface of copper metal and the surface of copper metal begins to shine.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q14
examples.problem: Differentiate between metals and non-metals on the basis of their chemical properties.
examples.solution:
Differences in chemical properties of metals and non-metals:
| Properties | Metals | Non-metals |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Nature of oxides | They generally form basic oxides which form alkalies with water. For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> Sodium hydroxide (alkali) | They form acidic oxides. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>8</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><mn>8</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> (acid) </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math> |
| Electrochemical nature | They are electropositive elements and form cation. They are liberated at cathode during electrolysis. Some metals like chromium \& manganese form some anions also with other elements like oxygen. | They are electronegative elements and form anions. They are liberated at the anode during electrolysis (exception: hydrogen). |
| Action of acids | They generally dissolve in mineral acids forming a salt with the evolution of a gas. For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | They either do not dissolve in mineral acids or form the corresponding oxyacids. For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><munderover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow /><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></munderover><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> |
| Solubility | They generally dissolve by a chemical reaction. | Many non-metals dissolve without any chemical change taking place. For example: chlorine, bromine or iodine dissolves in water. |

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q15
examples.problem: A man went door to door posing as goldsmith. He promised to bring back the glitter on dull gold ornaments. An unsuspecting lady gave a set of gold bangles to him which he dipped in a particular solution. The bangles sparkled like new but their weight was reduced drastically. The lady got upset and after a futile argument, the man beat a hasty retreat. Can you predict the nature of solution used by the imposter?
examples.solution: The man has used an aqua-regia solution (mixture of conc. HCl and conc. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in the ratio of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> by volume). Gold dissolves in aqua-regia and forms gold (III) chloride, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (auric chloride). Since, gold dissolves in aqua-regia, so a loss in mass of gold bangles occurred. Since the dull layer of gold was removed from its surface so there was original shine on the bangles. It is an excellent oxidant and highly corrosive.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q16
examples.problem: Give reason as to why copper is used to make hot water tanks and not steel (an alloy of iron).
examples.solution: Copper does not react easily with water unlike iron (constituent of steel) and it is better conductor of heat than steel so it can be used to heat the water uniformly. It is less efficient in conserving heat but this disadvantage is corrected with heat insulation.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Exemplar Questions — Q1
examples.problem: Iqbal treated a lustrous, divalent element M with sodium hydroxide. He observed the formation of bubbles in reaction mixture. He made the same observations when this element was treated with hydrochloric acid. Suggest how can he identify the produced gas. Write chemical equations for both the reactions.
examples.solution:
The produced gas can be identified by bringing a burning match stick near the reaction vessel. If it is hydrogen gas, a pop sound is produced.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
The element is a metal.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Exemplar Questions — Q2
examples.problem:
A non-metal A is an important constituent of our food and forms two oxides B and C. Oxide B is toxic, whereas C causes global warming.
(i) Identify <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and C .
(ii) To which group of periodic table does A belong?
examples.solution:
(i) A is carbon, B is carbon monoxide and C is carbon dioxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></munder><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></munder></mrow></mrow></math>
(ii) A belongs to Group -14 of the periodic table.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Exemplar Questions — Q3
examples.problem: An alkali metal A gives a compound B (molecular mass <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> on reacting with water. The compound B gives a soluble compound C on treatment with aluminium oxide. Identify <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and C and give the reaction involved.
examples.solution:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mi>;</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mi>;</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Exemplar Questions — Q4
examples.problem: Of the three metals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> reacts with cold water, Y with hot water and Z with steam only. Identify X , Y and Z and also arrange them in order of increasing reactivity.
examples.solution:
X is alkali metal, Na or K .
Y is alkaline earth metal, Mg or Ca .
Z is Fe .
Increasing reactivity series : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>></mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>></mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Exemplar Questions — Q5
examples.problem:
A non-metal A which is the largest constituent of air, when heated with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in 1:3 ratio in the presence of catalyst ( Fe ) gives a gas B . On heating with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> it gives an oxide C . If this oxide is passed into water in the presence of air it gives an acid D which acts as a strong oxidising agent.
(i) Identify <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and D
(ii) To which group of periodic table does this nonmetal belong?
examples.solution:
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>;</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>;</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mi>;</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
Nitric oxide (NO) is oxidised to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in presence of air and then reacts with water to produce nitric acid ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) D.
(ii) Element A belongs to Group -15 of the periodic table.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q1
examples.problem:
A student by mistake used a wet gas jar to collect sulphur dioxide. Which one of the following tests of the gas is likely to fail ?
(a) Odour
(b) Effect on acidified <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution
(c) Solubility test
(d) None of these

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q2
examples.problem:
Silicon is used in :
(a) solar energy devices
(b) semiconductors
(c) transistors
(d) all of these
examples.solution: (d) All are characteristics of metal.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q3
examples.problem:
Which of the following is not a characteristics of metal ?
(a) Malleable
(b) Electropositive nature
(c) Ductile

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q4

The following observations are given for four metals:
[NTSE]

Choose the correct decreasing order of reactivity of these metals amongst the following:
(a) M <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> L <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> H <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> K
(b) K <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> M <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> H <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> L
(c) M <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> K <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> L <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> H
(d) L <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> H <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> K <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> M
examples.solution:
(c) Metals below hydrogen in a reactivity series does not react with dilute HCl . Medium reactive metals reacts with warm water and highly reactive metals react with cold water.
As per the given information <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> and M can be identified as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> respectively. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

examples.solution: The man has used an aqua-regia solution (mixture of conc. HCl and conc. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in the ratio of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> by volume). Gold dissolves in aqua-regia and forms gold (III) chloride, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (auric chloride). Since, gold dissolves in aqua-regia, so a loss in mass of gold bangles occurred. Since the dull layer of gold was removed from its surface so there was original shine on the bangles. It is an excellent oxidant and highly corrosive.

## Physical properties of metals
- Metallic lusture
- Usually solid (except Hg which is a liquid)
- Show ductility and malleability.
- Good conductor of heat and electricity.
## Chemical properties of metals
Chemical properties of metals
- Form basic oxides with oxygen (Al and Zn forms amphoteric oxides)
- Form metal oxide and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
- Na and K reacts violently with cold water.
- Mg reacts only with hot water.
- <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and Fe react with steam.
- Form salts and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> gas with acids.
- Reactive metals displaces less reactive metals from their solution.
## Reaction of metals with non metals
- Metal loses the valence electrons while non-metal accepts these electron to form ionic bond.
- Properties of ionic compounds :

## TETRAVALENCY IN CARBON
A carbon atom has a total of six electrons occupying the first two shells, i.e., the K-shell has two electrons and the L-shell has four electrons. This distribution indicates that in the outermost shell there are one completely filled ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ' orbital and two half-filled ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ' orbitals, showing carbon to be a divalent atom. But in reality, carbon displays tetravalency in the combined state. Therefore, a carbon atom has four valence electrons. It could gain four electrons to form C anion or lose four electrons to form C cation. Both these conditions require large amount of energy. Thus it has a very little tendency to form ionic compounds. To overcome this problem carbon undergoes bonding by sharing its valence electron with other carbon atoms or with atoms of other elements. This allows it to be covalently bonded to one, two, three or four carbon atoms or atoms of other elements or groups of atoms (molecule).
This characteristic of carbon atom by virtue of which it form four covalent bonds is generally referred to as tetracovalency of carbon.
Not just carbon, but many other elements form molecules by sharing valence electrons. The shared electrons 'belong' to the outer shells of both the atoms and lead to both atoms attaining the noble gas configuration.
## CONNECTING TOPIC
To understand the bonding of carbon with other atoms in its compound we should understand the concept of covalent bonding.
## COVALENT BOND
According to Lewis, covalent bond is formed by the sharing of same number of electron between two atoms to complete their octet".
If one electron is shared between two atoms then it forms single bond. Similarly double \& triple bonds are formed by the sharing of two and three electrons respectively. For example:-
Only the electrons of valence shell take part in sharing. The electrons of valence shell which do not take part in chemical bonding are called lone pair or non bonding electrons. For example, in oxygen six valence electrons of oxygen atom (2, 6) can take part in bonding. Out of six electrons two electrons, are shared by one oxygen atom thus after bond formation each oxygen possesses four non bonding electrons (or two lone pairs).
## Octet Rule
The octet rule requires all atoms in a molecule to have 8 valence electrons; either by sharing, losing or gaining electrons; to become stable. For covalent bonds, atoms tend to share their electrons with each other to satisfy the octet rule. It requires 8 electrons because that is the amount of electrons needed to fill its outer most orbital (electron configuration); also known as a noble gas configuration. Each atom wants to become as stable as the noble gases that have their outer valence shell filled. Although it is important to remember the "magic number", 8, yet there are many octet rule exceptions.
Example: There are many stable molecules in which central atom have more than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>in its valence shell e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ( I has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>14</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>in valence shell), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ( P has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>10</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>in valence shell), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ( S has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>12</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>in valence shell) etc.
## General properties of covalent molecules
(a) Solubility : These compounds are usually insoluble or less soluble in water and in other polar solvents. Polar covalent molecules are more soluble in water in comparison to that of non polar covalent molecules.
(b) Low melting point and boiling point: The intermolecular forces of attractions between the molecules of covalent compounds are generally weak. As a result, lesser amount of energy is needed to overcome these intermolecular forces. Thus, these compounds usually have low melting point and boiling point than ionic compounds.
(c) Conducting nature: These are generally poor conductors of electricity in the fused or dissolved state due to unavailability of ions. or gases at room temperature. However, a few covalent compounds also exist in the solid state e.g. glucose, urea, thiourea \& sugar etc.
## Electron Dot (Lewis Dot) Structures
Lewis dot structures for many species can be written according to the following steps :
(i) Pick up the central atom of the species in question.
(ii) Recall the number of electrons in the outermost orbit (valence electrons) in each atom of the species.
(iii) Recall the valency of the central atom and other atoms too.
(iv) Write down the structural formula of the species on the basis of point no. (ii) and (iii).
(v) Supply the required number of electrons to each bond (1 pair of electrons for a single bond, 2 pairs for a double bond and 3 pairs for a triple bond).
(vi) Verify that each atom of the species has inert gas configuration, i.e., either 2 (in case of hydrogen) or 8 electrons in the outermost orbit. Let us apply these points on few examples.
For main group elements, the number of valence electrons which an atom contributes in a Lewis structure is the same as its group number in the periodic table.

## ALLOTROPES OF CARBON
Carbon (Latin carbo means charcoal) is an element of prehistoric discovery. It is very widely distributed in nature. It is found in abundance in the sun, stars, comets, and atmospheres of most planets.
Carbon can either be in structural crystalline forms or may occur in a structure-less amorphous form. Some elements like carbon, sulphur, tin, oxygen, etc. are found in more than one structural forms. Therefore, some elements can have several different structural forms while in the same physical state. These forms are called allotropes and such phenomenon is called allotropy. The various allotropic forms of carbon can be broadly classified into two classes : wurtzite are polymorphs of ZnS.

These differences in the properties of diamond and graphite are due to the difference in their structures.
In diamond, each C atom is linked to its neighbours by four single covalent bonds. This leads to a three-dimensional network of covalent bonds. In graphite, the carbon atoms are arranged in flat parallel layers as regular hexagons. Each carbon in these layers is bonded to three others by covalent bonds. Graphite thus acquires some double bond character.
Each layer is bonded to adjacent layers by weak van der Waal's forces. Moreover, one electron is free at each carbon atom. This allows each layer to slide over the other easily. Due to this type of structure graphite is soft and slippery, and can act as a lubricant. Graphite is also a good conductor of electricity due to mobile electrons in it.
Graphite is also used as a industrial lubricant because it possesses high melting point. Thus no change in structure occur even if machineries are working at high temperature.

## CATENATION IN CARBON
Carbon atom is unique amongst all the elements that are found in nature. It can form long chain molecules. The ability of carbon to form a long chain is called catenation. Carbon forms strong bond because of its small size which enables the nucleus to held on to the shared pairs of electrons strongly. The chains are formed because carbon atoms form tetravalent bonds with other carbon atoms. This structure can be repeated endlessly without disturbing the stability of the bonds and the compounds formed. The chains can form branches, and sub-branches. The carbon atoms also form rings. The rings themselves can have more rings attached to them. Protein molecules and amino acids are long chain carbon molecules.
Figure : Variety of carbon chains formed when carbon atoms join together.
In addition, carbon atoms may be linked by single, double or triple bonds. Compounds of carbon, which has only single bonds between the carbon atoms are called saturated compounds. Compounds of carbon having double or triple bonds between their carbon atoms are called unsaturated compounds.

## COMPOUNDS OF CARBON
Compounds of carbon can broadly classified into two main categories, namely inorganic and organic compounds.
Inorganic compounds : These include compounds of carbon with metals and non-metals (other than hydrogen) such as oxygen, halogens etc. These do not have carbon-carbon bonds.
Organic compounds : Organic compounds are those chemical compounds in which one or more atoms of carbon are covalently linked to atoms of other elements, most commonly oxygen or nitrogen.
## Inorganic Compounds of Carbon
Carbon combines with a variety of other elements like oxygen, halogens, metals, etc., to form binary compounds respectively named as oxides, halides and carbides.
## Oxides of carbon :
(a) Carbon monoxide, CO
(i) Carbon monoxide is a colourless, tasteless gas with faint odour.
(ii) Carbon monoxide is extremely poisonous in nature. The poisonous nature of CO is due to the fact that it combines with haemoglobin (a red colouring matter of blood), oxygen carrier of blood, to form a stable compound carboxyhaemoglobin. As a result, oxygen transporation is disturbed and thus brain and body tissues do not get necessary oxygen and ultimately death occurs. This explains, why people sleeping in closed rooms with charcoal fire burning inside, dies.
A victim of carbon monoxide poisoning, if unconscious, should be brought in the open place and Know!
given artificial respiration with carbogen (mixture of oxygen and 5-10\% <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ).

## Organic Compounds
## Origin and Definition of Organic Compounds :
According to the earlier definition, organic chemistry was defined as the chemistry of substances found in the living matter (Berzelius in 1808). Further, Berzelius in 1815 also suggested that the organic compounds could be prepared only by living organisms under the influence of a mysterious force known as the vital force (life-force). The vital force theory remain unchallanged until 1828, when Friedrich Wohler, a German chemist, reported the synthesis of a typical organic compound urea by heating an inorganic compound, ammonium cyanate.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Ammonium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> chloride </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Potassium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> cyanate </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Ammonium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> cyanate </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
The synthesis of urea from inorganic compounds gave a blow to the vital force theory and thus the distinction between organic and inorganic compounds based on vital force soon started fading away. The vital force theory was completely discarded after the synthesis of acetic acid from C, H and O (Kolbe, 1845) and methane (Berthelet, 1856). Subsequently, a large number of naturally occurring organic compounds were synthesized in the laboratory and the vital force theory was decisively disproved.
However, all the organic compounds were found to contain carbon as one of the elements. Thus the emphasis for the definition of organic compounds was shifted from origin to composition. Accordingly, organic chemistry has now been defined as the chemistry of carbon compounds.
On the basis of this definition, the study of compounds like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, carbonates, cyanides, cyanates, carbides, etc., should be included in organic chemistry, but due to their greater resemblance with inorganic compounds these are studied under inorganic chemistry.
Further, since all the organic compounds could be considered as derivatives of hydrocarbons, a more appropriate definition for the organic chemistry is the study of hydrocarbons and their derivatives.
## HYDROCARBONS
Compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen are known as hydrocarbons. Petroleum and coal are the two important natural sources of hydrocarbons. Petroleum is a major source of aliphatic hydrocarbons while coal is a source of aromatic hydrocarbons.
On the basis of structure and properties, hydrocarbons can be classified broadly into two classes.

## 2. Closed Chain or Cyclic Hydrocarbons
As the name represents, these compounds contain closed chain (ring) of carbon atoms in their molecules. These are further divided into two types namely cycloalkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons or arenes.
(i) Cycloalkanes : Those saturated hydrocarbons in which carbon atoms are joined together to form ring are known as cycloalkanes. For example,
Cyclopropane
Cyclopentane
Cyclohexane
(ii) Aromatic hydrocarbons or Arenes: Those hydrocarbons which contain at least one benzene ring in their molecules are called arenes. For example,
Toluene
Naphthalene
All the above types of hydrocarbons may also be grouped in a different manner into two types depending upon the basis of nature of carbon-carbon bonds in their molecules.
(i) Saturated hydrocarbons: These contain carbon-carbon single bonds in their molecules. Alkanes and cycloalkanes are grouped in this category.
(ii) Unsaturated hydrocarbons: These contains carbon-carbon multiple bond (double or triple) in their molecules. Alkenes, alkynes and arenes are grouped in this category.

## FUNCTIONAL GROUPS
In organic chemistry, functional groups (or moieties) are specific groups of atoms within molecules that are responsible for the characteristic chemical reactions of those molecules. The same functional group will undergo the same or similar chemical reaction(s) regardless of the size of the molecule for example, - OH (alcohol), - CHO (aldehyde) etc.

## HOMOLOGOUS SERIES
In chemistry, a homologous series is a series of organic compounds with a similar general formula, possessing similar chemical properties due to the presence of the same functional group, and shows a gradation in physical properties as a result of increase in molecular size and mass (see relative molecular mass). For example, ethane has a higher boiling point than methane since it has more van der Waal's forces(intermolecular forces) with neighbouring molecules. This is due to increase in the number of atoms making up the molecule.
Organic compounds in the same homologous series differ by a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> group. Alkanes (paraffins), alkenes (olefins), methoxyethane (ethers), and alkynes (acetylenes) form such series in which members differ in mass by 14 atomic mass units. For example, the alkane homologous series have methane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, ethane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, propane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, butane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, and pentane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, each member differing from the previous one by a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> group (or 14 atomic mass units).
Similarly, alcohol homologous series starts with methanol ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ), ethanol ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ), propylalcohol ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ) etc.
- A homologation reaction is any chemical process converting one member of a homologous series to the next.
## NOMENCLATURE OF CARBON COMPOUNDS
In the early stages of the development, the various organic compounds were named on the basis of either the source of origin of the compounds or on some specific property of the compounds. For example, methane gas is found to get released in marshy places. Hence it is called marsh gas. These names are called trivial or common names.
In order to give names for the huge number of organic compounds used all over the world, a more systematic method was required. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) developed a systematic approach to the nomenclature of organic compounds based on its structure and reflects the physical and chemical properties. This IUPAC system has three parts: root word, suffix and prefix.

Combustion usually occurs when a hydrocarbon reacts with oxygen to produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>.
In more general sense, combustion involves a reaction between any combustible materials and an oxidizer to form an oxidized product. Combustion is an exothermic reaction, so it release heat. General reaction is:
Hydrocarbon + Oxygen ⟶ Carbondioxide + Water

## Important Substitution Reactions
In substitution reactions the hydrogen of the alkane molecule is replaced by another atom or a group of atoms (like alkyl) resulting in the formation of the derivatives of that hydrocarbon. Substitution by halogen atom is generally called halogenation. This type of substitution results in chlorination, bromination or iodination.
Like methane, ethane also forms a series of substitution products in the presence of excess chlorine and sunlight.

## Preparation of ethanol by fermentation of sugar
Fermentation is a process whereby an organic compound is broken into smaller molecules by enzymes such as yeast. Ethanol is prepared by fermentation of molasses. Molasses, a by product of sugar industry, has traces of sugar. The fermentation is initiated by yeast, which secretes two enzymes called invertase and zymase. These enzymes act as catalyst for converting sugar into ethanol. The reaction is exothermic and carbon dioxide is released in the process.

## How Do Alcohols Affect Living Beings?
Superficially, ethanol evokes a distinctive heat-like sensation in the mouth and a stinging sensation on the skin. In the body it is metabolized to other substances, affecting the central nervous system in particular. The effect varies between individuals, and can be worse when applied in addition to certain drugs. When applied to open wounds (as for disinfection) it produces a strong stinging sensation. Pure or highly concentrated ethanol may permanently damage living tissue on contact. When large quantities of ethanol are consumed, it tends to slow metabolic processes and depresses the central nervous system. This results in lack of coordination, mental confusion, drowsiness, lowering of the normal inhibitions, and finally stupour.
The individual ethanol consuming may feel relaxed but does not realise that his sense of judgement, sense of timing, and muscular coordination have been seriously impaired. Ethanol within the human body is converted into acetaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase and then into acetic acid by acetaldehyde dehydrogenase. The product of the first step of this breakdown, acetaldehyde, is more toxic than ethanol. It has been shown to increase the risk of developing cirrhosis of the liver, multiple forms of cancer, and alcoholism. Death from ethyl alcohol consumption is possible when blood alcohol level reaches <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.4</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math>. A blood alcohol level of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> or more is commonly fatal.

## SOAPS AND DETERGENTS
Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of higher fatty acids, produced from the alkaline hydrolysis of fats (higher fatty acids) in a chemical reaction. The reaction is called saponification. They are of biological origin. Each soap molecule has a long hydrocarbon chain, sometimes called its 'tail', with a carboxylate 'head'. In water, the sodium or potassium ions float free, leaving a negatively charged head.
- When the alkali is sodium hydroxide, a sodium soap is formed. Sodium soaps are "hard" soaps. When the alkali is potassium hydroxide, a potassium soap is formed. Potassium soaps are softer and are found in some liquid hand soaps and shaving creams.
- Soap is an excellent cleanser because of its ability to act as an emulsifying agent. An emulsifier is capable of dispersing one liquid into another immiscible liquid. This means that while oil (which attracts dirt) doesn't naturally mix with water, soap can suspends oil/dirt in such a way that it can be removed.
Detergents (syndets) are emulsifying agents that are very similar to soaps but they do not have a biological origin and they do not have a carboxylate group instead of it they have sulphonate group as they are sodium salt of long chain sulphonic acids. Synthetic detergents usually have a long hydrocarbon chain of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></math> carbon atoms. At the head of this chain there is a polar group that forms a strong hydrogen bond with water but does not form strong ionic bonds with the ions of hard water.

(i) The salts of fatty acids have an ionic polar head group, the carboxylate and a long non-polar hydrocarbon chain.

(iv) Here the polar groups are exposed to the water and the hydrocarbon portions are buried within the core, away from the water.
## How Soap Cleans :
The things we call "dirt" are actually grease, oils, and fats which are insoluble in water. When cleaning, soap micelles come into contact with the "dirt" and because like dissolves like, a minute amount of "dirt" dissolves within the central region of the soap micelle. Nonpolar dirts are emulsified and washed away in polar wash water. This is why soaps are said to be good emulsifying agents.
## How Does Detergent Remove Grease From Clothing ?
Detergent molecules contain hydrophobic tails (hydrocarbon chain) which are water hating and will attach themselves to any substance which is non-polar (grease). The tails surround the grease with the polar heads in the aqueous phase, forming the structure shown. On agitation, the grease is pulled from the clothing allowing the grease to be completely surrounded and moved into the aqueous phase. This is then washed away leaving only clean clothes behind.

## Surface Tension/Surfactants :
The property of a liquid due to which its free surface tries to have minimum surface area and behaves as if it were under tension some what like a stretched elastic membrane is called surface tension. Chemicals that are able to reduce the surface tension of the solvent effectively are called surface active agents, or surfactants. Surfactants perform other important functions in cleaning, such as loosening, emulsifying (dispersing in water) and holding soil in suspension until it can be rinsed away. Surfactants can also provide alkalinity, which is useful in removing acidic soils. Surfactants are classified by their ionic (electrical charge) properties in water: anionic (negative charge), nonionic (no charge), cationic (positive charge) and amphoteric (either positive or negative charge). Soap is an anionic surfactant. Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) is a compound which is added to synthetic detergent to keep the dust particles suspended in water, and helps in cleansing process.

## Markownikoff's rule
When an unsymmetrical alkene or alkyne reacts with unsymmetrical reagent, then negative part of reagent attach with that carbon atom which contains lesser number of hydrogen atom during the addition.
For example:
(Markownikoff's addition)
Addition of HBr (not <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and HF ) on alkenes in presence of peroxides takes place in anti-Markownikoff's way (Peroxide effect).

1. Differences in the properties of diamond and graphite are due to the difference in their structures. In diamond, each C atom is linked to its neighbours by four single covalent bonds. This leads to a three-dimensional network of covalent bonds. In graphite, the carbon atoms are arranged in flat parallel layers as regular hexagons. Each carbon in these layers is bonded to three others by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> hybrid orbitals. Graphite thus acquires some double bond character. Each layer is bonded to adjacent layers by weak van der Waal's forces. Moreover, one electron is free at each carbon atom. This allows each layer to slide over the other easily. Due to this type of structure graphite is soft and slippery, and can act as a lubricant. Graphite is also a good conductor of electricity due to presence of mobile electrons in it.

The molecule of methane has four carbon-hydrogen single covalent bonds. These covalent bonds are called nonpolar covalent bonds.
(i) These compounds are poor conductor of electricity because covalent bonds are formed by sharing of electrons. They don't have a free electron that is required for electricity transfer. Thus, they are bad conductors.

Cooking oil consists of unsaturated hydrocarbon which decolourise bromine solution while butter consists of saturated hydrocarbons and it will not decolorise bromine solution.
15. Cleaning Action of Soap and Detergent : Both of them follow the same principle. They contain two parts, a large hydrocarbon which is hydrophobic (water repelling) and a negative charged head, which is hydrophillic (water attracting). In solution water molecules being polar in nature, surround the head and not the organic part of the molecule. When a soap or detergent is dissolved in water, the molecule gather together as clusters, called micelles. The tails stick inwards and the head outwards oily dirt will be collected in the centre of the micelle. The hydrocarbon tail attaches itself to oily dirt. When water is agitated, the oily dirt tends to lift off from the dirty surface and dissociates into fragments. The solution now contains small globules of oil surrounded by detergent molecules. The negatively charged heads present in water prevent the small globules from coming together and form aggregates. Thus the oily dirt is removed from the object.
Micelle formed by detergent molecules in water. The hydrocarbon tail sticks to oily dirt

## 4. Carbon and its Compounds
A
Strong
Foundation

## TETRAVALENCY IN CARBON
A carbon atom has a total of six electrons occupying the first two shells, i.e., the K-shell has two electrons and the L-shell has four electrons. This distribution indicates that in the outermost shell there are one completely filled ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ' orbital and two half-filled ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> ' orbitals, showing carbon to be a divalent atom. But in reality, carbon displays tetravalency in the combined state. Therefore, a carbon atom has four valence electrons. It could gain four electrons to form C anion or lose four electrons to form C cation. Both these conditions require large amount of energy. Thus it has a very little tendency to form ionic compounds. To overcome this problem carbon undergoes bonding by sharing its valence electron with other carbon atoms or with atoms of other elements. This allows it to be covalently bonded to one, two, three or four carbon atoms or atoms of other elements or groups of atoms (molecule).
This characteristic of carbon atom by virtue of which it form four covalent bonds is generally referred to as tetracovalency of carbon.
Not just carbon, but many other elements form molecules by sharing valence electrons. The shared electrons 'belong' to the outer shells of both the atoms and lead to both atoms attaining the noble gas configuration.

## CONNECTING TOPIC
To understand the bonding of carbon with other atoms in its compound we should understand the concept of covalent bonding.

## COVALENT BOND
According to Lewis, covalent bond is formed by the sharing of same number of electron between two atoms to complete their octet".
If one electron is shared between two atoms then it forms single bond. Similarly double \& triple bonds are formed by the sharing of two and three electrons respectively. For example:-
Only the electrons of valence shell take part in sharing. The electrons of valence shell which do not take part in chemical bonding are called lone pair or non bonding electrons. For example, in oxygen six valence electrons of oxygen atom (2, 6) can take part in bonding. Out of six electrons two electrons, are shared by one oxygen atom thus after bond formation each oxygen possesses four non bonding electrons (or two lone pairs).

## Octet Rule
The octet rule requires all atoms in a molecule to have 8 valence electrons; either by sharing, losing or gaining electrons; to become stable. For covalent bonds, atoms tend to share their electrons with each other to satisfy the octet rule. It requires 8 electrons because that is the amount of electrons needed to fill its outer most orbital (electron configuration); also known as a noble gas configuration. Each atom wants to become as stable as the noble gases that have their outer valence shell filled. Although it is important to remember the "magic number", 8, yet there are many octet rule exceptions.
Example: There are many stable molecules in which central atom have more than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>in its valence shell e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ( I has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>14</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>in valence shell), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ( P has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>10</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>in valence shell), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ( S has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>12</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>in valence shell) etc.

## General properties of covalent molecules
(a) Solubility : These compounds are usually insoluble or less soluble in water and in other polar solvents. Polar covalent molecules are more soluble in water in comparison to that of non polar covalent molecules.
(b) Low melting point and boiling point: The intermolecular forces of attractions between the molecules of covalent compounds are generally weak. As a result, lesser amount of energy is needed to overcome these intermolecular forces. Thus, these compounds usually have low melting point and boiling point than ionic compounds.
(c) Conducting nature: These are generally poor conductors of electricity in the fused or dissolved state due to unavailability of ions. or gases at room temperature. However, a few covalent compounds also exist in the solid state e.g. glucose, urea, thiourea \& sugar etc.

## Electron Dot (Lewis Dot) Structures
Lewis dot structures for many species can be written according to the following steps :
(i) Pick up the central atom of the species in question.
(ii) Recall the number of electrons in the outermost orbit (valence electrons) in each atom of the species.
(iii) Recall the valency of the central atom and other atoms too.
(iv) Write down the structural formula of the species on the basis of point no. (ii) and (iii).
(v) Supply the required number of electrons to each bond (1 pair of electrons for a single bond, 2 pairs for a double bond and 3 pairs for a triple bond).
(vi) Verify that each atom of the species has inert gas configuration, i.e., either 2 (in case of hydrogen) or 8 electrons in the outermost orbit. Let us apply these points on few examples.
For main group elements, the number of valence electrons which an atom contributes in a Lewis structure is the same as its group number in the periodic table.

## Carbon Dioxide Molecule (CO2)
Carbon atom has four electrons in its outermost shell and oxygen atom has six electrons in its outermost shell.
Thus, each carbon atom requires four, and each oxygen atom requires two more electrons to acquire noble gas configurations. To achieve this, two oxygen atoms form a covalent double bond with carbon as follows

Each carbon then requires three more electrons to acquire a stable configuration of the nearest noble gas (neon). ## ALLOTROPES OF CARBON
Carbon (Latin carbo means charcoal) is an element of prehistoric discovery. It is very widely distributed in nature. It is found in abundance in the sun, stars, comets, and atmospheres of most planets.
Carbon can either be in structural crystalline forms or may occur in a structure-less amorphous form. Some elements like carbon, sulphur, tin, oxygen, etc. are found in more than one structural forms. Therefore, some elements can have several different structural forms while in the same physical state. These forms are called allotropes and such phenomenon is called allotropy. The various allotropic forms of carbon can be broadly classified into two classes : wurtzite are polymorphs of ZnS.
(a) Crystalline form : Pure carbon is found as graphite, diamond, Buckministerfullerene
Structure of Diamond
Structure of Graphite
Structure of Buckministerfullerene
- There is another form of crystalline carbon known as "white" carbon, but not much is known about it. Conditions such as temperature and pressure determine which allotrope of carbon occurs.
- A diamond is hard, clear, and shiny substance. It is formed under very high temperatures and pressure. Diamond has ability to reflect and refract light which makes it an important material for making jewellary.
Graphite is black, with a slippery, greasy feel. Graphite is formed on heating coke or coal.
- Though non-metallic, graphite possesses a metallic lustre. It is insoluble in ordinary solvents. Graphite is used in making electrodes, in electric furnances and electric ores. It is also used in lead pencils.

## Comparison between Diamond and Graphite
| | Diamond | Graphite |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| i. | Diamond is the hardest material known. | Graphite is one of the softest materials known. |
| ii. | Diamond is the ultimate abrasive. | Graphite is a very good lubricant. |
| iii. | Diamond is an excellent electrical insulator. | Graphite is a conductor of electricity. |
| iv. | Diamond is the best known naturally occurring thermal conductor. | Some forms of graphite are used for thermal insulation. (i.e. firebreaks and heat shields) |
| v. | Diamond is highly transparent. | Graphite is opaque. |
| vi. | Diamond crystallizes in the cubic system. | Graphite crystallizes in the hexagonal system. |
These differences in the properties of diamond and graphite are due to the difference in their structures.
In diamond, each C atom is linked to its neighbours by four single covalent bonds. This leads to a three-dimensional network of covalent bonds. In graphite, the carbon atoms are arranged in flat parallel layers as regular hexagons. Each carbon in these layers is bonded to three others by covalent bonds. Graphite thus acquires some double bond character.
Each layer is bonded to adjacent layers by weak van der Waal's forces. Moreover, one electron is free at each carbon atom. This allows each layer to slide over the other easily. Due to this type of structure graphite is soft and slippery, and can act as a lubricant. Graphite is also a good conductor of electricity due to mobile electrons in it.
Graphite is also used as a industrial lubricant because it possesses high melting point. Thus no change in structure occur even if machineries are working at high temperature.
Why graphite is used as lubricant?

## CATENATION IN CARBON
Carbon atom is unique amongst all the elements that are found in nature. It can form long chain molecules. The ability of carbon to form a long chain is called catenation. Carbon forms strong bond because of its small size which enables the nucleus to held on to the shared pairs of electrons strongly. The chains are formed because carbon atoms form tetravalent bonds with other carbon atoms. This structure can be repeated endlessly without disturbing the stability of the bonds and the compounds formed. The chains can form branches, and sub-branches. The carbon atoms also form rings. The rings themselves can have more rings attached to them. Protein molecules and amino acids are long chain carbon molecules.
Figure : Variety of carbon chains formed when carbon atoms join together.
In addition, carbon atoms may be linked by single, double or triple bonds. Compounds of carbon, which has only single bonds between the carbon atoms are called saturated compounds. Compounds of carbon having double or triple bonds between their carbon atoms are called unsaturated compounds.

## COMPOUNDS OF CARBON
Compounds of carbon can broadly classified into two main categories, namely inorganic and organic compounds.
Inorganic compounds : These include compounds of carbon with metals and non-metals (other than hydrogen) such as oxygen, halogens etc. These do not have carbon-carbon bonds.
Organic compounds : Organic compounds are those chemical compounds in which one or more atoms of carbon are covalently linked to atoms of other elements, most commonly oxygen or nitrogen.

## Inorganic Compounds of Carbon
Carbon combines with a variety of other elements like oxygen, halogens, metals, etc., to form binary compounds respectively named as oxides, halides and carbides.

## Oxides of carbon :
(a) Carbon monoxide, CO
(i) Carbon monoxide is a colourless, tasteless gas with faint odour.
(ii) Carbon monoxide is extremely poisonous in nature. The poisonous nature of CO is due to the fact that it combines with haemoglobin (a red colouring matter of blood), oxygen carrier of blood, to form a stable compound carboxyhaemoglobin. As a result, oxygen transporation is disturbed and thus brain and body tissues do not get necessary oxygen and ultimately death occurs. This explains, why people sleeping in closed rooms with charcoal fire burning inside, dies.
A victim of carbon monoxide poisoning, if unconscious, should be brought in the open place and Know!
given artificial respiration with carbogen (mixture of oxygen and 5-10\% <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ).

## Uses :
(i) Carbon monoxide is used as a fuel in the form of water gas ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) and producer gas ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ).
(ii) It is used in making metal carbonyls among which nickel tetracarbonyl is used in the extraction of nickel (Mond's process).
(iii) It is used in the manufacture of methanol, synthetic petrol and phosgene.
(iv) It is used as a reducing agent in metallurgy of iron and in the manufacture of hydrogen.
(v) Iron carbonyl is used in the manufacture of magnetic tapes for videos and tape recorders.
(b) Carbon dioxide, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
It is present in air to the extent of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.03</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> by volume. It is found in caves, mines, etc., and it evolves from volcanoes.
(i) Carbon dioxide can be easily liquefied under pressure (50-60 atmospheres) and also solidified. Solid carbon dioxide is technically known as dry ice because it evaporates (sublimes) without liquefying (it sublimes at 195 K ). It is used as a refrigerant (coolant) under the commercial name of drikold. When it is placed in an organic solvent like ether, it gives a constant temperature of 173 K .
(ii) Although <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is not poisonous in nature, it does not support life.
(iii) It is neither combustible nor a supporter of combustion. But certain active metals like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> and Mg continue burning in atmosphere of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. It is due to the fact that the active metals combine with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to form the oxides. The latter combine with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to form carbonates.
