theory_sections.topics: Origin and Definition of Organic Compounds :
theory_sections.markdown:
## Origin and Definition of Organic Compounds :
According to the earlier definition, organic chemistry was defined as the chemistry of substances found in the living matter (Berzelius in 1808). Further, Berzelius in 1815 also suggested that the organic compounds could be prepared only by living organisms under the influence of a mysterious force known as the vital force (life-force). The vital force theory remain unchallanged until 1828, when Friedrich Wohler, a German chemist, reported the synthesis of a typical organic compound urea by heating an inorganic compound, ammonium cyanate.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Ammonium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> chloride </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Potassium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> cyanate </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Ammonium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> cyanate </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
The synthesis of urea from inorganic compounds gave a blow to the vital force theory and thus the distinction between organic and inorganic compounds based on vital force soon started fading away. The vital force theory was completely discarded after the synthesis of acetic acid from C, H and O (Kolbe, 1845) and methane (Berthelet, 1856). Subsequently, a large number of naturally occurring organic compounds were synthesized in the laboratory and the vital force theory was decisively disproved.
However, all the organic compounds were found to contain carbon as one of the elements. Thus the emphasis for the definition of organic compounds was shifted from origin to composition. Accordingly, organic chemistry has now been defined as the chemistry of carbon compounds.
On the basis of this definition, the study of compounds like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, carbonates, cyanides, cyanates, carbides, etc., should be included in organic chemistry, but due to their greater resemblance with inorganic compounds these are studied under inorganic chemistry.
Further, since all the organic compounds could be considered as derivatives of hydrocarbons, a more appropriate definition for the organic chemistry is the study of hydrocarbons and their derivatives.

## HYDROCARBONS
Compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen are known as hydrocarbons. Petroleum and coal are the two important natural sources of hydrocarbons. Petroleum is a major source of aliphatic hydrocarbons while coal is a source of aromatic hydrocarbons.
On the basis of structure and properties, hydrocarbons can be classified broadly into two classes.

## 1. Open Chain or Acyclic Hydrocarbons
As the name represents, these hydrocarbons contain open chain of carbon atoms in their molecules. These are also called aliphatic hydrocarbons. These are further classified into three types depending on the nature of carbon-carbon bonds in their molecules namely alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.
(i) Alkanes : These contain carbon-carbon single bonds e.g.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mtext> Ethane </mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mtext> Butane </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math>
General formula of alkane is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and are commonly called paraffins.
(ii) Alkenes : These contain at least one carbon-carbon double bonds, e.g.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Ethene </mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mtext> Butene-2 </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math>
General formula of alkene is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. They are commonly called olefins.
(iii) Alkynes : These contain at least one carbon-carbon triple bonds, e.g.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>≡</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Ethyne
Propyne
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>≡</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Butyne-2
General formula of alkyne is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. They are traditionally called acetylenes, although the name acetylene also refers specifically to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.

## 2. Closed Chain or Cyclic Hydrocarbons
As the name represents, these compounds contain closed chain (ring) of carbon atoms in their molecules. These are further divided into two types namely cycloalkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons or arenes.
(i) Cycloalkanes : Those saturated hydrocarbons in which carbon atoms are joined together to form ring are known as cycloalkanes. For example,
Cyclopropane
Cyclopentane
Cyclohexane
(ii) Aromatic hydrocarbons or Arenes: Those hydrocarbons which contain at least one benzene ring in their molecules are called arenes. For example,
Toluene
Naphthalene
All the above types of hydrocarbons may also be grouped in a different manner into two types depending upon the basis of nature of carbon-carbon bonds in their molecules.
(i) Saturated hydrocarbons: These contain carbon-carbon single bonds in their molecules. Alkanes and cycloalkanes are grouped in this category.
(ii) Unsaturated hydrocarbons: These contains carbon-carbon multiple bond (double or triple) in their molecules. Alkenes, alkynes and arenes are grouped in this category.

## FUNCTIONAL GROUPS
In organic chemistry, functional groups (or moieties) are specific groups of atoms within molecules that are responsible for the characteristic chemical reactions of those molecules. The same functional group will undergo the same or similar chemical reaction(s) regardless of the size of the molecule for example, - OH (alcohol), - CHO (aldehyde) etc.

## HOMOLOGOUS SERIES
In chemistry, a homologous series is a series of organic compounds with a similar general formula, possessing similar chemical properties due to the presence of the same functional group, and shows a gradation in physical properties as a result of increase in molecular size and mass (see relative molecular mass). For example, ethane has a higher boiling point than methane since it has more van der Waal's forces(intermolecular forces) with neighbouring molecules. This is due to increase in the number of atoms making up the molecule.
Organic compounds in the same homologous series differ by a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> group. Alkanes (paraffins), alkenes (olefins), methoxyethane (ethers), and alkynes (acetylenes) form such series in which members differ in mass by 14 atomic mass units. For example, the alkane homologous series have methane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, ethane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, propane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, butane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, and pentane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, each member differing from the previous one by a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> group (or 14 atomic mass units).
Similarly, alcohol homologous series starts with methanol ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ), ethanol ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ), propylalcohol ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ) etc.
- A homologation reaction is any chemical process converting one member of a homologous series to the next.

## NOMENCLATURE OF CARBON COMPOUNDS
In the early stages of the development, the various organic compounds were named on the basis of either the source of origin of the compounds or on some specific property of the compounds. For example, methane gas is found to get released in marshy places. Hence it is called marsh gas. These names are called trivial or common names.
In order to give names for the huge number of organic compounds used all over the world, a more systematic method was required. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) developed a systematic approach to the nomenclature of organic compounds based on its structure and reflects the physical and chemical properties. This IUPAC system has three parts: root word, suffix and prefix.

## CHEMICAL PROPERTIES OF CARBON COMPOUNDS

## Combustion
Combustion usually occurs when a hydrocarbon reacts with oxygen to produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>.
In more general sense, combustion involves a reaction between any combustible materials and an oxidizer to form an oxidized product. Combustion is an exothermic reaction, so it release heat. General reaction is:
Hydrocarbon + Oxygen ⟶ Carbondioxide + Water
For examples:

- If compound undergoing combustion contains nitrogen (it burns to form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) or sulfur (it burns to form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></math>
- There are complexities with combustion as you get deeper into it. For example, a combustion with insufficient oxygen yields carbon monoxide rather than carbon dioxide.
- In a very limited supply of air, methane gives carbon black.

## Learn More
Saturated hydrocarbons will generally give a clean flame while unsaturated carbon compounds will give a yellow flame with lots of black smoke,limiting the supply of air results in incomplete combustion of even saturated hydrocarbons giving a sooty flame. The gas/kerosene stove used at home has inlets for air so that a sufficiently oxygen-rich mixture is burnt to give a clean blue flame. If you observe the bottom of cooking vessels getting blackened, it means that the air holes are blocked and fuel is getting wasted. Fuels such as coal and petroleum have some amount of nitrogen and sulphur in them. Their combustion results in the formation of oxides of sulphur and nitrogen which are major pollutants in the environment.

## Oxidation
Carbon undergoes oxidation by combining with oxygen at higher temperature to form oxides, viz., carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon dioxide ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ). Carbon monoxide is formed, when incomplete combustion of carbon or carbon containing fuels takes place.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
CO is present in automobile exhausts (when there is incomplete combustion), volcanic gases, chimney gases etc. Carbon dioxide is formed by the complete combustion of carbon, hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide etc.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mtext> Heat </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mtext> Heat </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Carbon containing compounds undergo oxidation reactions when burnt in air or oxygen in the presence of catalyst to give useful products other then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>. For example, when methane is mixed with oxygen and heated in presence of molybdenum oxide, it gets oxidized to methanal or formaldehyde.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>350</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>500</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Molybdenum oxide </mtext></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
Oxidation of carbon compounds is used for producing other carbon compounds like alcohols, carboxylic acids, ethers etc. Methanol, an industrial alcohol, for instance, is prepared by the oxidation of methane.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><munderover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Copper tube </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><msup><mn>200</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></munderover><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Acetic acid is manufactured by the oxidation of fermented liquors ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> alcohol) in air along with the presence of mycoderma aceti. A 3-7\% solution of acetic acid is obtained and it is called vinegar.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

## Addition Reaction
Reactions in which an atoms or group of atoms are added to a molecule (i.e., there is simply a net gain of the reagent atoms in product molecule) are called addition reactions. The important examples of addition reactions are summarised below.
(a) Addition of hydrogen (Catalytic hydrogenation, hydrogenation in presence of catalyst): Hydrogen adds to unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkenes, and alkynes) in presence of metallic catalyst, such as finely divided platinum, palladium or nickel and form the corresponding alkane. For example,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethene </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>473</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>573</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow></mfrac><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethane </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
This reaction is used industrially in preparation of vegetable ghee which contains mainly saturate fatty acids from vegetable oils which mainly contains unsaturated fatty acids.
(b) Addition of halogens : When an alkene is treated at room temperature with chlorine or bromine in an inert solvent (usually chloroform or carbon tetrachloride), halogen adds rapidly to the double bond of the alkene and produces a vicinal dihalide.
Vicinal dibromide
Reaction of alkenes with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> with fluorine is explosive whereas iodine does not react under normal conditions. This reaction can be used as a test for unsaturation of alkenes because the brown colour of bromine will get decolourised by alkenes.
This reaction is also given by alkynes.
In your school lab, take two beakers containing bromine solution and label them A and B. Then add vanaspati ghee in beaker A and vegetable oil in B respectively. In beaker A , color of bromine solution remains same but in beaker B color of solution gets faded up or discharged. What is the reason for this observation? Consult your friends and teacher in case of any problem.
(c) Addition of hydrogen halides (hydrohalogenation) : On addition of hydrogen halide to an alkene, it forms an alkyl halides, e.g.
If the alkene is unsymmetrical, then the negative part of attacking molecule joins with the carbon atom which carries lesser number of hydrogen atoms as per Markovnikov's rule.
In the presence of organic peroxides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> e.g. benzoyl peroxide the reaction takes place opposite to the Markovnikov's rule. This is known as an anti Markovnikov's rule or Kharasch effect,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Propene </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Only HBr shows this peroxide effect, but not HF, HCl and HI, where addition occur according to Markovnikov's rule even in presence of peroxides.
(d) Addition of hypohalous acids : Alkenes react with hypochlorous and hypobromous acids readily to form the corresponding halohydrin.

## CONNECTING TOPIC
When the reagent has two different atoms, e.g. but addition of unsymmetrical reagent to unsymmetrical alkene (when the two doubly bond carbon atoms have different number of H atoms, e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) may form two different products.
But in practice, one of the products (here 2-chloropropane formed in major amount, while the other here 1-chloropropane is formed in minor amount.
Additions in such reactions, is governed by Markovnikov's rule according to which negative part of the reagent (e.g. Cl in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math> in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, etc ) adds on that carbon atom of the alkene which has lesser number of carbon atoms. ## Substitution Reaction
The reactions in which an atom or group of atoms in a molecule is replaced or substituted by different atoms or group of atoms are called substitution reaction. For example,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mtext> (H replaced by </mtext><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>I</mi><mtext> replaced by </mtext><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
## CONNECTING TOPIC

## Important Substitution Reactions
In substitution reactions the hydrogen of the alkane molecule is replaced by another atom or a group of atoms (like alkyl) resulting in the formation of the derivatives of that hydrocarbon. Substitution by halogen atom is generally called halogenation. This type of substitution results in chlorination, bromination or iodination.
Like methane, ethane also forms a series of substitution products in the presence of excess chlorine and sunlight.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethane </mtext></mrow></munder><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> uv light </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Chloroethane </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(a) Bromination : Bromination of alkanes is similar to chlorination but not so vigorous.
(b) Iodination : Iodination of alkanes is reversible and slow.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mrow><mo>⇌</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow></mover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Iodination may be carried out in the presence of an oxidising agent such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, etc. which destroys the HI as it is formed and so drives the reaction to the right.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
(c) Nitration : When a mixture of alkane and vapours of fuming nitric acid is heated between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>150</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>475</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>, a complex mixture of nitroalkanes is obtained.

theory_sections.markdown:
## Preparation of ethanol by fermentation of sugar
Fermentation is a process whereby an organic compound is broken into smaller molecules by enzymes such as yeast. Ethanol is prepared by fermentation of molasses. Molasses, a by product of sugar industry, has traces of sugar. The fermentation is initiated by yeast, which secretes two enzymes called invertase and zymase. These enzymes act as catalyst for converting sugar into ethanol. The reaction is exothermic and carbon dioxide is released in the process.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Sucrose </mtext></mrow></munder><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Invertase </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Glucose </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Fructose </mtext></mrow></munder><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Glucose or fructose </mtext></mrow></munder><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Zymase </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethanol </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></mrow></math>
- Presence of air will tend to oxidise the mixture whose resultant is vinegar (acetic acid or ethanoic acid) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. This is undesirable.
- Ethanol can also be made by fermentation of starchy materials such as barley, potatoes and maize. The starch is first converted to sugar by fermentation and then to ethanol.

## Ethanol preparation by hydration of ethene
An addition of a water molecule will convert ethene into ethanol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

Addition of water to a molecule is known as hydration.

## Physical Properties :
Ethanol is a versatile solvent, miscible in all proportions with water and many organic solvents, including acetic acid, acetone, benzene, carbon tetrachloride, chloroform. Solubility of higher alcohols ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> or more) decreases rapidly as the number of carbons increases. The polar nature of the hydroxyl group causes ethanol to dissolve in many ionic compounds.

Ethanol can also form esters with inorganic acids. Diethyl sulfate and triethyl phosphate, prepared by reacting ethanol with sulfuric and phosphoric acid respectively, are both useful ethylating agents in organic synthesis. Ethyl nitrite, prepared from the reaction of ethanol with sodium nitrite and sulfuric acid, was formerly a widely-used diuretic.

theory_sections.topics: How Do Alcohols Affect Living Beings?
theory_sections.markdown:
## How Do Alcohols Affect Living Beings?
Superficially, ethanol evokes a distinctive heat-like sensation in the mouth and a stinging sensation on the skin. In the body it is metabolized to other substances, affecting the central nervous system in particular. The effect varies between individuals, and can be worse when applied in addition to certain drugs. When applied to open wounds (as for disinfection) it produces a strong stinging sensation. Pure or highly concentrated ethanol may permanently damage living tissue on contact. When large quantities of ethanol are consumed, it tends to slow metabolic processes and depresses the central nervous system. This results in lack of coordination, mental confusion, drowsiness, lowering of the normal inhibitions, and finally stupour.
The individual ethanol consuming may feel relaxed but does not realise that his sense of judgement, sense of timing, and muscular coordination have been seriously impaired. Ethanol within the human body is converted into acetaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase and then into acetic acid by acetaldehyde dehydrogenase. The product of the first step of this breakdown, acetaldehyde, is more toxic than ethanol. It has been shown to increase the risk of developing cirrhosis of the liver, multiple forms of cancer, and alcoholism. Death from ethyl alcohol consumption is possible when blood alcohol level reaches <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.4</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math>. A blood alcohol level of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> or more is commonly fatal.

## Uses of Ethanol
(a) Ethanol is used in manufacturing of paints, dyes, varnishes etc.
(b) Ethanol is used in medicines especially for disinfecting area on the skin before giving an injection. It is used for sterilization of syringes in hospitals.
(c) Ethanol is used for preparation of compounds such as chloroform and ether.
(d) Ethanol is used for making thermometer that is used for measuring low temperatures.
(e) Ethanol is used in spirit lamps.
(f) Ethanol blended fuel called rectified spirit is used as a substitute for fuels in vehicles that are environmental pollutant. They give off low emissions of carbon monoxide gas that is harmful to the environment. Ethanol is the main component of alcoholic beverages such as rum, whisky and beer.
(g) Ethanol is used as an organic solvent.
(h) Ethanol is used as an antifreeze mixture for radiators in cars. Ethanol mixed with water freezes at a lower temperature than water. Such an antifreeze mixture is used for radiators in cold countries.
Make a project report on the use of ethyl alcohol as a fuel. Mention which type of ethyl alcohol blended fuels are currently or in near by future sold in market. Also mention the composition of these fuels. Make into account the merits and demerits of using ethyl alcohol as fuel. You can consult your teacher and can take help of internet, television, science magazine etc.

## ACETIC ACID (ETHANOIC ACID)
Acetic acid, also known as ethanoic acid, is an organic chemical compound best recognized for giving vinegar its sour taste and pungent smell. Its chemical formula is represented as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. The trivial name acetic acid is commonly used. Glacial acetic acid is a trivial name for water-free acetic acid, the name comes from the ice-like crystals formed slightly below room temperature at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>16.7</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> (about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>62</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> ).
It is a weak acid because at standard temperature and pressure the dissociated acid exists in
Did You Know! equilibrium with the undissociated form in aqueous solutions, in contrast to strong acids, which are fully dissociated.

## Physical Properties
Pure, acetic acid (glacial acetic acid) is a colourless liquid that attracts water from the environment (hygroscopy), and freezes below <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>16.7</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>62</mn><msup><mrow /><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> ) to a colourless crystalline solid. Acetic acid is the second simplest carboxylic acids (first being formic acid, HCOOH ). Acetic acid is corrosive, and its vapour causes irritation to the eyes, a dry and burning nose, sore throat and congestion to lungs.

## Chemical Properties
Carboxylic acids <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ionises in aqueous solution to give H , hence these are acidic in nature. Acetic acid is a weak, monoprotic acid. Acetic acid is corrosive to metals including iron, magnesium, and zinc, forming hydrogen gas and metal salts called acetates.

## Reactions of Acetic Acid (Ethanoic Acid) :
(a) Esterification reaction : Esterification is the reaction between an acid and an alcohol producing ester( sweet-smelling substances).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Alkanol </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mtext> Alkanoic acid </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>⇌</mo><munder><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ester </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Water </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
Esters are used in making perfumes and as flavouring agents.
Esters react in the presence of an acid or a base to give back the alcohol and carboxylic acid. This reaction is known as ester hydrolysis or saponification (hydrolysis in presence of base) because it is used in the preparation of soap.
(b) Reaction with a base: Like mineral acids, ethanoic acid reacts with a base such as sodium hydroxide to give a salt (sodium ethanoate or commonly called sodium acetate) and water:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
(c) Reaction with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates: Ethanoic acid reacts with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates to give rise to a salt, carbon dioxide and water. The salt produced is commonly called sodium acetate.

- What are the products obtained on reaction of acetic acid with magnesium carbonate?

## Uses
It is an important chemical reagent and industrial chemical that is used in the production of polyethylene terephthalate, mainly used in soft drink bottles; cellulose acetate, mainly for photographic film; and polyvinyl acetate for wood glue, as well as synthetic fibres and fabrics. In households, dilute acetic acid is often used in descaling agents. In the food industry, acetic acid is used under the food additive code E260 as an acidity regulator.

## SOAPS AND DETERGENTS
Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of higher fatty acids, produced from the alkaline hydrolysis of fats (higher fatty acids) in a chemical reaction. The reaction is called saponification. They are of biological origin. Each soap molecule has a long hydrocarbon chain, sometimes called its 'tail', with a carboxylate 'head'. In water, the sodium or potassium ions float free, leaving a negatively charged head.
- When the alkali is sodium hydroxide, a sodium soap is formed. Sodium soaps are "hard" soaps. When the alkali is potassium hydroxide, a potassium soap is formed. Potassium soaps are softer and are found in some liquid hand soaps and shaving creams.
- Soap is an excellent cleanser because of its ability to act as an emulsifying agent. An emulsifier is capable of dispersing one liquid into another immiscible liquid. This means that while oil (which attracts dirt) doesn't naturally mix with water, soap can suspends oil/dirt in such a way that it can be removed.
Detergents (syndets) are emulsifying agents that are very similar to soaps but they do not have a biological origin and they do not have a carboxylate group instead of it they have sulphonate group as they are sodium salt of long chain sulphonic acids. Synthetic detergents usually have a long hydrocarbon chain of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></math> carbon atoms. At the head of this chain there is a polar group that forms a strong hydrogen bond with water but does not form strong ionic bonds with the ions of hard water.
Before dealing with cleansing action of soap let us understand few points:
(i) The salts of fatty acids have an ionic polar head group, the carboxylate and a long non-polar hydrocarbon chain.
Figure : Structure of a detergent molecule and it's cleansing action
(ii) The polar group is hydrophilic (i.e. water-loving), the non-polar portion is hydrophobic (i.e. water-hating) or lipophilic.
(iii) An aqueous solutions of this type of compound tend to form ordered aggregates such as micelles and bilayers.
(iv) Here the polar groups are exposed to the water and the hydrocarbon portions are buried within the core, away from the water.

## How Soap Cleans :
The things we call "dirt" are actually grease, oils, and fats which are insoluble in water. When cleaning, soap micelles come into contact with the "dirt" and because like dissolves like, a minute amount of "dirt" dissolves within the central region of the soap micelle. Nonpolar dirts are emulsified and washed away in polar wash water. This is why soaps are said to be good emulsifying agents.

theory_sections.topics: How Does Detergent Remove Grease From Clothing ?
theory_sections.markdown:
## How Does Detergent Remove Grease From Clothing ?
Detergent molecules contain hydrophobic tails (hydrocarbon chain) which are water hating and will attach themselves to any substance which is non-polar (grease). The tails surround the grease with the polar heads in the aqueous phase, forming the structure shown. On agitation, the grease is pulled from the clothing allowing the grease to be completely surrounded and moved into the aqueous phase. This is then washed away leaving only clean clothes behind.
Figure : Structure of a detergent molecule and it's cleansing action

## Surface Tension/Surfactants :
The property of a liquid due to which its free surface tries to have minimum surface area and behaves as if it were under tension some what like a stretched elastic membrane is called surface tension. Chemicals that are able to reduce the surface tension of the solvent effectively are called surface active agents, or surfactants. Surfactants perform other important functions in cleaning, such as loosening, emulsifying (dispersing in water) and holding soil in suspension until it can be rinsed away. Surfactants can also provide alkalinity, which is useful in removing acidic soils. Surfactants are classified by their ionic (electrical charge) properties in water: anionic (negative charge), nonionic (no charge), cationic (positive charge) and amphoteric (either positive or negative charge). Soap is an anionic surfactant. Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) is a compound which is added to synthetic detergent to keep the dust particles suspended in water, and helps in cleansing process.

## CASE III : Detergents have number of
advantages over soaps but detergents are the main pollutants to cause water pollution. Why?
An important disadvantage of detergents over soap is that some of the detergents are non biodegradable, that is they cannot be decomposed by micro-organisms and hence cause water pollution in water bodies. Detergents sometimes could be carcinogenic, so they should be eliminated from the water e.g. phosphate salt. It is the main constituent of the laundry detergents, which tends to inhibit the biodegradation of organic substances. Non-biodegradable substances cannot be eliminated by public waste water treatment. In addition to that, some phosphate based detergents can also cause eutrophication.
CASE II : The cleaning action of soap is very effective in soft water but it is not effective in hard water. If detergents are used for cleaning purpose, it
Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts whereas soft water contains negligible amount of calcium and magnesium ions. Generally, soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long chain fatty acids. When soap is added to hard water, the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ions present in hard water react with soap. The sodium salts present in soap are converted to their corresponding calcium and magnesium salts which are precipitated as scum. The insoluble scum sticks on the clothes thus the cleaning capacity of soap is reduced. Soft water, however, does not contain any calcium or magnesium ions, therefore, lathers easily when soap is added. A detergent is the sodium salt of long chain benzene sulphonic acid. Detergent can form lather easily even in hard water because they do not form insoluble <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> salts on reacting with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ions present in hard water.

## Markownikoff's rule
When an unsymmetrical alkene or alkyne reacts with unsymmetrical reagent, then negative part of reagent attach with that carbon atom which contains lesser number of hydrogen atom during the addition.
For example:
(Markownikoff's addition)
Addition of HBr (not <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and HF ) on alkenes in presence of peroxides takes place in anti-Markownikoff's way (Peroxide effect).

15. Cleaning Action of Soap and Detergent : Both of them follow the same principle. They contain two parts, a large hydrocarbon which is hydrophobic (water repelling) and a negative charged head, which is hydrophillic (water attracting). In solution water molecules being polar in nature, surround the head and not the organic part of the molecule. When a soap or detergent is dissolved in water, the molecule gather together as clusters, called micelles. The tails stick inwards and the head outwards oily dirt will be collected in the centre of the micelle. The hydrocarbon tail attaches itself to oily dirt. When water is agitated, the oily dirt tends to lift off from the dirty surface and dissociates into fragments. The solution now contains small globules of oil surrounded by detergent molecules. The negatively charged heads present in water prevent the small globules from coming together and form aggregates. Thus the oily dirt is removed from the object.
Micelle formed by detergent molecules in water. The hydrocarbon tail sticks to oily dirt

## CATENATION IN CARBON
Carbon atom is unique amongst all the elements that are found in nature. It can form long chain molecules. The ability of carbon to form a long chain is called catenation. Carbon forms strong bond because of its small size which enables the nucleus to held on to the shared pairs of electrons strongly. The chains are formed because carbon atoms form tetravalent bonds with other carbon atoms. This structure can be repeated endlessly without disturbing the stability of the bonds and the compounds formed. The chains can form branches, and sub-branches. The carbon atoms also form rings. The rings themselves can have more rings attached to them. Protein molecules and amino acids are long chain carbon molecules.
Figure : Variety of carbon chains formed when carbon atoms join together.
In addition, carbon atoms may be linked by single, double or triple bonds. Compounds of carbon, which has only single bonds between the carbon atoms are called saturated compounds. Compounds of carbon having double or triple bonds between their carbon atoms are called unsaturated compounds.

## COMPOUNDS OF CARBON
Compounds of carbon can broadly classified into two main categories, namely inorganic and organic compounds.
Inorganic compounds : These include compounds of carbon with metals and non-metals (other than hydrogen) such as oxygen, halogens etc. These do not have carbon-carbon bonds.
Organic compounds : Organic compounds are those chemical compounds in which one or more atoms of carbon are covalently linked to atoms of other elements, most commonly oxygen or nitrogen.
## Inorganic Compounds of Carbon
Carbon combines with a variety of other elements like oxygen, halogens, metals, etc., to form binary compounds respectively named as oxides, halides and carbides.
## Oxides of carbon :
(a) Carbon monoxide, CO
(i) Carbon monoxide is a colourless, tasteless gas with faint odour.
(ii) Carbon monoxide is extremely poisonous in nature. The poisonous nature of CO is due to the fact that it combines with haemoglobin (a red colouring matter of blood), oxygen carrier of blood, to form a stable compound carboxyhaemoglobin. As a result, oxygen transporation is disturbed and thus brain and body tissues do not get necessary oxygen and ultimately death occurs. This explains, why people sleeping in closed rooms with charcoal fire burning inside, dies.
A victim of carbon monoxide poisoning, if unconscious, should be brought in the open place and Know!
given artificial respiration with carbogen (mixture of oxygen and 5-10\% <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ).
## Uses :
(i) Carbon monoxide is used as a fuel in the form of water gas ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) and producer gas ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ).
(ii) It is used in making metal carbonyls among which nickel tetracarbonyl is used in the extraction of nickel (Mond's process).
(iii) It is used in the manufacture of methanol, synthetic petrol and phosgene.
(iv) It is used as a reducing agent in metallurgy of iron and in the manufacture of hydrogen.
(v) Iron carbonyl is used in the manufacture of magnetic tapes for videos and tape recorders.
(b) Carbon dioxide, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
It is present in air to the extent of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.03</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> by volume. It is found in caves, mines, etc., and it evolves from volcanoes.
(i) Carbon dioxide can be easily liquefied under pressure (50-60 atmospheres) and also solidified. Solid carbon dioxide is technically known as dry ice because it evaporates (sublimes) without liquefying (it sublimes at 195 K ). It is used as a refrigerant (coolant) under the commercial name of drikold. When it is placed in an organic solvent like ether, it gives a constant temperature of 173 K .
(ii) Although <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is not poisonous in nature, it does not support life.
(iii) It is neither combustible nor a supporter of combustion. But certain active metals like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> and Mg continue burning in atmosphere of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. It is due to the fact that the active metals combine with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to form the oxides. The latter combine with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to form carbonates.

(iv) Carbon dioxide is absorbed by plants in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll (green colouring matter) to form glucose and higher carbohydrates. This process is known as photosynthesis.

## HOMOLOGOUS SERIES
In chemistry, a homologous series is a series of organic compounds with a similar general formula, possessing similar chemical properties due to the presence of the same functional group, and shows a gradation in physical properties as a result of increase in molecular size and mass (see relative molecular mass). For example, ethane has a higher boiling point than methane since it has more van der Waal's forces(intermolecular forces) with neighbouring molecules. This is due to increase in the number of atoms making up the molecule.
Organic compounds in the same homologous series differ by a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> group. Alkanes (paraffins), alkenes (olefins), methoxyethane (ethers), and alkynes (acetylenes) form such series in which members differ in mass by 14 atomic mass units. For example, the alkane homologous series have methane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, ethane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, propane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, butane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, and pentane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, each member differing from the previous one by a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> group (or 14 atomic mass units).
Similarly, alcohol homologous series starts with methanol ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ), ethanol ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ), propylalcohol ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ) etc.
- A homologation reaction is any chemical process converting one member of a homologous series to the next.
In homologous series each member differ from the previous one by a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> group (or 14 atomic mass units).
## NOMENCLATURE OF CARBON COMPOUNDS
In the early stages of the development, the various organic compounds were named on the basis of either the source of origin of the compounds or on some specific property of the compounds. For example, methane gas is found to get released in marshy places. Hence it is called marsh gas. These names are called trivial or common names.
In order to give names for the huge number of organic compounds used all over the world, a more systematic method was required. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) developed a systematic approach to the nomenclature of organic compounds based on its structure and reflects the physical and chemical properties. This IUPAC system has three parts: root word, suffix and prefix.
## For detail explanation please refer chapter-8
## CHEMICAL PROPERTIES OF CARBON COMPOUNDS
## Combustion
Combustion usually occurs when a hydrocarbon reacts with oxygen to produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>.
In more general sense, combustion involves a reaction between any combustible materials and an oxidizer to form an oxidized product. Combustion is an exothermic reaction, so it release heat. General reaction is:
Hydrocarbon + Oxygen ⟶ Carbondioxide + Water

## Oxidation
Carbon undergoes oxidation by combining with oxygen at higher temperature to form oxides, viz., carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon dioxide ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ). Carbon monoxide is formed, when incomplete combustion of carbon or carbon containing fuels takes place.

## Addition Reaction
Reactions in which an atoms or group of atoms are added to a molecule (i.e., there is simply a net gain of the reagent atoms in product molecule) are called addition reactions. The important examples of addition reactions are summarised below.
(a) Addition of hydrogen (Catalytic hydrogenation, hydrogenation in presence of catalyst): Hydrogen adds to unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkenes, and alkynes) in presence of metallic catalyst, such as finely divided platinum, palladium or nickel and form the corresponding alkane. For example,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethene </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>473</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>573</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow></mfrac><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethane </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
This reaction is used industrially in preparation of vegetable ghee which contains mainly saturate fatty acids from vegetable oils which mainly contains unsaturated fatty acids.
(b) Addition of halogens : When an alkene is treated at room temperature with chlorine or bromine in an inert solvent (usually chloroform or carbon tetrachloride), halogen adds rapidly to the double bond of the alkene and produces a vicinal dihalide.

## How Do Alcohols Affect Living Beings?
Superficially, ethanol evokes a distinctive heat-like sensation in the mouth and a stinging sensation on the skin. In the body it is metabolized to other substances, affecting the central nervous system in particular. The effect varies between individuals, and can be worse when applied in addition to certain drugs. When applied to open wounds (as for disinfection) it produces a strong stinging sensation. Pure or highly concentrated ethanol may permanently damage living tissue on contact. When large quantities of ethanol are consumed, it tends to slow metabolic processes and depresses the central nervous system. This results in lack of coordination, mental confusion, drowsiness, lowering of the normal inhibitions, and finally stupour.
The individual ethanol consuming may feel relaxed but does not realise that his sense of judgement, sense of timing, and muscular coordination have been seriously impaired. Ethanol within the human body is converted into acetaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase and then into acetic acid by acetaldehyde dehydrogenase. The product of the first step of this breakdown, acetaldehyde, is more toxic than ethanol. It has been shown to increase the risk of developing cirrhosis of the liver, multiple forms of cancer, and alcoholism. Death from ethyl alcohol consumption is possible when blood alcohol level reaches <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.4</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math>. A blood alcohol level of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> or more is commonly fatal.
## Uses of Ethanol
(a) Ethanol is used in manufacturing of paints, dyes, varnishes etc.
(b) Ethanol is used in medicines especially for disinfecting area on the skin before giving an injection. It is used for sterilization of syringes in hospitals.
(c) Ethanol is used for preparation of compounds such as chloroform and ether.
(d) Ethanol is used for making thermometer that is used for measuring low temperatures.
(e) Ethanol is used in spirit lamps.
(f) Ethanol blended fuel called rectified spirit is used as a substitute for fuels in vehicles that are environmental pollutant. They give off low emissions of carbon monoxide gas that is harmful to the environment. Ethanol is the main component of alcoholic beverages such as rum, whisky and beer.
(g) Ethanol is used as an organic solvent.
(h) Ethanol is used as an antifreeze mixture for radiators in cars. Ethanol mixed with water freezes at a lower temperature than water. Such an antifreeze mixture is used for radiators in cold countries.

## ACETIC ACID (ETHANOIC ACID)
Acetic acid, also known as ethanoic acid, is an organic chemical compound best recognized for giving vinegar its sour taste and pungent smell. Its chemical formula is represented as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. The trivial name acetic acid is commonly used. Glacial acetic acid is a trivial name for water-free acetic acid, the name comes from the ice-like crystals formed slightly below room temperature at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>16.7</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> (about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>62</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> ).
It is a weak acid because at standard temperature and pressure the dissociated acid exists in
Did You Know! equilibrium with the undissociated form in aqueous solutions, in contrast to strong acids, which are fully dissociated.
## Physical Properties
Pure, acetic acid (glacial acetic acid) is a colourless liquid that attracts water from the environment (hygroscopy), and freezes below <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>16.7</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>62</mn><msup><mrow /><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> ) to a colourless crystalline solid. Acetic acid is the second simplest carboxylic acids (first being formic acid, HCOOH ). Acetic acid is corrosive, and its vapour causes irritation to the eyes, a dry and burning nose, sore throat and congestion to lungs.
## Chemical Properties
Carboxylic acids <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ionises in aqueous solution to give H , hence these are acidic in nature. Acetic acid is a weak, monoprotic acid. Acetic acid is corrosive to metals including iron, magnesium, and zinc, forming hydrogen gas and metal salts called acetates.
