Mendeleev predicted the existence and properties of unknown elements which he called eka? aluminum, eka-boron, and eka-silicon. The elements gallium, scandium and germanium were found later to fit his predictions quite well.
## Main Features of Mendeleev's Periodic Table
In Mendeleev's periodic table elements are arranged in tabular form in rows and columns. It has been modified from time to time. Now let us learn more about these rows and columns and the elements present in them.
a. The horizontal rows present in the periodic table are called periods. Originally, there were six periods and Mendeleev called them series.
b. Properties of elements in a particular period show regular gradation (i.e. increase or decrease) from left to right.
c. The vertical columns present in the periodic table are called groups. You must have noticed that these are nine in number and are numbered from I to VIII and Zero (Roman numerals).
d. Groups I to VII are subdivided into A and B subgroups. Groups zero and VIII don't have any subgroup.
Element placed on the right hand side in a column form sub group-B, while those placed on the left hand side form subgroup-A.
e. All the elements in a particular group are chemically similar in nature. They show regular gradation in their physical properties and chemical reactivities.
After learning about the main features we shall now learn about the main merits of Mendeleev's periodic table.
## Merits of Mendeleev's Periodic Classification
a. Classification of all elements : Mendeleev provide the first classification which successfully included all the elements.
b. Prediction of new elements: Mendeleev's periodic table had some blank spaces in it. These vacant spaces were for elements that were yet to be discovered. For example, he proposed the existence of an unknown element that he called eka aluminium. The element gallium was discovered four years later and its properties matched very closely with the predicted properties of eka aluminium.
c. Systematic study of all elements: Due to proper classification Mendeleev periodic table predicted properties of other elements, if one element is known. elements, if one element is known.

## Defects in Mendeleev's Periodic Classification
In spite of being a historic achievement, Mendeleev's periodic table had some defects in it. The following were the main defects in it:
a. Position of hydrogen : Hydrogen resembles alkali metals (forms <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion just like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions) as well as halogens (forms <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion similar to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion). Therefore, it could neither be placed comfortably with alkali metals (group I) nor with halogens (group VII).
b. Position of isotopes : Different isotopes of same elements have different atomic masses, therefore, each one of them should be given a different position in the periodic table. On the other hand, because they are chemically similar, they had to be given same position.
c. Anomalous pairs of elements : At certain places, an element of higher atomic mass has been placed before an element of lower atomic mass. For example, argon (39.91) is placed before potassium (39.1).
d. Position of element of group VIII: No proper place has been allotted to nine elements of group VIII which have been arranged in three triads without any justification.
## MODERN CLASSIFICATION
Henry Moseley, an English physicist discovered in the year 1913 that atomic number, is the most fundamental property of an element. Atomic number (Z), of an element is the number of protons in the nucleus of its atom. The number of electrons in the neutral atom is also equal to its atomic number. This discovery changed the whole perspective about elements and their properties to such an extent that a need was felt to change the periodic law also.
Moseley's Law describes the relationship between atomic number and wavelength of a spectral line : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>σ</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, where K and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>σ</mi></mrow></math> are constants for a given spectral line. Moseley's determination of this relationship provided a simple test of the order of the elements according to Z . It showed where elements were missing from the periodic table and led to the discovery of some of these elements. For example, hafnium (Hf), which is chemically almost identical to zirconium ( Zr ), was identified by D.Coster and G. von Hevesy in 1923 from its X-ray spectrum.
## MODERN PERIODIC LAW
After discovery of atomic number the periodic law was modified and the new law was based upon atomic numbers in place of atomic masses of elements. After the change in the periodic law many changes were suggested in the periodic table. When the elements are arranged in the increasing order of their atomic number, most of the defects of Mendeleev classification get rectified.
Modern periodic law states that 'the properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.'

Elements present in groups 1 and 2 on left side and groups 13 to 17 on the right side of the periodic table are called representative elements. Their outermost shells are incomplete. They are also called typical or main group elements. Elements present in groups 3 to 12 in the middle of the periodic table are called transition elements. However, it should be noted here that more number of electrons are added to valence shell only in case of main group elements. In transition elements, the electrons are added to incomplete inner shells.
Group 12 elements ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ) are not regarded as transition metals because according to modern IUPAC definition "an element whose atom has an incomplete <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> sub-shell, or which can give rise to cations with an incomplete <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> sub-shell, are considered as transition elements. Elements of group 12 do not satisfy this condition because their d sub-shells are complete to their capacity, however they resemble transition metals in their properties.
Group 18 on extreme right side of the periodic table contains noble gases. Their outermost shells are completely filled therefore they are inert.
Inner transition elements: 14 elements with atomic numbers 58 to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>71</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math> to Lu<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are called lanthanides and they are placed along with the element lanthanum (La), atomic number 57 in the same position (group 3 in period 6) because of very close resemblance between them. However, for, the sake of convenience they are shown separately below the main periodic table. 14 elements with atomic numbers 90 to103 (Th to Lr) are called actinides and they are placed along with the element actinium (Ac), atomic number 89 in the same position (group 3 in period 7) because of very close resemblance between them. They are shown separately below the main periodic table like lanthanides.

## Classification Based on Properties
(i) Elements classified as metalloids :
The 7 elements classified as metalloids are located in groups 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17 elements of the periodic table.
Elements classified as metalloids have properties of both metals and non-metals. Some are semi-conductors and can carry an electrical charge making them useful for electronic appliances like calculators and computers.
The metalloids in the periodic table are : Silicon, Germanium, Arsenic, Antimony, Tellurium, Polonium and Astatine.
(ii) Elements classified as alkali metals :
The 6 elements classified as alkali metals are located in group 1 of the periodic table. Elements classified as alkali metals are very reactive metals that do not occur freely in nature. Alkali metals are soft, malleable, ductile, and are good conductors of heat and electricity. The alkali metals are: Lithium, Sodium, Potassium, Rubidium, Cesium, Francium
(iii) Elements classified as alkaline earth metals :
The 6 elements classified as alkaline earth metals are located in group 2 of the periodic table. Elements classified as alkaline earth metals are all found in the Earth's crust, but not in the elemental form as they are very reactive (Inspite of being so reactive their reactivity is less than alkali metals). Instead, they are widely distributed in rock structures. The alkaline earth metals in the periodic table are : Beryllium, Magnesium, Calcium, Strontium, Barium and Radium.
Did You <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mtext>® </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ?
Elements of group 1 and group 2 are called alkali and alkaline earth metals respectively. As they all are basic in nature and form alkaline oxides and hydroxides.
(iv) Elements classified as transition metals :
The elements classified as transition metals are located in groups 3-12 of the periodic table. Elements classified as transition metals are ductile, malleable, and conduct electricity and heat. The transition metals in the periodic table are:
Scandium, Titanium, Vanadium, Chromium, Manganese, Iron, Cobalt, Nickel, Copper, Zinc, Yttrium, Zirconium, Platinum, Gold, Mercury, Rutherfordium, Dubnium, Seaborgium, Bohrium, Hassium, Meitnerium, Roentgenium, Niobium, Iridium, Darmstadtium, Molybdenum, Technetium, Ruthenium, Rhodium, Palladium, Silver, Cadmium, Hafnium, Tantalum, Tungsten, Rhenium and Osmium copernicium.
They are called transition elements because their position in the periodic table is between the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>-block and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block elements. Their properties are transitional between highly reactive metallic elements of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>-block which typically form ionic compounds, and the elements of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block which mostly forms covalent compounds.
(v) Elements classified as other metals :
The elements classified as 'other metals' are located in groups 13, 14, and 15 of the periodic table. All of these elements are solid, have a relatively high density and are opaque. The other metals of the periodic table are: Aluminum, Gallium, Indium, Tin, Thallium, Lead and Bismuth
(vi) Elements classified as non-metals :
The elements classified as non-metals are located in groups 14,15 and 16, 17 of the periodic table. Non-metals do not easily conduct electricity or heat and do not reflect light. Non-metallic elements are very brittle, and cannot be rolled into wires or pounded into sheets. Non-metallic elements exist, at room temperature, in two of the three states of matter; gases (such as oxygen) and solids (such as carbon). The non-metal elements in the periodic table are : Carbon, Nitrogen, Oxygen, Phosphorus, Sulfur, Selenium etc.

The general formula of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block elements is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> (where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> to 6 ).

## Merits of Modern Periodic Table Over Mendeleev's Periodic Table
The modern periodic table is based on atomic number which is more fundamental property of an atom than atomic mass. The long form of modern periodic table is therefore free of following defects of Mendeleev's periodic table.
a. Position of isotopes : All isotopes of an element have same atomic number but different atomic masses. Therefore, they occupy the same position in the modern periodic table which they should have because all of them are chemically similar.
b. Anomalous pairs of elements : When elements are arranged in the periodic table according to their atomic numbers, the anomaly regarding certain pairs of elements in Mendeleev's periodic table disappears. For example, atomic numbers of argon and potassium are 18 and 19 respectively. Therefore, argon with smaller atomic number comes before potassium although its atomic mass is greater.
c. It explains the periodicity of the properties of the elements and relates them to their electronic configurations.
d. The table is simple and easy way for remembering the properties of various elements and moreover lanthanides and actinides are placed separately.

## TRENDS IN THE MODERN PERIODIC TABLE
In a period, the number of valence electrons and the nuclear charge increases from left to right. It increases the force of attraction between valence electrons and the nucleus of the atom. In a group, the number of filled shells increases and valence electrons are present in higher shells. This decreases the force of attraction between valence electrons and the nucleus of the atom. These changes affect various properties of elements, they also show gradual variation in a group and a period which repeat themselves after a certain interval of atomic number. Such properties are called periodic properties.

## 2. Atomic Radii
A number of physical properties like density, melting and boiling points are related to the size of atoms. Atomic radius determines the size of an atom. For an isolated atom atomic radius may be taken as the distance between the centre of nucleus of atom and the outermost shell of electrons. Practically, measurement of size of an isolated atom is difficult; therefore, it is measured when an atom is in company of another atom of same element. It is defined as one-half the distance between the nuclei of two atoms when they are linked to each other by a single covalent bond.

In a period, there is a gradual increase in the nuclear charge with increase in atomic number. Since valence electrons are added in the same shell and the electrons in the same shell do not screen each other from the nucleus, the increase in nuclear charge is not neutralised by the extra valence electron. As a result, effective nuclear charge increases, therefore, valence electrons are more and more strongly attracted towards nucleus. This gradually decreases atomic radii.
## Variation of atomic radii in a group :
Atomic radii increases in a group from top to bottom. This can be seen from the following data for group 1 and 17 elements.
| Element (group 1) | Atomic radius (pm) | Element (group 17) | Atomic radius (pm) |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Li | 155 | F | 72 |
| Na | 190 | Cl | 99 |
| K | 235 | Br | 114 |
| Rb | 248 | I | 133 |
On moving down the group, the nuclear charge increases with increase in atomic number. However, while going down in a group from one atom to another the number of inner shells also increases, although the number of electrons in the outermost shell remains the same. The effect of increase in the size of the electron cloud (due to increase in number of shells) is more pronounced than the effect of increased nuclear charge. Thus, the distance of outermost electron from the nucleus increases as we move down a group. For example, in lithium the valence electron is present in 2nd shell while in sodium it is present in 3rd shell. Also, the number of filled shells between valence electrons and nucleus increases. Thus in group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> has one filled shell between its nucleus and valence electron while <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> has two filled shells between them. Both the factors decrease the force of attraction between nucleus and valence electron. Therefore, atomic size increases on moving down a group

Variation of metallic character in a group :
Metallic character of elements in a group increases from top to bottom. As we move down in a group, atomic size increases, therefore, distance between valence electrons and nucleus also increases. Thus, electrostatic force of attraction on valence electrons decreases and they can be easily removed, i.e. electropositive or metallic character increases. ## IONIZATION ENERGY
Negatively charged electrons in an atom are attracted by the positively charged nucleus. For removing an electron, this attractive force must be overcome by spending some energy. The minimum amount of energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom in its ground state to form a gaseous ion is called ionization energy. It is measured in unit of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
Ionization energy is a measure of the force of attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electron. Stronger the force of attraction, greater is the value of ionization energy.
It corresponds to the following process : If only one electron is removed, the ionization energy is known as the first ionization energy. If second electron is removed the ionization energy is called the second ionization energy, same goes for third ionization energy and so on. Now we shall study the variation of ionization energy in the periodic table.
## Variation of Ionization Energy in a Group
We have already seen earlier, that the force of attraction between valence electrons and nucleus decreases in a group from top to bottom because of increase in atomic size due to addition of inner shells. Moreover, there is an increase in shielding effect on outermost (valence) electrons due to increase in the number of inner electrons. As a result, the electron becomes less and less firmly held to nucleus as we move down the group. Therefore, ionization energy decreases in a group from top to bottom. This can be seen from ionization energy values (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ) of group 1 and 17 elements given below.

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Element | Ionization Energy | Element | Ionization Energy |
| Li | 520 | F | 1680 |
| Na | 496 | Cl | 1251 |
| K | 419 | Br | 1143 |
| Rb | 403 | I | 1009 |

## ELECTRON AFFINITY
Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is accepted by an atom in the gaseous state. It corresponds to the process : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>⟶</mi><msup><mi>X</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow></math>
Here, X is an atom of an element. The energy change is measured in the unit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. By convention, electron affinity is assigned a positive value when energy is released during the process. Greater the value of electron affinity, more energy is released during the process and greater is the tendency of the atom to gain electron. Electron affinity depends on factors like nuclear charge, size of atom and electronic configuration.
## Variation of Electron Affinity in a Group
In a group, the electron affinity decreases on moving from top to bottom, that is, less and less amount of energy is released. On moving down a group, atomic size and nuclear charge increases. The effect of increase in atomic size is much more pronounced than the effect of nuclear charge, therefore, additional electron feels less attraction by nucleus. Hence, lower is electron affinity. Such trends in its values (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ) for group 1 and group 17 elements are given below.

| Li | 58 | F | 333 |
| Na | 53 | Cl | 348 |
| K | 48 | Br | 324 |
| Rb | 45 | I | 295 |
## Variation of Electron Affinity Along a Period
On moving across a period, the size of atom decreases and nuclear charge increases. Both of these factors result into greater attraction for incoming electron. Thus, electron affinity increases in a period from left to right. However, certain irregularities are due to stable electronic configurations of certain atoms.

## ELECTRONEGATIVITY
We have learnt in the previous section that electron affinity of an element is a measure of an isolated atom to attract electrons towards itself. We normally do not deal with isolated atoms. Mostly we come across atoms which are bonded to other atoms. There is another property which deals with the power of bonded atoms to attract electrons. This property is known as electronegativity. Electronegativity is relative tendency of a bonded atom to attract the bond-electrons towards itself. Electronegativity is a dimensionless quantity and does not have any units. It just compares the tendency of various elements to attract the bond-electrons towards themselves. The most widely used scale of electronegativity was devised by Linus Pauling. Electronegativity generally decreases in a group from top to bottom. As we move in a group from top to bottom the atomic size increases. As a result, bonding electrons become away from the nucleus. Variation of electronegativity in groups 1 and 17 is given below.

| K | 0.8 | Br | 3.0 |
| Rb | 0.8 | I | 2.7 |
Fluorine atom has the greatest power of attracting electrons and is the most electronegative element.
Now let us see its variation in 2nd and 3rd period elements. Electronegativity generally increases in a period from left to right. This is due to decrease in atomic size and increase in effective nuclear charge. Now as a result of increase in effective nuclear charge, the attraction for the outermost electrons increases.

CASEI: The atomic size generally decreases from left to right in a period whereas it increases down the group. In the periodic table, noble gases comes after halogens, thus they should have smaller size than halogens. But this is not observed in reality, instead noble gases have exceptionally large size. Similarly, expected variation in the size of elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>6</mn><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> period is also not observed.
Why such anomalies are seen in periodic table? Inert gases have fully filled electronic configuration which results in greater inter electronic repulsion. Moreover in case of noble gases atomic radius is determined by van der Waal radius which is larger than both ionic as well as covalent radii. Consequently inert gases has larger atomic size than halogens in the corresponding period.
Atomic size of elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><msup><mrow /><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> period does not show much increase as in the corresponding group. Effect of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> orbitals does not allow the size to increase when we move from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> series. For example. Zr and Hf; Nb and Ta; Mo and W have approximately similar size. This resemblance in size is due to the presence of lanthanoids in between transition elements.

## PASSAGE-2
The way atomic radius varies with increasing atomic number can be explained by the arrangement of electrons in shells of fixed capacity. Shells closer to the nucleus, those with a smaller radius are generally filled first, since the negatively charged electrons are attracted by the positively charged protons in the nucleus. As the atomic number increases along a row of the periodic table, additional electrons are added to the same, outermost shell. The radius of this shell gradually contracts as the attraction between the additional electrons and the nucleus increases. On moving down in group, atomic radius increases due to increase in the number of shells. As the number of shells increases, the force of attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electron decreases and hence the size increases.

The size of atomic radius decreases on moving left to right in a horizontal row. When, we move across a period, the number of electrons in the same shell increases. This will experience greater attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electrons. This increased attraction bring the outermost electron closer to the nucleus, thereby decreases the atomic size.

theory_sections.markdown:
## Periodic Classification of Elements
Elements are the basic units of all types of matter. Earlier it was easy to study and remember properties of the elements individualy, as few elements were known, but later it become difficult due to the discovery of more number of elements. Thus, we needed a systematic way to organize our knowledge by classifying the elements. So that we can identify the physical and chemical properties of elements, and prediction of new elements can also be done. There were various attempts made to classify the elements, let's study them in detail.

theory_sections.topics: EARLY ATTEMPTS FOR THE CLASSIFICATION OF ELEMENTS
theory_sections.markdown:
## EARLY ATTEMPTS FOR THE CLASSIFICATION OF ELEMENTS
Elements like gold, tin, copper, lead, silver have been known since ancient times ; but the first element discovered through scientific inquiry by Hennig Brand was phosphorous (P) in 1649. By 1865, 63 elements had been discovered.

## Dobereiner's Triads
Between 1817-1829, Johann Dobereiner began to group elements with similar properties into groups of three elements called triads.
This began in 1817 when Johann Dobereiner noticed that the atomic weights of strontium, Sr , was halfway between the weights of calcium and barium. These elements possessed similar chemical properties. By 1829, he had discovered a halogen triad made up of chlorine, bromine and iodine and an alkali metal triad of lithium, sodium and potassium.
He postulated that nature contained triads of elements in which the middle element had properties that was an average of the other two elements.
In a triad, mean of the atomic masses of the first and the third elements was roughly equal to the atomic mass of the middle element. Observe the groups in the given table in which elements are arranged downwards in increasing order of atomic masses.
| A | | B | | C | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Element | Atomic mass | Element | Atomic mass | Element | Atomic mass |
| Lithium, Li | 7 | Calcium, Ca | 40 | Clorine, Cl | 35.5 |
| Sodium, Na | 23 | Strontium, Sr | 88 | Bromine, Br | 80 |
| Potassium, K | 39 | Barium, Ba | 137 | Iodine, I | 127 |
Mean of the atomic masses of the first and third element in triad <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>39</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>
Mean of the atomic masses of the first and third elements in triad <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>137</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>88.5</mn><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>
Mean of the first atomic masses of the first and third elements in triad <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>35.5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>127</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>81.25</mn><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>
Actual atomic mass of the second element in triad <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>
Actual atomic mass of the second element in triad (B) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>88</mn><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>
Actual atomic mass of the second element in triad (C) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>80</mn><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>
Dobereiner's idea of classification of elements into triads did not receive wide acceptance as he could arrange only a few elements in this manner.
Later, other scientists found other triads and recognized that elements could be grouped into set larger than three. The poor accuracy of measurements such as that of atomic weights hindered grouping of further elements.

## Learn More
In 1862, A.E. Beguyer de Chancourtois was the first person to make use of atomic weights to reveal that the elements were arranged according to their atomic weights with similar elements occurring at regular intervals. He drew the elements as a continuous spiral around a cylinder divided into 16 parts. A list of elements was wrapped around a cylinder so that several sets of similar elements lined up, creating the first geometric representation of the periodic law.

## NEWLAND'S LAW OF OCTAVES
In 1865 John Alexander Newland, an English chemist noticed that when elements are arranged in the increasing order of their atomic masses, every eighth element had properties similar to the first element. Newland called it the Law of Octaves.
Look carefully at the Newland's arrangement of elements shown below:

Similarly, aluminium is the eighth element from boron it shows properties similar to it.
However, Newland could arrange elements in this manner only up to calcium out of a total of over sixty elements known at that time. Because of this shortcoming, his work did not receive attention by the scientific community. The next breakthrough in classification of elements came in the form of Mendeleev's work.

## MENDELEEV'S LAW
Dmitri Ivanovich Mendeleev, a Russian chemist, arranged the elements on the basis of their fundamental property, the atomic mass, and gave a periodic law.
The chemical and physical properties of elements are periodic function of their atomic masses. A periodic function is the one which repeats itself after a certain interval. Thus, according to the periodic law (given by Mendeleev) the chemical and physical properties of elements repeat themselves after certain intervals when they are arranged in the increasing order of their atomic mass.
A tabular arrangement of the elements based on the periodic law is called periodic table. Mendeleev believed that atomic mass of elements was the most fundamental property and arranged elements in increasing order of atomic mass in horizontal rows till he encountered an element which had properties similar to the first element. He placed this element below the first element and thus started the second row of elements. Proceeding in this manner he could arrange all the known elements according to their properties and thus created the first periodic table.

theory_sections.markdown:
## Main Features of Mendeleev's Periodic Table
In Mendeleev's periodic table elements are arranged in tabular form in rows and columns. It has been modified from time to time. Now let us learn more about these rows and columns and the elements present in them.
a. The horizontal rows present in the periodic table are called periods. Originally, there were six periods and Mendeleev called them series.
b. Properties of elements in a particular period show regular gradation (i.e. increase or decrease) from left to right.
c. The vertical columns present in the periodic table are called groups. You must have noticed that these are nine in number and are numbered from I to VIII and Zero (Roman numerals).
d. Groups I to VII are subdivided into A and B subgroups. Groups zero and VIII don't have any subgroup.
Element placed on the right hand side in a column form sub group-B, while those placed on the left hand side form subgroup-A.
e. All the elements in a particular group are chemically similar in nature. They show regular gradation in their physical properties and chemical reactivities.
After learning about the main features we shall now learn about the main merits of Mendeleev's periodic table.

## Merits of Mendeleev's Periodic Classification
a. Classification of all elements : Mendeleev provide the first classification which successfully included all the elements.
b. Prediction of new elements: Mendeleev's periodic table had some blank spaces in it. These vacant spaces were for elements that were yet to be discovered. For example, he proposed the existence of an unknown element that he called eka aluminium. The element gallium was discovered four years later and its properties matched very closely with the predicted properties of eka aluminium.
c. Systematic study of all elements: Due to proper classification Mendeleev periodic table predicted properties of other elements, if one element is known. elements, if one element is known.
Time to
Check Your Knowledge
- Why Mendeleev left some places empty in his periodic table?

## Defects in Mendeleev's Periodic Classification
In spite of being a historic achievement, Mendeleev's periodic table had some defects in it. The following were the main defects in it:
a. Position of hydrogen : Hydrogen resembles alkali metals (forms <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion just like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ions) as well as halogens (forms <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion similar to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>ion). Therefore, it could neither be placed comfortably with alkali metals (group I) nor with halogens (group VII).
b. Position of isotopes : Different isotopes of same elements have different atomic masses, therefore, each one of them should be given a different position in the periodic table. On the other hand, because they are chemically similar, they had to be given same position.
c. Anomalous pairs of elements : At certain places, an element of higher atomic mass has been placed before an element of lower atomic mass. For example, argon (39.91) is placed before potassium (39.1).
d. Position of element of group VIII: No proper place has been allotted to nine elements of group VIII which have been arranged in three triads without any justification.

## MODERN CLASSIFICATION
Henry Moseley, an English physicist discovered in the year 1913 that atomic number, is the most fundamental property of an element. Atomic number (Z), of an element is the number of protons in the nucleus of its atom. The number of electrons in the neutral atom is also equal to its atomic number. This discovery changed the whole perspective about elements and their properties to such an extent that a need was felt to change the periodic law also.
Moseley's Law describes the relationship between atomic number and wavelength of a spectral line : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>σ</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, where K and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>σ</mi></mrow></math> are constants for a given spectral line. Moseley's determination of this relationship provided a simple test of the order of the elements according to Z . It showed where elements were missing from the periodic table and led to the discovery of some of these elements. For example, hafnium (Hf), which is chemically almost identical to zirconium ( Zr ), was identified by D.Coster and G. von Hevesy in 1923 from its X-ray spectrum.

## MODERN PERIODIC LAW
After discovery of atomic number the periodic law was modified and the new law was based upon atomic numbers in place of atomic masses of elements. After the change in the periodic law many changes were suggested in the periodic table. When the elements are arranged in the increasing order of their atomic number, most of the defects of Mendeleev classification get rectified.
Modern periodic law states that 'the properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.'

## More
#### Abstract
Henry Moseley discovered that the wavelength (energy) of an X-ray depend upon the nuclear charge of an atom. In 1913, working at the University of Manchester, he photographed the X-ray spectrum of 10 elements that occupied consecutive places in the periodic table. He concluded that there was 'a fundamental quantity which increases by regular steps as we pass from one element to the next.' In 1920, Rutherford at Cambridge identified this quantity as the atomic number.

## Groups:
There are 18 vertical columns in the modern periodic table. Each column is called a group. These groups have been numbered from 1 to 18 (in Arabic numerals) from left to right. Group 1at extreme left position contains alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs and Fr) and group 18 at extreme right side position contains noble gases ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and Rn ).
All elements present in a group have similar electronic configuration and have same number of valence electrons.

Elements present in groups 1 and 2 on left side and groups 13 to 17 on the right side of the periodic table are called representative elements. Their outermost shells are incomplete. They are also called typical or main group elements. Elements present in groups 3 to 12 in the middle of the periodic table are called transition elements. However, it should be noted here that more number of electrons are added to valence shell only in case of main group elements. In transition elements, the electrons are added to incomplete inner shells.
Group 12 elements ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ) are not regarded as transition metals because according to modern IUPAC definition "an element whose atom has an incomplete <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> sub-shell, or which can give rise to cations with an incomplete <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> sub-shell, are considered as transition elements. Elements of group 12 do not satisfy this condition because their d sub-shells are complete to their capacity, however they resemble transition metals in their properties.
Group 18 on extreme right side of the periodic table contains noble gases. Their outermost shells are completely filled therefore they are inert.
Inner transition elements: 14 elements with atomic numbers 58 to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>71</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math> to Lu<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are called lanthanides and they are placed along with the element lanthanum (La), atomic number 57 in the same position (group 3 in period 6) because of very close resemblance between them. However, for, the sake of convenience they are shown separately below the main periodic table. 14 elements with atomic numbers 90 to103 (Th to Lr) are called actinides and they are placed along with the element actinium (Ac), atomic number 89 in the same position (group 3 in period 7) because of very close resemblance between them. They are shown separately below the main periodic table like lanthanides.

## Periods :
There are seven rows in the periodic table. Each row is called a period. The periods have been numbered from 1 to 7 (Arabic numerals). In each period, a new shell starts filling up. The period number is also the number of shell which starts filling up in it. For example, in elements of 3rd period, the third shell (M shell) starts filling up as we move from left to right. The first element of this period, sodium, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> has only one electron in its valence shell (third shell), while the last element of this period, argon, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>Ar</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> has eight electrons in its valence shell. The gradual filling of the third shell can be seen below.

The first period is the shortest period of all and contains only 2 elements, H and He .
The second and third periods are called short periods and contain 8 elements each.
Fourth and fifth periods are long periods and contain 18 elements each.
Sixth and seventh periods are very long periods containing 32 elements each, including elements up to atomic number 118. Elements of atomic numbers 114, 116 and 118 have been reported only recently.
The period of an element signifies the highest energy level of an electron in that element, occupies in an unexcited state.
## CONNECTING TOPIC
## CLASSIFICATION OF ELEMENTS

## Classification Based on Properties
(i) Elements classified as metalloids :
The 7 elements classified as metalloids are located in groups 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17 elements of the periodic table.
Elements classified as metalloids have properties of both metals and non-metals. Some are semi-conductors and can carry an electrical charge making them useful for electronic appliances like calculators and computers.
The metalloids in the periodic table are : Silicon, Germanium, Arsenic, Antimony, Tellurium, Polonium and Astatine.
(ii) Elements classified as alkali metals :
The 6 elements classified as alkali metals are located in group 1 of the periodic table. Elements classified as alkali metals are very reactive metals that do not occur freely in nature. Alkali metals are soft, malleable, ductile, and are good conductors of heat and electricity. The alkali metals are: Lithium, Sodium, Potassium, Rubidium, Cesium, Francium
(iii) Elements classified as alkaline earth metals :
The 6 elements classified as alkaline earth metals are located in group 2 of the periodic table. Elements classified as alkaline earth metals are all found in the Earth's crust, but not in the elemental form as they are very reactive (Inspite of being so reactive their reactivity is less than alkali metals). Instead, they are widely distributed in rock structures. The alkaline earth metals in the periodic table are : Beryllium, Magnesium, Calcium, Strontium, Barium and Radium.
Did You <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mtext>® </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ?
Elements of group 1 and group 2 are called alkali and alkaline earth metals respectively. As they all are basic in nature and form alkaline oxides and hydroxides.
(iv) Elements classified as transition metals :
The elements classified as transition metals are located in groups 3-12 of the periodic table. Elements classified as transition metals are ductile, malleable, and conduct electricity and heat. The transition metals in the periodic table are:
Scandium, Titanium, Vanadium, Chromium, Manganese, Iron, Cobalt, Nickel, Copper, Zinc, Yttrium, Zirconium, Platinum, Gold, Mercury, Rutherfordium, Dubnium, Seaborgium, Bohrium, Hassium, Meitnerium, Roentgenium, Niobium, Iridium, Darmstadtium, Molybdenum, Technetium, Ruthenium, Rhodium, Palladium, Silver, Cadmium, Hafnium, Tantalum, Tungsten, Rhenium and Osmium copernicium.
They are called transition elements because their position in the periodic table is between the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>-block and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block elements. Their properties are transitional between highly reactive metallic elements of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>-block which typically form ionic compounds, and the elements of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block which mostly forms covalent compounds.
(v) Elements classified as other metals :
The elements classified as 'other metals' are located in groups 13, 14, and 15 of the periodic table. All of these elements are solid, have a relatively high density and are opaque. The other metals of the periodic table are: Aluminum, Gallium, Indium, Tin, Thallium, Lead and Bismuth
(vi) Elements classified as non-metals :
The elements classified as non-metals are located in groups 14,15 and 16, 17 of the periodic table. Non-metals do not easily conduct electricity or heat and do not reflect light. Non-metallic elements are very brittle, and cannot be rolled into wires or pounded into sheets. Non-metallic elements exist, at room temperature, in two of the three states of matter; gases (such as oxygen) and solids (such as carbon). The non-metal elements in the periodic table are : Carbon, Nitrogen, Oxygen, Phosphorus, Sulfur, Selenium etc.
Phosphorus does not conduct electricity whereas lithium does. Why ?

## Classification Based on Differentiating Electron
This classification divides the elements into four types. i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>−</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> - and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>-block elements depending on the type of the atomic shell into which the last electron enters.
The last electron is called differentiating electron.
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi></mrow></mrow></math>-Block elements : Those elements of the periodic table in which the last electron enters in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>-orbital, are called <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>-block elements.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>-orbital can accommodate a maximum of two electrons. Their general formula is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> to 7<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
I A Group elements are known as alkali metals because they react with water to form alkali. II A Group elements are known as alkaline earth metals because their oxides react with water to form alkali and these are found in the soil or earth. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>-block element are soft and have low melting and boiling points. They mostly form ionic compounds. The total number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>-block elements are 14. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mn>87</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mn>88</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are radioactive elements, H and He are gaseous elements. Cs and Fr are liquid elements belonging to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>-block.
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mi></mrow></mrow></math>-Block elements : Those elements of the periodic table in which the last electron gets filled up in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mi></mrow></mrow></math>-orbital, are called <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block elements. A <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-orbital can accommodate a maximum of six electrons. Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block elements are divided into six groups which are III A, IV A, V A, VI A, VII A and VIII A groups. They include both metals and non-metals. They form mostly covalent compounds. The general formula of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block elements is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> (where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> to 6 ).
The VIII A group elements having general formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> are inert, because their energy levels are fully filled. The total number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block elements in the periodic table is 30 (excluding He). There are nine gaseous elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> and N<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> belonging to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block. Gallium ( Ga ) and bromine ( Br ) are liquids.
(iii) d-Block elements : Those elements of the periodic table in which the last electron gets filled up in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>-orbital, called <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>-block elements. The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>-block elements are placed in groups named IIIB, IV B, V B, VI B, VII B, VIII, I B and II B. In <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>-block elements the electron gets filled up in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> orbital of the penultimate shell. Though the total number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>-block elements is 39 in the periodic table but there are only 36 transition elements. Because only those elements are transition elements in which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> orbital is partly filled. The general formula of these elements is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></msup><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> to 7 . They are metals having high melting and boiling points. Most of them form coloured compounds and exhibit several oxidation states
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi></mrow></mrow></math>-Block elements : Those elements of the periodic table in which the last electron gets filled up in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>-orbital, called <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>-block elements. There are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>28</mn><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>-block elements in the periodic table. The elements from atomic number 58 to 71 are called lanthanides because they come after lanthanum (57). The elements from 90 to 103 are called actinides because they come after actinium (89). They are heavy metals with high melting and boiling points. They form coloured ions. All the actinide elements are radioactive. All the elements after atomic number 92 (i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mn>92</mn></mrow></msup><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> ) are transuranic elements. The elements which do not occur in nature and are produced in the laboratories artificially are called transuranic or synthetic elements. The general formula of these elements is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>&</mi><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>
(Ev)
- Write general electronic configuration of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mi></mrow></mrow></math>-block elements.

theory_sections.topics: Merits of Modern Periodic Table Over Mendeleev's Periodic Table
theory_sections.markdown:
## Merits of Modern Periodic Table Over Mendeleev's Periodic Table
The modern periodic table is based on atomic number which is more fundamental property of an atom than atomic mass. The long form of modern periodic table is therefore free of following defects of Mendeleev's periodic table.
a. Position of isotopes : All isotopes of an element have same atomic number but different atomic masses. Therefore, they occupy the same position in the modern periodic table which they should have because all of them are chemically similar.
b. Anomalous pairs of elements : When elements are arranged in the periodic table according to their atomic numbers, the anomaly regarding certain pairs of elements in Mendeleev's periodic table disappears. For example, atomic numbers of argon and potassium are 18 and 19 respectively. Therefore, argon with smaller atomic number comes before potassium although its atomic mass is greater.
c. It explains the periodicity of the properties of the elements and relates them to their electronic configurations.
d. The table is simple and easy way for remembering the properties of various elements and moreover lanthanides and actinides are placed separately.
## CONNECTING TOPIC

## NOMENCLATURE OF NEWLY DISCOVERED ELEMENTS IN THE MODERN PERIODIC TABLE
According to IUPAC, until the name of newly discovered element is officially recognized, a systematic nomenclature is derived directly from the atomic number of the element using the numerical roots for 0 and numbers 1-9.
To derive the name, roots are arranged in order of the digits of atomic number and 'ium' is added at the end. To derive the symbol, abbreviations are arranged in order of the digits of atomic number.

theory_sections.topics: TRENDS IN THE MODERN PERIODIC TABLE
theory_sections.markdown:
## TRENDS IN THE MODERN PERIODIC TABLE
In a period, the number of valence electrons and the nuclear charge increases from left to right. It increases the force of attraction between valence electrons and the nucleus of the atom. In a group, the number of filled shells increases and valence electrons are present in higher shells. This decreases the force of attraction between valence electrons and the nucleus of the atom. These changes affect various properties of elements, they also show gradual variation in a group and a period which repeat themselves after a certain interval of atomic number. Such properties are called periodic properties.

## 1. Valency
The combining capacity of an atom or radical is known as its valency. It is measured in terms of hydrogen, chlorine and oxygen atom. Valency of an element is defined as the number of hydrogen, chlorine and double the number of oxygen atom with which atom of an element can combine, e.g.
Valency of oxygen in water <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is 2 .
Valency of carbon in methane ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is 4 .
(a) Valency in a period : We have already learnt in the previous section that the number of valence electrons increases in a period. In normal elements, it increases from 1 to 8 in a period from left to right. It reaches 8 in group 18 elements (noble gases) which show practically no chemical activity under ordinary conditions and their valency is taken as zero. Carefully look at the table given below. Valency of normal elements with respect to oxygen increases from 1 to 7 as shown below

## 2. Atomic Radii
A number of physical properties like density, melting and boiling points are related to the size of atoms. Atomic radius determines the size of an atom. For an isolated atom atomic radius may be taken as the distance between the centre of nucleus of atom and the outermost shell of electrons. Practically, measurement of size of an isolated atom is difficult; therefore, it is measured when an atom is in company of another atom of same element. It is defined as one-half the distance between the nuclei of two atoms when they are linked to each other by a single covalent bond.

theory_sections.topics: Variation of atomic radii in a period :
theory_sections.markdown:
## Variation of atomic radii in a period :
Atomic radii (in picometer) of 2nd and 3rd period elements are given in the following table. In a period, atomic radius generally decreases from left to right with increase in atomic number.
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow><mrow><mtext>nd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> period | Li | Be | B | C | N | O | F |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Atomic Radius | 152 | 111 | 88 | 77 | 74 | 66 | 42 |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow><mrow><mtext>rd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> period | Na | Mg | Al | Si | P | S | Cl |
| Atomic Radius | 190 | 145 | 118 | 111 | 98 | 88 | 79 |
In a period, there is a gradual increase in the nuclear charge with increase in atomic number. Since valence electrons are added in the same shell and the electrons in the same shell do not screen each other from the nucleus, the increase in nuclear charge is not neutralised by the extra valence electron. As a result, effective nuclear charge increases, therefore, valence electrons are more and more strongly attracted towards nucleus. This gradually decreases atomic radii.

theory_sections.topics: Variation of atomic radii in a group :
theory_sections.markdown:
## Variation of atomic radii in a group :
Atomic radii increases in a group from top to bottom. This can be seen from the following data for group 1 and 17 elements.
| Element (group 1) | Atomic radius (pm) | Element (group 17) | Atomic radius (pm) |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Li | 155 | F | 72 |
| Na | 190 | Cl | 99 |
| K | 235 | Br | 114 |
| Rb | 248 | I | 133 |
On moving down the group, the nuclear charge increases with increase in atomic number. However, while going down in a group from one atom to another the number of inner shells also increases, although the number of electrons in the outermost shell remains the same. The effect of increase in the size of the electron cloud (due to increase in number of shells) is more pronounced than the effect of increased nuclear charge. Thus, the distance of outermost electron from the nucleus increases as we move down a group. For example, in lithium the valence electron is present in 2nd shell while in sodium it is present in 3rd shell. Also, the number of filled shells between valence electrons and nucleus increases. Thus in group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> has one filled shell between its nucleus and valence electron while <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> has two filled shells between them. Both the factors decrease the force of attraction between nucleus and valence electron. Therefore, atomic size increases on moving down a group

Variation of metallic character in a group :
Metallic character of elements in a group increases from top to bottom. As we move down in a group, atomic size increases, therefore, distance between valence electrons and nucleus also increases. Thus, electrostatic force of attraction on valence electrons decreases and they can be easily removed, i.e. electropositive or metallic character increases. This can be best seen in elements of group 14. Its first element, carbon is a typical non metal, next two elements Si and Ge are metalloids and the remaining elements Sn and Pb , are typical metals as shown below.

## CONNECTING TOPIC

## IONIZATION ENERGY
Negatively charged electrons in an atom are attracted by the positively charged nucleus. For removing an electron, this attractive force must be overcome by spending some energy. The minimum amount of energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom in its ground state to form a gaseous ion is called ionization energy. It is measured in unit of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
Ionization energy is a measure of the force of attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electron. Stronger the force of attraction, greater is the value of ionization energy.
It corresponds to the following process : If only one electron is removed, the ionization energy is known as the first ionization energy. If second electron is removed the ionization energy is called the second ionization energy, same goes for third ionization energy and so on. Now we shall study the variation of ionization energy in the periodic table.

theory_sections.topics: Variation of Ionization Energy in a Group
theory_sections.markdown:
## Variation of Ionization Energy in a Group
We have already seen earlier, that the force of attraction between valence electrons and nucleus decreases in a group from top to bottom because of increase in atomic size due to addition of inner shells. Moreover, there is an increase in shielding effect on outermost (valence) electrons due to increase in the number of inner electrons. As a result, the electron becomes less and less firmly held to nucleus as we move down the group. Therefore, ionization energy decreases in a group from top to bottom. This can be seen from ionization energy values (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ) of group 1 and 17 elements given below.
| Group 1 | | Group 17 | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Element | Ionization Energy | Element | Ionization Energy |
| Li | 520 | F | 1680 |
| Na | 496 | Cl | 1251 |
| K | 419 | Br | 1143 |
| Rb | 403 | I | 1009 |

We know that the force of attraction between valence electron and nucleus increases in a period from left to right due to increase in nuclear charge. As a consequence of this, the ionization energy generally increases in a period from left to right. This trend can be seen in ionization energies (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ) of elements belonging to 2nd and 3rd periods.

However, some irregularities in the general trend have been noticed. These are due to extra stability of half filled and completely filled configurations. For example, as shown in above data nitrogen has more ionization energy in comparison to oxygen which is due to electronic configuration of nitrogen atom <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. ## ELECTRON AFFINITY
Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is accepted by an atom in the gaseous state. It corresponds to the process : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>⟶</mi><msup><mi>X</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow></math>
Here, X is an atom of an element. The energy change is measured in the unit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. By convention, electron affinity is assigned a positive value when energy is released during the process. Greater the value of electron affinity, more energy is released during the process and greater is the tendency of the atom to gain electron. Electron affinity depends on factors like nuclear charge, size of atom and electronic configuration.

theory_sections.topics: Variation of Electron Affinity in a Group
theory_sections.markdown:
## Variation of Electron Affinity in a Group
In a group, the electron affinity decreases on moving from top to bottom, that is, less and less amount of energy is released. On moving down a group, atomic size and nuclear charge increases. The effect of increase in atomic size is much more pronounced than the effect of nuclear charge, therefore, additional electron feels less attraction by nucleus. Hence, lower is electron affinity. Such trends in its values (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ) for group 1 and group 17 elements are given below.
| Group 1 | | Group 17 | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Element | Electron affinity | Element | Electron affinity |
| Li | 58 | F | 333 |
| Na | 53 | Cl | 348 |
| K | 48 | Br | 324 |
| Rb | 45 | I | 295 |

theory_sections.topics: Variation of Electron Affinity Along a Period
theory_sections.markdown:
## Variation of Electron Affinity Along a Period
On moving across a period, the size of atom decreases and nuclear charge increases. Both of these factors result into greater attraction for incoming electron. Thus, electron affinity increases in a period from left to right. However, certain irregularities are due to stable electronic configurations of certain atoms.
- Why electron affinity value of bromine atom is lower than of chlorine atom ?

## ELECTRONEGATIVITY
We have learnt in the previous section that electron affinity of an element is a measure of an isolated atom to attract electrons towards itself. We normally do not deal with isolated atoms. Mostly we come across atoms which are bonded to other atoms. There is another property which deals with the power of bonded atoms to attract electrons. This property is known as electronegativity. Electronegativity is relative tendency of a bonded atom to attract the bond-electrons towards itself. Electronegativity is a dimensionless quantity and does not have any units. It just compares the tendency of various elements to attract the bond-electrons towards themselves. The most widely used scale of electronegativity was devised by Linus Pauling. Electronegativity generally decreases in a group from top to bottom. As we move in a group from top to bottom the atomic size increases. As a result, bonding electrons become away from the nucleus. Variation of electronegativity in groups 1 and 17 is given below.
| Group 1 | | Group 17 | |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Element | Electronegativity | Element | Electronegativity |
| Li | 1.0 | F | 4.0 |
| Na | 0.9 | C | 3.2 |
| K | 0.8 | Br | 3.0 |
| Rb | 0.8 | I | 2.7 |
Fluorine atom has the greatest power of attracting electrons and is the most electronegative element.
Now let us see its variation in 2nd and 3rd period elements. Electronegativity generally increases in a period from left to right. This is due to decrease in atomic size and increase in effective nuclear charge. Now as a result of increase in effective nuclear charge, the attraction for the outermost electrons increases.

- Non-metals have high electronegativity values in comparison to metals.

CASEI: The atomic size generally decreases from left to right in a period whereas it increases down the group. In the periodic table, noble gases comes after halogens, thus they should have smaller size than halogens. But this is not observed in reality, instead noble gases have exceptionally large size. Similarly, expected variation in the size of elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>6</mn><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> period is also not observed.
Why such anomalies are seen in periodic table? Inert gases have fully filled electronic configuration which results in greater inter electronic repulsion. Moreover in case of noble gases atomic radius is determined by van der Waal radius which is larger than both ionic as well as covalent radii. Consequently inert gases has larger atomic size than halogens in the corresponding period.
Atomic size of elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><msup><mrow /><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> period does not show much increase as in the corresponding group. Effect of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> orbitals does not allow the size to increase when we move from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> series. For example. Zr and Hf; Nb and Ta; Mo and W have approximately similar size. This resemblance in size is due to the presence of lanthanoids in between transition elements.

## PASSAGE-1
In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic numbers which is related to the electronic configuration. Depending upon the type of orbitals receiving the last electron, the elements in the periodic table have been divided into four blocks, viz, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>. The modern periodic table consists of 7 periods and 18 groups. Each period begins with the filling of a new energy shell. In accordance with the Afbau principle, the seven periods ( 1 to 7 ) have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>18</mn></mrow></math>, 18, 32 and 32 elements respectively. The seventh period is still incomplete. To avoid the periodic table being too long, the two series of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>-block elements, called lanthanoids and actinoids are placed at the bottom of the main body of the periodic table.
