## PASSAGE-2
The way atomic radius varies with increasing atomic number can be explained by the arrangement of electrons in shells of fixed capacity. Shells closer to the nucleus, those with a smaller radius are generally filled first, since the negatively charged electrons are attracted by the positively charged protons in the nucleus. As the atomic number increases along a row of the periodic table, additional electrons are added to the same, outermost shell. The radius of this shell gradually contracts as the attraction between the additional electrons and the nucleus increases. On moving down in group, atomic radius increases due to increase in the number of shells. As the number of shells increases, the force of attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electron decreases and hence the size increases.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Very Short Answer Questions — Q1
exercises.problem: What is the basis of the modern periodic table ?
exercises.solution: The basis of the modern periodic table is Mosley periodic law according to which the properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Very Short Answer Questions — Q2
exercises.problem: In how many blocks has the modern periodic table been divided?
exercises.solution: The periodic table is divided into four blocks ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>-block, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>-block and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>-block) on the basis of their electronic configuration.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Very Short Answer Questions — Q3
exercises.problem: What was Dobereiner's basis of classifying elements ?
exercises.solution: According to Doberenier, elements having similar properties can be arranged in triads in which atomic mass of the middle element is the mean of the atomic mass of the other two elements.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Very Short Answer Questions — Q4
exercises.problem: Out of Li, Ge and N, which forms the most basic oxide and which forms the most acidic oxide ?
exercises.solution: Lithium forms the most basic oxide as it is a metal and nitrogen forms the most acidic oxide as it is a non-metal.

exercises.problem: The size of atoms decreases as we move from left to right. Explain the trend.
exercises.solution: The effective nuclear charge on the outermost electrons increases across the period. Therefore the size of the atom decreases as we move from left to right.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q1
exercises.problem: Arrange these atoms and ions in order of decreasing size: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and Ca .
exercises.solution: Cations are smaller than their parent atoms, so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is smaller than the Ca atom. Because Ca is below Mg in group IIA of the periodic table, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is larger than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Consequently, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q2
exercises.problem: What do you understand by the term periodicity ? Are the properties of the elements placed in a group, same ? Illustrate.
exercises.solution: When the elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic numbers, elements with similar chemical properties appear at definite intervals, this is known as periodicity. Yes, this periodicity is due to the periodicity in the number of electrons in the outermost shell of the atoms of the elements. Elements placed in the same group have same number of valance electrons and show similar properties.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q3
exercises.problem: Define and explain Mendeleev's periodic law ?
exercises.solution: Mendeleev's periodic law : It states that, the properties of elements are the periodic functions of their atomic masses. It means that the properties of the elements depend on their atomic masses and elements were placed in the periodic table on the basis of their increasing atomic masses.

(b) Among <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> which ions are isoelectronic with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ?
exercises.solution:
(a) The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>cation has 14 electrons. Ar and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> have 18 electrons, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>has 15 electrons, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> has 14 electrons. Only <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is isoelectronic with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(b) The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> cation has 23 electrons with electron configuration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ion also has 23 electrons and the same electronic configuration as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>; thus they are isoelectronic. The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ion has 25 electrons <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> has 24 electrons <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. Neither of which is isoelectronic with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q5
exercises.problem:
What is the general electronic configuration for the valence electrons in
(a) group IA
(b) group IV A
(c) group VIIA?
exercises.solution: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> (a) </mtext><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> (b) </mtext><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> (c) </mtext><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q6
exercises.problem:
Write the symbol for a cation with a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> charge that has the electron configuration
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
exercises.solution: (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> (c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q7
exercises.problem:
Which species in each of the following pairs is larger ? Give an explanation for your answer.
(a) Na or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
exercises.solution:
(a) Na, cation always has smaller size than neutral atom.
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, the size of anion increase as the charge increases.
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, the size of cation decreases as the charge increases.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q8
exercises.problem:
Using periodic table as a guide, arrange each of the following series of atoms in order of increasing size.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
exercises.solution: (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo><</mo><mi>B</mi><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> (b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo><</mo><mi>C</mi><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> (c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q9
exercises.problem:
Using periodic table as a guide, arrange each of the following series of species in order of increasing size.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
exercises.solution: (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math> (b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mi>S</mi><mo><</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q10
exercises.problem:
Indicate which species in each pair has the higher ionization energy. Explain the reason for your answer.
(a) Na and Rb
(b) O and F
exercises.solution:
(a) In a group, the ionisation potential decreases from top to bottom, hence ionisation potential of Na will be higher than Rb .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(b) In a period ionisation potential increases from left to right, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>></mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q11
exercises.problem: Which has greater, second ionization energy: boron or beryllium ? Explain your answer.
exercises.solution: Boron. In both cases a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> valence electron is being removed, but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>has fully filled inert configuration.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q12
exercises.problem: What are the names and chemical symbols of the elements that are vertical and horizontal neighbours of sulfur in the periodic table? Which of these have chemical properties similar to those of sulfur?
exercises.solution: Vertical neighbours are oxygen ( O ) and selenium ( Se ), horizontal neighbours are phosphorus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and chlorine (Cl). Oxygen and selenium have similar chemical properties to that of sulphur.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q13
exercises.problem: Arrange the following atoms in order of decreasing atomic radius : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
exercises.solution:
As we move from left to right across a period there is a regular decrease in atomic radii of the representative elements. This is due to the fact that number of energy shells remain the same in a period but nuclear charge increases gradually as the atomic number increases, hence the correct order will be
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mi>P</mi><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q14
exercises.problem: Arrange the following atoms in order of increasing radius: P, Si, N.
exercises.solution: N and P are in the same group and N is above P . Therefore, the radius of N is smaller than that of P (atomic radius increases as we go down a group). Both Si and P are in the third period, and Si is to the left of P. Therefore, the radius of P is smaller than that of Si (atomic radius decreases as we move from left to right across a period). Thus the order of radius is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo><</mo><mi>P</mi><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q15
exercises.problem:
(i) Predict which of the following elements will form cation and which will form anions?
(a) Na
(b) Al
(c) Cl
(d) O
(ii) Name two elements that are inert in nature.
exercises.solution:
(i) Cations -Na and Al
Anions -Cl and O
(ii) He and Ne are inert elements

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q16
exercises.problem:
From the following elements :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>19</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(i) Select the element having one electron in the outermost shell.
(ii) Two elements of the same group.
(iii) Write the formula and mention the nature of the compound formed by the union of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>19</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
exercises.solution:
(i) The element which have one electron in the outermost shell is
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>19</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
(ii) Two elements of the same group are Be and Ca .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mtext> Valency Same </mtext><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
(iii) Formula of element K and element X : Both elements K and X have valency one
Since between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> an ionic bond is formed. Hence, it is an electrovalent compound.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q17
exercises.problem:
Calcium is an element with atomic number 20. State reason for each of the following questions:
(i) Is calcium metal or non-metal?
(ii) Will its atomic radius be larger or smaller than that of potassium with atomic number 19 ?
(iii) Write the formula of its oxide.
exercises.solution:
(i) It is a metal because it has two electrons in its outermost shell i.e. two valence electrons, which it can lose easily.
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>19</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is placed before <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>20</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> in the same period. Since, the atomic radius decrease across a period so, the atomic radius of calcium is smaller than that of potassium.
(iii) The formula of oxide of calcium is CaO , because the valency of both calcium and oxygen is 2 .

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q18
exercises.problem: Name any two elements of group one and write their electronic configurations. What similarity do you observe in their electronic configurations? Write the formula of oxide of any of the above said element.
exercises.solution:
(i) Two elements of group 1 are sodium (Na) and potassium (K)
Electronic configurations :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>11</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>;</mi><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>19</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
(ii) Similarity : Both the elements have one valence electron in outermost shell.
(iii) Oxide : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q19
exercises.problem: An element ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> ' with electronic configuration ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ) combines separately with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> radicals. Write the formula of the three compounds so formed. To which group and period of the modern periodic table does the element 'M' belong? Will 'M' form covalent or ionic compounds? Give reason to justify your answer.
exercises.solution:
The electronic configuration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> confirm that it belongs to group 2 and period 3 of the modern periodic table and its valency is 2 .
The chemical formula of the compounds are :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>M</mi><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
'M' will form ionic compounds, because it has only two electrons in its outer most shell. Hence it can lose electrons easily.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q20
exercises.problem:
An element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> (atomic number 20) reacts with an element Q (atomic number 17) to form a compound. Answer the following questions giving reason:
Write the position of P and Q in the modern periodic table and the molecular formula of the compound formed when P reacts with Q .
exercises.solution:
The position of P in the modern periodic table:
Period <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>, Group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
The position of Q in the modern Periodic table:
Period = 3, Group = <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
When P reacts with Q , it loses two valence electrons (valency 2)
These two valence electrons are received by two
Q atoms. Hence, the formula is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q21
exercises.problem:
The electronic configuration of an element is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>. State its :
(a) group and period in the modern periodic table.
(b) name and write its one physical property.
exercises.solution:

∴ Number of shells <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
It has four electrons in its valence shell.
Hence it is in 3rd period and 14th group.
(b) The name of the element is silicon .
Physical property : Pure silicon exists in solid state and has a dark grey colour.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q1
exercises.problem:
Identify the larger species of each of the following pairs:
(a) K or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
exercises.solution:
(a) K has the electronic configuration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>has the electronic configuration of [Ar]. The electron in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> orbital makes K much larger than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(b) These two species have the same electronic configuration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math> as these two species are
isoelectronic. The size of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is larger than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> because generally anions with more negative charge are larger in size. Moreover, sulphur is at left to chlorine in periodic table. Therefore, periodic trend also favours larger size of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(c) Both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> have valence electrons in the same sublevel, but the size <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is larger because additional shielding caused by the extra electron will expand the electron cloud.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q2
exercises.problem:
(a) Which atom in Group VIA should have a smaller first ionization energy : oxygen or sulfur?
(b) Specify the group of the periodic table in which each of the following elements is found :
(I) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(II) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(III) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
exercises.solution:
(a) Oxygen and sulfur are members of group VIA. They have the same valence electron configuration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, but the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> electron in sulfur is farther away from the nucleus and experiences less nuclear attraction than the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> electron in oxygen. Thus, following the general rule that the ionization energy of elements decreases as we move down a periodic group, we predict that sulfur should have a smaller first ionization energy.
(b)
(I) Group IA
(II) Group VA
(III) Group VIIIA

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q3
exercises.problem: What were the limitations of Newlands' Law of Octaves?
exercises.solution:
(i) It was found that law of octaves was applicable only up to calcium because after Ca , every eighth element did not possess properties similar to first.
(ii) New elements discovered could not fit into the law of octaves on the basis of their properties.
(iii) Newland adjusted two elements in same slot e.g., Co and Ni were placed along with halogens which differ entirely from halogens. Iron resembles with Co and Ni , but placed far away from these elements.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q4
exercises.problem: Write the main aim of classifying elements. Name the basic property of elements used in the development of modern periodic table. State the modern periodic law. On which side (part) of the modern periodic table do you find metals, metalloids and non-metals?
exercises.solution:
The main aim of classifying elements is the systematic and simplified study of elements and their compounds. The basic property of elements used in development of modern periodic table was atomic number.
Modern periodic law : The properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number.
Metals are found on the left side and at the centre of the modern periodic table.
Metalloids are present in a zig-zag manner between the metals and the non-metals.
Non-metals are present on the right side of the modern periodic table.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q5
exercises.problem: Write the names given to the vertical columns and horizontal rows in the modern periodic table. How does the metallic character of elements vary on moving down a vertical column? How does the size of atomic radius vary on moving left to right in a horizontal row? Give reason in support of your answer in the above two cases.
exercises.solution:
18 vertical columns are known as groups and 7 horizontal rows are known as periods. Metallic character increases on moving down a group in the modern periodic table. As we move down the group, the attraction between the nucleus and the outermost shell electron decreases due to the addition of new shell between them. Therefore, the valence electron can be easily lost by the element.
The size of atomic radius decreases on moving left to right in a horizontal row. When, we move across a period, the number of electrons in the same shell increases. This will experience greater attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electrons. This increased attraction bring the outermost electron closer to the nucleus, thereby decreases the atomic size.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q6
exercises.problem:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and Al are the elements of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext>rd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> period of the modern periodic table having group number 1, 2 and 13 respectively. Which one of these elements has the
(i) highest valency,
(ii) largest atomic radius, and
(iii) maximum chemical reactivity? Justify your answer stating the reason for each.
exercises.solution:
(i) Na: Electronic configuration: 2, 8, 1
for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mi>:</mi></mrow></math> Valency = 1
for, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>;</mi><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Valency = 2
Al: 2, 8, 3; Valency = 3
Al has the highest valency beacause it contains the maximum number of electrons in the outermost orbital.
(ii) Na has the largest atomic radius in given elements because atomic radius decreases across the period due to increase in number of electrons and nuclear charge which tends to pull the electrons closer to the nucleus.
(iii) Na has the maximum chemical reactivity as it contains only one electron in its valence shell so it can lose electron easily to form cation in comparison to Mg and Al .

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q7
exercises.problem:
(a) The modern periodic table has been evolved through the early attempts of Dobereiner, Newland and Mendeleev. List one advantage and one limitation of all the three attempts.
(b) Name the scientists who first of all showed that atomic number of an element is a more fundamental property than its atomic mass.
(c) State modern periodic law.
exercises.solution:
(a) Dobereiner:
Advantage:- He gave an idea of classification of elements in the form of triads.
Disadvantage:- He could arrange only a few elements in triads.
Newland:
Advantage:- He arranged known elements in order of increasing atomic mass and encouraged other chemist to correlate the properties of elements with their atomic masses.
Disadvantage:- Newland could arrange elements only upto calcium.
Mendeleev:
Advantage:- Mendeleev's periodic table had some blank spaces in it. These vacant spaces were for elements that were yet to be discovered.
Disadvantage: Argon (39.91) is placed before potassium (39.1)
(b) Henry Moseley
(c) The properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

exercises.problem:

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Long Answer Questions — Q9
exercises.problem: How it can be proved that the basic structure of the modern periodic table is based on the electronic configuration of atoms of different elements?
exercises.solution:
The basic structure of the modern periodic table has vertical columns known as groups and horizontal rows known as periods.
If we know the electronic configuration of an element, we can know its period from the number of shells present in its atom and we can know its group from number of electrons in the valence shell.
For example, Atomic number of chlorine <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow></math>
Its electronic configuration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>
KLM
Number of shells <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
∴ Chlorine belongs to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext>rd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> period
As Cl atom has seven electron in its valence shell
∴ Chlorine is present in seventeenth group.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q1
exercises.problem: Why elements in any given group have similar properties?
exercises.solution: The chemical properties of an atom are largely determined by its valance electrons. In a given group, the number of valance electrons in all elements is same, hence they have similar chemical properties.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q2
exercises.problem: Why some gaps were left in Mendeleev's periodic table?
exercises.solution: Mendeleev left some gaps in his periodic table for the elements yet to be discovered. He even predicted the properties of these elements by studying the properties of the neighbouring elements.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q3
exercises.problem: Why are the group 2 elements called alkaline earth metals?
exercises.solution: These elements are called alkaline earth metals because their oxides and hydroxides are alkaline in nature and these metal oxides are found in the earth's crust.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q4
exercises.problem: Why the size of the atom increases down the group?
exercises.solution: On moving down a group, the charge on the nucleus increases with increase in atomic number, but at the same time, there is an increase in the energy levels. The number of electrons in the outermost shell, however, remains the same. Since the effect of additional energy levels outweigh the effect of increased atomic or nuclear charge, the distance of the outermost electron from the nucleus increase on going down the group. Hence size of the atom increases down the group.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q5
exercises.problem: Explain why the first ionization energy of lithium is less than that for beryllium, but the second ionization energy of beryllium is less than lithium.
exercises.solution:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>;</mi><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
First ionization energy of lithium is less than beryllium because electron has been removed from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> subshell which is partially filled in Li and fully filled in Be. While second ionisation energy of Be is less than Li because second electron has been removed from partially filled <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> subshell in Be and from fully filled subshell in Li. Half filled and completely filled subshell are stable configuration therefore require more energy for electron removal.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q6
exercises.problem: Why does the metallic character increase down the group?
exercises.solution: As we move down the group atomic size increases and effective nuclear charge experienced by the valence electrons decreases, consequently valence electrons can be removed easily. Therefore metallic character increase down the group.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q7
exercises.problem: In the modern periodic table, why does cobalt with higher atomic mass of 58.93 appear before nickel having lower atomic mass of 58.71?
exercises.solution: Modern periodic table is based on modern periodic law and the elements are arranged in the order of increasing atomic number. Therefore, cobalt with atomic number 27 should come first followed by nickel with atomic number 28 .

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q8
exercises.problem: Why could no fixed position be given to hydrogen in Mendeleev's periodic table?
exercises.solution:
Fixed position could not be given to hydrogen in Mendeleev's periodic table because hydrogen resembles both halogens and alkali metals in its properties.
Resemblence with halogen:
(i) Hydrogen exists as diatomic molecules <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
(ii) Hydrogen combines with certain metals to form ionic compounds.
(iii) It also react with non metals to form covalent compounds.
Resemblence with alkali metals:
(i) Hydrogen combines with halogens, oxygen and sulphur to form compounds having similar formulae as of alkali metals.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Reasoning Based Questions — Q9
exercises.problem: Why the properties of elements are repeated after 2,8 , 18 and 32 elements in the periodic table?
exercises.solution: The electronic configuration of elements are repeated after 2, 8, 18 and 32 elements because 2, 8, 18 and 32 is the maximum number of electrons which can be accomodated in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> and N shells of the atoms of the elements. The properties of elements are repeated after 2, 8, 18 and 32 elements because electronic configuration of the elements are repeated after 2, 8, 18 and 32 element.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q1
exercises.problem: Referring to a periodic table, arrange the following atoms in order of increasing first ionization energy : Ne, Na, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>.
exercises.solution:
The ionization energy increases as we move left to right across a period. It decreases as we move from the top of a group to the bottom. Because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>, and Ar are in the same period of the periodic table, therefore ionisation energy vary in the order : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mi>P</mi><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Because Ne is above Ar in group 18, we expect Ne to exhibit the greater first ionization energy : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Similarly, K is the alkali metal directly below Na in group IA, so we expect IE1 for K to be less than that of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mi>:</mi><mi>K</mi><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
From these observations we conclude that the first ionization energies follow the order : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mi>P</mi><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q2
exercises.solution:
In comparing ionic radii, it is useful to classify the ions into three categories: (1) isoelectronic ions, (2) ions carrying the same charge and are generated from atoms of the same periodic group, and (3) ions carrying different charges but are generated from the same atom. In case (1), ions carrying a greater negative charge are always larger; in case (2), ions from atoms having a greater atomic number are always larger; in case (3), ions having a greater positive charge are always smaller.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>are isoelectronic anions. Because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> has only seven protons and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>has nine, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is larger.
(b) Both Mg and Ca belong to Group 2A (the alkaline earth metals). The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ion is larger than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> because valence electrons in Ca are in 4th shell while in Mg valence electrons are in 3rd shell.
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is larger

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q3
exercises.problem:
Using only a periodic table as a guide, arrange each of the following series of species in order of increasing first ionization energy.
(a) O, C, F
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
exercises.solution:
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo><</mo><mi>O</mi><mo><</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q4
exercises.solution:
(a) W , because density increases with atomic number
(b) Os, density increases with atomic number
(c) Pd, density decreases at the end of a row
(d) Nb , density increases with atomic number.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q5
exercises.problem: Why are the elements of group 18 called zero valent ?
exercises.solution: Group 18 elements have their outermost shell completely filled and the atoms of these elements have no tendency to gain or lose electrons. Thus, the elements of this group are zero valent and almost unreactive.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q6
exercises.problem: List the following series of elements in order of increasing atomic radius : (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math> (b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
exercises.solution:
(a) Beryllium is in the same period with carbon and is to its left, so it is larger of the two. Magnesium is below beryllium in the same group and is larger. The order of increasing size is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(b) Rubidium is far to the left in the same period as iodine and is larger; bromine is above iodine and is the smallest among the three: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mi>I</mi><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q7
exercises.problem: Arrange the ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> in order of decreasing ionic radii.
exercises.solution:
This is an isoelectronic series of ions, with all ions having 18 electrons. In such a series, size decreases as the charge of the cation increases and size increases as the charge of anion increases. The atomic numbers of the ions are S (16), Cl (17), K (19) and Ca (20). Thus, size of the ions decrease in the order :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q8
exercises.problem: List the following ions in order of increasing ionic radius: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
exercises.solution:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo><</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo><</mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo><</mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo><</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
In a group ionic radii increases as the atomic number increases. In a period ionic radii decreases as we move from left to right

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — HOTS Questions — Q9
exercises.problem: Why are the electron affinities of the alkaline earth metals, either negative or small positive values?
exercises.solution:
The outermost shell of alkaline earth metals has two electrons. For the process
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>⟶</mi><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
where M denotes a member of the Group IIA, extra electron to be added must enter the outermost subshell. The outermost shell is completely filled means there is no vacancy for electron to be added. Therefore, electron affinity for IIA elements is negative value or small positive value.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q1
exercises.problem: Did Dobereiner's triads also exist in the columns of Newland's octaves? Compare and find out.
exercises.solution:
Yes, Dobereiner's triads exists in the column of Newland's octaves e.g.
Li Be
Na Mg
K Ca

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q2
exercises.problem: What were the limitations of Dobereiner's classification?
exercises.solution: Dobereiner's triads were dismissed because all the known elements of that time could not be arranged in triads.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q3
exercises.problem:
Use Mendeleev's periodic table to predict the formulae for the oxides of following elements :
K, C, Al, Si, Ba
exercises.solution: K is in 1st group and has valency one. Thus the formula of its oxide formed is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>. C and Si are in group 14, hence have valency 4. Thus the formulae of oxides formed are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> \& <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Aluminium is in group 13 and has valency 3, thus the formula of its oxide formed is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> is in second group and has valency 2 , thus the formula of its oxide formed is BaO .

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q4
exercises.problem: Besides galium, which other elements have since been discovered to fill the gaps left by Mendeleev in his periodic table? (any two)
exercises.solution: Germanium and scandium.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q5
exercises.problem: What were the criteria used by Mendeleev in creating his periodic table?
exercises.solution: The criteria used by Mendeleev in creating his periodic table was classfication of elements on the basis of their atomic masses.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q6
exercises.problem: Why do you think the noble gases are placed in a separate group?
exercises.solution: Noble gases are placed in a separate 18th group because all of them have completely filled outermost shell.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q7
exercises.problem: How could the modern periodic table remove various anomalies of Mendeleev's periodic table?
exercises.solution:
(i) Classification of elements in modern periodic table is based on the atomic number of the elements, which is their fundamental property.
(ii) Same position of the isotopes of an element in the periodic table can be justified as isotopes have same atomic number but different mass number .
(iii) The systematic grouping of elements into four blocks i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> has made the study of these elements quite simple.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q8
exercises.problem: Name two elements you would expect to show same kind of chemical reactivity as magnesium. What is the basis for your choice?
exercises.solution: Calcium and barium because they have same number of valence electrons as magnesium, i.e., they are in same group of periodic table.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q9
exercises.problem:
Name :
(a) Three elements that have only a single electron in their outermost shell.
(b) Two elements that have two electrons in their outermost shell.
(c) Three elements with completely filled outermost shell.
exercises.solution:
(a) Lithium (Li), Sodium (Na) and Potassium (K).
(b) Magnesium (Mg) and Calcium (Ca).
(c) Neon (Ne), Argon (Ar) and Krypton (Kr)

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q10
exercises.problem:
(a) Lithium, Sodium and Potassium are all metals that react with water to liberate hydrogen gas. Is there any similarity in the atoms of these elements?
(b) Helium is an unreactive gas and neon is a gas of extremely low reactivity. What, if anything, do their atoms have in common?
exercises.solution:
(a) All these are alkali metals, placed in group 1 of periodic table and has one electron in their valence shell.
(b) Both are noble gases and have completely filled electrons valence shells.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q11
exercises.problem: In the modern periodic table, among the first ten elements, which are metals?
exercises.solution: Lithium and Berylium.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Questions — Q12
exercises.problem:
By considering their position in the periodic table, which one of the following elements would you expect to have the most metallic characteristics?
Ga Ge As Se Be
exercises.solution: Be, the elements placed on the extreme left side of the periodic table have maximum metallic character. Among the given elements Be is placed in group 2, thus has maximum metallic character.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q1
exercises.problem:
Which of the following statements is not a correct statement about the trends when going from left to right across the periods of periodic table.
(a) The elements become less metallic in nature.
(b) The number of valence electrons increases.
(c) The atoms lose their electrons more easily.
(d) The oxides become more acidic.
exercises.solution:
(c) As we move from left to right in a period no. of shells remains same whereas one more electron is
added thus the size of atom decreases and hence the valence electron becomes more and more near to the nucleus and hold of nucleus on valence electron increases, due to this, the tendency of an atom to lose valence electron decreases.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q2
exercises.problem:
Element X forms a chloride with the formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, which is a solid with a high melting point? X would most likely be in the same group of the periodic table as :
(a) Na
(b) Mg
(c) Al
(d) Si
exercises.solution: (b) X forms <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> suggests that X is in +2 state in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Therefore X would most like be in gp 2 of periodic table.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q3
exercises.problem:
Which element has :
(a) two shells, both of which are completely filled with electrons?
(b) the electronic configuration 2, 8, 2?
(c) a total of three shells, with four electrons in its valence shell?
(d) a total of two shells, with three electrons in its valence shell?
(e) twice as many electrons in its second shell as in its first shell?
exercises.solution:
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>12</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>14</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
(e) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q4
exercises.problem:
(a) What property do all elements in the same column of the periodic table as boron have in common?
(b) What property do all elements in the same column of the periodic table as fluorine have in common?
exercises.solution:
(a) All of them have common valency 3 .
(b) All of them have common valency 1 .

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q5
exercises.problem:
An atom has electronic configuration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>.
(a) What is the atomic number of this element?
(b) To which of the following elements would it be chemically similar? (Atomic numbers are given in parentheses).
N (7)
F(9)
P (15)
Ar(18)
exercises.solution:
(a) Atomic number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow></math>
(b) This element will be similar to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> as it also has 7 electrons in its valence shell. Therefore, they both belong to group 17th of the periodic table.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q6
exercises.problem:
The position of three elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and C in the periodic table are shown below :
| Group 16 | Group 17 |
| :--- | :---: |
| - | - |
| - | A |
| - | - |
| B | C |
(a) State whether A is a metal or non-metal.
(b) State whether C is more reactive or less reactive than A .
(c) Will C be larger or smaller in size than B ?
(d) Which type of ion, cation or anion will be formed by an element A ?
exercises.solution:
(a) Element A belongs to group 17 which is on the extreme right side of the periodic table. Hence, A is a non-metal. It is a halogen.
(b) In group 17 (halogens) the reactivity decreases from fluorine to iodine.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>></mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>></mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>></mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Hence, C will be less reactive than A . This is due to increase in size of atom.
(c) On moving left to right along a period the atomic size decreases. Hence, C is smaller than B .
(d) Since, A has 7 valence electrons.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>17</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>
Therefore this will show a tendency to gain one electron and hence form an anion.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q7
exercises.problem: Nitrogen (atomic number 7) and phosphorus (atomic number 15) belong to group 15 of the periodic table. Write the electronic configuration of these two elements. Which of these will be more electronegative? Why?
exercises.solution:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>15</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
Atomic size increases on moving down the group consequently effective nuclear charge decreases which results in decreases in electronegativity of an atom. Therefore N is more electronegative than P .

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q8
exercises.problem: How does the electronic configuration of an atom relate to its position in the modern periodic table?
exercises.solution:
If we know the electronic configuration of an element, we can know its period from the number of shells present in its atom and from number of electrons in the valence shell of its atoms we can know its group e.g.
Atomic number of chlorine <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></mrow></math>
Its electronic configuration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Number of shells <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
∴ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Chlorine belongs to 3rd period.
As chlorine atom has seven electron in its valence shell.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> It is present in group 17.

exercises.solution:
Element with atomic numbers 12 and 38 resembles calcium since they have two electrons in their valence shell like calcium.
Atomic number increase on moving down the group.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Text - Book Exercise — Q10
exercises.problem: Compare and contrast the arrangement of elements in Mendeleev's periodic table and the modern periodic table.
exercises.solution:
| | Mendeleev's Periodic Table | | Modern Periodic Table |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. | Elements are arranged in the order of increasing atomic mass. | 1. | Elements are arranged in the order of increasing atomic number. |
| 2. | There are nine vertical columns called groups. | 2. | There are 18 vertical column called groups. |
| 3. | Transition elements are arbitrarily placed together in group VIII. | 3. | Transition elements are placed in the middle of long periods. |

exercises.solution:
The position of P in the modern periodic table:
Period <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>, Group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

Period = 3, Group = <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

When Z/e ratio increases, the size decreases and when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> ratio decreases, size increases.
