(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo><</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mn>37</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q54
exercises.problem:
Consider following as a portion of the periodic table from Group No. 13 to 17. Which of the following statements is/are true about the elements shown in it?
[NTSE]
I. V., W, Y and Z are less electropositive than X.
II. V, W, X and Y are more .electronegative than Z.
III. Atomic size of Y is greater than that of W .
IV. Atomic size of W is smaller than that of X .
| | | | V | Z |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| | | | | Y |
| W | | | | |
| | | | | |
| X | | | | |
(a) I, II and III
(b) II and III
(c) I and IV
(d) III and IV
exercises.solution:
(c) Electropositive nature increases from top to bottom in a group and decrease along a period. Therefore X is most electropositive.
Atomic size decreases along a period and increases down the group. Therefore <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo><</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q55
exercises.problem:
Mendeleev's periodic law states that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their
[KVPY]
(a) reactivity of elements
(b) atomic size
(c) atomic mass
(d) electronic configuration
exercises.solution: (c) Mendeleev's periodic law states that the physical and chemical properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic mass.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q61
exercises.problem:
The ionic radii of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>follow the decreasing order
[JSTSE]
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
exercises.solution: (a) Increase in positive charge decrease the ionic radii of cation while increase in negative charge increases the ionic size of anion. So <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q63
exercises.problem:
Which of the following statement can help a chemistry student to predict chemical properties of an element?
[NTSE]

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q66
exercises.problem:
Manya, Kartik, Gurnoor and Sheena had arranged the ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> in decreasing orders of their ionic radii.
[NTSE]
| Manya - | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> |
| :--- | :--- |
| Kartik - | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> |
| Gurnoor- | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> |
| Sheena - | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> |
Who had provided the correct order of their decreasing ionic radii?
(a) Manya
(b) Kartik
(c) Gurnoor
(d) Sheena
exercises.solution:
(c) The ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> are isoelectronic species having same electronic configuration but their nuclear charges differ from each other because of their difference in the number of protons in the nucleus. With increase in the number of protons in the nucleus, the electrons are more attracted towards nucleus thereby causing the decrease in ionic radius. Therefore, the given ions are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>: no. of proton <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math> and no. of electron <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>: no. of proton <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></math> and no. of electron <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>:</mi></mrow></math> no. of proton <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> and no. of electron <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> : no. of proton <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> and no. of electron <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q67
exercises.problem:
Consider the elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and D with atomic numbers 11, 12, 16 and 17, respectively. Which among the following statements regarding these elements are correct?
[NTSE]
I. The element C will gain electron more easily than element D .
II. The element B tends to lose electron more readily than C .
III. The oxide of A will be least basic while that of D will be most basic.
IV. The energy required to remove an electron from outermost shell from A will be minimum while that from D will be maximum.
(a) I and III only
(b) I and IV only
(c) II and III only
(d) II and IV only
exercises.solution:
(d)
| Atomic Number | Element | Electronic configuration |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>11</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> | Na | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>12</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> | Mg | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> | S | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>17</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> | Cl | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> |
From the above table it is clear that:
(a) Chlorine (D) will gain electrons more easily than sulphur (C).
(b) The oxide of sodium (A) which is an alkali metal, will be the most basic while that of chlorine (D) which is a halogen, will be the most acidic.

exercises.title: Passage Based Questions — Multiple Choice Questions — Q68
exercises.problem:

[JSTSE]
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
exercises.solution:
(a) The correct order of reactivity is as follows.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Alkali metals and alkaline earth metals are very reactive elements in the periodic table and reactivity decreases on moving from left to right in the periodic table.

exercises.title: Assertion \& Reason — Directions — Q13
exercises.problem:
Consider the following changes
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>→</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>:</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>→</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mi>:</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
The energy required to pull out the two electrons are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> respectively. The correct relationship between two energies would be-
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo><</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>></mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
exercises.solution:
As we move from left to right across a period there is a regular decrease in atomic radii of the representative elements. This is due to the fact that number of energy shells remain the same in a period but nuclear charge increases gradually as the atomic number increases, hence the correct order will be
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mi>P</mi><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>

(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

exercises.solution: N and P are in the same group and N is above P . Therefore, the radius of N is smaller than that of P (atomic radius increases as we go down a group). Both Si and P are in the third period, and Si is to the left of P. Therefore, the radius of P is smaller than that of Si (atomic radius decreases as we move from left to right across a period). Thus the order of radius is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo><</mo><mi>P</mi><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

As we move down the group, the attraction between the nucleus and the outermost shell electron decreases due to the addition of new shell between them. Therefore, the valence electron can be easily lost by the element.
The size of atomic radius decreases on moving left to right in a horizontal row. When, we move across a period, the number of electrons in the same shell increases. This will experience greater attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electrons. This increased attraction bring the outermost electron closer to the nucleus, thereby decreases the atomic size.

Disadvantage: Argon (39.91) is placed before potassium (39.1)
(b) Henry Moseley
(c) The properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

Hence size of the atom increases down the group.

Neon and fluorine both are gases in which fluorine is extremely reactive whereas neon is completely non reactive?
Elements classified as rare earth elements :

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi></mrow></mrow></math>-Block elements : Those elements of the periodic table in which the last electron enters in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>-orbital, are called <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>-block elements.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mi></mrow></mrow></math>-Block elements : Those elements of the periodic table in which the last electron gets filled up in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mi></mrow></mrow></math>-orbital, are called <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block elements. A <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-orbital can accommodate a maximum of six electrons. Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block elements are divided into six groups which are III A, IV A, V A, VI A, VII A and VIII A groups. They include both metals and non-metals. They form mostly covalent compounds. The general formula of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>-block elements is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> (where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> to 6 ).

d-Block elements : Those elements of the periodic table in which the last electron gets filled up in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>-orbital, called <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>-block elements. The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>-block elements are placed in groups named IIIB, IV B, V B, VI B, VII B, VIII, I B and II B. In <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>-block elements the electron gets filled up in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> orbital of the penultimate shell. Though the total number of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>-block elements is 39 in the periodic table but there are only 36 transition elements. Because only those elements are transition elements in which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> orbital is partly filled. The general formula of these elements is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></msup><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> to 7 . They are metals having high melting and boiling points. Most of them form coloured compounds and exhibit several oxidation states

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi></mrow></mrow></math>-Block elements : Those elements of the periodic table in which the last electron gets filled up in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>-orbital, called <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>-block elements. There are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>28</mn><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>-block elements in the periodic table. The elements from atomic number 58 to 71 are called lanthanides because they come after lanthanum (57). The elements from 90 to 103 are called actinides because they come after actinium (89). They are heavy metals with high melting and boiling points. They form coloured ions. All the actinide elements are radioactive. All the elements after atomic number 92 (i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mn>92</mn></mrow></msup><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> ) are transuranic elements. The elements which do not occur in nature and are produced in the laboratories artificially are called transuranic or synthetic elements. The general formula of these elements is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>&</mi><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>
Write general electronic configuration of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mi></mrow></mrow></math>-block elements.

Valency in a period : We have already learnt in the previous section that the number of valence electrons increases in a period. In normal elements, it increases from 1 to 8 in a period from left to right. It reaches 8 in group 18 elements (noble gases) which show practically no chemical activity under ordinary conditions and their valency is taken as zero. Carefully look at the table given below. Valency of normal elements with respect to oxygen increases from 1 to 7 as shown below

Valency in a group : All the elements of a group have the same number of valence electrons. Therefore, they all have the same valency. Thus valency of all elements of group 1, alkali metals, is 1 . Similarly, valency of all elements of group 17, halogens, is 1 with respect to hydrogen and 7 with respect to oxygen.
Valency remains constant for elements in group or in period ?

CASE II: Ionization energy is the minimum amount of energy required to remove the outermost electron from an atom or ion in the gas phase. Ionization energy generally increases from left to right along a period whereas it decreases top to bottom in a group. If you look at a chart of first ionization energies. Energy of boron is less than that of beryllium and the first ionization energy of oxygen is less than that of nitrogen. Why these variation are seen in ionisation energy trend?
Li <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo><</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>e</mi><mo><</mo><mi>B</mi><mo><</mo><mi>C</mi><mo><</mo><mi>N</mi><mo><</mo><mi>O</mi><mo><</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> Expected
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">L</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">O</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">N</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">F</mi></mrow><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Observed
The electronic configuration of all 4 elements which shows variation, can be written as follows. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mspace width="1em" /><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mspace width="1em" /><mn>7</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mspace width="1em" /><mn>8</mn><mi>O</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Generally, the fully filled or half filled orbitals are more stable as compared to other. That means more energy is required to remove electrons from these orbitals. Beryllium atom has fully filled 2s orbital hence more energy is required to remove an electron as compared to boron, where electron has to be removed from singly occupied <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> orbital. Similarly, nitrogen atom has half filled <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> orbital, therefore, more energy is required for electron removal than oxygen atom.
CASE III: Electron affinity is the amount of energy released when an electron is added to an atom in the gaseous phase to produce an anion. It follows similar trend as ionisation energy. Electron affinity increases across the period whereas it decreases down the group. Generally noble gases show zero electron affinity. Atoms of the element having low electron affinity has more tendency to lose electrons than gain electrons. Why? The noble gases show zero electron affinity because the addition of an electron to these atoms is not possible. Atoms with a low electron affinity readily loses valence electron because in these atom nucleus does not have strong hold on valence electrons.

(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
8. Using periodic table as a guide, arrange each of the following series of atoms in order of increasing size.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
9. Using periodic table as a guide, arrange each of the following series of species in order of increasing size.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
10. Indicate which species in each pair has the higher ionization energy. Explain the reason for your answer.
(a) Na and Rb
(b) O and F
11. Which has greater, second ionization energy: boron or beryllium ? Explain your answer.
12. What are the names and chemical symbols of the elements that are vertical and horizontal neighbours of sulfur in the periodic table? Which of these have chemical properties similar to those of sulfur?
13. Arrange the following atoms in order of decreasing atomic radius : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
14. Arrange the following atoms in order of increasing radius: P, Si, N.
15. (i) Predict which of the following elements will form cation and which will form anions?
(a) Na
(b) Al
(c) Cl
(d) O
(ii) Name two elements that are inert in nature.
16. From the following elements :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>19</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(i) Select the element having one electron in the outermost shell.
(ii) Two elements of the same group.
(iii) Write the formula and mention the nature of the compound formed by the union of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>19</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
17. Calcium is an element with atomic number 20. State reason for each of the following questions:
(i) Is calcium metal or non-metal?
(ii) Will its atomic radius be larger or smaller than that of potassium with atomic number 19 ?
(iii) Write the formula of its oxide.
18. Name any two elements of group one and write their electronic configurations. What similarity do you observe in their electronic configurations? Write the formula of oxide of any of the above said element.
19. An element ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> ' with electronic configuration ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> ) combines separately with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> radicals. Write the formula of the three compounds so formed. To which group and period of the modern periodic table does the element 'M' belong? Will 'M' form covalent or ionic compounds? Give reason to justify your answer.
20. An element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> (atomic number 20) reacts with an element Q (atomic number 17) to form a compound. Answer the following questions giving reason:
Write the position of P and Q in the modern periodic table and the molecular formula of the compound formed when P reacts with Q .
21. The electronic configuration of an element is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>. State its :
(a) group and period in the modern periodic table.
(b) name and write its one physical property.
## Long Answer Questions
1. Identify the larger species of each of the following pairs:
(a) K or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
2. (a) Which atom in Group VIA should have a smaller first ionization energy : oxygen or sulfur?
(b) Specify the group of the periodic table in which each of the following elements is found :
(I) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(II) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(III) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
3. What were the limitations of Newlands' Law of Octaves?
4. Write the main aim of classifying elements. Name the basic property of elements used in the development of modern periodic table. State the modern periodic law. On which side (part) of the modern periodic table do you find metals, metalloids and non-metals?
5. Write the names given to the vertical columns and horizontal rows in the modern periodic table. How does the metallic character of elements vary on moving down a vertical column? How does the size of atomic radius vary on moving left to right in a horizontal row? Give reason in support of your answer in the above two cases.
6. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and Al are the elements of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext>rd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> period of the modern periodic table having group number 1, 2 and 13 respectively. Which one of these elements has the
(i) highest valency,
(ii) largest atomic radius, and
(iii) maximum chemical reactivity? Justify your answer stating the reason for each.
7. (a) The modern periodic table has been evolved through the early attempts of Dobereiner, Newland and Mendeleev. List one advantage and one limitation of all the three attempts.
(b) Name the scientists who first of all showed that atomic number of an element is a more fundamental property than its atomic mass.
(c) State modern periodic law.
8. Based on the group valency of elements write the molecular formula of the following compounds giving justification for each:
(i) Oxide of first group elements.
(ii) Halide of the elements of group thirteen, and
(iii) Compound formed when an element, A of group 2 combines with an element, B of group seventeen.
9. How it can be proved that the basic structure of the modern periodic table is based on the electronic configuration of atoms of different elements?
## Reasoning Based Questions
1. Why elements in any given group have similar properties?
2. Why some gaps were left in Mendeleev's periodic table?
3. Why are the group 2 elements called alkaline earth metals?
4. Why the size of the atom increases down the group?
5. Explain why the first ionization energy of lithium is less than that for beryllium, but the second ionization energy of beryllium is less than lithium.
6. Why does the metallic character increase down the group?
7. In the modern periodic table, why does cobalt with higher atomic mass of 58.93 appear before nickel having lower atomic mass of 58.71?
8. Why could no fixed position be given to hydrogen in Mendeleev's periodic table?
9. Why the properties of elements are repeated after 2,8 , 18 and 32 elements in the periodic table?
## HOTS Questions
1. Referring to a periodic table, arrange the following atoms in order of increasing first ionization energy : Ne, Na, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>.
2. For each of the following pairs, indicate which one of the two species is larger:

(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>;
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
3. Using only a periodic table as a guide, arrange each of the following series of species in order of increasing first ionization energy.
(a) O, C, F
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
4. Predict which element of the following pairs will have the higher density and support your prediction using periodic trends :
(a) Cr or W ;
(b) W or Os;
(c) Pd or Ag ; and
(d) Y or Nb .
5. Why are the elements of group 18 called zero valent ?
6. List the following series of elements in order of increasing atomic radius : (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math> (b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
7. Arrange the ions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> in order of decreasing ionic radii.

List the following ions in order of increasing ionic radius: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
9. Why are the electron affinities of the alkaline earth metals, either negative or small positive values?

case_studies.title: Case Study Based MCQs (CBSE Sample Issued 2021)
case_studies.description:
1. Read the following and answer any four questions from (i) to (v).
Metallic Character The ability of an atom to donate electrons and form positive ion (cation) is known as electropositivity or metallic character. Down the group, metallic character increases due to increase in atomic size and across the period, from left to right electropositivity decreases due to decrease in atomic size. Non-Metallic Character The ability of an atom to
accept electrons to form a negative ion (anion) is called non-metallic character or electronegativity. The elements having high electro-negativity have a higher tendency to gain electrons and form anion. Down the group, electronegativity decreases due to increase in atomic size and across the period, from left to right electronegativity increases due to decrease in atomic size.
(i) Which of the following correctly represents the decreasing order of metallic character of Alkali metals plotted in the graph?
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mi>K</mi><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mi>K</mi><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(ii) Hydrogen is placed along with Alkali metals in the modern periodic table though it shows non-metallic character
(a) as Hydrogen has one electron \& readily loses electron to form negative ion
(b) as Hydrogen can easily lose one electron like alkali metals to form positive ion
(c) as Hydrogen can gain one electron easily like Halogens to form negative ion
(d) as Hydrogen shows the properties of nonmetals
(iii) Which of the following has highest electronegativity?
(a) F
(b) Cl
(c) Br
(d) I
(iv) Identify the reason for the gradual change in electronegativity in halogens down the group.
(a) Electronegativity increases down the group due to decrease in atomic size
(b) Electronegativity decreases down the group due to decrease in tendency to lose electrons
(c) Electronegativity decreases down the group due to increase in atomic radius/ tendency to gain electron decreases
(d) Electronegativity increases down the group due to increase in forces of attractions between nucleus \& valence electrons
(v) Which of the following reason correctly justifies that "Fluorine (72pm) has smaller atomic radius than Lithium ( 152 pm )"?
(a) F and Li are in the same group. Atomic size increases down the group
(b) F and Li are in the same period. Atomic size increases across the period due to increase in number of shells
(c) F and Li are in the same group. Atomic size decreases down the group
(d) F and Li are in the same period and across the period atomic size/radius decreases from left to right.
## Exercise 2 Lil Master NCERT (Textbook \& Exemplar)
## Text - Book Questions
1. Did Dobereiner's triads also exist in the columns of Newland's octaves? Compare and find out.
2. What were the limitations of Dobereiner's classification?
3. Use Mendeleev's periodic table to predict the formulae for the oxides of following elements :
K, C, Al, Si, Ba
4. Besides galium, which other elements have since been discovered to fill the gaps left by Mendeleev in his periodic table? (any two)
5. What were the criteria used by Mendeleev in creating his periodic table?
6. Why do you think the noble gases are placed in a separate group?
7. How could the modern periodic table remove various anomalies of Mendeleev's periodic table?
8. Name two elements you would expect to show same kind of chemical reactivity as magnesium. What is the basis for your choice?
9. Name :
(a) Three elements that have only a single electron in their outermost shell.
(b) Two elements that have two electrons in their outermost shell.
(c) Three elements with completely filled outermost shell.
10. (a) Lithium, Sodium and Potassium are all metals that react with water to liberate hydrogen gas. Is there any similarity in the atoms of these elements?
(b) Helium is an unreactive gas and neon is a gas of extremely low reactivity. What, if anything, do their atoms have in common?
11. In the modern periodic table, among the first ten elements, which are metals?
12. By considering their position in the periodic table, which one of the following elements would you expect to have the most metallic characteristics?
Ga Ge As Se Be
## Text - Book Exercise
1. Which of the following statements is not a correct statement about the trends when going from left to right across the periods of periodic table.
(a) The elements become less metallic in nature.
(b) The number of valence electrons increases.
(c) The atoms lose their electrons more easily.
(d) The oxides become more acidic.
2. Element X forms a chloride with the formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, which is a solid with a high melting point? X would most likely be in the same group of the periodic table as :
(a) Na
(b) Mg
(c) Al
(d) Si
3. Which element has :
(a) two shells, both of which are completely filled with electrons?
(b) the electronic configuration 2, 8, 2?
(c) a total of three shells, with four electrons in its valence shell?
(d) a total of two shells, with three electrons in its valence shell?
(e) twice as many electrons in its second shell as in its first shell?
4. (a) What property do all elements in the same column of the periodic table as boron have in common?
(b) What property do all elements in the same column of the periodic table as fluorine have in common?
5. An atom has electronic configuration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>.
(a) What is the atomic number of this element?
(b) To which of the following elements would it be chemically similar? (Atomic numbers are given in parentheses).
N (7)
F(9)
P (15)
Ar(18)
6. The position of three elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and C in the periodic table are shown below :
| Group 16 | Group 17 |
| :--- | :---: |
| - | - |
| - | A |
| - | - |
| B | C |
(a) State whether A is a metal or non-metal.
(b) State whether C is more reactive or less reactive than A .
(c) Will C be larger or smaller in size than B ?
(d) Which type of ion, cation or anion will be formed by an element A ?

In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic numbers which is related to the electronic configuration. The modern periodic table consists of 7 periods and 18 groups. Each period begins with the filling of a new energy shell. In accordance with the Afbau principle, the seven periods ( 1 to 7 ) have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>18</mn></mrow></math>, 18, 32 and 32 elements respectively. ## PASSAGE-2
The way atomic radius varies with increasing atomic number can be explained by the arrangement of electrons in shells of fixed capacity. Shells closer to the nucleus, those with a smaller radius are generally filled first, since the negatively charged electrons are attracted by the positively charged protons in the nucleus. As the atomic number increases along a row of the periodic table, additional electrons are added to the same, outermost shell. The radius of this shell gradually contracts as the attraction between the additional electrons and the nucleus increases. On moving down in group, atomic radius increases due to increase in the number of shells. As the number of shells increases, the force of attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electron decreases and hence the size increases.

case_studies.title: CASE STUDY
case_studies.description:
1. When an electron is present in the valence shell of an atom, it is attracted toward nucleus by nuclear force of attraction. In order to remove this electron, energy is required to overcome this force of attraction. During the addition of an electron to a neutral atom, the electron approaches neutral atom due to nuclear force of attraction. This process involves work done towards the force of attraction and hence energy is released. Thus, ionization potential is the energy absorbed and electron affinity is the energy released.
2. The given elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> and z are Ti, Zr and Hf respectively. They belong to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>6</mn><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> period of transitions series. Since they belong to same group and the value of ionization potential (I.P.) decreases down the group, hence the I.P. decrease from Ti to Zr. However, the I.P. value of Hf is double to the I.P. value of Zr due of the presence of lanthanide elements that causes lanthanide contraction.

examples.problem: State one reason for placing Mg and Ca in the same group of the periodic table.
examples.solution: Due to the presence of 2 electrons in the valence shell and similar chemical properties.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Very Short Answer Questions — Q14
examples.problem:
The atomic radii of first group elements are given below :
| Group-I element | Atomic Radii (pm) |
| :---: | :---: |
| Na | 86 |
| K | 231 |
| Rb | 244 |
| Cs | 282 |
State the reason behind the observed trend in the above elements.
examples.solution: The atomic size (atomic radii) increases while going down the group because new shells are being added at each step.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q1
examples.problem: Arrange these atoms and ions in order of decreasing size: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and Ca .
examples.solution: Cations are smaller than their parent atoms, so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is smaller than the Ca atom. Because Ca is below Mg in group IIA of the periodic table, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is larger than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Consequently, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q2
examples.problem: What do you understand by the term periodicity ? Are the properties of the elements placed in a group, same ? Illustrate.
examples.solution: When the elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic numbers, elements with similar chemical properties appear at definite intervals, this is known as periodicity. Yes, this periodicity is due to the periodicity in the number of electrons in the outermost shell of the atoms of the elements. Elements placed in the same group have same number of valance electrons and show similar properties.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q3
examples.problem: Define and explain Mendeleev's periodic law ?
examples.solution: Mendeleev's periodic law : It states that, the properties of elements are the periodic functions of their atomic masses. It means that the properties of the elements depend on their atomic masses and elements were placed in the periodic table on the basis of their increasing atomic masses.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q4
examples.problem:
(a) Which elements or ions among <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> are isoelectronic with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>?
(b) Among <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> which ions are isoelectronic with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ?
examples.solution:
(a) The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>cation has 14 electrons. Ar and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> have 18 electrons, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>has 15 electrons, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> has 14 electrons. Only <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is isoelectronic with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(b) The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> cation has 23 electrons with electron configuration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ion also has 23 electrons and the same electronic configuration as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>; thus they are isoelectronic. The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ion has 25 electrons <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> has 24 electrons <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. Neither of which is isoelectronic with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q7
examples.problem:
Which species in each of the following pairs is larger ? Give an explanation for your answer.
(a) Na or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
examples.solution:
(a) Na, cation always has smaller size than neutral atom.
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, the size of anion increase as the charge increases.
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, the size of cation decreases as the charge increases.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q10
examples.problem:
Indicate which species in each pair has the higher ionization energy. Explain the reason for your answer.
(a) Na and Rb
(b) O and F
examples.solution:
(a) In a group, the ionisation potential decreases from top to bottom, hence ionisation potential of Na will be higher than Rb .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(b) In a period ionisation potential increases from left to right, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>></mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q11
examples.problem: Which has greater, second ionization energy: boron or beryllium ? Explain your answer.
examples.solution: Boron. In both cases a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> valence electron is being removed, but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>has fully filled inert configuration.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q12
examples.problem: What are the names and chemical symbols of the elements that are vertical and horizontal neighbours of sulfur in the periodic table? Which of these have chemical properties similar to those of sulfur?
examples.solution: Vertical neighbours are oxygen ( O ) and selenium ( Se ), horizontal neighbours are phosphorus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and chlorine (Cl). Oxygen and selenium have similar chemical properties to that of sulphur.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q13
examples.problem: Arrange the following atoms in order of decreasing atomic radius : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
examples.solution:
As we move from left to right across a period there is a regular decrease in atomic radii of the representative elements. This is due to the fact that number of energy shells remain the same in a period but nuclear charge increases gradually as the atomic number increases, hence the correct order will be
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mi>P</mi><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q14
examples.problem: Arrange the following atoms in order of increasing radius: P, Si, N.
examples.solution: N and P are in the same group and N is above P . Therefore, the radius of N is smaller than that of P (atomic radius increases as we go down a group). Both Si and P are in the third period, and Si is to the left of P. Therefore, the radius of P is smaller than that of Si (atomic radius decreases as we move from left to right across a period). Thus the order of radius is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo><</mo><mi>P</mi><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q15
examples.problem:
(i) Predict which of the following elements will form cation and which will form anions?
(a) Na
(b) Al
(c) Cl
(d) O
(ii) Name two elements that are inert in nature.
examples.solution:
(i) Cations -Na and Al
Anions -Cl and O
(ii) He and Ne are inert elements

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q16
examples.problem:
From the following elements :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>19</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(i) Select the element having one electron in the outermost shell.
(ii) Two elements of the same group.
(iii) Write the formula and mention the nature of the compound formed by the union of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>19</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
examples.solution:
(i) The element which have one electron in the outermost shell is
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow /><mrow><mn>19</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
(ii) Two elements of the same group are Be and Ca .

examples.title: Passage Based Questions — Short Answer Questions — Q17
examples.problem:
Calcium is an element with atomic number 20. State reason for each of the following questions:
(i) Is calcium metal or non-metal?
(ii) Will its atomic radius be larger or smaller than that of potassium with atomic number 19 ?
(iii) Write the formula of its oxide.
examples.solution:
(i) It is a metal because it has two electrons in its outermost shell i.e. two valence electrons, which it can lose easily.
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>19</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is placed before <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>20</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> in the same period. Since, the atomic radius decrease across a period so, the atomic radius of calcium is smaller than that of potassium.
(iii) The formula of oxide of calcium is CaO , because the valency of both calcium and oxygen is 2 .
