- What kitchen device is used to lower the rate at which microorganisms grow on food ?
Microorganisms, such as bread mold, are everywhere and difficult to avoid. Lowering the temperatures of microorganism contaminated food by using the refrigerator, decreases the rate of the chemical reactions necessary for the growth of microorganisms. This ultimately prevents decaying of food.
## (c) Effect of Catalyst
A catalyst is a foreign substance which is added to reaction mixture to change the rate of chemical reaction (either increases or decreases) without itself undergoing any change. A catalyst is recovered unchanged in mass and composition at the end of the reaction.
e.g.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is acting as a catalyst to increase the rate of reaction.
## On the basis of physical state, catalyst are of two types -
(i) Homogeneous Catalysts : Those catalysts in which physical states of reactants \& catalyst are same.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Sulphur trioxide </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
(ii) Heterogeneous Catalysts : Those catalysts in which physical states of reactants \& catalyst are different.

Know!
On the basis of action of catalyst, catalyst are of two types -
(i) Positive Catalyst : Those catalysts which increase the rate of reaction are called positive catalyst.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> water </mtext></mrow></munder><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Urease </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ammonia </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Carbondioxide </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow><mrow><mtext> Urea </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
(ii) Negative Catalyst : Those catalysts which decrease the rate of reaction are called negative catalyst. They are also known as inhibitors.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Hydrogen peroxide </mtext></mrow></munder><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Glycerine </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Glycerine inhibits the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.
Thus, a catalyst can have both positive and negative effects on the rate of a chemical reaction.
(d) Effect of Light on Reaction Rate
Those chemical reactions which are carried in the presence of light are known as photochemical reactions. Examples :
(i) Plants in presence of sunlight produces glucose. This is known as photosynthesis.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><munderover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Sunlight </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Chlorophyll </mtext></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></munderover><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Glucose </mtext></mrow></munder><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
(ii) Oxygen in the upper atmosphere absorbs U. V. radiations \& gets converted into ozone.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(iii) When silver bromide is exposed to light it will break into silver \& bromine. This reaction occurs in photography.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>ν</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

## (e) Effect of Surface Area
Rate of reaction is directly proportional to the surface area of the reactants. More will be the surface area, more will be the rate of reaction.
Rate of reaction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∝</mo></mrow></math> Surface area of reactants
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Iron </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Hydrochloric acid </mtext></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ferrous chloride </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
In this case, if metal is in powdered form then reaction would be more rapid than when taken in a ribbon form.
It is a common observation that small pieces of wood burn more rapidly than large logs of wood. This is due to the fact that the total surface area of the smaller particles is greater than that of large particles and this permits more molecules of the reactants to come in contact and form products.

- Generally, if the solid is more finely divided the reaction will be faster but it does not happen in the case of gas reacting with powered solid.
If the solid powder was in one big heap, the gas may not be able to penetrate it. That means its effective surface area is much the same as (or even less than) it would be if it were present in a single lump.

Time to Check Your Knowledge
- What kitchen device is used to lower the rate at which microorganisms grow on food ?
check_your_knowledge_items.solution: Microorganisms, such as bread mold, are everywhere and difficult to avoid. Lowering the temperatures of microorganism contaminated food by using the refrigerator, decreases the rate of the chemical reactions necessary for the growth of microorganisms. This ultimately prevents decaying of food.

The rate of a reaction is expressed by the change in concentration divided by the time taken for the change.

The rate of reaction can be expessed in terms of the reactant or the product both. Since molar concentration of reactant decreases with time and that of the product increases with time, the change in molar concentration of reactant is negative whereas that of product is positive.
The different expressions for the rate can be made equivalent by dividing the rate expression by the stoichiometric coefficient shown by the balanced chemical equation.

## AVERAGE RATE AND INSTANTANEOUS RATE
Since the rate of reaction does not remain constant throughout the reaction time the average rate over the time, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> discussed in above expressions is used as the rate of reaction. However, remember that the average rate does not specify the true rate of reaction at a particular time. So, a new term instantaneous rate of reaction is used to specify the rate of reaction at a particular instant. Therefore, the instantaneous rate may be defined as the rate of change of concentration of any one of the reactants or products at a specific instant of time.
To get instantaneous rate, the time interval ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ) is made infinitesimally small ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ) so that the change in concentration during that time interval remains almost uniform, i.e., the concentration changes when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> approaches zero. Mathematically, instantaneous rate may be expressed by the expression <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> instead of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> is infinitesimally small time change. For example, for a gaseous reaction
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Average rate is given as,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
But the instantaneous rate,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> As </mtext><mi>t</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn><mfrac><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Hence the instantaneous rate expression for the reaction will be,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
A clear distinction between average rate and instantaneous rate can be made by following example. Suppose you travelled 10 km distance in 15 min , then your speed is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>40</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></math>. It is average speed and it is not necessary that you travelled with this speed all the time. Instantaneous speed is your speed at a particular moment and it can be calculated by dividing 15 minutes into infinitely small time intervals.
## For the given general reaction write average and instantaneous rate
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>
Average rate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Instantaneous rate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
## FACTORS AFFECTING RATE OF A REACTION
The rate of a chemical reaction is not a fixed quantity and varies with the experimental conditions. The rate of reaction depends on the following factors :
(a) Effect of Concentration
(b) Effect of Temperature
(c) Effect of Catalyst
(d) Effect of Light
(e) Effect of Surface Area
(a) Effect of Concentration on Reaction Rate
The rate of reaction increases as the concentration of reactant increases and vice versa.
Rate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∝</mo></mrow></math> Concentration of reactant
Example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Zinc </mtext></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Zulphuric acid </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
On increasing the conc. of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> the rate of evolution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> will increase.
Different reactants can affect the rate of a particular reaction to different extents.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mtext> Nitric oxide </mtext></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mtext> Nitrogen dioxide </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
(i) The rate of this reaction becomes double when concentration of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is doubled.
(ii) The rate of this reaction becomes four times or quadruples when the concentration of NO is doubled.
Reason : For a reaction to occur, the reactant molecules must collide with each other. The probability of such collisions increases with increase in concentration of reactants.Thus, more is the number of collisions taking place per unit volume, more will be the rate of reaction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> i.e </mtext><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> Rate of reaction </mtext><mo>∝</mo><mtext> [Reactants] </mtext></mrow></math>
## Rate Law and Rate Constant
The mathematical expression which denotes the experimentally observed rate of a reaction in terms of the concentrations of the reacting species which influence the rate of reaction is termed as rate law.
Consider a general reaction
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> Products </mtext></mrow></math>
Where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and C are the reactants and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> are stoichiometric coefficients of the balanced equation.
Rate of above reaction
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mtext> Rate </mtext><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>C</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msup><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>k</mi><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext> Rate constant </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
For example
Rate law expression :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>⟶</mi><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Rate </mtext><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Rate law expression according to law of mass action; Rate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Did You Know?
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are coefficients of reactants in reaction. It is not necessary that they represent true
powers of concentration of these reactants that should be determined experimentally.
If all the concentration of reactants are taken as unity i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> mole/litre then Rate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>; where rate is termed as the specific reaction rate and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is called as rate constant. Thus rate constant may be defined as the rate of reaction when the concentration of each reactant is taken as unity. Therefore, the rate constant is also referred as specific reaction rate.
## Order of a Reaction
Order of a reaction is an important parameter which is always determined experimentally. Let us consider a hypothetical reaction
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>X</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>Y</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>Z</mi><mo>→</mo><mtext> Product </mtext></mrow></math>
Where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> and Z are the reactants and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> are the stoichiometric coefficients. Rate law expression for this reaction based on the experimental determination is
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Rate </mtext><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>X</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>Y</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>Z</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is the rate constant and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math> are molar concentrations of the reactants <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> and Z respectively. The exponents <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> are the order with respect to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> and Z respectively.
The sum of exponents <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is known as the overall order of the reaction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Order of reaction </mtext><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>
These power or exponents ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ) have no relation with the stoichiometric coefficients <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> of reactants. Following examples illsutrate the order of reaction.

Thus the order of a reaction can be defined as the sum of the powers of the concentration terms, as expressed in rate law.
## Molecularity of a Reaction
The molecularity of a reaction is defined as the total number of molecules of the reactants taking part in a reaction, i.e., the molecularity represents the number of reactant molecules undergoing collisions to bring about the chemical reaction. Thus in the reaction,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><mtext> Product. </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mtext> Molecularity </mtext><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
The molecularity of the reaction may be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> etc. according to the participation of one, two or three reactant molecules in the reaction.

## (b) Effect of Temperature on Reaction Rate
Generally reactions take place much faster at a higher temperature. It means on increasing temperature rate of reaction increases.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Rate </mtext><mo>∝</mo><mtext> Temperature </mtext></mrow></math>
Reason : (i) As the temperature increases, the kinetic energy of the reactant molecules increases, hence, the number of collisions also increases.
(ii) At higher temperature the reactant molecules have greater chance of energy greater than the activation energy.
Note : Activation energy is the minimum amount of energy required to initiate the reaction.
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Calcium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> carbonate </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Hydrochloric </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> acid </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="1"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext> Calcium </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext> chloride </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mstyle></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
At 273 K the evolution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is very slow, but at 323 K the evolution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is rapid.
This graph shows that at higher temperature rate of evolution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is also high.
The reactants do not change directly in the products, reactants first absorb a certain amount of energy above the average potential energy of the reactants so that they overcome energy barrier between reactants and products. Thus this minimum amount of energy required to overcome this energy barrier between reactant and product is called activation energy ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ). For fast reactions, activation energies are low whereas for slow reactions, activation energies are high.
Activation energy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> [Threshold energy] - [Average energy of the reactants]
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>-Activation energy
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> - Threshold energy
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> - Average energy of reactant
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> - Energy of products
Note : The minimum amount of energy which the colliding reactant molecules must possess to react is known as threshold energy.

## More
- Effect of temperature on rate of reaction is observed for exothermic as well as for endothermic reactions. Reaction rate for most of the chemical reactions becomes almost double, for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> rise in temperature. This is expressed in terms of temperature coefficient.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Temperature coefficient </mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Rate constant at </mtext><mn>308</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Rate constant at </mtext><mn>298</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
So temperature coefficient may be defined as the ratio of the constants of the reaction at two temperature differing by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
- For some exceptional reactions, rate of reaction decreases with increase in temperature. For example rate of reaction between NO and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, decreases with increase in temperature.
- Effect of temperature on reaction rate depends upon the nature of reaction.
(i) For Most Reactions : As temperature increases rate of reaction increases uniformly. (Fig. 1)
(ii) For Explosive Reactions : Initially as temperature increases reaction rate increases. As explosion occurs there is sudden rise in reaction rate. (Fig. 2)
(iii) For Enzyme Catalysed Reactions : Initially as temperature increases reaction rate increases, reaches a maximum value and then it drops. Thus a bell shaped curve is obtained. (Fig. 3)

Thus, a catalyst can have both positive and negative effects on the rate of a chemical reaction.
(d) Effect of Light on Reaction Rate
Those chemical reactions which are carried in the presence of light are known as photochemical reactions. Examples :
(i) Plants in presence of sunlight produces glucose. This is known as photosynthesis.

(ii) Oxygen in the upper atmosphere absorbs U. V. radiations \& gets converted into ozone.

## (e) Effect of Surface Area
Rate of reaction is directly proportional to the surface area of the reactants. More will be the surface area, more will be the rate of reaction.

In this case, if metal is in powdered form then reaction would be more rapid than when taken in a ribbon form.
It is a common observation that small pieces of wood burn more rapidly than large logs of wood. This is due to the fact that the total surface area of the smaller particles is greater than that of large particles and this permits more molecules of the reactants to come in contact and form products.

Time to Check Your Knowledge
- What kitchen device is used to lower the rate at which microorganisms grow on food ?
examples.solution: Microorganisms, such as bread mold, are everywhere and difficult to avoid. Lowering the temperatures of microorganism contaminated food by using the refrigerator, decreases the rate of the chemical reactions necessary for the growth of microorganisms. This ultimately prevents decaying of food.

## 6 Chemical Kinetics
## Foundation
## (CONCEPT MAP )
## CLASSIFICATION OF CHEMICAL REACTIONS BASED ON THEIR SPEED
In a chemical reaction, the bonds present in the reactants are broken and new bonds are formed to give the products. The speed of bond formation and bond breaking in different reactions is different. Chemical kinetics tells about the rate of a reaction. Depending upon the rate of reaction, by which the reactants are converted into products, reactions are classified in three types.
## (a) Fast or Instantaneous Reactions
Those reactions in which the reactants readily change into products within few seconds are fast reactions. Ionic reactions are fast reactions.
## Example :
Acid-base reactions complete in a fraction of second, e.g. Neutralisation of sodium hydroxide by hydrochloric acid.

## ELECTROCHEMISTRY
Electrochemistry deals with the study of electrical properties of solutions of electrolytes and with the interrelation of chemical phenomenon and electrical energy. It is the study of production of electricity from energy released during spontaneous chemical reactions and the use of electrical energy to bring about non-spontaneous chemical transformations.
Electricity has an important place in modern society. What constitutes an electric current? How does it flow? An electric current is a flow of particles (electrons) flowing through wires and components.
Substances which allow the electricity to pass through them are called conductors, whereas those which do not allow electricity to pass through them are called insulators.
Conductors are classified into two types based on the nature of decomposition: electronic and electrolytic.
Electronic conductors: The conductors which conduct electricity without causing decomposition of substance are electronic conductors. The flow of electricity is due to flow of electrons in the conductor.
Examples : Metals, graphite, and certain minerals.
Electrolytic conductors: The conductors which decompose when current is passed through them are electronic conductors. In these conductors flow of electricity is due to flow of ions.
Examples : Aqueous solutions of acids, bases, and salt or even fused salts.
Compounds which conduct electricity in solution or in the fused state are called electrolytes and those which do not conduct electricity are called non-electrolytes.
Aqueous solutions of electrolyte is a better conductor than fused electrolyte. Concentration of
free ions in aqueous solution is greater than in fused state, because an electrolyte dissociates to a greater extent in its aqueous solution than in fused state. Therefore, conductivity of aqueous solution of electrolyte is greater than that of fused electrolyte.
## ELECTROLYSIS
Electrolysis is the process of conduction of electricity through a chemical compound in an aqueous solutions or in the molten state accompanied by a chemical change. The process of electrolysis is carried out in an electrolytic cell.
An electrolytic cell has two electrodes immersed in a solution placed in a container. The electrode connected to the negative pole is called cathode and the one connected to the positive pole is called anode.
An aqueous solution of electrolyte contains both positive and negative ions. When electricity is passed, positive ions migrate towards the cathode and negative ions move towards the anode. A compound is converted into its respective elements at cathode by accepting electrons, and at anode by donating electrons.
## Properties of Electrolysis
(i) The phenomenon of electrolysis appears only at the electrodes.
(ii) The electrolyte as a whole remains neutral during the process of electrolysis as equal number of charges are neutralised at the electrodes.
(iii) The deposition of different ions at the electrodes takes place only when electricity passes.
(iv) If two or more positive and negative ions are present in the solution, the least active ion is discharged first at the respective electrode.
## Applications of Electrolysis
The process of electrolysis has various applications.

## CELLS
The process of eletrolysis requires chemical reaction to occur, which is carried out by using electrical energy. Similarly, electrical energy can also be generated by undergoing chemical reaction in an electrochemical cell.
Cell is a system or arrangement in which two electrodes are fitted in the same electrolyte or in two different electrolytes which are joined by a salt bridge. Cells are of two types :
(a) Electrolytic cell
(b) Galvanic or voltaic cell
## Electrolytic Cell
It is a device in which a non-spontaneous chemical reaction is carried out by using electricity or in which conversion of electrical energy into chemical energy is done.
## Galvanic or Voltaic Cell
It is a device in which chemical energy liberated during a chemical reaction is converted into electrical energy, i.e., electricity can be obtained with the help of oxidation and reduction reaction.
The chemical reaction responsible for production of electricity takes place in two separate compartments. Each compartment consists of a suitable electrolyte solution and a metallic conductor. The metallic conductor acts as an electrode. The compartments containing the electrode and the solution of the electrolyte are called half-cells. When the two compartments are connected by a salt bridge and electrodes are joined by a wire through galvanometer, the electricity begins to flow. This is the simple form of voltaic cell.

## Difference between Electrolytic Cell and Galvanic Cell
| Electrolytic cell | Galvanic cell |
| :--- | :--- |
| (i) Electrical energy is converted into chemical energy. | (i) Chemical energy is converted into electrical energy |
| (ii) Anode is positive electrode. Cathode is negative electrode. | (ii) Anode is negative electrode. Cathode is positive electrode. |
| (iii) Ions are discharged on both the electrodes. | (iii) Ions are discharged only on the cathode. |
| (iv) Both the electrodes can be fitted in the same compartment. | (iv) The electrodes are fitted in different compartments. |

## Applications of Electrochemical Series
(a) Reactivity of metals :
(i) Alkali metals and alkaline earth metals react with cold water and evolve hydrogen and readily dissolve in acids.
(ii) Metals like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, etc. do not react with cold water but react with steam to evolve hydrogen.
(iii) Metals like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, and Au which lie below hydrogen are less reactive and do not evolve hydrogen from water.
(b) Electropositive character of metals : Electropositive character of metals decreases from top to bottom.
(c) Displacement reactions : The metal having low SRP will displace the metal from its salt solution which has higher value of SRP.
(d) Reducing power of metals : Reducing nature decreases from top to bottom in the electrochemical series.
(e) Oxidizing nature of non-metals : Oxidizing nature increases from top to bottom in the electrochemical series.
(f) Products of electrolysis : The ion which is a stronger oxidizing agent is discharged first at cathode.
(g) Corrosion of metals : The corrosion tendency increases from top to bottom.
Platinum and gold do not occur in combined state unlike other metals. They do not possess
Did You Know! tendency to form positive ions due to the high negative value of oxidation potential. Hence, they occur in free state in nature.

## Important Points about this Series
(a) Metals near the top of the series are strongly electropositive (or weakly electronegative). They lose electrons readily to give cations.
(b) Weakly electronegative metals in the upper part can displace more electronegative metals below them from their salts. For example, iron displaces copper from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution, Cu displaces silver from silver salt solution, silver displaces gold from gold salt solution as in photography during gold toning process.
(c) Hydroxides of metals in the upper part of the series are strongly basic and their salts do not undergo hydrolysis. On the other hand, hydroxides of the metals in the lower part of the series are weakly basic and their salts undergo hydrolysis.
(d) Metals lying above hydrogen are easily rusted. Those situated below are not rusted.
(e) Metals above hydrogen displace hydrogen from dilute acids and water.
(f) Iron and other metals above it decompose steam and liberate hydrogen.
(g) Oxides of iron and other metals below it can be reduced easily.
(h) Oxides of manganese and other metals above it are reduced when heated in a current of hydrogen.
(i) Oxides of mercury and other metals below it are decomposed on heating.

## Secondary Cell
In these cells, electrode reactions can be reversed by an external electric energy source, i.e., these cells can be recharged by passing electric current in opposite direction. Common examples are lead storage battery and nickel-cadmium storage cell.
## Lead Storage Battery
It consists of a lead anode and a grid of lead packed with lead dioxide as cathode. A solution of sulphuric acid is used as an electrolyte.

## CORROSION
Corrosion is basically an electrochemical phenomenon. The rusting of iron, the tarnishing of silver, development of a green coating on copper and bronze are some of the examples of corrosion.
In corrosion, a metal is oxidised by loss of electrons to oxygen and forms metal oxide. Corrosion of iron (which is commonly known as rusting) occurs in presence of water and oxygen (air).
Chemically, rust is hydrated form of ferric oxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>.
## Electrochemical Theory of Rusting
According to this theory, flow of electric current between separate anode and cathode bars is the reason why corrosion occurs. The ferrous ions formed by action of moisture or water move through water and come at the surface of iron object where these are further oxidised to ferric state by atmospheric oxygen and constitute rust which is hydrated iron (III) oxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>→</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
## Factors Which Promote Corrosion
(a) More active metals are readily corroded.
(b) Presence of impurities in metals enhances the chances of corrosion. Pure metals do not corrode e.g. pure iron does not rust.
(c) Air and moisture accelerate corrosion. Presence of gases like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in air catalyses the process of corrosion. Iron when placed in vacuum does not rust.
(d) Corrosion (e.g. rusting of iron) takes place rapidly at bends, scratches, nicks and cuts in the metal.
(e) Electrolytes, if present, also increase the rate of corrosion.

## ELECTROCHEMISTRY
Electrochemistry deals with the study of electrical properties of solutions of electrolytes and with the interrelation of chemical phenomenon and electrical energy. It is the study of production of electricity from energy released during spontaneous chemical reactions and the use of electrical energy to bring about non-spontaneous chemical transformations.
Electricity has an important place in modern society. What constitutes an electric current? How does it flow? An electric current is a flow of particles (electrons) flowing through wires and components.
Substances which allow the electricity to pass through them are called conductors, whereas those which do not allow electricity to pass through them are called insulators.
Conductors are classified into two types based on the nature of decomposition: electronic and electrolytic.
Electronic conductors: The conductors which conduct electricity without causing decomposition of substance are electronic conductors. The flow of electricity is due to flow of electrons in the conductor.
Examples : Metals, graphite, and certain minerals.
Electrolytic conductors: The conductors which decompose when current is passed through them are electronic conductors. In these conductors flow of electricity is due to flow of ions.
Examples : Aqueous solutions of acids, bases, and salt or even fused salts.
Compounds which conduct electricity in solution or in the fused state are called electrolytes and those which do not conduct electricity are called non-electrolytes.
Aqueous solutions of electrolyte is a better conductor than fused electrolyte. Concentration of
free ions in aqueous solution is greater than in fused state, because an electrolyte dissociates to a greater extent in its aqueous solution than in fused state. Therefore, conductivity of aqueous solution of electrolyte is greater than that of fused electrolyte.

## ELECTROLYSIS
Electrolysis is the process of conduction of electricity through a chemical compound in an aqueous solutions or in the molten state accompanied by a chemical change. The process of electrolysis is carried out in an electrolytic cell.
An electrolytic cell has two electrodes immersed in a solution placed in a container. The electrode connected to the negative pole is called cathode and the one connected to the positive pole is called anode.
An aqueous solution of electrolyte contains both positive and negative ions. When electricity is passed, positive ions migrate towards the cathode and negative ions move towards the anode. A compound is converted into its respective elements at cathode by accepting electrons, and at anode by donating electrons.

## Properties of Electrolysis
(i) The phenomenon of electrolysis appears only at the electrodes.
(ii) The electrolyte as a whole remains neutral during the process of electrolysis as equal number of charges are neutralised at the electrodes.
(iii) The deposition of different ions at the electrodes takes place only when electricity passes.
(iv) If two or more positive and negative ions are present in the solution, the least active ion is discharged first at the respective electrode.

## Applications of Electrolysis
The process of electrolysis has various applications.

## Electroplating
The process of plating a thin layer of one metal over the other with the help of electric current is called electroplating.
For example, for nickel plating of steel articles, take an aqueous solution of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> as an electrolyte in an electrolytic container. The steel article to be electroplated is made the cathode ( - ) and a pure nickel plate is made the anode ( + ). When electric current is passed through the electrolytic solution, the following reactions take place-

## Eletro-Refining of Metals
The process of purifying metal by electrolysis is called electro refining. The impure metal is made the anode and a plate of the same pure metal is made the cathode. Aqueous solution of the metal salt is taken as an electrolyte.
For example, in the refining of copper, impure copper plates are made anodes and suspended between pure copper sheets acting as the cathode. Acidified copper sulphate solution is taken as an electrolyte.

## CELLS
The process of eletrolysis requires chemical reaction to occur, which is carried out by using electrical energy. Similarly, electrical energy can also be generated by undergoing chemical reaction in an electrochemical cell.
Cell is a system or arrangement in which two electrodes are fitted in the same electrolyte or in two different electrolytes which are joined by a salt bridge. Cells are of two types :
(a) Electrolytic cell
(b) Galvanic or voltaic cell

## Electrolytic Cell
It is a device in which a non-spontaneous chemical reaction is carried out by using electricity or in which conversion of electrical energy into chemical energy is done.

## Galvanic or Voltaic Cell
It is a device in which chemical energy liberated during a chemical reaction is converted into electrical energy, i.e., electricity can be obtained with the help of oxidation and reduction reaction.
The chemical reaction responsible for production of electricity takes place in two separate compartments. Each compartment consists of a suitable electrolyte solution and a metallic conductor. The metallic conductor acts as an electrode. The compartments containing the electrode and the solution of the electrolyte are called half-cells. When the two compartments are connected by a salt bridge and electrodes are joined by a wire through galvanometer, the electricity begins to flow. This is the simple form of voltaic cell.

theory_sections.markdown:
## Difference between Electrolytic Cell and Galvanic Cell
| Electrolytic cell | Galvanic cell |
| :--- | :--- |
| (i) Electrical energy is converted into chemical energy. | (i) Chemical energy is converted into electrical energy |
| (ii) Anode is positive electrode. Cathode is negative electrode. | (ii) Anode is negative electrode. Cathode is positive electrode. |
| (iii) Ions are discharged on both the electrodes. | (iii) Ions are discharged only on the cathode. |
| (iv) Both the electrodes can be fitted in the same compartment. | (iv) The electrodes are fitted in different compartments. |

## Cell Notation
By seeing the cell notation we can easily understand reactions undergoing in electrochemical cell. The first half of the notation represents anode reaction, whereas the second half represents cathode reaction.
In the notation, the anode or oxidation half cell is always written on the left. The cathode or reduction half cell is written on the right. The two electrodes are connected by means of a salt bridge, denoted by two vertical lines.
In a beaker take some salt water. Now place copper and zinc plates connected with wire to the positive and negative ends of LCD clock in the beaker. Note whether the clock functions or not. Repeat this process with distilled water and cold drink also. find which solution conducts electricity.

## ELECTRODE POTENTIAL
When a strip of metal is brought in contact with the solution containing its own ions, then the strip of metal gets positively charged or negatively charged and results into a potential difference developed between the metallic strip and its solution, which is known as electrode potential.

## Applications of Electrochemical Series
(a) Reactivity of metals :
(i) Alkali metals and alkaline earth metals react with cold water and evolve hydrogen and readily dissolve in acids.
(ii) Metals like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, etc. do not react with cold water but react with steam to evolve hydrogen.
(iii) Metals like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, and Au which lie below hydrogen are less reactive and do not evolve hydrogen from water.
(b) Electropositive character of metals : Electropositive character of metals decreases from top to bottom.
(c) Displacement reactions : The metal having low SRP will displace the metal from its salt solution which has higher value of SRP.
(d) Reducing power of metals : Reducing nature decreases from top to bottom in the electrochemical series.
(e) Oxidizing nature of non-metals : Oxidizing nature increases from top to bottom in the electrochemical series.
(f) Products of electrolysis : The ion which is a stronger oxidizing agent is discharged first at cathode.
(g) Corrosion of metals : The corrosion tendency increases from top to bottom.
Platinum and gold do not occur in combined state unlike other metals. They do not possess
Did You Know! tendency to form positive ions due to the high negative value of oxidation potential. Hence, they occur in free state in nature.

## Important Points about this Series
(a) Metals near the top of the series are strongly electropositive (or weakly electronegative). They lose electrons readily to give cations.
(b) Weakly electronegative metals in the upper part can displace more electronegative metals below them from their salts. For example, iron displaces copper from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution, Cu displaces silver from silver salt solution, silver displaces gold from gold salt solution as in photography during gold toning process.
(c) Hydroxides of metals in the upper part of the series are strongly basic and their salts do not undergo hydrolysis. On the other hand, hydroxides of the metals in the lower part of the series are weakly basic and their salts undergo hydrolysis.
(d) Metals lying above hydrogen are easily rusted. Those situated below are not rusted.
(e) Metals above hydrogen displace hydrogen from dilute acids and water.
(f) Iron and other metals above it decompose steam and liberate hydrogen.
(g) Oxides of iron and other metals below it can be reduced easily.
(h) Oxides of manganese and other metals above it are reduced when heated in a current of hydrogen.
(i) Oxides of mercury and other metals below it are decomposed on heating.

## Secondary Cell
In these cells, electrode reactions can be reversed by an external electric energy source, i.e., these cells can be recharged by passing electric current in opposite direction. Common examples are lead storage battery and nickel-cadmium storage cell.

## CORROSION
Corrosion is basically an electrochemical phenomenon. The rusting of iron, the tarnishing of silver, development of a green coating on copper and bronze are some of the examples of corrosion.
In corrosion, a metal is oxidised by loss of electrons to oxygen and forms metal oxide. Corrosion of iron (which is commonly known as rusting) occurs in presence of water and oxygen (air).
Chemically, rust is hydrated form of ferric oxide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>.

## Electrochemical Theory of Rusting
According to this theory, flow of electric current between separate anode and cathode bars is the reason why corrosion occurs. The ferrous ions formed by action of moisture or water move through water and come at the surface of iron object where these are further oxidised to ferric state by atmospheric oxygen and constitute rust which is hydrated iron (III) oxide.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>→</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

## Factors Which Promote Corrosion
(a) More active metals are readily corroded.
(b) Presence of impurities in metals enhances the chances of corrosion. Pure metals do not corrode e.g. pure iron does not rust.
(c) Air and moisture accelerate corrosion. Presence of gases like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in air catalyses the process of corrosion. Iron when placed in vacuum does not rust.
(d) Corrosion (e.g. rusting of iron) takes place rapidly at bends, scratches, nicks and cuts in the metal.
(e) Electrolytes, if present, also increase the rate of corrosion.

## Applications of Electrochemical Series
(a) Reactivity of metals :
(i) Alkali metals and alkaline earth metals react with cold water and evolve hydrogen and readily dissolve in acids.
(ii) Metals like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, etc. do not react with cold water but react with steam to evolve hydrogen.
(iii) Metals like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, and Au which lie below hydrogen are less reactive and do not evolve hydrogen from water.
(b) Electropositive character of metals : Electropositive character of metals decreases from top to bottom.
(c) Displacement reactions : The metal having low SRP will displace the metal from its salt solution which has higher value of SRP.
(d) Reducing power of metals : Reducing nature decreases from top to bottom in the electrochemical series.
(e) Oxidizing nature of non-metals : Oxidizing nature increases from top to bottom in the electrochemical series.
(f) Products of electrolysis : The ion which is a stronger oxidizing agent is discharged first at cathode.
(g) Corrosion of metals : The corrosion tendency increases from top to bottom.
Platinum and gold do not occur in combined state unlike other metals. They do not possess
Did You Know! tendency to form positive ions due to the high negative value of oxidation potential. Hence, they occur in free state in nature.

## Important Points about this Series
(a) Metals near the top of the series are strongly electropositive (or weakly electronegative). They lose electrons readily to give cations.
(b) Weakly electronegative metals in the upper part can displace more electronegative metals below them from their salts. For example, iron displaces copper from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution, Cu displaces silver from silver salt solution, silver displaces gold from gold salt solution as in photography during gold toning process.
(c) Hydroxides of metals in the upper part of the series are strongly basic and their salts do not undergo hydrolysis. On the other hand, hydroxides of the metals in the lower part of the series are weakly basic and their salts undergo hydrolysis.
(d) Metals lying above hydrogen are easily rusted. Those situated below are not rusted.
(e) Metals above hydrogen displace hydrogen from dilute acids and water.
(f) Iron and other metals above it decompose steam and liberate hydrogen.
(g) Oxides of iron and other metals below it can be reduced easily.
(h) Oxides of manganese and other metals above it are reduced when heated in a current of hydrogen.
(i) Oxides of mercury and other metals below it are decomposed on heating.

## Primary Cell

## Secondary Cell
In these cells, electrode reactions can be reversed by an external electric energy source, i.e., these cells can be recharged by passing electric current in opposite direction. Common examples are lead storage battery and nickel-cadmium storage cell.
## Lead Storage Battery
It consists of a lead anode and a grid of lead packed with lead dioxide as cathode. A solution of sulphuric acid is used as an electrolyte.
When the cell discharges, it operates as a voltaic cell.

## Fuel Cell
Galvanic cells that are designed to convert the energy of combustion of fuels like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> etc., directly into electrical energy are called fuel cells. Such a cell converts <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>70</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> of chemical energy into electrical energy. The fuel used is in the gaseous state; <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> fuel cell is a common example.

key_points.text: The phenomenon of electrolysis appears only at the electrodes.
The electrolyte as a whole remains neutral during the process of electrolysis as equal number of charges are neutralised at the electrodes.
The deposition of different ions at the electrodes takes place only when electricity passes.
If two or more positive and negative ions are present in the solution, the least active ion is discharged first at the respective electrode.

Reactivity of metals :
Alkali metals and alkaline earth metals react with cold water and evolve hydrogen and readily dissolve in acids.

Metals like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, etc. do not react with cold water but react with steam to evolve hydrogen.

Metals like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, and Au which lie below hydrogen are less reactive and do not evolve hydrogen from water.
Electropositive character of metals : Electropositive character of metals decreases from top to bottom.
Displacement reactions : The metal having low SRP will displace the metal from its salt solution which has higher value of SRP.
Reducing power of metals : Reducing nature decreases from top to bottom in the electrochemical series.

## Applications of Electrochemical Series
(a) Reactivity of metals :
(i) Alkali metals and alkaline earth metals react with cold water and evolve hydrogen and readily dissolve in acids.
(ii) Metals like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, etc. do not react with cold water but react with steam to evolve hydrogen.
(iii) Metals like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, and Au which lie below hydrogen are less reactive and do not evolve hydrogen from water.
(b) Electropositive character of metals : Electropositive character of metals decreases from top to bottom.
(c) Displacement reactions : The metal having low SRP will displace the metal from its salt solution which has higher value of SRP.
(d) Reducing power of metals : Reducing nature decreases from top to bottom in the electrochemical series.
(e) Oxidizing nature of non-metals : Oxidizing nature increases from top to bottom in the electrochemical series.
(f) Products of electrolysis : The ion which is a stronger oxidizing agent is discharged first at cathode.
(g) Corrosion of metals : The corrosion tendency increases from top to bottom.
Platinum and gold do not occur in combined state unlike other metals. They do not possess
Did You Know! tendency to form positive ions due to the high negative value of oxidation potential. Hence, they occur in free state in nature.
