## Important Points about this Series
(a) Metals near the top of the series are strongly electropositive (or weakly electronegative). They lose electrons readily to give cations.
(b) Weakly electronegative metals in the upper part can displace more electronegative metals below them from their salts. For example, iron displaces copper from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution, Cu displaces silver from silver salt solution, silver displaces gold from gold salt solution as in photography during gold toning process.
(c) Hydroxides of metals in the upper part of the series are strongly basic and their salts do not undergo hydrolysis. On the other hand, hydroxides of the metals in the lower part of the series are weakly basic and their salts undergo hydrolysis.
(d) Metals lying above hydrogen are easily rusted. Those situated below are not rusted.
(e) Metals above hydrogen displace hydrogen from dilute acids and water.
(f) Iron and other metals above it decompose steam and liberate hydrogen.
(g) Oxides of iron and other metals below it can be reduced easily.
(h) Oxides of manganese and other metals above it are reduced when heated in a current of hydrogen.
(i) Oxides of mercury and other metals below it are decomposed on heating.

## Primary Cell
The most familiar type of battery is the dry cell which is a compact form of Leclanche cell (fig.) known after its discoverer, Leclanche.

## Secondary Cell
In these cells, electrode reactions can be reversed by an external electric energy source, i.e., these cells can be recharged by passing electric current in opposite direction. Common examples are lead storage battery and nickel-cadmium storage cell.
## Lead Storage Battery
It consists of a lead anode and a grid of lead packed with lead dioxide as cathode. A solution of sulphuric acid is used as an electrolyte.
When the cell discharges, it operates as a voltaic cell.

Another secondary cell is the nickel-cadmium storage cell which has a longer life than the lead storage cell.

## Fuel Cell
Galvanic cells that are designed to convert the energy of combustion of fuels like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> etc., directly into electrical energy are called fuel cells. Such a cell converts <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>70</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> of chemical energy into electrical energy. The fuel used is in the gaseous state; <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> fuel cell is a common example.

## IUPAC NOMENCLATURE
According to IUPAC system, the name of an organic compound consists of three parts :
(a) Root word
(b) Suffix
(c) Prefix
## Root word
Word root denotes the number of carbon atoms present in the principal chain which is the longest possible chain of carbon atoms. However, from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> common names have been retained.

## Suffix
The root word is linked to the suffix which can be primary or secondary or both.
## (a) Primary suffix
A primary suffix indicates the type of linkage in the carbon atoms. If the carbon atoms are linked by single covalent bonds, the primary suffix is 'ane'. If these are linked by double and triple bonds, the primary suffixes 'ene' and 'yne' are respectively used to represent them. Thus,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mtext> ane : primary suffix for </mtext><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi><mtext> bond </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mtext> ene : primary suffix for </mtext><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mtext> bond </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mtext> yne : primary suffix for </mtext><mi>C</mi><mo>≡</mo><mi>C</mi><mtext> bond </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
If the parent chain of carbon atoms contains more than one double or triple bonds, numerical prefixes like di (for two), tri (for three), tetra (for four) etc. are added to primary suffix.

## Rules for IUPAC Nomenclature of Organic Compounds
There are certain (following) rules for naming a complex organic molecule according to IUPAC system. These rules are illustrated below.
(a) Longest chain rule : The first step for naming an organic compound is to select the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms which may or may not be horizontal (straight). This is called the parent chain or main chain, and other carbon chains attached to it are known as side chains. On the basis of the number of carbon atoms present in the parent chain, the parent hydrocarbon is ascertained. For example, if the parent chain contains six carbon atoms, the compound is considered to be a derivative of hexane.
For example : The structure I has the longest chain of six carbon atoms present in a straight line; therefore it is said to be a derivative of hexane. On the other hand, in structutre II the straight chain has only four or three carbon atoms, while the longest possible chain may have as many as six carbon atoms (zig-zag chain).
I
Longest chain, straight
II
Longest chain, zig-zag
Therefore, both the structures are derivatives of hexane.
In case a molecule contains two equally long carbon chains, the one carrying larger number of side chains is selected. For example, structures A and B have carbon chains of equal lengths <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, but the one carrying three substituents is selected.
(A)
Straight parent chain of C7 (correct) with three side chains
(B)
Zig-zag parent chain of C7 (incorrect) with only one side chain

## (m) Amines
Amines can be regarded as derived from ammonia by the replacement of one, two or three hydrogen atoms by the corresponding number of alkyl groups. Amines are of three types depending upon the number of alkyl groups attached to nitrogen.
(i) Primary amines : These are monoalkyl derivatives of ammonia.
(ii) Secondary amines : These are dialkyl derivatives of ammonia.
(iii) Tertiary amines : These are trialkyl derivatives of ammonia.

Rules for nomenclature of poly functional organic compounds:
(i) If the organic compound contains two or more functional groups, one of the group is selected as principal functional group containing longest possible chain of carbon atoms and all the remaining functional groups are treated as substituents.

## ISOMERISM
In the study of organic chemistry we come across many cases when two or more compounds are made of equal number of like atoms. A molecular formula does not tell the nature of organic compound, sometimes several organic compounds may have same molecular formula. These compounds possess the same molecular formula but differ from each other in physical or chemical properties, and called as isomers and the phenomenon is termed isomerism proposed by Berzelius (Greek, iso <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> equal ; meros <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> parts). Since isomers have the same molecular formula, the difference in their properties must be due to different modes of the combination or arrangement of atoms within the molecule. Broadly speaking, isomerism is of two types.
(i) Structural isomerism
(ii) Stereoisomerism

## Structural Isomerism (Constitutional Isomerism)
Structural isomers possess the same molecular formula but different arrangement of atoms or groups within the molecules. The phenomenon is called structural isomerism.
The term constitutional isomerism is a more modern term of structural isomerism. It arises
Did You Know! because of the difference in the sequence of covalently bonded atoms in the molecule without reference to space.
## Types of Structural Isomerism :
(a) Chain / nuclear / skeleton isomerism :
This type of isomerism arises from the difference in the structure of carbon chain which forms the nucleus of the molecules. Here isomers have same molecular formula but different arrangement of carbon chain. e.g.
Chain isomerism is observed when the number of carbon atoms is four or more than four in an organic compound. Chain isomer differ in the nature of carbon chain, i.e., in the length of the carbon chain.
- The isomer showing chain isomerism belong to the same homologous series, i.e., functional group, class of the compound (cyclic or open) remains unchanged.

## IUPAC NOMENCLATURE
According to IUPAC system, the name of an organic compound consists of three parts :
(a) Root word
(b) Suffix
(c) Prefix

## Root word
Word root denotes the number of carbon atoms present in the principal chain which is the longest possible chain of carbon atoms. However, from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> common names have been retained.

## Suffix
The root word is linked to the suffix which can be primary or secondary or both.

## (a) Primary suffix
A primary suffix indicates the type of linkage in the carbon atoms. If the carbon atoms are linked by single covalent bonds, the primary suffix is 'ane'. If these are linked by double and triple bonds, the primary suffixes 'ene' and 'yne' are respectively used to represent them. Thus,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mtext> ane : primary suffix for </mtext><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi><mtext> bond </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mtext> ene : primary suffix for </mtext><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mtext> bond </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mtext> yne : primary suffix for </mtext><mi>C</mi><mo>≡</mo><mi>C</mi><mtext> bond </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
If the parent chain of carbon atoms contains more than one double or triple bonds, numerical prefixes like di (for two), tri (for three), tetra (for four) etc. are added to primary suffix.

theory_sections.markdown:
## Rules for IUPAC Nomenclature of Organic Compounds
There are certain (following) rules for naming a complex organic molecule according to IUPAC system. These rules are illustrated below.
(a) Longest chain rule : The first step for naming an organic compound is to select the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms which may or may not be horizontal (straight). This is called the parent chain or main chain, and other carbon chains attached to it are known as side chains. On the basis of the number of carbon atoms present in the parent chain, the parent hydrocarbon is ascertained. For example, if the parent chain contains six carbon atoms, the compound is considered to be a derivative of hexane.
For example : The structure I has the longest chain of six carbon atoms present in a straight line; therefore it is said to be a derivative of hexane. On the other hand, in structutre II the straight chain has only four or three carbon atoms, while the longest possible chain may have as many as six carbon atoms (zig-zag chain).
I
Longest chain, straight
II
Longest chain, zig-zag
Therefore, both the structures are derivatives of hexane.
In case a molecule contains two equally long carbon chains, the one carrying larger number of side chains is selected. For example, structures A and B have carbon chains of equal lengths <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, but the one carrying three substituents is selected.
(A)
Straight parent chain of C7 (correct) with three side chains
(B)
Zig-zag parent chain of C7 (incorrect) with only one side chain

## NOMENCLATURE OF DIFFERENT CLASSES OF ORGANIC COMPOUNDS
The names of various homologous series and their simple members are given below.

## (a) Alkanes or Paraffins (Saturated Hydrocarbons):
These are such compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen atoms. The various carbon atoms present in the molecule are linked by single covalent bonds ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ). These are represented by the general formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. The IUPAC name for this homologous series is alkanes and the names of all alkanes will be ending with the suffix -ane. The common and IUPAC names for the first few members are identical.

| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | Methane | Methane |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | Ethane | Ethane |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | Propane | Propane |

## (c) Alkynes or Acetylenic Hydrocarbons
These are characterised by the presence of a triple bond between two carbon atoms, and contain four hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkanes. Their names are derived from the corresponding alkanes by substituting the suffix -ane by -yne.

## (d) Halogen Derivatives
These are derived from alkanes by the replacement of one or more hydrogen atoms by halogen atoms <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, or I). They are thus further classified as mono-, di-, tri-, or tetra-halogen derivatives when they contain 1,2 , 3 or 4 halogen atoms respectively in their molecules.
(i) Mono-halogen derivatives or alkyl halides : These are monohalogen derivatives of the alkanes.
General foumula : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>, where R stands for an alkyl radical and X for a halogen atom.
Common names of alkyl halides are derived from the alkyl radical, while in IUPAC system these are named as substituted alkanes.

## (f) Ethers
These are derived from alkanes by the replacement of one hydrogen atom by an alkoxy group (-OR).
When the two alkyl groups on either side of oxygen ( O ) are same, the ether is called as simple or symmetrical ether; and when they are different, it is called mixed or unsymmetrical ether. Thus
General formula :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Simple ether
Mixed ether
Functional group : -O-
The IUPAC (systematic) name for ethers is alkoxyalkanes.

## (g) Thio-alcohols, Thiols, Mercaptans or Alkanethiols
Thioalcohols are derived by replacing O (oxygen) atom of alcohol by S (sulphur) atom.
General formula: R-SH
Characteristic group: -SH (mercapto or thiol group)
The secondary suffix used for thio alcohols or mercaptans in IUPAC system is thiol (in place of -ol used in alcohols), while the common names are obtained by adding thio alcohol to the name of the alkyl group.

## (i) Aldehydes or Alkanals
These are derived from alkanes by the replacement of one hydrogen atom by aldehydic (- CHO ) group.

## (j) Ketones or Alkanones
These are derived by replacing two hydrogen atoms from two molecules of alkanes by a divalent ketonic ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> ) group.
General formula : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>
Characteristic group : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
The two alkyl groups of a ketone may be similar (simple ketones) or different (mixed ketones).
The IUPAC names (alkanones) are derived by replacing terminal ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> ' of the alkane by 'one'. The position of the CO group is indicated by placing the number of the carbon atom to which oxygen is attached at the end. For example,

The prefix 2 or 3, indicates the position of the functional group carbon atom which must always get the lowest possible number.
(k) Carboxylic Acids

Functional group : - COOH

## (m) Amines
Amines can be regarded as derived from ammonia by the replacement of one, two or three hydrogen atoms by the corresponding number of alkyl groups. Amines are of three types depending upon the number of alkyl groups attached to nitrogen.
(i) Primary amines : These are monoalkyl derivatives of ammonia.
(ii) Secondary amines : These are dialkyl derivatives of ammonia.
(iii) Tertiary amines : These are trialkyl derivatives of ammonia.
| Types of amine | General formula | Functional group |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Primary amine | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> |
| Secondary amine | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> |
| Tertiary amine | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>↘</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>↗</mo></mrow></mfrac><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> |
Common names of amines are derived according to the alkyl group (s) attached to the nitrogen
atom and adding the suffix amine.
The systematic (IUPAC) names for primary, secondary and tertiary amines are alkanamine, alkylalkanamine, and dialkylalkanamine respectively.
| Formula | Type of amine | Common name | IUPAC name |

Rules for nomenclature of poly functional organic compounds:
(i) If the organic compound contains two or more functional groups, one of the group is selected as principal functional group containing longest possible chain of carbon atoms and all the remaining functional groups are treated as substituents.

## ISOMERISM
In the study of organic chemistry we come across many cases when two or more compounds are made of equal number of like atoms. A molecular formula does not tell the nature of organic compound, sometimes several organic compounds may have same molecular formula. These compounds possess the same molecular formula but differ from each other in physical or chemical properties, and called as isomers and the phenomenon is termed isomerism proposed by Berzelius (Greek, iso <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> equal ; meros <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> parts). Since isomers have the same molecular formula, the difference in their properties must be due to different modes of the combination or arrangement of atoms within the molecule. Broadly speaking, isomerism is of two types.
(i) Structural isomerism
(ii) Stereoisomerism
The following figure shows the pictorial representation of different types of isomerism

## Structural Isomerism (Constitutional Isomerism)
Structural isomers possess the same molecular formula but different arrangement of atoms or groups within the molecules. The phenomenon is called structural isomerism.
The term constitutional isomerism is a more modern term of structural isomerism. It arises
Did You Know! because of the difference in the sequence of covalently bonded atoms in the molecule without reference to space.

## Types of Structural Isomerism :
(a) Chain / nuclear / skeleton isomerism :
This type of isomerism arises from the difference in the structure of carbon chain which forms the nucleus of the molecules. Here isomers have same molecular formula but different arrangement of carbon chain. e.g.
Chain isomerism is observed when the number of carbon atoms is four or more than four in an organic compound. Chain isomer differ in the nature of carbon chain, i.e., in the length of the carbon chain.
- The isomer showing chain isomerism belong to the same homologous series, i.e., functional group, class of the compound (cyclic or open) remains unchanged.

## (m) Amines
Amines can be regarded as derived from ammonia by the replacement of one, two or three hydrogen atoms by the corresponding number of alkyl groups. Amines are of three types depending upon the number of alkyl groups attached to nitrogen.
(i) Primary amines : These are monoalkyl derivatives of ammonia.
(ii) Secondary amines : These are dialkyl derivatives of ammonia.
(iii) Tertiary amines : These are trialkyl derivatives of ammonia.

In the trivial (common) system these are named as alkyl isocyanides or alkyl isonitriles; while in the systematic names, the word carbylamine is added to the name of the alkyl radical.
| Formula | Common name | IUPAC name |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> | Methyl isocyanide | Methyl carbylamine |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> | Ethyl isocyanide | Ethyl carbylamine |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> | Butyl isocyanide | Butyl carbylamine |
## (p) Nitroalkanes or Nitroparaffins
These may be regarded as derived from alkanes by the replacement of a hydrogen atom by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (nitro) group.
General formula : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Functional group : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><msub><mo>↘</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
The common and systematic names are generally the same.
They are named by adding the prefix nitro before the name of the corresponding alkane, e.g.
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | Nitromethane |
| :--- | :--- |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | Nitroethane |
## (q) Alkyl Nitrites
These are derived from alkanes by the replacement of a hydrogen atom by nitrite ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> ) group.
General formula : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
Functional group : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
The common and IUPAC names are same. These are named by adding the suffix nitrite to the name of the alkyl group, e.g.
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> | Methyl nitrite |
| :--- | :--- |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>-Propyl nitrite |

(e) Tautomerism : This isomerism is due to spontaneous intreconversion of two isomeric forms with different functional groups. The prerequisites for this is the presence of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> in the usual cases and an alpha H atom. The most usual is the 'keto-enol' tautomerism, but there can be other like nitro-aci and amine-imine forms. In general the keto form is more stable. Enols can be formed by acid or base catalysis from the ketone and are extensively used in making <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> single bonds in organic synthesis.

Longest chain rule : The first step for naming an organic compound is to select the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms which may or may not be horizontal (straight). This is called the parent chain or main chain, and other carbon chains attached to it are known as side chains. On the basis of the number of carbon atoms present in the parent chain, the parent hydrocarbon is ascertained. For example, if the parent chain contains six carbon atoms, the compound is considered to be a derivative of hexane.

Lowest number or lowest sum rule : The carbon atom of longest carbon chain is numbered as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi></mrow></math> etc., starting from the end that gives the lowest possible number to the substituent. For example, in structures A and B numbering may be done in two ways;

Naming of simple alkanes : The name of the substituent is prefixed to the name of the parent hydrocarbon and its position on the main chain is indicated by writing the locant before the prefix. A hyphen ( - ) is inserted between the locant and the substituent name. The final name is always written as one word. Thus the following compound is written as 2-Methylpentane.

These are derived from alkanes by the replacement of one hydrogen atom by an alkoxy group (-OR).

Thioalcohols are derived by replacing O (oxygen) atom of alcohol by S (sulphur) atom.

Characteristic group: -SH (mercapto or thiol group)
The secondary suffix used for thio alcohols or mercaptans in IUPAC system is thiol (in place of -ol used in alcohols), while the common names are obtained by adding thio alcohol to the name of the alkyl group.

## (j) Ketones or Alkanones
These are derived by replacing two hydrogen atoms from two molecules of alkanes by a divalent ketonic ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> ) group.
General formula : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>
Characteristic group : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
The two alkyl groups of a ketone may be similar (simple ketones) or different (mixed ketones).
The IUPAC names (alkanones) are derived by replacing terminal ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> ' of the alkane by 'one'. (ii) Acid amides : These are derived by the replacement of -OH part of the -COOH group by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> General formula </mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>:</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mtext> or </mtext><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Functional group </mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>:</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math>

| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> (Acetic acid or Ethanoic acid) | Acetamide | Ethanamide |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> (Propionic acid or Propanoic acid) | Propionamide | Propanamide |
(iii) Acid anhydrides : These are considered to be derived from two (similar or different) carboxylic acid molecules by the elimination of a molecule of water.
The common names of acid anhydrides are derived from the name of the parent acid or acids; while the systematic names are obtained by replacing 'acid' from the name of the acid by 'anhydride', e.g.,

| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math> | (Ethanoic acid) | | |

## (m) Amines
Amines can be regarded as derived from ammonia by the replacement of one, two or three hydrogen atoms by the corresponding number of alkyl groups. Amines are of three types depending upon the number of alkyl groups attached to nitrogen.
(i) Primary amines : These are monoalkyl derivatives of ammonia.
(ii) Secondary amines : These are dialkyl derivatives of ammonia.
(iii) Tertiary amines : These are trialkyl derivatives of ammonia.
| Types of amine | General formula | Functional group |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Primary amine | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> |
| Secondary amine | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> |
| Tertiary amine | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>↘</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>↗</mo></mrow></mfrac><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> |
Common names of amines are derived according to the alkyl group (s) attached to the nitrogen
atom and adding the suffix amine.
The systematic (IUPAC) names for primary, secondary and tertiary amines are alkanamine, alkylalkanamine, and dialkylalkanamine respectively.

| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | Primary | Ethyl amine | Ethanamine |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | Secondary | Dimethyl amine (N-Methyl methyl amine) | Methylmethanamine |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | Secondary | Ethyl methyl amine ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo></mrow></math> Methyl ethyl amine) | N -Methylethanamine |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow></mrow></math> | Tertiary | Trimethyl amine (N, N-Dimethyl methyl amine) | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>-Dimethylmethanamine |

## (n) Alkyl Cyanides, or Carbonitriles
These are derived by replacing a hydrogen atom of the alkanes or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> group of the acid by nitrile (-CN) group.
General forumula : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Functional group : -CN or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>≡</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>
Their common names are obtained by adding suffix cyanide to the alkyl group or by replacing - ic acid from the name of the corresponding acid by the suffix onitrile, while systematic names are derived by adding suffix nitrile to the parent alkane, e.g.

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| HCN | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | Hydrogen cyanide | Methanenitrile |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow></mrow></math> | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | Methyl cyanide or Acetonitrile | Ethanenitrile |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow></mrow></math> | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | Propyl cyanide or Propiononitrile | Butanenitrile |
Did You Know!
While counting number of carbon atom in parent chain the carbon atom present in -CN group is also taken into consideration.
## (o) Alkyl Isocyanides, Isonitriles, Carbylamines
These may be derived by replacing a hydrogen atom of alkanes or a -COOH group of carboxylic acid by isonitrile (-NC) group. Thus
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> General formula </mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>:</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mtext> or </mtext><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Functional group </mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>:</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi><mover><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>→</mo></mrow></mover><mtext> or </mtext><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math>
In the trivial (common) system these are named as alkyl isocyanides or alkyl isonitriles; while in the systematic names, the word carbylamine is added to the name of the alkyl radical.
| Formula | Common name | IUPAC name |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> | Methyl isocyanide | Methyl carbylamine |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> | Ethyl isocyanide | Ethyl carbylamine |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> | Butyl isocyanide | Butyl carbylamine |
## (p) Nitroalkanes or Nitroparaffins
These may be regarded as derived from alkanes by the replacement of a hydrogen atom by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (nitro) group.
General formula : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Functional group : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><msub><mo>↘</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
The common and systematic names are generally the same.
They are named by adding the prefix nitro before the name of the corresponding alkane, e.g.
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | Nitromethane |
| :--- | :--- |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> | Nitroethane |
## (q) Alkyl Nitrites
These are derived from alkanes by the replacement of a hydrogen atom by nitrite ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> ) group.
General formula : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
Functional group : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
The common and IUPAC names are same. These are named by adding the suffix nitrite to the name of the alkyl group, e.g.
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> | Methyl nitrite |
| :--- | :--- |
| <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> | <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>-Propyl nitrite |

## 9. Organic Compounds
Foundation
## (CONCEPTMAP)
## ALKANES
Alkanes or saturated hydrocarbons are those in which all the four valencies of carbon atom(s) are satisfied by four atoms or groups i.e. the carbon valencies are fully satisfied. These compounds contain only <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></math> types of covalent bonds. Since they are relatively inert towards most of the chemical reagents under ordinary conditions, they are called paraffins (Latin-parum, little; affinis-affinity). The IUPAC name for these compounds is alkanes. Their general formula is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Alkanes are quite stable compounds and give substitution reactions while alkenes and alkynes are more reactive and generally give addition reactions.

(a) Alkanes from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are colourless, odourless gases. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are colourless liquids, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>18</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo></mrow></math> onwards are waxy, white solids.
## (b) Boiling points
Boiling points of alkanes are lowest of all the groups of organic compounds. The forces of attraction among alkane molecules are weakest van der Waal's forces of attraction. With the increase in the number of carbon chain length (molecular size), the magnitude of van der Waal's forces also increases.
Among isomeric alkanes, boiling point decreases with increasing branching.
Example : n-Pentane > iso-Pentane > neo-Pentane
## (c) Melting point
The melting point of alkanes does not show regular variation with increase in molecular size. Unbranched alkanes containing 2, 4, 6, 8 etc. carbon atoms have higher melting points than the unbranched alkanes containing 3, 5, 7, 9 etc. carbon atoms respectively.

Alkenes are those unsaturated hydrocarbons which contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond in their molecules. Their general formula is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and hence they contain two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkane and hence designated as unsaturated hydrocarbon having general formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. The process in which simple molecules combine together to form large molecule is called polymerisation; the starting simple molecule is called a monomer while the larger molecule (final product) is called a polymer. ## (b) Ozonolysis
Addition of ozone to an unsaturated hydrocarbon, forms an intermediate called ozonide, which on further hydrolysis in the presence of zinc dust gives corresponding carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and ketones). This reaction is used to identify and locate the position of multiple bonds in an unsaturated hydrocarbon.
For example, ethene on such reaction gives two molecules of formaldehyde.

## Physical Properties of Alkynes
(a) Alkynes are colourless, odourless and tasteless.
(b) Lower alkynes are partially soluble in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>.
(c) Higher alkynes are insoluble in water while completely soluble in organic solvents.
(d) Melting point and boiling point are directly proportional to molecular mass and inversely proportional to number of branches.
(e) Upto <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, alkynes are gaseous, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are liquids, while <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> \& above are solids.
(f) Acetylene \& 1 - alkynes are acidic in nature. It is due to presence of active H .
(g) Oxyacetylene flame is used for cutting and welding metals.
Order of solubility, density, B.P., M.P. and acidic nature of above hydrocarbons is :
Alkyne > Alkene > Alkane
All terminal alkynes are acidic in nature.

## ALKYL HALIDES
Alkyl halides (haloalkanes) are those compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms in an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms.
Halogen derivatives of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes are known as alkyl halides (haloalkanes), alkenyl halides (haloalkenes) and alkynyl halides (haloalkynes) respectively.
On the basis of the number of halogen atom, alkyl halides are further classified as mono-, di-, tri-,
Did You Know? poly- and per-halohydrocarbons. The word perhalohydrocarbon means all the hydrogen atoms of the hydrocarbon are replaced by corresponding number of halogen atoms.

Alkyl halide when heated with alcoholic KOH solution, a molecule of hydrogen halide is eliminated and alkenes are formed. Generally <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>β</mi></mrow></math>-carbon (the carbon atom next to the carbon carrying the halogen) is eliminated during the reaction. In case of unsymmetrical alkyl halide there is the possibility of formation of two products. The more substituted alkene will be formed as a major product. This phenomenon was explained by Saytzeff, so its called Saytzeff's rule.

Alcohols are classified according to number of hydroxyl groups present in the molecule. Alcohols with one, two and three hydroxyl groups are called monohydric, dihydric \& trihydric alcohols respectively. Alcohols which contain four or more hydroxyl groups are called polyhydric alcohols.

## ETHERS
Ethers are a class of compounds which contain an oxygen atom bonded to two alkyl groups (same or different). When both the alkyl groups are same they are designated as simple or symmetrical ethers and when both are different, they are called mixed or unsymmetrical ethers.

## Physical Properties of Ethers
(a) The first two members, i.e., dimethyl ether and methylethyl ether are gases; while all others are colourless, volatile pleasant smelling liquids. Among aromatic ethers anisole <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and phenetole <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> are liquids; diphenyl ether is solid at room temperature.
(b) Lower ethers are highly volatile and inflammable and also act as anaesthetics.
(c) They are sparingly soluble in water, but readily soluble in organic solvents such as benzene, chloroform, etc.
## Chemical Properties of Ethers
(a) Properties due to alkyl groups
(i) Halogenation : When ethers are treated with chlorine or bromine in dark, substitution reaction occurs at the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math>-carbon atom. The extent of substitution depends upon the reaction conditions.
(ii) Combustion : Since ethers are volatile and highly inflammable, they burn in air to form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and water.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>4</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
## (b) Properties due to ethereal oxygen
(i) Chemical inertness : Since ethers do not have any active group in their molecules, so they do not react with active metals like Na , strong bases like NaOH , reducing or oxidising agents.
(ii) Basic nature : Owing to the presence of unshared electron pairs on oxygen, ethers behave as Lewis bases. Hence they dissolve in strong acids (e.g., conc. HCl , conc. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) at low temperature to form oxonium salts.
Dialkyloxonium chloride

(i) Hydrolysis : Ethers, when heated with dilute sulphuric acid under pressure are hydrolysed to the corresponding alcohols.

(ii) Action of conc. sulphuric acid : On heating with concentrated sulphuric acid, ethers are converted to alkyl hydrogen sulphates.

## Uses of Ethers
(a) The most important use of ethers is a laboratory and industrial solvent (for oils, resins, gums, etc.)
(b) Ether is used as an anaesthic in surgery.

(d) By ozonolysis of ethylene
Ethylene is dissolved in an organic solvent such as chloroform or carbon tetrachloride and a stream of ozonised oxygen is passed. The ozonide formed is decomposed by passing hydrogen in presence of palladium as catalyst.
In the above reaction methanal can also be obtained by hydrolysis of ozonide in presence of zinc.

## Physical Properties of Methanal
(a) It is a colourless, pungent smelling gas.
(b) It is extremely soluble in water.
(c) It can easily be condensed into liquid. The liquid formaldehyde boils at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>21</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
(d) It causes irritation to skin, eyes, nose and throat.
(e) Its solution acts as antiseptic and disinfectant.

## Uses of Methanal
(a) The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>40</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> solution of formaldehyde (formalin) is used as disinfectant, germicide and antiseptic. It is used for the preservation of biological specimens.
(b) It is used in the preparation of hexamethylene tetramine (urotropine) which is used as an antiseptic and germicide.
(c) It is used in silvering of mirror.
(d) It is employed in the manufacture of synthetic dyes such as para-rosaniline, indigo, etc.
(e) It is used in the manufacture of forma mint (by mixing formaldehyde with lactose) - a throat lozenges.
(f) It is used for making synthetic plastics like bakelite, urea-formaldehyde resin, etc.

## Uses of Acetone
(a) As a solvent for cellulose acetate, cellulose nitrate, celluloid, lacquers, resins, etc.
(b) For storing acetylene.
(c) In the manufacture of cordite - a smokeless powder explosive.
(d) In the preparation of chloroform, iodoform, sulphonal and chloretone.
(e) As a nailpolish remover.
(f) In the preparation of an artificial scent (ionone), plexiglass (unbreakable glass) and synthetic rubber.

## CARBOXYLIC ACIDS
The compounds containing the carboxyl functional group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are called carboxylic acids. The word carboxyl is a combination of two words carbonyl ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> ) and hydroxyl ( -OH ).
## Classification of Carboxylic Acids
Depending upon the number of -COOH groups, they are classified as (i) monocarboxylic acids: containing one -COOH group (ii) dicarboxylic acids-containing two -COOH groups and so on.
Fatty acids: Aliphatic monocarboxylic acids are commonly called fatty acids because higher members are obtained by the hydrolysis of oils and fats.
## Isomerism in Carboxylic Acids
They exhibit following type of isomerism.
(a) Position and chain isomerism
e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> represents
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> 1-Hexanoic acid </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> 2-Methylpentanoic acid </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> 2-Ethylbutanoic acid </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> Position isomers
4-Methylpentanoic acid and 1-hexanoic acid are chain isomers
(b) Functional isomerism

Compounds derived from hydrocarbons by the replacement of one or more hydrogen atom(s) by the halogen atoms(s) are known as halogen derivatives. The halogen derivatives of alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and arenes are known as alkyl halides (haloalkanes), alkenyl halides (haloalkenes), alkynyl halides (haloalkynes), aryl halides (haloarenes) respectively. Halogen derivatives may be classified depending upon the number of the halogen atom. Thus halogen derivatives of alkanes may be monohalogen derivatives, dihalogen derivatives, tri- and tetra-halogen derivatives.

## 9. Organic Compounds
Foundation
## (CONCEPTMAP)

## ALKANES
Alkanes or saturated hydrocarbons are those in which all the four valencies of carbon atom(s) are satisfied by four atoms or groups i.e. the carbon valencies are fully satisfied. These compounds contain only <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></math> types of covalent bonds. Since they are relatively inert towards most of the chemical reagents under ordinary conditions, they are called paraffins (Latin-parum, little; affinis-affinity). The IUPAC name for these compounds is alkanes. Their general formula is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Alkanes are quite stable compounds and give substitution reactions while alkenes and alkynes are more reactive and generally give addition reactions.

## Physical Properties of Alkanes
(a) Alkanes from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are colourless, odourless gases. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are colourless liquids, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>18</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo></mrow></math> onwards are waxy, white solids.

## (b) Boiling points
Boiling points of alkanes are lowest of all the groups of organic compounds. The forces of attraction among alkane molecules are weakest van der Waal's forces of attraction. With the increase in the number of carbon chain length (molecular size), the magnitude of van der Waal's forces also increases.
Among isomeric alkanes, boiling point decreases with increasing branching.
Example : n-Pentane > iso-Pentane > neo-Pentane

## (c) Melting point
The melting point of alkanes does not show regular variation with increase in molecular size. Unbranched alkanes containing 2, 4, 6, 8 etc. carbon atoms have higher melting points than the unbranched alkanes containing 3, 5, 7, 9 etc. carbon atoms respectively.
Example :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>-Pentane
(both methyl groups are directed on same side)
n-Hexane
(both methyl groups are adversely directed)
M.P. of even No. of carbon atoms > M.P. of odd No. of carbon atoms
M.P. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∝</mo></mrow></math> mol.wt.

## (e) Solubility
Alkanes are lighter than water. These are insoluble in water while soluble in organic solvents.

## Chemical Properties of Alkanes
(a) Thermal decomposition, cracking or pyrolysis
The decomposition of a compound by heat is known as pyrolysis. Thermal decomposition when applied to alkanes is known as cracking and leads to the formation of lower alkanes, alkenes and hydrogen, e.g.
Note : Cracking has been used in the manufacture of petrol, petrol gas, oil gas, etc.

## (b) Isomerisation
The process of conversion of one isomer of a compound to another isomer is known as isomerisation. ## ALKENES
Alkenes are those unsaturated hydrocarbons which contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond in their molecules. Their general formula is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and hence they contain two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkane and hence designated as unsaturated hydrocarbon having general formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. These are also known as olefins or olifines (olifiant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> oil forming) and their IUPAC name is alkenes.
The carbon-carbon double bond ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ), commonly known as ethylenic or olifinic bond or linkage, is the characteristic group of alkenes.

Ethylene <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a sweet smelling gas. It produces anaesthetic effect in large amounts.
(b) Alkenes are practically insoluble in water. They dissolve freely in organic solvents like benzene, chloroform, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, petroleum ether, etc.
(c) The boiling and melting points of alkenes are slightly higher than the corresponding alkanes. Alkenes are therefore, lesser volatile than the corresponding alkanes. The branched chain alkenes, however, have lower boiling points than the corresponding straight chain alkenes.
Their boiling points, melting points and specific gravities rise with the increase of molecular weight.
The increase in branching in carbon chain decreases the boiling point among isomeric alkenes.

(a) Polymerisation
The process in which simple molecules combine together to form large molecule is called polymerisation; the starting simple molecule is called a monomer while the larger molecule (final product) is called a polymer. Polymers are used as plastics, rubber and several other important products. Lower alkenes and alkynes undergo polymerisation to form products of great importance.
Lower alkenes (e.g. ethene, propene etc.) readily undergo polymerisation at high temperature and pressure and in the presence of a suitable catalyst like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, etc.

## (b) Ozonolysis
Addition of ozone to an unsaturated hydrocarbon, forms an intermediate called ozonide, which on further hydrolysis in the presence of zinc dust gives corresponding carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and ketones). This reaction is used to identify and locate the position of multiple bonds in an unsaturated hydrocarbon.
For example, ethene on such reaction gives two molecules of formaldehyde.

(a) Alkynes are colourless, odourless and tasteless.

(c) Higher alkynes are insoluble in water while completely soluble in organic solvents.
(d) Melting point and boiling point are directly proportional to molecular mass and inversely proportional to number of branches.
(e) Upto <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, alkynes are gaseous, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are liquids, while <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> \& above are solids.
(f) Acetylene \& 1 - alkynes are acidic in nature. It is due to presence of active H .
(g) Oxyacetylene flame is used for cutting and welding metals.
Order of solubility, density, B.P., M.P. and acidic nature of above hydrocarbons is :
Alkyne > Alkene > Alkane
All terminal alkynes are acidic in nature.

Make a project report on fuel value comparison of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes. Mention which of these classes of hydrocarbons have maximum and minimum fuel value. Also provide reasons for that why a particular class has highest fuel value while other has lowest. Provide some statistical data to support your answer. You can consult your teacher and can take help of internet.

## ALKYL HALIDES
Alkyl halides (haloalkanes) are those compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms in an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms.
Halogen derivatives of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes are known as alkyl halides (haloalkanes), alkenyl halides (haloalkenes) and alkynyl halides (haloalkynes) respectively.
On the basis of the number of halogen atom, alkyl halides are further classified as mono-, di-, tri-,
Did You Know? poly- and per-halohydrocarbons. The word perhalohydrocarbon means all the hydrogen atoms of the hydrocarbon are replaced by corresponding number of halogen atoms.
Besides the nature and number of halogen atoms, alkyl halides may be classified into primary <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, secondary <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and tertiary <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> according to the nature of the carbon atom bearing halogen.

## (g) Elimination reaction
Alkyl halide when heated with alcoholic KOH solution, a molecule of hydrogen halide is eliminated and alkenes are formed. Generally <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>β</mi></mrow></math>-carbon (the carbon atom next to the carbon carrying the halogen) is eliminated during the reaction. In case of unsymmetrical alkyl halide there is the possibility of formation of two products. The more substituted alkene will be formed as a major product. This phenomenon was explained by Saytzeff, so its called Saytzeff's rule.

## ALCOHOLS
Alcohols, generally indicated by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, can be regarded as a derivative of alkanes where one hydrogen atom is replaced by a hydroxyl group (- OH ). The general molecular formula for alcohols is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. Alcohols are very important in organic chemistry because they can be converted to many other types of compounds.
Examples :

## Classification of Alcohols
Alcohols are classified according to number of hydroxyl groups present in the molecule. Alcohols with one, two and three hydroxyl groups are called monohydric, dihydric \& trihydric alcohols respectively. Alcohols which contain four or more hydroxyl groups are called polyhydric alcohols.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Methanol
Ethylene glycol
Glycerol
Butane-1,2,3,4-tetrol
When two or more hydroxyl groups attached to the same carbon atom of the compound is generally unstable. Such type of compound loses a water molecule easily and converted into a stable compound.
Monohydric alcohols are further divided into three classes:

## (a) Primary alcohols
The hydroxyl group is attached with primary carbon atom. They possess a characteristic group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(b) Secondary alcohols
The hydroxyl group is attached to secondary carbon atom. They possess <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> group.

## (c) Tertiary alcohols
The hydroxyl group is attached to tertiary carbon atom. They possess a characteristic group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><munder><mrow><mo>∣</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>∣</mo></mrow></munder><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
2-Methylbutan-2-ol
2-Methylpropan-2-ol
Time to
