## Isomerism in Alcohols
Alcohols exhibit following types of isomerism:
(a) Position isomerism
e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
1-Propanol
2-Propanol
(b) Chain isomerism
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mtext> e.g. </mtext><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mtext> 1-Butanol(straight chain) </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
2-Methyl-1-propanol (branched chain)
ETHYL ALCOHOL : Preparations and properties are already discussed in ch. 4

## ETHERS
Ethers are a class of compounds which contain an oxygen atom bonded to two alkyl groups (same or different). When both the alkyl groups are same they are designated as simple or symmetrical ethers and when both are different, they are called mixed or unsymmetrical ethers.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mtext> e.g. </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mspace width="2em" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>R</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>′</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Simple ethers </mtext></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> Mixed ethers </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow></math>
Ethers form a homologous series with the general formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> where the value of ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ' is always more than 1 ; the functional group of ether is (- - - ). Ethers may be regarded as anhydrides of alcohol as they may be obtained by elimination of water molecule from two alcohol molecules.
Just as alcohols are considered as monoalkyl derivatives of water, ethers may be considered as dialkyl derivatives of water.

## Isomerism in Ethers
Ethers exhibit two types of isomerism which are as follows.
(a) Functional isomerism
Ethers are isomeric with monohydric alcohols, e.g.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Methoxymethane
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Ethyl alcohol
(b) Metamerism
It is a type of structural isomerism in which different alkyl groups are attached to the same functional group.
e.g.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethoxyethane </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
Preparation of Ethers
2-Methoxypropane

## (a) By dehydrating excess of alcohols
Simple ethers can be prepared by heating an excess of primary alcohols with conc. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> at 413 K . Alcohol should be taken in excess so as to avoid its dehydration to alkenes.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethanol (2 molecules) </mtext></mrow></munder><munderover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mn>413</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Conc. </mtext><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></munderover><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Diethyl ether </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
(b) By heating alkyl halide with dry silver oxide : (Only for simple ethers)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(c) By heating alkyl halide with sod. or pot. alkoxides (Williamson synthesis)
This is the most important industrial and laboratory method for preparing simple as well as mixed ethers. For example,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
In this method generally primary alkyl halide is allowed to react with sodium ethoxide. If secondary or tertiary alkyl halide is taken for the synthesis of ether, along with ether alkene is also formed, that means elimination reaction competes over substitution. For example, the reaction of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> alkyl halide) gives only alkene instead of ether.
It is because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are not only nucleophiles but strong bases as well, therefore, it leading to elimination reaction.

theory_sections.topics: How can you prepare methyl butyl ether by methyl iodide?
theory_sections.markdown: ## How can you prepare methyl butyl ether by methyl iodide?

## Physical Properties of Ethers
(a) The first two members, i.e., dimethyl ether and methylethyl ether are gases; while all others are colourless, volatile pleasant smelling liquids. Among aromatic ethers anisole <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and phenetole <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> are liquids; diphenyl ether is solid at room temperature.
(b) Lower ethers are highly volatile and inflammable and also act as anaesthetics.
(c) They are sparingly soluble in water, but readily soluble in organic solvents such as benzene, chloroform, etc.

## Chemical Properties of Ethers
(a) Properties due to alkyl groups
(i) Halogenation : When ethers are treated with chlorine or bromine in dark, substitution reaction occurs at the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math>-carbon atom. The extent of substitution depends upon the reaction conditions.
(ii) Combustion : Since ethers are volatile and highly inflammable, they burn in air to form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and water.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>4</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>

## (b) Properties due to ethereal oxygen
(i) Chemical inertness : Since ethers do not have any active group in their molecules, so they do not react with active metals like Na , strong bases like NaOH , reducing or oxidising agents.
(ii) Basic nature : Owing to the presence of unshared electron pairs on oxygen, ethers behave as Lewis bases. Hence they dissolve in strong acids (e.g., conc. HCl , conc. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) at low temperature to form oxonium salts.
Dialkyloxonium chloride
Being Lewis bases, ethers also form coordination complexes with Lewis acids like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>,

## (c) Properties due to carbon-oxygen bond
(i) Hydrolysis : Ethers, when heated with dilute sulphuric acid under pressure are hydrolysed to the corresponding alcohols.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethyl alcohol </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
The hydrolysis may also be effected by boiling the ether with water or by treating it with steam.
(ii) Action of conc. sulphuric acid : On heating with concentrated sulphuric acid, ethers are converted to alkyl hydrogen sulphates.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mtext> (conc.) </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethyl alcohol </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethyl hydrogen sulphate </mtext></mrow></munder><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(iii) Action of hydroiodic or hydrobromic acid : In this reaction, the ethereal linkage is broken; the product depends upon the temperature of the reaction.
- In cold, ethers react with HI or HBr to give the corresponding alkyl halide and alcohol.

(d) By ozonolysis of ethylene
Ethylene is dissolved in an organic solvent such as chloroform or carbon tetrachloride and a stream of ozonised oxygen is passed. The ozonide formed is decomposed by passing hydrogen in presence of palladium as catalyst.
In the above reaction methanal can also be obtained by hydrolysis of ozonide in presence of zinc.

## Physical Properties of Methanal
(a) It is a colourless, pungent smelling gas.
(b) It is extremely soluble in water.
(c) It can easily be condensed into liquid. The liquid formaldehyde boils at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>21</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
(d) It causes irritation to skin, eyes, nose and throat.
(e) Its solution acts as antiseptic and disinfectant.

(b) Reaction with sodium hydroxide (Cannizzaro's reaction)
It does not form resin with sodium hydroxide like acetaldehyde but when treated with a concentrated solution of sodium hydroxide, two molecules of formaldehyde undergo mutual oxidation and reduction forming formic acid salt and methyl alcohol (Disproportionation).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Formaldehyde </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mtext> (Conc.) </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Sod. formate </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Methyl alcohol </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
The above reaction is also called Cannizaro's reaction and is only given by those aldehydes which do not have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math>-hydrogen atom (hydrogen atom present at carbon atom bonded to functional group of organic compounds).
(c) Aldol condensation
Formaldehyde in presence of a weak base undergoes repeated aldol condensation to give formose.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><mn>6</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Formaldehyde </mtext></mrow></munder><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Formose (hexose) </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>

## Uses of Methanal
(a) The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>40</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> solution of formaldehyde (formalin) is used as disinfectant, germicide and antiseptic. It is used for the preservation of biological specimens.
(b) It is used in the preparation of hexamethylene tetramine (urotropine) which is used as an antiseptic and germicide.
(c) It is used in silvering of mirror.
(d) It is employed in the manufacture of synthetic dyes such as para-rosaniline, indigo, etc.
(e) It is used in the manufacture of forma mint (by mixing formaldehyde with lactose) - a throat lozenges.
(f) It is used for making synthetic plastics like bakelite, urea-formaldehyde resin, etc.

theory_sections.markdown:
## 2. ACETONE OR PROPANONE, OR DIMETHYL KETONE, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
It is a symmetrical (simple) ketone and is the first member of the homologous series of ketones. In traces, it is present in blood and urine.

## Preparation of Acetone
Acetone is prepared in laboratory by heating anhydrous calcium acetate.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Calcium acetate </mtext></mrow></munder><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Acetone </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>

## Manufacture of Acetone (Industrial Process)
Acetone is manufactured by following methods.
(a) By air oxidation of isopropyl alcohol
The air oxidation occurs at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>500</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Isopropyl alcohol </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><msup><mn>500</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Acetone </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
(b) By dehydrogenation of isopropyl alcohol

## Physical Properties of Acetone
(a) It is a colourless liquid with characteristic pleasant odour.
(b) It is highly inflammable liquid. It boils at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>56</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
(c) It is highly miscible with water, alcohol and ether.

## Chemical Properties of Acetone
It shows general properties of ketones. Some special properties of acetone are described below :

## (a) Haloform reaction
When heated with iodine and sodium hydroxide, it forms yellow crystals of iodoform.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ariiodo acetone </mtext></mrow></munder><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Iodoform </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Sodium acetate </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) Acetone forms chloroform when heated with bleaching powder in water.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>&</mi><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Chloroform </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Calcium acetate </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></mrow></math>

## Uses of Acetone
(a) As a solvent for cellulose acetate, cellulose nitrate, celluloid, lacquers, resins, etc.
(b) For storing acetylene.
(c) In the manufacture of cordite - a smokeless powder explosive.
(d) In the preparation of chloroform, iodoform, sulphonal and chloretone.
(e) As a nailpolish remover.
(f) In the preparation of an artificial scent (ionone), plexiglass (unbreakable glass) and synthetic rubber.

theory_sections.markdown: ## For which alkyne, acetone is used as a storage material?

## CARBOXYLIC ACIDS
The compounds containing the carboxyl functional group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are called carboxylic acids. The word carboxyl is a combination of two words carbonyl ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> ) and hydroxyl ( -OH ).

## Classification of Carboxylic Acids
Depending upon the number of -COOH groups, they are classified as (i) monocarboxylic acids: containing one -COOH group (ii) dicarboxylic acids-containing two -COOH groups and so on.
Fatty acids: Aliphatic monocarboxylic acids are commonly called fatty acids because higher members are obtained by the hydrolysis of oils and fats.

## Isomerism in Carboxylic Acids
They exhibit following type of isomerism.
(a) Position and chain isomerism
e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> represents
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> 1-Hexanoic acid </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> 2-Methylpentanoic acid </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> 2-Ethylbutanoic acid </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> Position isomers
4-Methylpentanoic acid and 1-hexanoic acid are chain isomers
(b) Functional isomerism
Formula
Functional Isomers
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> :
Propanoic acid
2, 3 - Dimethylbutanoic acid
3, 3 - Dimethylbutanoic acid
All are chain isomers of 1-hexanoic acid.

## More than One Option Correct
DIRECTIONS : This section contains multiple choice questions. Each question has four choices (a), (b), (c) and (d) out of which ONE OR MORE may be correct.
1. Which of the following statements is not true for ethane?
(a) It can be chlorinated with chlorine.
(b) Ethane undergoes addition reactions.
(c) When oxidised produces <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>.
(d) It can be catalytically hydrogenated.
2. Which gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> when treated with water ?
(a) Aluminium carbide
(b) Iron carbide
(c) Beryllium carbide
(d) Calcium carbide
3. When ethyl iodide and propyl iodide react with Na in the presence of dry ether, they form
(a) pentane
(b) butane
(c) hexane
(d) propane
4. In which test-tube effervescences will occur?
(a)
(b)
(c)
(d)
5. Which of the following compound decolorises alkaline <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> solution ?
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) Butanol
(c) Butan-2-ol
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
6. Alkynes have in their molecule
(a) two hydrogen atoms less than in a molecule of corresponding alkene.
(b) two hydrogen atoms less than in a molecule of corresponding alkane.
(c) - <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>≡</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> - linkage
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>\</mi></mrow></math> linkage
7. Which of the following are used as dehydrating agent ?
(a) Conc. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(c) Alkaline <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(d) Pd or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
8. Which of the following aldehydes undergo Cannizzaro's reaction?
(a) HCHO
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
9. Which of the following are the uses of formaldehyde?
(a) It is used in silvering of mirror.
(b) It is used as disinfectant.
(c) It is used in the preparation of iodoform.
(d) It is used in the preparation of an artificial scent.
10. Which of the following exhibits chain isomerism?
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(c)
(d) HCHO

## Passage-2
Compounds derived from hydrocarbons by the replacement of one or more hydrogen atom(s) by the halogen atoms(s) are known as halogen derivatives. The halogen derivatives of alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and arenes are known as alkyl halides (haloalkanes), alkenyl halides (haloalkenes), alkynyl halides (haloalkynes), aryl halides (haloarenes) respectively. Halogen derivatives may be classified depending upon the number of the halogen atom. Thus halogen derivatives of alkanes may be monohalogen derivatives, dihalogen derivatives, tri- and tetra-halogen derivatives.

## Physical Properties of Alkanes
(a) Alkanes from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are colourless, odourless gases. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are colourless liquids, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>18</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo></mrow></math> onwards are waxy, white solids.
## (b) Boiling points
Boiling points of alkanes are lowest of all the groups of organic compounds. The forces of attraction among alkane molecules are weakest van der Waal's forces of attraction. With the increase in the number of carbon chain length (molecular size), the magnitude of van der Waal's forces also increases.
Among isomeric alkanes, boiling point decreases with increasing branching.
Example : n-Pentane > iso-Pentane > neo-Pentane
## (c) Melting point
The melting point of alkanes does not show regular variation with increase in molecular size. Unbranched alkanes containing 2, 4, 6, 8 etc. carbon atoms have higher melting points than the unbranched alkanes containing 3, 5, 7, 9 etc. carbon atoms respectively.
Example :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>-Pentane
(both methyl groups are directed on same side)
n-Hexane
(both methyl groups are adversely directed)
M.P. of even No. of carbon atoms > M.P. of odd No. of carbon atoms
M.P. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∝</mo></mrow></math> mol.wt.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> because alkanes with even number of carbon atoms has higher melting point.

Decreasing order of fuel capacity is

## (e) Solubility
Alkanes are lighter than water. These are insoluble in water while soluble in organic solvents.
## Chemical Properties of Alkanes

## (b) Isomerisation
The process of conversion of one isomer of a compound to another isomer is known as isomerisation. This is achieved by heating the normal alkane with anhydrous <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and HCl or anhydrous <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and HBr under pressure of 35 atmospheres.
Isomerisation of alkanes is of great importance in petroleum industry.

illustrations.problem: Why hydrocarbons are used as a fuel?
illustrations.solution:
It is because during their combustion, a large amount of heat is evolved; for example cooking gas, which is often called L.P.G. is a mixture of propane and butane which is used as a fuel.
## ALKENES
Alkenes are those unsaturated hydrocarbons which contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond in their molecules. Their general formula is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and hence they contain two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkane and hence designated as unsaturated hydrocarbon having general formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. These are also known as olefins or olifines (olifiant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> oil forming) and their IUPAC name is alkenes.
The carbon-carbon double bond ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ), commonly known as ethylenic or olifinic bond or linkage, is the characteristic group of alkenes.

## Physical Properties of Alkenes
(a) From <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> they are colourless, odourless gases, from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> they are colourless liquids, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>18</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> onwards alkenes are solids. Ethylene <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a sweet smelling gas. It produces anaesthetic effect in large amounts.
(b) Alkenes are practically insoluble in water. They dissolve freely in organic solvents like benzene, chloroform, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, petroleum ether, etc.
(c) The boiling and melting points of alkenes are slightly higher than the corresponding alkanes. Alkenes are therefore, lesser volatile than the corresponding alkanes. The branched chain alkenes, however, have lower boiling points than the corresponding straight chain alkenes.
Their boiling points, melting points and specific gravities rise with the increase of molecular weight.
The increase in branching in carbon chain decreases the boiling point among isomeric alkenes.

(a) Polymerisation
The process in which simple molecules combine together to form large molecule is called polymerisation; the starting simple molecule is called a monomer while the larger molecule (final product) is called a polymer. Polymers are used as plastics, rubber and several other important products. Lower alkenes and alkynes undergo polymerisation to form products of great importance.
Lower alkenes (e.g. ethene, propene etc.) readily undergo polymerisation at high temperature and pressure and in the presence of a suitable catalyst like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, etc.

## (b) Ozonolysis
Addition of ozone to an unsaturated hydrocarbon, forms an intermediate called ozonide, which on further hydrolysis in the presence of zinc dust gives corresponding carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and ketones). This reaction is used to identify and locate the position of multiple bonds in an unsaturated hydrocarbon.
For example, ethene on such reaction gives two molecules of formaldehyde.

## Physical Properties of Alkynes
(a) Alkynes are colourless, odourless and tasteless.
(b) Lower alkynes are partially soluble in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>.
(c) Higher alkynes are insoluble in water while completely soluble in organic solvents.
(d) Melting point and boiling point are directly proportional to molecular mass and inversely proportional to number of branches.
(e) Upto <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, alkynes are gaseous, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are liquids, while <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> \& above are solids.
(f) Acetylene \& 1 - alkynes are acidic in nature. It is due to presence of active H .
(g) Oxyacetylene flame is used for cutting and welding metals.
Order of solubility, density, B.P., M.P. and acidic nature of above hydrocarbons is :
Alkyne > Alkene > Alkane
All terminal alkynes are acidic in nature.

## ALKYL HALIDES
Alkyl halides (haloalkanes) are those compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms in an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms.
Halogen derivatives of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes are known as alkyl halides (haloalkanes), alkenyl halides (haloalkenes) and alkynyl halides (haloalkynes) respectively.
On the basis of the number of halogen atom, alkyl halides are further classified as mono-, di-, tri-,
Did You Know? poly- and per-halohydrocarbons. The word perhalohydrocarbon means all the hydrogen atoms of the hydrocarbon are replaced by corresponding number of halogen atoms.

## Physical Properties of Alkyl Halides
(a) Alkyl halide is insoluble in water though the molecule is polar. This is due to the fact that haloalkenes can neither form hydrogen bonds with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> nor break the hydrogen bonds, already existing.
(b) Boiling points
Greater the molecular mass, stronger the van der Waal's forces of attraction and hence higher is the boiling point.

## (g) Elimination reaction
Alkyl halide when heated with alcoholic KOH solution, a molecule of hydrogen halide is eliminated and alkenes are formed. Generally <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>β</mi></mrow></math>-carbon (the carbon atom next to the carbon carrying the halogen) is eliminated during the reaction. In case of unsymmetrical alkyl halide there is the possibility of formation of two products. The more substituted alkene will be formed as a major product. This phenomenon was explained by Saytzeff, so its called Saytzeff's rule.

## Classification of Alcohols
Alcohols are classified according to number of hydroxyl groups present in the molecule. Alcohols with one, two and three hydroxyl groups are called monohydric, dihydric \& trihydric alcohols respectively. Alcohols which contain four or more hydroxyl groups are called polyhydric alcohols.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Methanol
Ethylene glycol
Glycerol
Butane-1,2,3,4-tetrol
When two or more hydroxyl groups attached to the same carbon atom of the compound is generally unstable. Such type of compound loses a water molecule easily and converted into a stable compound.
Monohydric alcohols are further divided into three classes:
## (a) Primary alcohols
The hydroxyl group is attached with primary carbon atom. They possess a characteristic group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(b) Secondary alcohols
The hydroxyl group is attached to secondary carbon atom. They possess <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> group.
## (c) Tertiary alcohols
The hydroxyl group is attached to tertiary carbon atom. They possess a characteristic group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><munder><mrow><mo>∣</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>∣</mo></mrow></munder><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

## ETHERS
Ethers are a class of compounds which contain an oxygen atom bonded to two alkyl groups (same or different). When both the alkyl groups are same they are designated as simple or symmetrical ethers and when both are different, they are called mixed or unsymmetrical ethers.

Ethers form a homologous series with the general formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> where the value of ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ' is always more than 1 ; the functional group of ether is (- - - ). Ethers may be regarded as anhydrides of alcohol as they may be obtained by elimination of water molecule from two alcohol molecules.
Just as alcohols are considered as monoalkyl derivatives of water, ethers may be considered as dialkyl derivatives of water.

This is the most important industrial and laboratory method for preparing simple as well as mixed ethers. For example,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
In this method generally primary alkyl halide is allowed to react with sodium ethoxide. If secondary or tertiary alkyl halide is taken for the synthesis of ether, along with ether alkene is also formed, that means elimination reaction competes over substitution. For example, the reaction of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> alkyl halide) gives only alkene instead of ether.
It is because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are not only nucleophiles but strong bases as well, therefore, it leading to elimination reaction.
## How can you prepare methyl butyl ether by methyl iodide?
Sodium butoxide reacts with methyl iodide leading to methylbutyl ether (Williamson's synthesis).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
## Physical Properties of Ethers
(a) The first two members, i.e., dimethyl ether and methylethyl ether are gases; while all others are colourless, volatile pleasant smelling liquids. Among aromatic ethers anisole <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and phenetole <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> are liquids; diphenyl ether is solid at room temperature.
(b) Lower ethers are highly volatile and inflammable and also act as anaesthetics.
(c) They are sparingly soluble in water, but readily soluble in organic solvents such as benzene, chloroform, etc.
## Chemical Properties of Ethers
(a) Properties due to alkyl groups
(i) Halogenation : When ethers are treated with chlorine or bromine in dark, substitution reaction occurs at the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math>-carbon atom. The extent of substitution depends upon the reaction conditions.
(ii) Combustion : Since ethers are volatile and highly inflammable, they burn in air to form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and water.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>4</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
## (b) Properties due to ethereal oxygen
(i) Chemical inertness : Since ethers do not have any active group in their molecules, so they do not react with active metals like Na , strong bases like NaOH , reducing or oxidising agents.
(ii) Basic nature : Owing to the presence of unshared electron pairs on oxygen, ethers behave as Lewis bases. Hence they dissolve in strong acids (e.g., conc. HCl , conc. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) at low temperature to form oxonium salts.
Dialkyloxonium chloride

## Uses of Ethers
(a) The most important use of ethers is a laboratory and industrial solvent (for oils, resins, gums, etc.)
(b) Ether is used as an anaesthic in surgery.

## Physical Properties of Methanal
(a) It is a colourless, pungent smelling gas.
(b) It is extremely soluble in water.
(c) It can easily be condensed into liquid. The liquid formaldehyde boils at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>21</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
(d) It causes irritation to skin, eyes, nose and throat.
(e) Its solution acts as antiseptic and disinfectant.

## Uses of Methanal
(a) The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>40</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> solution of formaldehyde (formalin) is used as disinfectant, germicide and antiseptic. It is used for the preservation of biological specimens.
(b) It is used in the preparation of hexamethylene tetramine (urotropine) which is used as an antiseptic and germicide.
(c) It is used in silvering of mirror.
(d) It is employed in the manufacture of synthetic dyes such as para-rosaniline, indigo, etc.
(e) It is used in the manufacture of forma mint (by mixing formaldehyde with lactose) - a throat lozenges.
(f) It is used for making synthetic plastics like bakelite, urea-formaldehyde resin, etc.

(a) It is a colourless liquid with characteristic pleasant odour.

## Chemical Properties of Acetone
It shows general properties of ketones. Some special properties of acetone are described below :

## Uses of Acetone
(a) As a solvent for cellulose acetate, cellulose nitrate, celluloid, lacquers, resins, etc.
(b) For storing acetylene.
(c) In the manufacture of cordite - a smokeless powder explosive.
(d) In the preparation of chloroform, iodoform, sulphonal and chloretone.
(e) As a nailpolish remover.
(f) In the preparation of an artificial scent (ionone), plexiglass (unbreakable glass) and synthetic rubber.

## CARBOXYLIC ACIDS
The compounds containing the carboxyl functional group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are called carboxylic acids. The word carboxyl is a combination of two words carbonyl ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> ) and hydroxyl ( -OH ).
## Classification of Carboxylic Acids
Depending upon the number of -COOH groups, they are classified as (i) monocarboxylic acids: containing one -COOH group (ii) dicarboxylic acids-containing two -COOH groups and so on.
Fatty acids: Aliphatic monocarboxylic acids are commonly called fatty acids because higher members are obtained by the hydrolysis of oils and fats.
## Isomerism in Carboxylic Acids
They exhibit following type of isomerism.
(a) Position and chain isomerism
e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> represents
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> 1-Hexanoic acid </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> 2-Methylpentanoic acid </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> 2-Ethylbutanoic acid </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> Position isomers

Compounds derived from hydrocarbons by the replacement of one or more hydrogen atom(s) by the halogen atoms(s) are known as halogen derivatives. The halogen derivatives of alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and arenes are known as alkyl halides (haloalkanes), alkenyl halides (haloalkenes), alkynyl halides (haloalkynes), aryl halides (haloarenes) respectively. Halogen derivatives may be classified depending upon the number of the halogen atom. Thus halogen derivatives of alkanes may be monohalogen derivatives, dihalogen derivatives, tri- and tetra-halogen derivatives.

## Physical Properties of Alkanes
(a) Alkanes from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are colourless, odourless gases. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are colourless liquids, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>18</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo></mrow></math> onwards are waxy, white solids.
## (b) Boiling points
Boiling points of alkanes are lowest of all the groups of organic compounds. The forces of attraction among alkane molecules are weakest van der Waal's forces of attraction. With the increase in the number of carbon chain length (molecular size), the magnitude of van der Waal's forces also increases.
Among isomeric alkanes, boiling point decreases with increasing branching.
Example : n-Pentane > iso-Pentane > neo-Pentane
## (c) Melting point
The melting point of alkanes does not show regular variation with increase in molecular size. Unbranched alkanes containing 2, 4, 6, 8 etc. carbon atoms have higher melting points than the unbranched alkanes containing 3, 5, 7, 9 etc. carbon atoms respectively.
Example :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>-Pentane
(both methyl groups are directed on same side)
n-Hexane
(both methyl groups are adversely directed)
M.P. of even No. of carbon atoms > M.P. of odd No. of carbon atoms
M.P. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∝</mo></mrow></math> mol.wt.
## Out of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> which one has high melting point?
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> because alkanes with even number of carbon atoms has higher melting point.
## (d) Fuel capacity
Decreasing order of fuel capacity is
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mtext> More branched </mtext><mo>></mo><mtext> Less branched </mtext><mo>></mo><mtext> Unbranched </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mtext> Lower mol.wt. </mtext><mo>></mo><mtext> Higher mol. wt. </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
## (e) Solubility
Alkanes are lighter than water. These are insoluble in water while soluble in organic solvents.
## Chemical Properties of Alkanes
(a) Thermal decomposition, cracking or pyrolysis
The decomposition of a compound by heat is known as pyrolysis. Thermal decomposition when applied to alkanes is known as cracking and leads to the formation of lower alkanes, alkenes and hydrogen, e.g.
Note : Cracking has been used in the manufacture of petrol, petrol gas, oil gas, etc.
## (b) Isomerisation
The process of conversion of one isomer of a compound to another isomer is known as isomerisation. This is achieved by heating the normal alkane with anhydrous <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and HCl or anhydrous <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and HBr under pressure of 35 atmospheres.
Isomerisation of alkanes is of great importance in petroleum industry.

examples.problem: Why hydrocarbons are used as a fuel?
examples.solution:
It is because during their combustion, a large amount of heat is evolved; for example cooking gas, which is often called L.P.G. is a mixture of propane and butane which is used as a fuel.
## ALKENES
Alkenes are those unsaturated hydrocarbons which contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond in their molecules. Their general formula is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and hence they contain two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkane and hence designated as unsaturated hydrocarbon having general formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. These are also known as olefins or olifines (olifiant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> oil forming) and their IUPAC name is alkenes.
The carbon-carbon double bond ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ), commonly known as ethylenic or olifinic bond or linkage, is the characteristic group of alkenes.

## (b) Ozonolysis
Addition of ozone to an unsaturated hydrocarbon, forms an intermediate called ozonide, which on further hydrolysis in the presence of zinc dust gives corresponding carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and ketones). This reaction is used to identify and locate the position of multiple bonds in an unsaturated hydrocarbon.
For example, ethene on such reaction gives two molecules of formaldehyde.

(a) Alkynes are colourless, odourless and tasteless.

(d) Melting point and boiling point are directly proportional to molecular mass and inversely proportional to number of branches.
(e) Upto <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, alkynes are gaseous, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are liquids, while <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> \& above are solids.
(f) Acetylene \& 1 - alkynes are acidic in nature. It is due to presence of active H .
(g) Oxyacetylene flame is used for cutting and welding metals.
Order of solubility, density, B.P., M.P. and acidic nature of above hydrocarbons is :
Alkyne > Alkene > Alkane
All terminal alkynes are acidic in nature.

## ALKYL HALIDES
Alkyl halides (haloalkanes) are those compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms in an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms.
Halogen derivatives of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes are known as alkyl halides (haloalkanes), alkenyl halides (haloalkenes) and alkynyl halides (haloalkynes) respectively.
On the basis of the number of halogen atom, alkyl halides are further classified as mono-, di-, tri-,
Did You Know? poly- and per-halohydrocarbons. The word perhalohydrocarbon means all the hydrogen atoms of the hydrocarbon are replaced by corresponding number of halogen atoms.
Besides the nature and number of halogen atoms, alkyl halides may be classified into primary <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, secondary <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and tertiary <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> according to the nature of the carbon atom bearing halogen.

## (g) Elimination reaction
Alkyl halide when heated with alcoholic KOH solution, a molecule of hydrogen halide is eliminated and alkenes are formed. Generally <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>β</mi></mrow></math>-carbon (the carbon atom next to the carbon carrying the halogen) is eliminated during the reaction. In case of unsymmetrical alkyl halide there is the possibility of formation of two products. The more substituted alkene will be formed as a major product. This phenomenon was explained by Saytzeff, so its called Saytzeff's rule.

## Classification of Alcohols
Alcohols are classified according to number of hydroxyl groups present in the molecule. Alcohols with one, two and three hydroxyl groups are called monohydric, dihydric \& trihydric alcohols respectively. Alcohols which contain four or more hydroxyl groups are called polyhydric alcohols.

Ethylene glycol
Glycerol
Butane-1,2,3,4-tetrol
When two or more hydroxyl groups attached to the same carbon atom of the compound is generally unstable. Such type of compound loses a water molecule easily and converted into a stable compound.
Monohydric alcohols are further divided into three classes:
## (a) Primary alcohols
The hydroxyl group is attached with primary carbon atom. They possess a characteristic group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(b) Secondary alcohols
The hydroxyl group is attached to secondary carbon atom. They possess <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> group.

## ETHERS
Ethers are a class of compounds which contain an oxygen atom bonded to two alkyl groups (same or different). When both the alkyl groups are same they are designated as simple or symmetrical ethers and when both are different, they are called mixed or unsymmetrical ethers.

Ethers form a homologous series with the general formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> where the value of ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ' is always more than 1 ; the functional group of ether is (- - - ). Ethers may be regarded as anhydrides of alcohol as they may be obtained by elimination of water molecule from two alcohol molecules.
Just as alcohols are considered as monoalkyl derivatives of water, ethers may be considered as dialkyl derivatives of water.
