Simple ethers can be prepared by heating an excess of primary alcohols with conc. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> at 413 K . Alcohol should be taken in excess so as to avoid its dehydration to alkenes.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethanol (2 molecules) </mtext></mrow></munder><munderover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mn>413</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mtext> Conc. </mtext><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></munderover><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Diethyl ether </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
(b) By heating alkyl halide with dry silver oxide : (Only for simple ethers)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(c) By heating alkyl halide with sod. or pot. alkoxides (Williamson synthesis)
This is the most important industrial and laboratory method for preparing simple as well as mixed ethers. For example,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
In this method generally primary alkyl halide is allowed to react with sodium ethoxide. If secondary or tertiary alkyl halide is taken for the synthesis of ether, along with ether alkene is also formed, that means elimination reaction competes over substitution. For example, the reaction of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> alkyl halide) gives only alkene instead of ether.
It is because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are not only nucleophiles but strong bases as well, therefore, it leading to elimination reaction.
## How can you prepare methyl butyl ether by methyl iodide?
Sodium butoxide reacts with methyl iodide leading to methylbutyl ether (Williamson's synthesis).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
## Physical Properties of Ethers
(a) The first two members, i.e., dimethyl ether and methylethyl ether are gases; while all others are colourless, volatile pleasant smelling liquids. Among aromatic ethers anisole <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and phenetole <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> are liquids; diphenyl ether is solid at room temperature.
(b) Lower ethers are highly volatile and inflammable and also act as anaesthetics.
(c) They are sparingly soluble in water, but readily soluble in organic solvents such as benzene, chloroform, etc.
## Chemical Properties of Ethers
(a) Properties due to alkyl groups
(i) Halogenation : When ethers are treated with chlorine or bromine in dark, substitution reaction occurs at the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math>-carbon atom. The extent of substitution depends upon the reaction conditions.
(ii) Combustion : Since ethers are volatile and highly inflammable, they burn in air to form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and water.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><mn>4</mn><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>
## (b) Properties due to ethereal oxygen
(i) Chemical inertness : Since ethers do not have any active group in their molecules, so they do not react with active metals like Na , strong bases like NaOH , reducing or oxidising agents.
(ii) Basic nature : Owing to the presence of unshared electron pairs on oxygen, ethers behave as Lewis bases. Hence they dissolve in strong acids (e.g., conc. HCl , conc. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) at low temperature to form oxonium salts.
Dialkyloxonium chloride
Being Lewis bases, ethers also form coordination complexes with Lewis acids like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>,
## (c) Properties due to carbon-oxygen bond
(i) Hydrolysis : Ethers, when heated with dilute sulphuric acid under pressure are hydrolysed to the corresponding alcohols.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><munder><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethyl alcohol </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
The hydrolysis may also be effected by boiling the ether with water or by treating it with steam.
(ii) Action of conc. sulphuric acid : On heating with concentrated sulphuric acid, ethers are converted to alkyl hydrogen sulphates.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mtext> (conc.) </mtext><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethyl alcohol </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethyl hydrogen sulphate </mtext></mrow></munder><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mi>⟶</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(iii) Action of hydroiodic or hydrobromic acid : In this reaction, the ethereal linkage is broken; the product depends upon the temperature of the reaction.
- In cold, ethers react with HI or HBr to give the corresponding alkyl halide and alcohol.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mi>I</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethyl iodide </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethyl alcohol </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethyl ether </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
In case of mixed ethers, the nucleophile ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math>) attacks to the lower alkyl group side.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mi>⟶</mi><munder><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>I</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Mehyl iodide </mtext></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethyl alcohol </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow><mrow><mtext> Ethylmethyl ether </mtext></mrow></munder></mrow></math>
However, one of the alkyl group is a tertiary group, the halide formed is a tertiary halide.
- Ethers when heated with conc. halogen acids form two molecules of alkyl halides.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mo>→</mo></mstyle><mpadded width="+0.833em" lspace="0.556em" voffset="-.2em" height="-.2em"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow><mspace depth=".25em" /></mpadded></mover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>O</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
When HI is used in excess and the reaction is carried out at high temperature, ethanol further reacts with HI and is converted to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mi>I</mi></mrow></math>.

(d) By ozonolysis of ethylene
Ethylene is dissolved in an organic solvent such as chloroform or carbon tetrachloride and a stream of ozonised oxygen is passed. The ozonide formed is decomposed by passing hydrogen in presence of palladium as catalyst.
In the above reaction methanal can also be obtained by hydrolysis of ozonide in presence of zinc.

## Physical Properties of Methanal
(a) It is a colourless, pungent smelling gas.
(b) It is extremely soluble in water.
(c) It can easily be condensed into liquid. The liquid formaldehyde boils at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>21</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
(d) It causes irritation to skin, eyes, nose and throat.
(e) Its solution acts as antiseptic and disinfectant.

(c) Aldol condensation
Formaldehyde in presence of a weak base undergoes repeated aldol condensation to give formose.

## Uses of Methanal
(a) The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>40</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> solution of formaldehyde (formalin) is used as disinfectant, germicide and antiseptic. It is used for the preservation of biological specimens.
(b) It is used in the preparation of hexamethylene tetramine (urotropine) which is used as an antiseptic and germicide.
(c) It is used in silvering of mirror.
(d) It is employed in the manufacture of synthetic dyes such as para-rosaniline, indigo, etc.
(e) It is used in the manufacture of forma mint (by mixing formaldehyde with lactose) - a throat lozenges.
(f) It is used for making synthetic plastics like bakelite, urea-formaldehyde resin, etc.
## 2. ACETONE OR PROPANONE, OR DIMETHYL KETONE, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
It is a symmetrical (simple) ketone and is the first member of the homologous series of ketones. In traces, it is present in blood and urine.

Acetone is prepared in laboratory by heating anhydrous calcium acetate.

Acetone is manufactured by following methods.
(a) By air oxidation of isopropyl alcohol
The air oxidation occurs at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>500</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.

## Physical Properties of Acetone
(a) It is a colourless liquid with characteristic pleasant odour.
(b) It is highly inflammable liquid. It boils at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>56</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
(c) It is highly miscible with water, alcohol and ether.

## Uses of Acetone
(a) As a solvent for cellulose acetate, cellulose nitrate, celluloid, lacquers, resins, etc.
(b) For storing acetylene.
(c) In the manufacture of cordite - a smokeless powder explosive.
(d) In the preparation of chloroform, iodoform, sulphonal and chloretone.
(e) As a nailpolish remover.
(f) In the preparation of an artificial scent (ionone), plexiglass (unbreakable glass) and synthetic rubber.

## CARBOXYLIC ACIDS
The compounds containing the carboxyl functional group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are called carboxylic acids. The word carboxyl is a combination of two words carbonyl ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> ) and hydroxyl ( -OH ).
## Classification of Carboxylic Acids
Depending upon the number of -COOH groups, they are classified as (i) monocarboxylic acids: containing one -COOH group (ii) dicarboxylic acids-containing two -COOH groups and so on.
Fatty acids: Aliphatic monocarboxylic acids are commonly called fatty acids because higher members are obtained by the hydrolysis of oils and fats.
## Isomerism in Carboxylic Acids
They exhibit following type of isomerism.
(a) Position and chain isomerism
e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> represents
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> 1-Hexanoic acid </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> 2-Methylpentanoic acid </mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> 2-Ethylbutanoic acid </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> Position isomers
4-Methylpentanoic acid and 1-hexanoic acid are chain isomers
(b) Functional isomerism

Functional Isomers
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> :

## ALKANES
Alkanes or saturated hydrocarbons are those in which all the four valencies of carbon atom(s) are satisfied by four atoms or groups i.e. the carbon valencies are fully satisfied. These compounds contain only <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></math> types of covalent bonds. Since they are relatively inert towards most of the chemical reagents under ordinary conditions, they are called paraffins (Latin-parum, little; affinis-affinity). The IUPAC name for these compounds is alkanes. Their general formula is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Alkanes are quite stable compounds and give substitution reactions while alkenes and alkynes are more reactive and generally give addition reactions.
## General Methods of Preparation of Alkanes
